Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival

Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: The two recurring issues that hampered Verstappen and Red Bull again at the US GP
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen secured his 10th podium of the 2026 Formula 1 season in Austin, his sixth in succession since his crash at Zandvoort. It is an impressive statistic, although it did little to satisfy him at the Circuit of the Americas.

On Saturday, the pace appeared to be there to take pole position – at least judging by Verstappen's impressive Q2 lap – but he inexplicably lost grip in Q3. Based on the practice sessions, his race pace still appeared good enough to challenge for the win, but according to Verstappen, too many small things went wrong during the race.

"It was pretty frustrating, to be honest, just not a really good race for us," Verstappen said in the post-race press conference.

Why Red Bull's recent strength turned into a weakness in Austin

That frustration stems partly from problems that have been troubling Red Bull for some time and partly from decisions specific to this race that ultimately backfired.

"In hindsight, of course, it’s very easy to say, but for whatever reason, the softer compounds were not really working that well today. Then also, I think the way that we used our tyres was wrong, the order of the stints," the Dutchman added.

"I think at one point, it was quite clear that the people on the harder compounds were finding a lot of grip, so I guess we didn't really react to that. We were probably sticking a bit too much to our belief from the last two races, where the softer compounds were the fastest. But clearly here, that didn't work."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

In recent race weekends, that had been one of the areas where Red Bull made the difference. The RB22 had been particularly good at managing the softer tyres and keeping them alive in the right operating window, but in Austin the opposite proved to be the case, as team principal Laurent Mekies also admitted after the race.

Verstappen also complained over the team radio about issues related to the power unit, to which the team responded with some engine braking suggestions.

"Besides the strategy, we had too many issues with the power unit, where it was just very inconsistent behaviour around the corners. Every lap and every corner, the behaviour was different," Verstappen said.

"You can't build up a rhythm, you can't build any kind of consistency in the car. And then I had a slow pit stop as well, so yeah, too many things today that just didn't go well."

Two recurring problems continue to trouble Red Bull

While the strategy and power unit problems were specific to this race, there are two other factors Red Bull has been struggling with throughout the year: radio communication and poor starts. Regarding the latter, Verstappen explained that his start in Austin was not so much bad as simply in line with Red Bull's average this year – which has been consistently below par.

"I didn't lose a position, so it wasn't that bad. It's normal. My start was normal, just consistently sh**," Verstappen said, stopping short of finishing the final word to avoid swearing during the FIA press conference.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

Radio communication has also become a recurring problem. In Singapore, his regular race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase could not hear Verstappen, forcing them to switch to coded communication. Mekies subsequently said Red Bull was taking the problem very seriously and wanted to come up with a "strong solution", but that solution had evidently not yet materialised in Austin.

At the extremely bumpy Circuit of the Americas, both Hadjar and Verstappen experienced communication problems with the team. In Verstappen's case, he could not hear Tom Hart, who was standing in as his race engineer this weekend to begin building their working relationship for the future.

"It's not the second time. It's already, I don't know how many times this year. Maybe we should just start communicating in sign language! It's probably cheaper as well," Verstappen joked.

"But yeah, it’s a disaster. It's really frustrating, to be honest."

Taken together, all these setbacks meant Red Bull was unable to extract the full potential of the RB22 in Texas. Team members acknowledge that Kimi Antonelli also had the upper hand in terms of outright pace, although Verstappen's frustration mainly stems from the fact that Red Bull did not even reach the level it had been aiming for.

Sports.title: Alonso criticises quality of F1 backmarkers after Albon clash at United States GP
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso let rip at Williams' Alex Albon after contact between their cars on the opening lap of the Formula 1 United States Grand Prix. It cost the Aston Martin driver four places in Austin and left him with floor damage, which compromised the AMR26 for the rest of the race.

The two-time world champion lost one position at the start from 12th on the grid as Esteban Ocon surged from 15th to 11th. Albon picked up three places with a clean launch to run 14th and challenged Alonso for position all the way through the Esses on the opening lap.

At Turn 11, Alonso made a bid to pass the squabbling Haas cars on the inside line into the left-hander, but Albon had also launched on a similar trajectory. The Williams was already committed as the gap narrowed, and Albon's front-right wheel crunched into Alonso's left-hand bargeboard and floor edge.

Alonso was pushed onto the outside kerb, losing a further four places. The damage to the Aston Martin's floor was clearly visible from Albon's on-board camera. Alonso recovered to 12th place at the chequered flag, but was clearly disgruntled when he spoke to the media.

"That was the biggest damage," he said. "I think we lost half a second or more [per lap]. The car is destroyed, I saw it in parc ferme. Half of the floor is not there. I don't know how we kept on going and how we were semi-competitive.

"I imagine if the car was in one piece, probably today the points were a strong possibility because we were running P12 with half a car. I lost even further pieces of the floor. I couldn't turn. So we stopped. I thought about retiring the car. I was ready to switch it off.

Alexander Albon, Williams, Fernando Alonso, Aston Martin Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

"But then they put a new front wing and I went out again. Obviously the car was turning ok to the right and not ok to the left for the last 15 laps of the race. But we wanted to finish and collect a little bit more data.

"When you start at the back, there is this risk always. I think the quality of the drivers in the low third of the grid is very low. As we saw today with Alex. So I think we need to improve the car and start a little bit higher up."

The contact wasn't deemed worthy of investigation by the stewards, being a typical consequence of three cars fighting for the same patch of real estate at that corner.

"It felt like there was a car on the right side of Fernando," explained Albon. "And he gave Fernando enough space as if he thought there was only one car on his inside. But then I was on the inside of Fernando.

"So then I think it pinched and I tried to get out of the way and get on the kerb. But I didn't make good of it. So I imagine he got damage. I know I got damaged as we were driving around with a broken wing for the race."

Sports.title: Russell scrambling for answers after "not being quick enough" at US GP
Sports.content:
George Russell is desperately searching for answers after “not being quick enough” at the United States Grand Prix as team-mate Kimi Antonelli closes in on the Formula 1 world title.

Antonelli dominated Sunday’s race at Austin from pole, whereas Russell started sixth but finished eighth, having received a five-second penalty for gaining an advantage by running off-track on the opening lap.

It came on lap one when the Briton was defending from Oscar Piastri heading into Turn 12, where he left the track and rejoined ahead of the McLaren to keep his position.

But that penalty had little impact on his finishing position anyway since, without it, he’d have theoretically finished seventh instead of the Australian with a point gain of just two.

So when asked by Sky Sports what he’s particularly struggling with, Russell replied: “Just not being quick enough, to be honest.

“I need to try and understand why it is. It’s strange when you’re so far off, so hopefully there’s some answers somewhere. But, anyway, I don’t have one.”

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

Russell’s result came despite a recently upgraded W17, which he claims has a ‘narrow set-up window’ as evidenced by his up-and-down form since it was introduced in Malaysia.

There, Antonelli finished runner-up to the dominant Max Verstappen while Russell was set to finish third until a late power unit failure caused him to retire.

In Singapore, Verstappen won again with Antonelli third, while Russell took a lowly ninth meaning it is now three grands prix without a podium for the Briton amid a horrid 2026.

Speaking later with the written media in Austin, Russell said: “The pace wasn't good on the first stint.

“But when I came out of the pits on the hard [tyres], I probably did six laps where I was lapping the same pace as Kimi. But then I caught up with Oscar and I just couldn't overtake.

“Six good laps, 50 bad laps. I want to understand why the pace was so bad on the first stint. The penalty was a bit ridiculous as well, but that was at least some of my worries after such a bad weekend.”

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Pierluigi Orsi, Mercedes Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

The results means that Antonelli is likely to become champion in Mexico next weekend, holding a 123-point advantage over Russell with 125 left available ahead of the final five rounds.

Russell is then only one-point above third-placed Lewis Hamilton and sixth ahead of Verstappen in fourth, while Mercedes is set to win the constructors’ title as it’s 133 points in front of Ferrari.

“For me, as long as we win the constructors’ [championship], that's the main thing,” said Russell. “For the team, obviously I'd like to finish best of the rest but P2, P3, P5 is not champion so it doesn't mean anything.”

Sports.title: The maths behind Antonelli becoming F1 world champion at Mexico GP
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has taken another giant step towards becoming Formula 1 world champion by dominating the United States Grand Prix from pole on Sunday.

The Mercedes driver consequently took his ninth victory of the 2026 season and it leaves him with one hand on the championship trophy - though it has been for a while.

So, when will he do it and become F1’s youngest ever world champion?

How many drivers can still win the F1 2026 title?

There were six mathematical contenders heading into Austin - Antonelli, George Russell, Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen, Charles Leclerc and Lando Norris - as 139 points separated the drivers with 150 left available pre-Texas.

Three of those - Verstappen, Leclerc and Norris - have now dropped out of contention though, due to them finishing third, second and fifth respectively. All solid results, but it just shows how unlikely world championship glory was for them as it meant their hopes had ended.

For Antonelli to become champion at Circuit of the Americas, he needed to win with Russell finishing ninth or below and Hamilton taking fifth. But as his Mercedes team-mate took eighth and the Ferrari driver, who he succeeded at the Silver Arrows, finished fourth, the fight goes on to next weekend.

How Antonelli becomes world champion at Mexico GP

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

There are now 125 points left available in the 2026 campaign with five rounds remaining - Mexico, Sao Paulo, Las Vegas, Qatar and Abu Dhabi - provided the Middle Eastern grands prix go ahead amid the conflict.

Russell is now 123 points behind Antonelli and Hamilton is 124, so the 20-year-old Italian is all-but certain to take the crown at Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. After that race there will be 100 points left on the table, but the other two must be behind Antonelli by 99 or fewer, due to the championship leader having the most wins this season by a comfortable margin - so he would win it on countback.

This means both must outscore Antonelli by 24 and 25 points respectively. So for Russell, that entails him winning and his team-mate finishing no higher than 10th, while for Hamilton, he must also take victory but Antonelli not take any points.

Sports.title: F1 United States GP: Antonelli dominates from pole - but forced to wait for title
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli has taken another step towards an inevitable Formula 1 title with a sovereign United States Grand Prix win, defeating Charles Leclerc at Austin's Circuit of the Americas.

From pole, the Mercedes driver warded off a challenge from the Ferrari man and Max Verstappen as he stuck to the Silver Arrows’ masterplan and executed a clean one-stop race.

Antonelli's ninth grand prix win of 2026 wasn't quite enough to secure the title just yet, but the 20-year-old Italian now looks set to become F1's youngest ever world champion at next weekend's Mexico Grand Prix.

Antonelli held onto his lead at the start of the 56-lap race as second-placed Verstappen suffered a poor getaway. That left the Red Bull driver vulnerable to Leclerc, who had picked off Isack Hadjar and then swept past Verstappen with a high commitment move through the Esses.

Lewis Hamilton, starting on used softs, also worked his way past Hadjar. Behind him, George Russell was handed a five-second time penalty for going off the track on lap one while defending his position. As the top of the order settled down, Oscar Piastri was told to let quicker Lando Norris past on lap eight for seventh.

At the front, Antonelli controlled a narrow but sovereign three-second lead on Verstappen. That prompted Red Bull to roll the dice and call the Dutchman in on lap 14 for a second set of soft tyres, putting him on a two-stop race.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Mercedes didn't take the bait and kept Antonelli out as it looked determined to stay on a one-stop strategy. Struggling for grip on used softs, Hamilton came in for mediums next, as did his team-mate Leclerc and the two McLarens.

That left a temporary top three of Antonelli, Hadjar and Russell until all came in for what was supposed to be their only pitstop, with Antonelli eschewing the soft tyres entirely to go from mediums to hards on lap 25.

Verstappen didn't enjoy his new-found lead all that long as he started struggling with engine braking issues, calling his Red Bull "undriveable". It forced him into the pits on lap 32 for a second stop for mediums, dropping down to fifth, 18 seconds behind new leader Antonelli.

On the slower hard tyres Antonelli faced a challenge from Leclerc, but both he and Ferrari team-mate Hamilton were yet to stop again as Verstappen remained Antonelli's real challenger. The two Ferraris both moved to hard tyres in the final third, which droppèd them behind Verstappen.

To get to Antonelli, though, Verstappen first had to clear second-placed Norris, who also banked on a one-stop strategy. Verstappen's battle with Norris allowed Leclerc to exploit his fresher tyres and close the gap, with the three cars converging with 10 laps to go.

At the start of lap 47, Verstappen made a late lunge on Norris to the inside of COTA's steep Turn 1 hairpin, snatching second away before Leclerc also found a way through. On much fresher tyres, Leclerc then picked off Verstappen on the back straight on lap 49 to take second.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Alex Slitz / Getty Images

Antonelli's win never came under real threat as he led Leclerc by 13 seconds, with Verstappen another four seconds behind in third.

Norris also fell into the clutches of Hamilton as the latter secured fourth from the reigning world champion on lap 51, which also meant the seven-time world champion remained in mathematical title contention until next week.

Hadjar finished sixth ahead of Piastri, who held off Russell for a distant seventh. With Russell needing to avoid finishing ninth or lower to prolong his theoretical title chances, he only just managed to do so after a frustrating weekend.

Liam Lawson continued Racing Bulls' canter to fifth in the constructors' championship by finishing ninth, with the final point going to Alpine's Pierre Gasly. Antonelli is now all but certain to wrap up the championship in Mexico, needing just two points to become the youngest ever title winner aged 20.

Haas driver Oliver Bearman was one of three retirements, the eventual result of first-lap damage from contact with Gasly, which the Briton was handed a 10-second penalty for and provoked a brief VSC period.

Alpine's Franco Colapinto also disappeared from the race, while Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas retired late on with engine trouble, causing the second brief virtual safety car period of the race.

Sports.title: Inside COTA's Turn 1 clubhouse and its plans to build a second track
Sports.content:
For spectators and TV viewers tuning into coverage of Formula 1's United States Grand Prix, it's been hard to miss. Turn 1 of the Circuit of the Americas has a distinctly different look to it this year with the addition of a mammoth multi-storey clubhouse.

Connected to the main paddock area via a cable car that crosses the track, this weekend the new hospitality structure serves as an extension of F1's swanky Paddock Club. From 2 January it becomes a year-round members-only club, dubbed 'The Circuit', as the venue turns private at the start of next year.

"It isn’t an annual membership in the traditional sense," said Parris Mullins, COTA’s Senior Vice President of Motorsports. "It’s much more like a country club. There are annual dues to maintain the facilities and cover staffing, but the initiation fee is a one-time payment that essentially provides a lifetime membership.

"We’ve had more than 50 additional submissions in the past 24 hours, and that was before this race weekend. Before this race weekend, around 600 people had reached out. We’ve had one-to-one conversations with approximately 140 of them, and many have started putting down deposits and signing contracts.

"There will never be more than 300 members. We’re limiting North American membership to 250. The remaining 50 places will be a mix of international and corporate memberships."

A view from COTA's new Turn 1 clubhouse. Photo by: Filip Cleeren

The new facility isn't just COTA president Bobby Epstein's brainchild alone, though. It fits a calendar-wide push by F1 management for races to significantly ramp up their hospitality offerings.

"A lot of our contract renewal was dependent on this as well," Mullins added. "We needed to improve both the members’ experience and the experience for the Paddock Club guests. F1 has made a big commitment to it. The sport has grown, and certain markets demand these kinds of amenities. They have to keep improving what they offer."

Why COTA is building a second circuit

COTA's decision to go private has some side effects, with the venue now no longer available for track days or for regional driving clubs. But there's a solution on the horizon. On an empty plot of land to the north of the existing F1 track, COTA has crafted advanced plans to build a second, shorter circuit designed for both cars and motorcycles.

"A second track will be built, primarily because we recognise that we’re displacing a number of people and organisations that have been partners of ours since the circuit opened," Mullins explained.

"Growing motorsport, particularly in the local area, is very important to us. We’re not going to build another FIA Grade 1 facility because there’s no need for one. Instead, we want to build something that suits the local motorsport community, allows them to continue using a circuit and gives them access at a much lower price point.

"There’s obviously prestige associated with COTA. I know people love being able to say they’ve driven their car on the grand prix circuit, and we’re sorry that this won’t always be possible unless they’re members. But we want to give people somewhere they can drive, enjoy motorsport and continue participating at a grassroots level."

While details remain sparse, the circuit's undisclosed layout has already been defined. COTA is also open to the new circuit, built to FIA Grade 3 standards suitable for touring cars, sportscars and entry-level single-seaters, hosting smaller motorsports series. But by not having to cater to F1 cars, Mullins feels there is an opportunity to come up with a track more suited to high-performance sports cars and the people who drive them.

"We want to create something fun with a different personality from the grand prix circuit," he said. "COTA was built around the requirements of a single major race weekend. I’d like it to have corners we don’t have here. We don’t have a banked corner, for example, so I think the new circuit should have one. It should also have an iconic chicane. We want features that people can enjoy in the kinds of cars they bring to the track. The layout should suit them much better."

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

When asked about the timelines for the secondary track, Mullins didn't want to commit to a firm date, but there is a sense of urgency not to leave local driving and car clubs without a track for too long.

"We still need to finalise everything and work through the process with the city," he said. "We’re far enough along that we’re comfortable saying we want to get it done sooner rather than later. We don’t want the local motorsport community to go without a facility for too long, but we also need to get the project right."

COTA still sees itself as the "people's race" with its enormous spectator numbers of up to 440,000 across the F1 weekend, and by gradually turning the entire venue into one giant theme park the organisers want to lean into F1's changed demographic in the post-Netflix era. Some of that can be taken quite literally, with the rollercoaster rides of the new COTALAND amusement running alongside the circuit's third sector. But the grand prix also continues its tradition of big-name end-of-day concerts, roping in Austin's popular college sports and food culture.

Earning a new F1 deal to 2034 gives COTA the long-term stability to write off those investments, and turn them into ways to make the circuit a year-round source of revenue alongside hosting the likes of F1, MotoGP, WEC and - from 2027 - Formula E. COTALAND fits into that picture, and so does the exclusive members club and the secondary track.

But COTA hasn't forgotten that its core business is to keep the hordes of F1 fans entertained over a weekend. "Formula 1 provides the on-track action. Our job is to complement that between sessions," Mullins said. "The concerts were the first step. What Bobby did with those was really groundbreaking.

"At the end of the day, this is sport, but it’s also entertainment. We want to entertain people."

Sports.title: Red Bull no longer falls away on difficult days: What Austin qualifying reveals about its progress
Sports.content:
In Austin, the battle for pole position looked for a long time as though it would be between Max Verstappen and Ferrari. By the end of qualifying, however, the Scuderia had failed to get either car into the top three, while Kimi Antonelli emerged as a surprise contender.

Verstappen had to settle for second place, making his conclusion during the Dutch media session in the paddock clear: yes, the Red Bull driver could certainly live with that starting position, but there was still more potential to be unlocked.

That was especially evident from the Q2 lap with which Verstappen impressed his rivals. On a set of scrubbed tyres, the Dutchman was faster than some drivers from the other top teams on fresh rubber, making a third consecutive pole position seem within reach.

When Autosport asked Verstappen why the picture in Q3 was so different from the second qualifying segment, the four-time world champion explained: "I just didn't have the same grip anymore. It's as simple as that.

"I simply couldn't carry the speed that I wanted through the slow corners anymore. That's something we obviously need to understand, because there was for sure more in it. I just couldn't get it out of the car in Q3."

The wind appears to have been an important factor in that story. In the closing minutes of Q3, many drivers were caught out by gusts of wind, explaining why there were only three improvements on the second runs. Lando Norris spoke of the worst gusts of wind he had ever experienced behind the wheel, which caused him to lock up despite braking earlier as a precaution.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Ronaldo Schemidt / AFP via Getty Images

Verstappen clarified, however, that this could not explain the whole story of Q3.

"On the final run, the wind was really bad, but not on the first run. So I don't really understand why it was so disappointing. But anyway, if that's still good enough for second place, then that's okay."

Ferrari's pace also dropped away in Q3, with Charles Leclerc – like George Russell, incidentally – pointing to the increased cloud cover and falling track temperature, which pushed the Pirelli tyres slightly outside the ideal operating window for them.

Red Bull no longer falls away on challenging days

Qualifying in Austin was nevertheless revealing about the progress Red Bull has made in recent weeks, particularly since the Baku upgrade. On a day when neither driver was particularly happy with the feeling in the car, the team still managed to secure second and third places on the grid.

That marks a considerable contrast with the first half of this season, when Red Bull would often slip towards seventh and eighth on a difficult day – right at the back of the group comprising the four leading teams.

Verstappen acknowledged this too and recognised that qualifying in Austin was, in that sense, representative of the team's recent resurgence.

"Yes, absolutely. The car has been a lot better over the last few weekends, that's clear. And as I've said over the past few weekends as well, some circuits will simply suit us a little better than others. I think this one is still okay, but I think Singapore and Malaysia were clearly better for our car."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

Nevertheless, Verstappen's race pace in Austin looked more than respectable on Friday, giving him confidence heading into Sunday.

"Normally, yes. It's a bit difficult to judge who's really the fastest in race pace, but over the last few weekends it's been pretty good for us. I hope the set-up we have on the car is the right direction for the race."

The start remains a major question mark for Red Bull, although second place on the inside of the grid offers opportunities if Verstappen manages to get away well.

"Yes, but I don't think about that too much. If an overtake happens in the first corner, then it happens. And if it doesn't, then it's still such a long race in which so many things can go right or wrong. If you have a good balance and enough speed in the car, you can race here through strategy or even by overtaking someone on track."

Sports.title: Verstappen responds to COTA boss and proposes drastic measures to tackle bumps
Sports.content:
It is one of the main talking points in the Formula 1 paddock this weekend: the extreme bumps at the Circuit of the Americas. Drivers raised their concerns during Friday evening's drivers' briefing, after which Verstappen stayed behind for some time to speak further with representatives of the FIA and the circuit.

Because the track was built on Texas' infamous high-plasticity clay, it suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect. Two years ago, it was completely resurfaced, while two further interventions were carried out ahead of this year's event. The section between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced again, while efforts were made to remove the worst bumps between Turns 12 and 19.

According to the drivers, however, that is not enough. Verstappen already described the track conditions as "unacceptable" and "out of control" on Thursday, adding on Saturday that he is taking painkillers every day in Austin, just as Lando Norris needs headache tablets for every session.

When the bumps came up again after qualifying during Verstappen’s Dutch media round in the paddock, he said: "There are a few corners here that are simply really unacceptable."

That appears to refer primarily to the enormous bump under braking for Turn 1 and a rather dangerous one at Turn 19, but when Autosport put that to Verstappen, he explained that there are more problem areas.

"Turns 1 and 19 are indeed really bad, but also that whole fast section between Turns 4 and 5, there are such big bumps there... Of course I understand that the ground here is a problem, but that's something you should have looked at beforehand. That really shouldn't be an excuse."

Besides placing considerable physical strain on the drivers, the bumps through the Esses are also potentially dangerous. Several drivers have already come close to losing control of their cars at that point during the practice sessions in Austin, and if things actually go wrong through the sequence of high-speed corners, the consequences could be immense.

"Yes, those are things that really shouldn't happen at such high speeds, when the car bottoms out like that", Verstappen said.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Verstappen proposes far-reaching measures

Bobby Epstein, chairman of the Circuit of the Americas, responded to Verstappen's initial comments by suggesting that the situation was not as bad in practice as the Dutchman had made it sound.

"We don't feel good that there's a bump at the bottom of Turn 1. We didn't know about it until this week. We would have fixed it. But the other things Max spoke about, all the bumps around the track, we've fixed them. The track is in really good shape", Epstein told ESPN.

He even expressed the expectation that Verstappen would change his mind after Friday practice.

"Max doesn't say I'm wrong a lot, but he's also right a lot. He's usually very frank, and I appreciate that about him. I had no problem with him saying what he said, but I think he might be surprised in some areas that bumps he thought were here aren't [there] anymore."

However, when those comments were put to Verstappen during the Dutch media session, that proved to be anything but the case. The four-time world champion is still far from impressed with the condition of the circuit and believes Epstein would say the same if he were to drive the RB22.

"I invite him to drive my car", Verstappen said. "I think he'd have to get out after five laps and wouldn't be able to walk anymore."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

According to Verstappen, far-reaching measures will be needed in the coming years. On Thursday, he had already said that F1 drivers should no longer have to accept such conditions because of the damage to their spines, and after qualifying the Dutchman put forward a concrete proposal for the years ahead.

"You can put down a new layer of asphalt again, but a year or two later you'll have the same problem, so you need to look deeper.

"I think the FIA and Formula 1 should also be stricter about that. I understand that it all costs a lot of money, but this is really just putting a plaster over the problem. You need to dig the whole thing up and put in a proper foundation if you know the ground underneath is moving."

Sports.title: More radio problems vex Verstappen: “‘Maybe we should use sign language’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen revealed he had yet more problems with his radio during the United States Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver suffered serious disruption to his pit-to-car communications when he won the previous round in Singapore. He said the radio fault in Austin was “not the second time” it has happened this year.

“It’s already, I don’t know how many times this year,” he said. “Maybe we should just start communicating in sign language. It’s probably cheaper as well.”

“It’s a disaster. It’s really frustrating, to be honest.”

Verstappen qualified second in Austin but fell to third place in the race as he struggled with his car’s balance. During one radio exchange Verstappen admitted he did not know how to change his front wing angle at his next pit stop.

Afterwards he said Red Bull had not been especially strong or weak anywhere at the Austin track.

“We are balanced as a car,” he said. “We are not the fastest in high-speed, we’re not the fastest in low-speed, and I think maybe here you either need to be very fast in high-speed or you need to be the quickest in low-speed.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“When you’re none of it, you’re just a little bit average, and I think we were just a little bit average in the race.”

However he does believe there was potential for Red Bull to perform better last weekend.

“Of course, if we chose different tyres, probably we could have maybe been second, but that’s always easy to say afterwards. Plus, when you have too many issues with the consistency of your power unit, then that already costs you free lap time.

“So it’s normal that you can’t execute everything to the limit or at least be at your best. There are still a lot of things that we need to look at and do better.”

Sports.title: Antonelli was “concerned” by threat from Verstappen’s early pit stop in Austin | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted he was concerned to see rival Max Verstappen make an early pit stop in the United States Grand Prix.

Verstappen committed to a two-stop strategy early in the race, pitting on lap 14 for a second set of soft tyres which meant he would have to come in again. Mercedes delayed Antonelli’s first pit stop but the tactics paid off as he was able to reach the end of the race with a single tyre change.

However Antonelli admitted he was “a bit concerned in the beginning” when he stayed out after Verstappen’s pit stop. “But we were able to extend and actually the pace came back with the medium, and we were able to extend without losing too much time.

“So then, as you know, after doing the first stint on the medium, we were like, ‘Oh, right, we’re going to go for one-stop.’ And the hard, to be fair, felt very robust, so I felt pretty confident to go all the way to the end.

“I just didn’t know how much management was required, but it was good, and the car felt very good today.”

Verstappen saved two sets of soft tyres from qualifying which appeared to give him a strategic advantage before the race began.

“We didn’t have much choice, to be fair,” said Antonelli. “We didn’t have any new softs, so the new medium was the only choice we really had, or the hard.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“But the medium was not amazing. I think today the best tyre was the hard, just because it was the most resilient tyre. It was quite surprising because in recent races the soft has always been probably the best tyre. So it was a good surprise, and luckily it worked for us.”

Antonelli scored Mercedes’ first win since it introduced a major upgrade for its W17 in Malaysia. He said there is still room for improvement with the car.

“In some places, I would say it’s still not [delivering] as much as we expected, but in other places it is delivering very well,” he said. “I think in the high- and medium-speed [corners] the car is very strong. The balance is good.

“We’re still struggling a little bit in low-speed with front locking. But overall, I feel like the package is finally starting to deliver, and we’re starting to see the results and the improvements from the package.”

Sports.title: Alonso says F1 has ‘very low quality drivers’ at back of grid after Albon collision | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Fernando Alonso believes Aston Martin failed to score points despite their strongest showing this year because of his first-lap collision with Alexander Albon.

The pair made contact when Albon tried to pass Alonso on the inside of turn 11. The clash damaged Alonso’s car and he finished the race 16th, four places lower than he started.

“Albon forgot that corner 11 was there and he had to turn left,” said Alonso after the race. “But we need to get better and start a little bit higher up because I think the bottom third of the grid, the quality of the drivers is very low at the moment.”

The stewards did not investigate the collision between the pair.

The two-times world champion believes he could have finished as high as ninth place without the damage he picked up on the first lap.

“I think it was the best race of the year by far for us in terms of competitiveness,” he said. “The car was very strong in the race good tyre management.

“We got a lot of damage on lap one with Albon incident, despite that the car was still competitive. So I think we today we could have had maybe a P9, P10 on merit.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“So the best and the strongest race of the year, but ruined in the first lap with the turn 11 incident.”

Albon said he wasn’t sure if Alonso had noticed him trying to pass on the inside. “I need to review it,” he said, “but I just thought it was lap one, I felt like there was a car on his right side at the time – maybe I’m wrong, I need to have a look.

“But I was on the inside for most of the corner and then it eventually tightened up as it always does in that corner. I tried to get out the way, I was completely on the on the inside kerb. There was a point when I realised he didn’t see me or he was pinched by the car on his right-hand side. I’m sure he got damage, I got damage, so not ideal.

“But we had a second fight. I enjoyed that one a little bit more. I thought that was quite fun, but maybe he doesn’t agree, I’m sure.”

2026 United States Grand Prix

Sports.title: Hadjar urges Red Bull to redesign clutch after another poor start | Formula 1
Sports.content:
A frustrated Isack Hadjar blamed Red Bull’s clutch design for his poor start in the United States Grand Prix.

Hadjar fell from third place to fifth at the start of the race. He went on to finish sixth.

“The clutch needs a redesign because at the moment it’s too fragile, it’s not coping well with temperatures,” he told Sky. “It is a real struggle.”

“I do everything perfect in terms of procedure and then I just have clutch over-delivery,” he added. “These things that are just out of my control, it’s starting to piss me off.”

However Hadjar said the clutch wasn’t the only problem he had to cope with. He complained about the team’s decision to switch him to the hard tyre compound for his second stint.

“I have poor radio coverage, I can’t hear what’s happening like in the pits,” he said. “Then I leave the pits with the wrong [throttle] map and then I’m losing a second a lap every lap on that hard tyre.”

Hadjar’s team mate Max Verstappen, who finished third, also had a list of problems after his race, including a poor start.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“It was just the same always in the start, the problem that we have,” he said. “But then the pace is just probably not where we wanted it to be.

“Also I think, for whatever reason, the softer compounds this weekend didn’t really seem to work that well in the race for the first time in a long time. So we were just on the wrong tyres.

“Also I think the way that we used the tyres in the races was the wrong way around, so very quickly it gave away that we had to do a two-stop.

“Then the whole weekend already the power unit has not been consistent, so lap after lap, corner after corner, I’m having different kinds of problems with my engine braking or shifts as well, so I cannot be consistent. That makes it of course very difficult.”

But having won the two grands prix prior to this weekend, Verstappen does not think his car was quick enough to take three in a row.

“Even if we would have done the tyres in the right order or chosen the right compounds, I don’t think we had the pace of Kimi [Antonelli],” he said, “but maybe we could have been second.”

Sports.title: Bearman disagrees with penalty for Gasly collision: ‘I don’t regret going for it’ | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Oliver Bearman disputed the stewards’ decision to penalise him for his collision with Pierre Gasly during the United States Grand Prix.

The pair made contact as Bearman tried to pass Gasly for 10th place. The incident left him with damage which led Haas to retire his car after Bearman served his 10-second time penalty.

“After the [Virtual Safety Car] I managed to get a good launch and [had] good battery level,” Bearman explained. “I caught the two in front of me very quickly and managed to make the Pierre go defensive into turn 12 and then into 13 I sent one up the inside.

“To be honest, yeah I went up his inside, he saw me because he left space, but for me it didn’t really feel like enough. It was a bit of space but only half a car and by the time I was committed, I wasn’t disappearing. So we made a bit of contact.

“I picked up a huge amount of damage on my car. I probably damaged Pierre’s car as well. It was a shame because I felt like I was massively penalised for it anyway. It actually ruined my race, to have that amount of damaged. I was losing a second a lap due to downforce.

“Then on top of that, I picked up a penalty. In my view, it was a racing incident. I sent a move, okay, but I felt like I was entitled to a bit more space than I got. I didn’t lose control. I had to even climb up onto the kerb to try and avoid contact, because I didn’t feel like I was given enough space. So one of those things. The main thing was that I picked up a heck of a lot of damage, and the car was terrible after that, so it was a shame.”

The stewards ruled Bearman was not close enough to Gasly to be entitled to space. “The front axle of car 87 [Bearman] was not ahead of the mirror of car 10 [Gasly] at the apex where a collision occurred

between the two cars,” they noted.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The stewards determined that the driver of Car 87 was wholly to blame for the collision and imposed a 10-second penalty accordingly.”

Bearman was surprised to learn of his penalty, replying “you’re kidding me?” when told on his radio.

Gasly went on to finish in 10th place. Bearman said “I don’t regret going for the move” despite the penalty and damage. “At this stage if we don’t do something special and get a bit lucky and be aggressive and go for it, then we’re not going to score points because we’re fast enough to do that on merit.

“Looking where he is now, I’m happy that he’s likely going to score points after the contact that we had, but I feel like that could have been me and of course that was what I was going for.”

2026 United States Grand Prix

Sports.title: Stewards explain reason for Russell’s “mitigated” US GP penalty | Formula 1
Sports.content:
George Russell received a five-second time penalty for a first-lap incident in the United States Grand Prix but the stewards considered a harsher sanction.

The Mercedes driver was penalised for leaving the track at turn 12 and gaining an advantage while fighting for position with Oscar Piastri . Russell stayed ahead of the McLaren.

“I was on the inside, he was overtaking on the outside, that’s his risk,” said Russell when his race engineer Marcus Dudley warned him he was under investigation.

The stewards decided that because Russell was also fighting Isack Hadjar at the time, and the incident happened on the first lap, a harsher penalty was not deserved.

“The driver of car 63 [Russell] was defending position from car 81 [Piastri], into turn 12 and left the track, then proceeded to rejoin in front of car 81, prior to turn 13. He retained that position. Accordingly he is determined by the stewards to have left the track, rejoined it and gained a lasting advantage.

“The normal penalty for this is a 10-second penalty, however the stewards considered that the driver of car 63 had previously been pressuring car six [Hadjar] and that put car 81 into an attacking position (and therefore car 63 into a defending position). Further, this was a first lap incident and in our determination, the penalty should be mitigated to five seconds.”

The stewards chose not to penalised Gabriel Bortoleto for a similar incident on the first lap of the race when he tried to pass Franco Colapinto. They said this was because they could not determine which driver was ahead at the apex.

“At the entry to turn 11, car five (Gabriel Bortoleto) moved to overtake car 43 (Franco Colapinto) on the outside. Car 43 stayed alongside and in that battle car five left the edge of the track and rejoined ahead of car 43.

“Under the Driving Standards Guidelines, had the front axle of car five been ahead at the apex, car five would have been entitled to racing room on the inside. There was no racing room on the inside which explained why car five left the edge of the track. Had the front axle of car 43 been ahead of the front axle of car five at the apex, car 43 was not obliged to leave racing room on the outside.

“The stewards were unable, by reference to the available evidence, to reach a level of comfortable satisfaction as to which of the two cars was ahead at the apex and in these circumstances determined to take no further action.”

Sports.title: Canelo Arrives in Riyadh for Mbilli Fight: Start Time, Ring Walks and DAZN PPV
Sports.content:
Canelo returns on October 31 to challenge for the WBC super middleweight belt, live on DAZN PPV and included with DAZN Ultimate.

Canelo Alvarez arrived in Riyadh on Monday morning ahead of his October 31 fight against WBC super middleweight champion Christian Mbilli. The Mexican challenges for a belt he previously held when they meet over 12 rounds at The Venue in Riyadh.

Mbilli had already reached Saudi Arabia. Canelo was welcomed by Faisal Bafarat, chief executive of the General Entertainment Authority, with Jaime Munguia and Rafael Espinoza among the fighters arriving alongside him.

Saturday ends Canelo’s 13-month absence from the ring. The 36-year-old has not fought since Terence Crawford outpointed him in September 2025, stripping him of his undisputed super middleweight championship.

Canelo enters at 63-3-2 with 39 knockouts, seeking to regain a title at 168 pounds. He has won championships in four divisions and twice collected all four major belts at super middleweight.

Mbilli makes his first defence of the full WBC title. The Cameroon-born, Montreal-based champion holds a 29-0-1 record with 24 knockouts, having stopped Maciej Sulecki in the opening round to capture the interim belt in June 2025.

His last fight ended in a split draw against Lester Martinez. He now faces Canelo with his championship and clean loss column at stake.

Canelo vs Mbilli Start Time and Ring Walks

The advertised running order lists preliminary coverage from 10:15 a.m. ET / 7:15 a.m. PT / 2:15 p.m. GMT on Saturday, October 31.

The PPV card begins at 2 p.m. ET / 11 a.m. PT / 6 p.m. GMT.

Canelo and Mbilli’s ring walks are listed for approximately 6 p.m. ET / 3 p.m. PT / 10 p.m. GMT, followed by the opening bell around 6:15 p.m. ET / 3:15 p.m. PT / 10:15 p.m. GMT.

The main event will not begin before 6 p.m. ET / 10 p.m. GMT under that timetable. Individual fight times remain estimates, particularly following changes to the undercard.

How to Watch on DAZN

DAZN PPV costs $79.99 in the United States. The event is also included with DAZN Ultimate, allowing subscribers to that tier to watch without a separate PPV purchase.

Undercard Changes Ahead of Saturday

Jaime Munguia faces Nikita Zon in a scheduled 12-round WBA super middleweight title bout. Their advertised slot is 5 p.m. ET / 9 p.m. GMT.

Rafael Espinoza now faces Ricardo Blandon, replacing Lorenzo Parra for the WBO featherweight title fight. The WBO approved Blandon as the substitute challenger; Espinoza’s original slot was 4 p.m. ET / 8 p.m. GMT.

Raymundo Rojas Garcia meets Reito Tsutsumi over 10 rounds at super featherweight, listed to open the PPV portion at 2 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. GMT.

Lindolfo Delgado’s planned IBF super lightweight title fight against Arthur Biyarslanov is off the card, according to reporter Lance Pugmire. Its previously advertised 2:55 p.m. ET slot should therefore no longer be treated as a confirmed bout time.

Sports.title: Hearn And Warren Let The Wolf In, Says Lou DiBella
Sports.content:
Lou DiBella isn’t buying the victory lap from boxing’s old guard over Zuffa’s early struggles, pointing out that rival promoters helped clear the path for TKO to muscle into the sport to begin with.

Shakur Stevenson walking out the door gave rival outfits an easy talking point, but grabbing free publicity does not suddenly balance a promotion’s checkbook, pack an arena, or supply the massive purse Stevenson expects.

DiBella cut through the noise to ask what these traditional promotional companies are actually gaining from the chaos.

“Is Eddie all of a sudden thriving? Does he have no worries? Is Oscar and Golden Boy great? Is Top Rank’s business getting better? Is anything changing?” said DiBella to Total Boxing.

Taking a victory lap looks hollow when signing an elite free agent immediately turns into a costly headache. Any promoter chasing Stevenson must still lock in an opponent, secure a broadcast budget, and generate enough public interest to justify the deal. Cheering because a fighter hits the open market costs nothing; financing his next outing is another matter entirely.

DiBella also turned the spotlight directly onto Eddie Hearn and Frank Warren for ushering Saudi influence into boxing.

“Who’s most responsible for letting the wolf into the hen house of boxing promotion? It’s Eddie Hearn and Frank Warren.”

Relying on external money delivered massive blockbusters, yet it built an independent power structure capable of pursuing fighters and television rights without needing the old establishment. Whining about an aggressive rival rings hollow after rolling out the red carpet for them.

Even as Zuffa hits growing pains, DiBella believes TKO still holds an edge in sheer muscle, deep political ties, and premier North American broadcast real estate.

“They still have better political and business connections. They still have the best TV deals in North America.”

Those advantages might not guarantee creative matchmaking or commercial success on their own, but deep pockets and broadcast reach give an enterprise plenty of room to absorb early stumbles.

DiBella admitted that everyone inside the sport shares blame for its fragmented condition. Still, his message lands with a thud: taking cheap shots at Dana White brings easy attention, but building a sustainable, busy boxing calendar takes real execution that no competitor can manufacture off another brand’s bad headlines.

Sports.title: Jaime Munguia Preps For Riyadh As Bektemir Melikuziev Gets Screwed
Sports.content:
Jaime Munguia is getting ready to fight Nikita Zon in Riyadh on October 31, but Bektemir Melikuziev is still stuck waiting for the WBA to enforce its own rules. Melikuziev reportedly turned down step-aside cash because he wanted his deserved shot at the belt. Now he risks getting hit with the exact delay he refused to take a check for.

That issue sits right behind the latest training clips floating out of Box Azteca. Munguia is wrapping his hands alongside trainer Eddy Reynoso, grinding through camp while his return date gets closer by the minute. Meanwhile, his number one challenger doesn’t have a clue when his title shot is coming.

The sanctioning body ordered Munguia to face Melikuziev back on September 21, giving both camps until October 21 to strike a deal. Officials pointed out that the mandatory defense window expired on August 30. Once the Zon fight was announced, the WBA posted that it hadn’t approved the bout at all.

It confirmed Melikuziev as the top contender, promising a full review. Yet here we are in late October, with zero public rulings to approve the Riyadh bout, strip the belt, or call a purse bid.

Turning down money to step aside ought to mean something. Melikuziev made it clear he wants the real prize. Letting Munguia cruise ahead without strict conditions gives the champion a pass, leaving the challenger frozen out with nothing to show for standing his ground.

Taking other fights creates real ripple effects. Zon could cause an unexpected cut, a prolonged recovery window, or fresh excuses to stall Melikuziev even longer. Detours like this show that loose promises about future title shots don’t protect anyone.

Missing the October 21 deadline didn’t trigger an automatic stripping, but the original order laid out a purse bid if negotiations crashed. The sanctioning body has a clear procedure ready to go. Leaving fight fans to watch Munguia prep for an unapproved opponent without a formal ruling looks terrible. The WBA needs to order that purse bid right now, or it tells every hungry contender that earning mandatory status means nothing when the champion wants to take a detour.
