Sports.title: Sebastian Fundora’s Inside Game Covers Poor Distance Control
Sports.content:
Sebastian Fundora’s towering stature is frequently billed as a nightmare puzzle for Jaron “Boots” Ennis. His gritty scrap against Ermal Hadribeaj exposed a deeper issue: height means little if you lack the hand speed and sharp timing to protect it.

Shawn Porter zeroed in on those deficiencies while breaking down Fundora’s October 17 win alongside Hadribeaj. The unheralded challenger slipped past the WBC junior middleweight champion’s reach all night, causing chaos until Fundora finally halted him with one tick remaining in round 12.

“He couldn’t time you last night,” Porter told Hadribeaj Porter’s channel. “You were coming after him, and there was not one moment where he saw you coming.”

Porter mentioned Timothy Bradley’s note that Fundora’s father deliberately schooled him in phone-booth infighting, knowing shorter foes would inevitably crowd him. Preparing for the trenches makes tactical sense. It does nothing to develop range control or a punishing perimeter game.

“You don’t have natural speed with the jab. You don’t have natural timing with the one-two,” Porter pointed out.

That gap undermines Fundora’s physical gifts. An 80-inch reach should turn the outside into a minefield, yet Hadribeaj walked into chest range round after round.

Labeling Fundora an inside specialist lets him off the hook. Smothering a foe by choice after dictating terms from the outside is one thing. Living on the inside because you lack the tools to keep opponents off your chest is entirely different. Porter’s critique puts Fundora squarely in that second camp.

Hadribeaj also smothered Fundora so effectively that the champion lost leverage on his trademark uppercuts. Porter observed that while a few broke through, the challenger took away the arc and velocity that crushed earlier rivals.

That pattern should set off alarm bells for Fundora’s camp ahead of a clash with Ennis.

Hadribeaj was an overlooked mandatory, not a pound-for-pound technician, yet he repeatedly forced the champion into disorganized exchanges.

Ennis would not have to wage a simple war of attrition. Boots could exploit those same entry lanes with explosive combinations, fluid stance switches, and evasive angles before Fundora resets his feet. Breaching Fundora’s perimeter would simply trigger a much heavier assault.

Hadribeaj maintains that Fundora’s rare height might still trouble Ennis. His own 12 rounds offered the opposite verdict: a modest puncher penetrated Fundora’s defenses at will.

Boots would still have to respect the champion’s durability, heavy inside clubs, and unrelenting output. Fundora eventually broke Hadribeaj through pure grit, and absorbing that type of heat drains any gas tank.

Fundora cannot gamble on elite punchers gassing out before his defensive gaps catch up to him. Halting Hadribeaj protected his belt, but it never answered Porter’s questions about how effortlessly he was reached.

Sports.title: Lindolfo Delgado Off Saudi Card Amid Safety Concerns
Sports.content:
Lindolfo Delgado is off the October 31 Canelo Alvarez–Christian Mbilli undercard in Riyadh, according to Lance Pugmire, after trainer Robert Garcia publicly questioned the safety of traveling to Saudi Arabia.

“Told definitively that Delgado is off the Saudi card,” Lance Pugmire posted on X.

Delgado was scheduled to face Arthur Biyarslanov for the vacant IBF light welterweight title. His absence follows days of uncertainty over travel arrangements against a backdrop of attacks on Saudi airports.

An October 21 U.S. Embassy security alert reported that operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh remained suspended. A separate travel advisory urged Americans to reconsider visiting Saudi Arabia because of drone and missile threats. Those warnings provide substantial context for the concerns Garcia raised before Delgado’s removal.

Garcia had spoken about his worries over taking Delgado and his team into the country while they still lacked travel arrangements. NY Fights reported those comments on October 22, several days before Pugmire’s update.

That makes this more serious than an ordinary fight-week cancellation. A boxer can spend months preparing for a championship opportunity and still face a decision that has little to do with the opponent across the ring. The importance of the belt does not remove the risks involved in reaching the venue.

Robert Garcia made the only sensible move a trainer can make in that spot. When a fighter enters title contention, the camp has to deal with enough variables inside the ropes without having to worry about closed airports, missile alerts, and basic travel logistics falling apart on fight week.

Pushing a fighter onto a plane under those conditions, especially with the U.S. Embassy issuing formal warnings in Riyadh, would have been reckless.

Biyarslanov has already arrived in Saudi Arabia, according to BoxingScene’s earlier reporting. He now faces uncertainty over whether he will fight Saturday and whether the vacant championship will remain available to him on this card.

Pugmire’s brief post does not specify the final decision-making process within Delgado’s camp or establish what happens to his IBF opportunity.

The organizers now have a missing title challenger days before the event. Finding another boxer may fill the slot, but it would not answer the travel and safety questions Garcia raised before Delgado was ruled out.

Sports.title: Terence Crawford Didn’t Deserve Fighter Of The Year
Sports.content:
Terence Crawford’s win over Canelo Alvarez secured him 2025 Fighter of the Year honors from The Ring and the BWAA. It belonged in the Performance of the Year discussion instead. Beating an aging champion in a lone appearance was simply not enough to capture the sport’s top annual award.

Mike Coppinger raised that point on X, agreeing with Stephen “Breadman” Edwards that boxing needs a recognized Performance of the Year category. Coppinger argued Fighter of the Year should require at least two bouts, noting he backed Naoya Inoue for that reason. One spectacular night does not equal a complete twelve-month campaign.

Crawford’s backers cite the climb from 154 to 168 pounds to claim undisputed status in a third division. Those accomplishments carry historical weight, but the state of the opponent cannot be ignored. Canelo was 35, well past his physical prime, and later had surgery to remove loose bodies from his left elbow. How much the joint limited him remains up for debate, yet it belongs in any honest assessment of the night.

The win also failed to answer key questions about Crawford at super middleweight. Taking on a dangerous contender like Osleys Iglesias would have tested him against prime physical power rather than an older, damaged champion. Crawford walked away and retired instead, leaving the Canelo bout as his sole 2025 appearance.

A factual detail also got lost in the online back-and-forth. Crawford did not capture the Ring or BWAA awards in 2023. Inoue swept both honors after stopping Stephen Fulton and Marlon Tapales, delivering two elite victories while Crawford fought just once against Errol Spence Jr.

Crawford earned recognition for beating Canelo, but Fighter of the Year went too far. Proving himself against an active, dangerous contender at 168 would have built a real case instead of relying strictly on the star value of a single name.

Sports.title: Zuffa Boxing Faces Expensive Gamble Rebuilding Conor Benn
Sports.content:
Conor Benn’s search for another massive payday puts him in treacherous territory after Ryan Garcia destroyed him in just two rounds. Eddie Hearn insists Chris Eubank Jr. stands as Benn’s lone viable move, openly wondering how Zuffa Boxing navigates this mess.

Benn commands enormous paydays, which makes soft matchmaking nearly impossible. Zuffa needs major events to justify its financial backing. Staging an uncompetitive tune-up becomes a brutal sell coming off an early knockout loss. Paying Benn top-tier money to beat up overmatched opponents turns into a fast way to burn through cash.

“The only fight for Conor Benn now is Chris Eubank. That’s it,” Hearn said to iFL TV. “Chris Eubank, ironically, holds the keys to Conor Benn’s next payday.”

A domestic clash with Eubank carries built-in nostalgia and guaranteed UK attention. In contrast, grinding out a rebuild at 147 pounds demands heavy lifting, since cruising past an overmatched opponent won’t erase the image of Garcia dropping him.

Benn must topple legitimate welterweight contenders to prove he belongs among the elite. His outings against Regis Prograis and Garcia offer plenty of reasons to doubt he can pull that off. Those bouts laid bare technical flaws that a soft touch can only paper over.

Zuffa might purchase some breathing room with careful matchmaking, yet Benn eventually has to face punchers capable of targeting those exact holes. That reality makes a gradual comeback an expensive gamble with zero guarantee of a payoff.

Hearn floated the idea that Zuffa could present Benn with lethal fights like Shakur Stevenson or Jaron Ennis, triggering immediate salary disputes.

“He’ll go, ‘I’m not fighting those guys for that kind of money,’ and they’ll go, ‘See you.’ He may never even fight again,” Hearn claimed.

Hearn didn’t quote Benn’s contract or point to a concrete offer Benn turned down. His forecast leans on speculation, though the underlying business logic holds up. Exactly how many setup bouts will Zuffa finance before demanding a dangerous matchup?

Old grievances clearly color Hearn’s comments. He still resents the way Benn walked out on Matchroom without picking up the phone after years of promotional loyalty.

“You can’t knock Conor Benn for taking the deal,” Hearn admitted. “What you can knock him for is the way that he treated me in terms of not even having a conversation with me.”

Personal bitterness aside, Hearn pinpoints a genuine dilemma. Benn’s price tag creates immediate pressure to deliver marquee fights, while his recent tape gives prospective rivals a clear roadmap to beat him.

Settling the score with Eubank delivers the quick cash grab Benn wants. Attempting to rebuild at welterweight forces Benn to take on dangerous contenders to restore his standing, which is precisely where the entire operation could unravel.

Sports.title: Shakur Stevenson Could Abandon WBO Title Over Raymond Muratalla
Sports.content:
Shakur Stevenson could soon face a tough business call if the WBO installs Raymond Muratalla as his mandatory challenger at 140 pounds. Taking that fight means accepting real physical risk without the massive financial windfall tied to bouts against Devin Haney, Ryan Garcia, or Gervonta Davis.

Top Rank took the first step by petitioning the sanctioning body to elevate their top-ranked contender. A petition doesn’t make the fight a done deal, yet it instantly forces the question of whether Shakur actually wants the matchup if it gets ordered.

Nobody can say Shakur is running just yet. At the same time, wanting to wear a world title strap and wanting the specific challenger standing behind it are completely separate things.

Muratalla brings zero box office power compared to the superstars Shakur keeps calling out. The challenger hits hard enough to turn lights out, but that kind of heavy-handed grit rarely guarantees a huge network budget or career-best purse. Without any clear financial guarantees on the table, Stevenson would effectively be asked to accept a discounted payday for a fight that could destroy his road to far bigger money.

That threat doesn’t mean Muratalla has to outbox the champion for twelve rounds. Stevenson could easily control long stretches with his southpaw jab, footwork, and outside defense. Still, he would need to stay locked in every second Muratalla steps inside to plant his feet. One slip against a true puncher wipes out entire rounds of clean boxing.

Defending the belt carries obvious perks for Shakur. He retains his hardware, adds a legitimate scalp to his resume, and silences critics who would otherwise claim he ducked the division’s toughest boogeyman. Chasing mega-fights with Haney, Garcia, or Tank always involves tricky promotional hurdles and clashing timelines. A hypothetical super-fight puts no cash in the bank until ink hits paper.

If a genuine blockbuster offer surfaces right as the WBO issues a firm order, dropping the title becomes a very real temptation. Shakur would take heat from fans for walking away from an elite challenger, but boxing remains a business first.

Holding that WBO belt helps Stevenson sell himself as the top dog at light welterweight. If Muratalla gets named mandatory, holding onto the hardware means taking a fight where the physical risk completely outweighs the financial reward. Until Shakur puts his signature on a bout agreement, nobody should be shocked if that belt suddenly loses its shine.

Ghana News.title: Netherlands pledges technical support and investment to boost Ghana’s poultry industry
Ghana News.content:
Deputy Agric Minister, John Dumelo and Hans Akerboom Ambassador desginate of the Netherlands to Ghana

The Netherlands has pledged to support Ghana’s efforts to develop a stronger and more competitive poultry industry through technical expertise, knowledge exchange and investment.

The Netherlands Ambassador to Ghana, H.E. Hans Akerboom, said his country was ready to work with Ghanaian stakeholders to identify practical solutions to challenges facing the sector and expand opportunities for local poultry farmers and businesses.

Speaking at a poultry round-table discussion in Accra on Monday, October 26, 2026, he said stronger collaboration between the two countries could help Ghana harness its growing poultry market to increase domestic production and create jobs.

H.E. Akerboom said the Netherlands welcomed the country’s ambition to strengthen its poultry sector and was committed to exploring ways to translate the partnership into tangible results.

“We warmly welcome this ambition and we are committed to exploring how we can translate it into a clear result,” he said.

He noted that the Netherlands had developed its poultry industry through sustained investment in knowledge, innovation and collaboration, adding that these experiences could help inform Ghana’s efforts, taking into account the country’s specific needs.

The Ambassador said the partnership was particularly important given Ghana’s reliance on imported poultry to meet domestic demand.

He disclosed that Ghana imported poultry worth approximately €18 million from the Netherlands alone in 2024, while other supplies came from countries including Belgium, the United States and Brazil.

The two countries have also signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on how to strengthen the sector

According to him, the figures highlighted the potential for Ghanaian farmers and businesses to increase their share of the domestic market.

Mr Akerboom stressed that the objective should go beyond reducing imports to creating conditions that would enable local farmers to expand production, supply the market consistently and benefit from existing demand.

Ghana News.title: TOR targets 55,000 barrels per stream day as F-61 crude heater work continues
Ghana News.content:
The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) is working to increase its crude-processing rate from approximately 28,000 barrels per stream day to between 45,000 and 55,000 barrels per stream day, Managing Director Edmond Kombat has announced.

He said engineers from Verga Engineering were working alongside TOR’s technical team to complete the tie-in and commission the F-61 crude heater, a critical component in the refinery’s ongoing operational recovery.

Speaking at the Government Accountability Series at Jubilee House on Monday, October 26, 2026, Mr Kombat said the work was expected to improve the performance of the Crude Distillation Unit (CDU) and move the plant towards its nameplate capacity.

“Engineers from Verga Engineering are currently on site, working on with TOR’s technical team to increase the throughput to between 45,000bpsd to 55,000bpsd,” he said.

The CDU was refurbished under a turnaround maintenance programme conducted between August 1 and October 30, 2025. Crude processing resumed on December 19, 2025, after the National Petroleum Authority inspected the plant and cleared it for operations.

President John Dramani Mahama subsequently commissioned the refurbished unit on August 1, 2026.

Mr Kombat said management had prioritised the CDU’s rehabilitation after inheriting a refinery whose major processing units had remained inactive for several years.

The CDU had been out of operation since April 2021, while the Residue Fluid Catalytic Cracking (RFCC) unit had been shut down since 2019.

He said the turnaround maintenance was funded entirely from TOR’s internally generated funds and carried out by the refinery’s engineers and technicians.

“Work also resumed on critical stalled projects, including Boiler No. 8, the F-61 Crude Heater, the Residue Air Cooler and the Steam Turbine Generator,” he said.

Management is also planning to install a new air cooler to increase processing capacity to 60,000 barrels per stream day and replace the existing 6,500-barrel-a-day catalytic reformers with a 10,000-barrel-per-day continuous catalytic reformer.

Mr Kombat said a new 120-tonne boiler had been installed, while work continued on the RFCC turnaround and the SCADA system.

Beyond the immediate engineering interventions, the government has directed TOR’s board and management to develop a roadmap for increasing processing capacity to 100,000 barrels per day, with a longer-term ambition of reaching 200,000 barrels per day.

Mr Kombat said the proposed improvements were intended to strengthen refining capacity, improve operational reliability and increase the refinery’s contribution to domestic petroleum supply.

He acknowledged that the recovery process was ongoing, adding that management remained focused on completing outstanding engineering works and sustaining the gains made since operations resumed.

Ghana News.title: ‘I’m not discouraged’ – Ablakwa responds to criticism over South Africa evacuation
Ghana News.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa says he remains committed to protecting the welfare and dignity of Ghanaians despite what he describes as “all the vilification” directed at him amid controversy over the cost of the evacuation exercise from South Africa.

He said criticism from the Minority and other commentators would not discourage him from carrying out his responsibilities.

Speaking at a press conference on Monday, October 26, organised by some of the evacuees to tell their part of the story, Mr Ablakwa reaffirmed his commitment to serving Ghanaians, insisting that the criticism would not distract him from his duties.

"I give you one assurance: despite all the vilification, I remain fully committed to the welfare, the protection, the dignity, and the rights of all Ghanaians. I am not discouraged at all," the minister said.

He also defended the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its finance officers against allegations of financial impropriety in the management of funds for the evacuation exercise.

The minister maintained that he had confidence in the work of the officials involved, insisting that no money had been stolen.

His comments follow media fact-checks and allegations by the Minority that not every evacuee received the reported GH¢5,500 in support payments.

Questions have also been raised about discrepancies in some dates of birth contained in documents provided by the ministry.

The controversy has triggered public scrutiny of the expenditure on the evacuation exercise and the accuracy of the records used to account for payments to returnees.

Mr Ablakwa's latest comments signal his determination to continue his work despite the mounting criticism, as calls for clarity over the payments and documentation remain part of the debate surrounding the exercise.

Ghana News.title: TOR targets 100,000 barrels-a-day capacity as Ghana eyes 70% local fuel supply by 2028
Ghana News.content:
The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) is working towards a major expansion of its crude-processing capacity to 100,000 barrels per day, as the government targets meeting about 70 per cent of Ghana’s national fuel demand through local refining by 2028.

Managing Director Edmond Kombat said the expansion formed part of a broader strategy to strengthen domestic refining, reduce dependence on imported finished petroleum products and improve the country’s energy security.

Speaking at the Government Accountability Series at Jubilee House on Monday, October 26, 2026, Mr Kombat said President John Dramani Mahama had directed the Energy and Green Transition Minister to work with TOR’s board and management on a strategic roadmap for the refinery’s expansion.

He said the President issued the directive when he commissioned the refurbished Crude Distillation Unit on August 1, 2026.

According to Mr Kombat, the roadmap includes an initial increase in capacity to 100,000 barrels per day, with a longer-term ambition of reaching 200,000 barrels per day.

“TOR is part of a national plan. With the refinery’s expansion from 45,000 to 100,000 barrels a day, the Government is targeting about 70 percent of national fuel demand from local refining by 2028,” he said.

In the immediate term, engineers from Verga Engineering are working with TOR’s technical team to complete the tie-in and commission the F-61 crude heater.

Mr Kombat said the work was expected to increase the CDU’s throughput from its current level of about 28,000 barrels per stream day to between 45,000 and 55,000 barrels per stream day.

Management also plans to install a new air cooler to increase processing capacity to 60,000 barrels per stream day and replace the existing 6,500-barrel-a-day catalytic reformers with a 10,000-barrel-per-day continuous catalytic reformer.

He said a new 120-tonne boiler had been installed, while work continued on the RFCC turnaround and the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system.

Beyond the immediate improvements, TOR is advancing plans for a new greenfield refinery and petrochemical facilities, alongside additional storage capacity.

The refinery’s longer-term Restoration and Legacy Projects programme for 2026 to 2029 proposes expanding the existing plant to 85,000 barrels per stream day and constructing a new refinery with a capacity of 115,000 barrels per stream day.

Together, the proposed developments would provide a combined capacity of 200,000 barrels per stream day.

Mr Kombat said the projects would be pursued with strategic partners and in line with the government’s climate-compliance principles.

He said increasing local refining capacity would strengthen Ghana’s ability to meet domestic demand while supporting industrial growth and reducing exposure to disruptions in international petroleum supply chains.

Ghana News.title: TOR receives over 5 million barrels of crude after zero receipts in 2024
Ghana News.content:
The Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) has received more than five million barrels of crude oil following a period in which it recorded no crude receipts in 2024, Managing Director Edmond Kombat has disclosed.

He said the renewed supply of crude reflected growing confidence among suppliers and business partners following efforts to restore the refinery’s operations.

Speaking at the Government Accountability Series at Jubilee House on Monday, October 26, 2026, Mr Kombat said TOR had received several crude cargoes since the recovery programme began, including shipments of Ghanaian indigenous crude.

“TOR has maintained a steady supply of crude oil for refinery operations, reflecting the renewed confidence among suppliers and business partners, who are once again willing to do business with the refinery,” he said.

The Managing Director listed Bonga, Baleine and Bonnie Light among the crude grades received since May 2026, followed by Ghana’s Jubilee Medium Sweet crude delivered aboard the MT Apache on July 15, 2026.

He said TOR paid for the Jubilee cargo in full, describing it as the refinery’s first Jubilee crude shipment in a decade.

On September 25, 2026, the refinery received a further 950,000-barrel shipment of Sankofa crude from the Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC).

The crude deliveries followed the restart of refining operations on December 19, 2025, after the completion of turnaround maintenance on the Crude Distillation Unit (CDU).

Mr Kombat said the restoration of crude supplies had been central to management’s efforts to return TOR to its core mandate of processing crude oil into petroleum products for the domestic market.

He explained that the refinery had been largely inactive when the current management took office in May 2025, with the CDU out of operation since April 2021 and the Residue Fluid Catalytic Cracking (RFCC) Unit shut down since 2019.

Management subsequently prioritised the rehabilitation of the CDU, with turnaround maintenance conducted between August 1 and October 30, 2025.

Following inspections by the National Petroleum Authority, the refinery received clearance to resume refining operations.

The refurbished CDU was commissioned by President John Dramani Mahama on August 1, 2026.

Mr Kombat said the crude deliveries and renewed commercial relationships demonstrated the importance of collaboration among state institutions and private-sector partners in restoring TOR.

He said management would continue working to ensure a steady supply of crude, improve operational efficiency and increase processing capacity.

Ghana News.title: NPP can welcome Alan Kyerematen back as a member, but not as flagbearer now – Joe Wise
Ghana News.content:
Former First Deputy Speaker of Parliament and Chairman of the New Patriotic Party’s Disciplinary Committee, Joseph Osei-Owusu, popularly known as Joe Wise, says the party is willing to welcome former Trade Minister Alan Kyerematen back as a member but will not consider him for the flagbearer position at this stage.

According to him, the NPP has already elected its flagbearer for the next general election, making it impossible for Mr Kyerematen to assume the position without going through the party’s established electoral process.

He says Mr Kyerematen would, however, be welcomed if he follows the party’s procedures for members who have left and wish to return.

Mr Osei-Owusu’s comments follow Mr Kyerematen’s public declaration that the only condition under which he would consider returning to the NPP is if he is offered the opportunity to lead the party as its flagbearer.

Speaking to the media at the Ashanti Region NPP sensitisation programme for the constituency secretaries in Kumasi, Joe Wise described the demand as unacceptable, adding that he initially considered the former minister’s comment a joke.

“The party has a channel of electing a flagbearer, and that procedure has been completed. So, if Bawumia finishes his term and Alan comes back, we will see whether he can go unopposed. But for now, I don’t think the party can accept him as flagbearer,” he said.

He explained that the NPP has established procedures governing the return of former members and urged Mr Kyerematen to follow the appropriate process if he is serious about rejoining the party.

Mr Osei-Owusu stressed that the NPP needs more members to strengthen its ranks, noting that Mr Kyerematen had served the party in various capacities during his time as a member.

“Alan Kyerematen has duly served the party in so many ways, so if he comes, we will accept him,” he stated.

Ghana News.title: 80% poultry import dependence highlights need to grow local production – Netherlands Ambassador
Ghana News.content:
Hans Akerboom Ambassador desginate of the Netherlands to Ghana

The Netherlands Ambassador to Ghana, H.E. Hans Akerboom, has expressed concern over Ghana’s dependence on imported poultry, saying the country imports about 80% of its poultry supply despite strong domestic demand.

He said the situation presented a significant opportunity for Ghana to strengthen local production, create jobs and improve the livelihoods of poultry farmers and businesses.

Speaking at a round-table discussion on the poultry industry in Accra on Monday, October 26, 2026, aimed at strengthening stakeholder collaboration in Ghana’s poultry sector, H.E. Akerboom said Ghana imported poultry worth approximately €18 million from the Netherlands alone in 2024.

He noted that the country also imports poultry from other countries, including Belgium, the United States and Brazil, further highlighting the country’s reliance on foreign supplies.

The Ambassador said the figures were worrying but also demonstrated the potential for Ghana to develop a stronger and more competitive domestic poultry industry.

“This is not simply about reducing imports. It is about creating the right conditions for Ghanaian farmers to grow their businesses, supply the market day by day and benefit from the demand that already exists,” he said.

He said chicken remained a popular source of protein for many Ghanaian households, creating a ready market for local farmers and businesses.

However, he stressed that meeting this demand would require stronger partnership between the government, private sector, financial institutions and knowledge institutions.

Ghana-Netherlands partnership

H.E. Akerboom said the Netherlands was ready to support Ghana’s efforts to expand domestic poultry production through the exchange of technical knowledge, innovation and investment.

He cited a visit by a Ghanaian delegation to the Netherlands earlier this year, during which officials explored opportunities to draw on Dutch expertise and investment to support the development of Ghana’s poultry industry.

According to him, the Netherlands’ poultry sector has grown through sustained investment in knowledge, innovation and collaboration, lessons he said could be adapted to Ghana’s needs.

He said the proposed interventions aligned with the government’s Feed Ghana programme and the 24-hour economy initiative, which could provide opportunities to strengthen agricultural production and create sustainable businesses.

The Ambassador announced that he would sign an addendum to the Memorandum of Understanding governing the Ghana-Netherlands Food and Agriculture Working Group, with a specific focus on the poultry sector.

He said the agreement would provide a framework for advancing cooperation and translating the shared ambition of both countries into practical outcomes.

As an initial step, H.E. Akerboom said a webinar would be organised in 2027 to present the key outcomes of the round-table discussion and facilitate connections between stakeholders to encourage further collaboration.

He expressed optimism that the partnership would help create opportunities for Ghanaian farmers, businesses and the wider food sector.

The round-table discussion forms part of broader efforts to identify practical solutions to the challenges facing Ghana’s poultry industry and improve its capacity to meet domestic demand.

Ghana News.title: ‘End the baseless attacks’ – Evacuees defend government over South Africa operation
Ghana News.content:
The leader of the Aggrieved South Africa Evacuees, Michael Addo, has called for an immediate end to what he describes as baseless attacks against Ghanaians evacuated from South Africa and the government that facilitated their return.

According to him, the ongoing public controversy surrounding the evacuation exercise has subjected returnees to humiliation, despite the trauma and hardship they endured while living in South Africa.

“We are here to seek answers and demand an immediate end to the baseless attacks on the government that was sympathetic towards us,” he stated.

His remarks come amid heightened scrutiny of the government's reported GH¢49.72 million expenditure on evacuating 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa.

The evacuation of over 1,900 Ghanaians from South Africa followed renewed xenophobic attacks in the country.

The government spent GH¢49.7 million on the evacuation exercise, with each evacuee receiving a GH¢5,000 reintegration grant and GH¢500 transportation allowance.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs, led by Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, provided a breakdown of the expenditure, which included chartered flights, accommodation, feeding, and medical care.

The Minority in Parliament has demanded a detailed breakdown of the expenditure, questioning the amount spent per evacuee. The Minority Caucus on the Foreign Affairs Committee boycotted a planned briefing by the Minister.

Mr Addo expressed disappointment that the pursuit of accountability had, in his view, turned into attacks on vulnerable returnees struggling to recover from their experiences.

“While we bravely recover from our trauma and pain, the very society we expect to protect us has reduced our pain to humiliation under the guise of seeking accountability,” he lamented.

He accused some elements within the Minority, the New Patriotic Party (NPP) and sections of the media of attempting to establish wrongdoing against the government.

Mr Addo also questioned allegations concerning financial assistance and relief packages reportedly given to evacuees, urging journalists who witnessed their arrival at the airport to provide an accurate account of the circumstances.

He further disclosed that 46 Ghanaians who were expected to be part of the evacuation exercise remain stranded in South Africa, but the ongoing controversy has discouraged the group from seeking additional government assistance.

“Currently, we still have 46 people who were supposed to be among the flight, but because of what is currently spreading on social media, we don’t even have the balls to beg the government to go and rescue them,” he said.

Expressing appreciation for the government's intervention, Mr Addo maintained that many Ghanaians had endured xenophobic attacks in South Africa for years without receiving similar assistance.

“We have experienced xenophobia for many years, but this is the first time a government has taken our plight into account and come to our rescue,” he added.

He consequently urged an end to the allegations and public attacks, stressing the need to protect the dignity of evacuees while addressing the plight of Ghanaians still awaiting assistance in South Africa.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Jordan arrests three suspects over church attack in dawn raid: What to know
World.content:
Jordanian authorities have not named the individuals or any group involved in the ‘terrorist incident’.

Share Jordan arrests three suspects over church attack in dawn raid: What to know on social media

Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a Greek Orthodox church on Friday.

At least eight people were killed and more than two dozen others were wounded in the rare attack in Karak governorate, located some 120km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman. Authorities said the attack was carried out by “extremist terrorists”.

Here’s what we know about the suspects.

What do we know about the operation to arrest suspects?

Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin al-Farrayeh said on Monday that all three suspects were Jordanians and “were identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident, and the security services employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them”.

They were hiding in an abandoned house in the village of al-Jadeeda in Karak, the Public Security Directorate said, adding that they refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three suspects.

They “put up fierce resistance against the security forces, but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries”, al-Farrayeh said.

He added that many locations were raided in efforts to apprehend the suspects, and the scope of the search was expanded until the suspects were surrounded during the final operation.

The Public Security Directorate said the suspects were injured, including one critically, during the dawn raid in Karak on Monday.

“Terrorism has no place among us,” the directorate said, adding that the ⁠suspects had met their “just fate”.



Security forces recovered firearms and ammunition at the suspects’ hideout, the state news agency Petra reported.

A Jordanian government source told Al Jazeera that the gun battle to arrest the suspects lasted about three hours in the village of al-Jadeeda, a six-minute drive from Hamoud, where the church attack happened.

Jordan’s King Abdullah II ordered security ⁠forces to respond with an “iron fist” to the unprecedented attack on the Christian minority community.

What happened during the church attack?

St George’s Church in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, which was attacked, is known for its medieval-era castle.

Armed men stormed the church compound during a funeral procession on Friday, killing eight people and wounding 34 others.

Security camera footage of the attack has been circulating online. Video broadcast by Al-Mamlaka TV shows three people shooting outside the church and running towards its entrance.

Other footage showed the attackers opening fire on a group of men outside the building trying to flee.

Have the suspects been named?

The Public ‌Security Directorate did not name the suspects or publicly identify possible affiliations with any armed group.

Interior Minister al-Farrayeh said a group of “extremists” that have “no relationship to humanity” were responsible for the attack, though no specific groups were mentioned.

No group has claimed responsibility for the attack so far.

What has been Jordan’s response to the attack?

“We have apprehended the killers, we are examining all the circumstances that lead young people toward extremism, and we will hold accountable everyone found to have been involved,” al-Farrayeh said in an X post on Monday.

He called for citizens to remain calm and said the tragedy would result in practical measures to protect civilians, urging Jordanians to reject violence.

King Abdullah II, who met the victims, said during a National Security Council meeting on Saturday, “The security and safety of Jordanians are a red line … the hand of justice will reach every terrorist.”

A day earlier, he had said the shooting would be met with the “harshest retaliation” possible.

Prime Minister Jafar Hassan ordered three days of national mourning, beginning on Friday, with flags to be flown at half-mast over government and public institutions.

Who were the victims?

Eight of the victims were laid to rest in Karak on Sunday in a funeral that drew a huge crowd.

Their coffins were draped with Jordanian flags as they were carried through the gathered mourners amid a large security presence.



Karak is home to a significant minority Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, where Christians make up between 2 percent and 3 percent of the population.

Social media showed images of the victims, including Mohammad al-Qasous, a Christian.

World.title: Key European defence ministers meet in Paris to discuss Ukraine support
World.content:
Defence ministers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK to discuss increasing military assistance to Ukraine.

Defence ministers of key European countries are meeting in the French capital to discuss military support for Ukraine amid continuing Russia-Ukraine attacks.

A Russian strike on ⁠Ukraine’s southeastern city ⁠of Zaporizhzhia injured four people on Monday morning, according to regional Governor Mykhailo Semikin, while a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s Voronezh killed two people and wounded 17, regional Governor Alexander Gusev said.

In Ukraine, two more people were injured in Russian strikes on the Chernihiv region, Ukraine’s emergency service ⁠said on Telegram on Monday.

The Russian Ministry of Defence also claimed its forces hit a power station in ‌Kharkiv, Ukraine’s second-largest city, as well as a nearby warehouse, and a power station in the Khmelnytskyi region.

The ministry said Russian forces also targeted port infrastructure in Chornomorsk in southwestern Ukraine, and a cargo vessel en route to Odesa, which it claimed was being used for military purposes.

Meanwhile, officials say that many of those wounded in the Ukrainian drone attack on Voronezh were passengers on a commuter train hit by falling debris.

“A significant number of the injured, including two seriously wounded, were on a train that was moving in the left-bank suburb of Voronezh when debris from a UAV fell on it,” Gusev said on Telegram.

The attack also caused fires at “a number of industrial businesses (without significant damage), a business centre in the central part of the city, and a residential building”, the governor added.

Four and a half years into the war, attacks have been escalating between Ukrainian and Russian forces, with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries and Russian forces bombarding Ukraine with relentless air strikes.



Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are expected to meet in Abu Dhabi, UAE, in the first half of November.

Meanwhile, defence ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom are set to meet in Paris on Monday to discuss additional support for Ukraine, European defence and the regional conflict in the Middle East, according to French officials.

At their previous meeting in Berlin in June, the five major European powers pledged continued support for Ukraine, seeking to send a clear signal to Moscow that Europe remains firmly behind Kyiv.

In an interview aired ⁠on Sunday, Zelenskyy said for Kyiv to halt the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which US President Donald Trump has demanded, Moscow must stop hitting Ukraine’s power ‌infrastructure.

Zelenskyy said if the Russians continue to hit Ukraine’s power infrastructure, the US should be willing to allow the use of Starshield over Russia to detect missile ‌launch ‌sites, or supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles.

Ukraine said on Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and its military version, Starshield, were now fully functional after ⁠more than a week of restrictions that disrupted military operations and intensified tensions with the US.

World.title: Saudi-led coalition says it struck Houthi missile facilities
World.content:
Coalition says it destroyed ballistic missile launchers as well as tunnels and a depot used by the Houthis to store missiles.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis has said it carried out a military operation “aimed at neutralising sources of threat”, as the armed group claimed attacks on infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said on Monday its forces destroyed four ballistic missile launchers and five tunnels used by the Houthis to store missiles.

In a post on X, he also said coalition forces attacked a missile depot, adding that the operation “focused on cutting off Houthi militia supply lines between areas under their control”.

The operation also targeted Houthi “fortifications, gatherings of their members, and their military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen”.

The Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – have carried out a wave of strikes in recent weeks against Saudi airports and other infrastructure. This follows a major escalation in fighting in Yemen’s war, in which Saudi Arabia is supporting the internationally recognised government fighting the Houthis.

A Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport this month killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade.

The attacks led to the airport’s temporary closure, forcing the postponement of Saudi Arabia’s flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.

The airport reopened and flights resumed on Sunday with the Houthis warning travellers to avoid the facility, calling it a “military target.”

Houthis claim new attacks

The Houthis later claimed they attacked the airport “with a ballistic missile, striking the target with precision”, according to a post by Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on social media on Monday.



Al-Maliki said on Monday that Saudi air defences “intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”

Saree also said that the Houthis had struck oil pumping stations in Saudi Arabia with drones.

In a separate statement, Saree also claimed responsibility for more ballistic missile attacks on “enemy” forces and weapons depots in Yemen.

He said the attacks targeted positions in the Salah al-Din area of Aden governorate and the al-Wahat area of Lahij governorate.

Yemen’s war reignited in the summer when the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, which intervened in 2015 to lead a coalition aimed at restoring the internationally recognised government that was ousted from the capital Sanaa by the Houthis in 2014.

A 2022 truce that had halted most fighting collapsed last month, as the Houthis launched a lightning offensive, seizing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast from government forces and also attacking Saudi energy facilities and airports.

Yemen’s government forces this month launched the “Operation Yemen Dawn” counteroffensive, aimed at recapturing territory held by the Houthis.

‘Everything is shaking’

As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) and discussed a key air defence system.

Mitsotakis “responded favourably to the kingdom’s request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances”, his office said, referring to a battery of the US-made air defence system deployed by Greece to Saudi Arabia in 2021, which protects energy infrastructure in Yanbu, on the Red Sea coast.

On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said air defences intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles.

The kingdom’s civil defence agency said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.

Images released by the kingdom’s official press agency showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

World.title: Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria
World.content:
Share Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria on social media

United States special envoy Tom Barrack recently spoke with a popular X personality about Syria and, in particular, Suwayda, which has been a hotbed of tensions between the government and Israel.

The southern governorate, which is majority Druze, is one of the last places in the country where the Syrian government does not have full control.

Barrack referred to “a particular Druze sheikh”, thought to be Hikmat al-Hijri, a leading political and religious figure in Suwayda. The National Guard, a Druze armed group linked to al-Hijri, has been accused of receiving support from Israel with separatist ambitions.

Barrack’s comment on al-Hijri is perceived by many as a firm message to Israel, which has attacked Syrian ministries and soldiers and tried to curry favour with Syria’s Druze community with the National Guard accused of acting as an Israeli proxy.

US President Donald Trump has built a strong relationship with his counterpart in Damascus, Ahmed al-Sharaa, and perceives any instability in Syria as dangerous for a country trying to rebuild after 13 years of war.

“[Barrack’s] message was totally clear,” Navvar Saban, a researcher in security and military affairs at the Arab Center for Contemporary Syrian Studies, told Al Jazeera. “Israel backing [al-Hijri] does not equal American backing. Washington has prioritised an agreement with Damascus while Israel retains its own security demands and relationship.”

Divergent views on Syria

Since the fall of Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024, the US has slowly rebuilt relations with Damascus and its new leader.



Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has received strong US support for his assaults in Lebanon, Palestine and Iran, has a view of the new Syrian government that is very different from Trump’s.

In the days immediately after the collapse of al-Assad’s government, Israel invaded Syria and seized land in Quneitra governorate and other strategically important areas of the country.

Israel has threatened President al-Sharaa’s government in Damascus, bombed the Ministry of Defence, and harassed and arrested Syrians in southern Syria. Israel has drawn an outcry from Syrian officials due to its repeated incursions into Syria.

Barrack, a Trump confidant who is the US ambassador to Turkiye and a special envoy to Syria and Iraq, has built a reputation for his direct approach to diplomacy, at times without regard to caution, as evidenced when he called some members of the media in Lebanon “animalistic” last year.

On Friday, Barrack spoke to Australian X personality Mario Nawfal and addressed the situation in southern Syria. He appeared to take the view that Washington favoured Damascus having control over Suwayda rather than a group aligned with al-Hijri and linked to Israel.

“[Barrack’s] remarks expose differences with Israel,” Nanar Hawach, a Syrian analyst who visited Suwayda in September, told Al Jazeera. “Washington is building a partner in Damascus while Israel appears to prefer a Damascus that is too weak to assert itself in the south.”

Israel and al-Hijri

Having grown tired of their worsening living conditions, residents in Suwayda, including many in its Druze majority, rose up against the al-Assad regime in 2023. They maintained their protests until the regime collapsed in December 2024.

Many in Suwayda celebrated this moment, which ended more than five decades of Baathist rule, although they were also hesitant to throw their support behind the new government.

That hesitancy turned to blatant opposition to al-Sharaa after fighting between Bedouin tribes and Druze in Suwayda turned into deadly sectarian killings in July 2025. Forces reportedly connected to the government joined the fighting on the side of the Bedouins. While there was violence and death on both sides, the casualties were overwhelmingly Druze.

Israel intervened in the fighting at one point, attacking what it said were Syrian government forces entering Suwayda. Since then, Israel has reportedly been trying to curry favour with locals there, including al-Hijri, who has been fervent in his opposition to Damascus’s new leadership.



“Israel appears intent on a lasting military presence in southern Syria, and it uses Suwayda as a lever against Damascus, offering enough support to keep the province reliant on Israeli protection and too little to secure its future,” Hawach said. “Along its line in Quneitra and Daraa [areas of southern Syria that Israel has invaded], Israel treats neighbouring communities differently, reviving wartime grievances between Syrians that any future Syria-Israel arrangement would struggle to undo.”

In Suwayda, analysts said, al-Hijri’s support is not universal but he benefits whenever the Druze community feels under attack.

“Sheikh al-Hijri’s authority rises with the community’s sense of threat and opens to debate as that threat recedes, so pressure from Damascus tends to strengthen the leadership it aims to weaken,” Hawach said. “Each side points to the other’s hard line to justify its own. That keeps Suwayda’s future framed in security terms and crowds out the many residents, clerics and local figures seeking a path between central rule and separation.”

Accountability needed for reconciliation

After the events of July 2025, the US began talks with the Syrian government hosted by Jordan to resolve the crisis. A trilateral agreement was signed in Amman in September 2025 that said Syria would invite an independent international commission to investigate what happened in Suwayda and perpetrators would be brought to justice.

While major fighting has not resumed between Damascus and Druze factions, the situation in Suwayda remains in a deadlock with many in the province having no trust in the government.

“Distrust has hardened, partly because Damascus has sought to bring Suwayda back by pressuring its leadership, and residents feel that pressure first, in their salaries, their children’s exams and the road to the capital,” Hawach said. “Trust tends to return through what the state delivers. Damascus stands a better chance of winning people back by serving residents directly and pursuing accountability for July 2025.”

Analysts said accountability is crucial if Damascus wants to bring Suwayda back into the Syrian fold.

“A durable settlement needs credible accountability for what happened in 2025,” Saban said. “The Druze need to be guaranteed protection of movement, education and security. Neither weakening Hijri, nor restoring government institutions alone will rebuild the trust.”

World.title: Thousands greet opposition leader Maria Machado upon return to Caracas
World.content:
NewsFeed Thousands greet opposition leader Maria Machado upon return to Caracas

Thousands lined the streets of Venezuela’s capital Caracas to welcome opposition leader Maria Corina Machado home after 10 months in exile. She fled last December, shortly before the US abducted President Nicolas Maduro and backed his deputy Delcy Rodriguez as leader.

World.title: Saudi Arabia confirms January start for Asian Cup 2027 despite attacks
World.content:
Asian Cup 2027 to kick off on January 7 with hosts Saudi Arabia facing Palestine in Riyadh as AFC announces schedule.

Saudi Arabia will host the 2027 Asian Cup in January and February despite recent doubts surrounding the tournament’s schedule due to ongoing attacks on the country and wider regional unrest.

The continental championship will get under way on January 7 in Riyadh, where the hosts will take on Palestine in a Group A fixture, according to the tournament schedule announced by the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) on Monday.

Riyadh’s 72,000-seat King Fahd Sports City Stadium will also host the inaugural match and serve as the venue for the final on February 5.

Eight venues – five in Riyadh, two in Jeddah and one in Al-Khobar – will host the 51 matches across the 29-day tournament.

Despite the confirmation from the organisers, the tournament’s fate remains under scrutiny as several of the 24 participating federations have raised concerns about security in the region.

Earlier on Monday, organisers of the Dakar Rally said the race would be moved out of Saudi Arabia for the 2027 edition due to the “recent developments in the region”.

Last week, a top Japanese football official said the ongoing security situation in Saudi Arabia would make it difficult for the country to host the Asian Cup as scheduled.

“Based on what I’ve learned from the news, the situation is still unsafe, so at this point, I don’t think it would be easy to hold the [Asian] Cup there,” Japan Football Association President Tsuneyasu Miyamoto said.

“I just had a meeting with the Saudi side, and they said that their top priority is the safety of the players, the fans and everyone who would be attending the tournament.”



Several major sporting events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled or postponed amid escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

The Saudi-led coalition intercepted a barrage of projectiles from Yemen that targeted cities across the kingdom on Sunday.

The Saudi Civil Defence said shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles, suspected to have been fired by Yemen’s Houthis, fell in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh and Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca province.

The kingdom has faced waves of Houthi missile and drone attacks in recent weeks that have targeted civilian and military infrastructure.

Riyadh announced late on Saturday that international flights from King Khalid International Airport would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.

This follows the suspension of flights from the Riyadh airport after waves of Houthi strikes, including one on 10 October that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.

AFC chief Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said this month that a postponement of the continental championships until 2028 was possible if necessary, but the local organising committee said it was sticking to the original schedule.

Defending champions Qatar will begin their title defence against Thailand on January 11 while Japan will open ⁠⁠their campaign against Indonesia the same day.

South Korea will face Yemen, ⁠⁠Australia will take on Singapore ⁠⁠and Iran will meet China in their opening matches.

The tournament’s group stage concludes on January 20 with the knockout rounds ‌‌beginning on January 22.

Saudi Arabia will host the Asian Cup for the first time, ‌‌seven ‌‌years before it stages the 2034 World Cup.

World.title: Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move?
World.content:
This will be Algeria’s first foreign troop deployment in 50 years as the country shifts its military doctrine amid new security challenges.

Share Algeria’s military deployment to Niger: What’s behind the move? on social media

Algeria’s parliament has approved a proposal to deploy troops to neighbouring Niger, in a major shift in the North African nation’s noninterventionist military doctrine.

Algeria’s lower house, the People’s National Assembly, ratified the deployment on Sunday after the upper house, the Council of the Nation, unanimously approved the proposal earlier in the day.

Details about the number of soldiers and when they will be deployed have yet to be made public.

It comes nearly two months after Algeria dispatched four Russian-made Sukhoi Su-30 jets, a transport aircraft and an aerial refuelling aircraft to Niamey, following what Algerian authorities described as an attempt to destabilise Niger’s military-led government.

The step comes amid a thawing of relations between Algiers and Niamey as Niger’s President Abdourahamane Tchiani visited Algeria in February and, months later, his defence minister, Salifou Mody, ⁠⁠travelled to Algiers to discuss security cooperation.

The shooting down of a Malian drone by the Algerian army last April triggered a diplomatic crisis after Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso recalled their ambassadors from Algiers. The condemnation of the 2023 coup in Niger by Algeria had also strained ties.

The troop deployment is reportedly intended to protect oil installations belonging to Algeria’s state-owned energy company, Sonatrach. Troops would be sent “to protect Algeria’s economic and strategic interests, particularly its oil facilities in Niger”, The Associated Press news agency reported, quoting Algerian Senator Belkacem Boulghiti.



It also comes as Algiers seeks to deepen security cooperation in the Sahel, a vast belt of territory stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, including several countries along Algeria’s southern frontier.

Why does this matter?

Algeria has historically been reluctant to deploy its armed forces beyond its borders, reflecting a longstanding foreign policy built around sovereignty, noninterference and opposition to foreign military intervention.

But that does not mean it has never done so.

Algerian forces participated in the 1973 Arab-Israeli war, although overseas military deployments have remained exceptionally rare in the decades since.

A constitutional revision in 2020 formalised the conditions under which Algerian troops could be sent abroad.

Under Article 91, the president may authorise such deployments, provided they receive the backing of at least two-thirds of the members of each chamber of parliament.

The constitution also provides for Algerian participation in peacekeeping operations under the auspices of the United Nations, the African Union and the Arab League.

The move is particularly significant given Algeria’s military capabilities. According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the country spent more than $25bn on its armed forces in 2025, making it Africa’s largest military spender.

But the decision also comes against a backdrop of growing diplomatic tensions and shifting regional alliances.

In September, Algeria severed diplomatic relations with the United Arab Emirates, accusing Abu Dhabi of repeated “hostile” and “provocative actions” without publicly detailing the incidents behind the decision.

The two countries have long disagreed over several regional issues, including Western Sahara and the UAE’s alleged interference in North African and Sahelian affairs.

Taken together, these developments suggest that Algeria is becoming increasingly willing to assert its security interests beyond its borders, even as it continues to emphasise the principles of sovereignty and noninterference.

Why the Sahel?

For Algeria, instability in the Sahel is not a distant security concern.

The country shares thousands of kilometres of borders with Mali, Niger and Libya, making developments in its southern neighbourhood particularly consequential.
