The roots of the current security crisis can be traced, in part, to the collapse of Muammar Gaddafi’s government in Libya in 2011.

At the height of the Arab Spring uprisings, Algeria took a firm stance against foreign military intervention and warned that the disintegration of the Libyan state could destabilise neighbouring countries.



Those concerns were not unfounded.

Following Gaddafi’s overthrow, weapons and armed fighters, including Tuareg who had served in Libya, spread into neighbouring countries.

Their return helped fuel a rebellion in northern Mali in 2012, contributing to a security crisis that preceded the military overthrow of President Amadou Toumani Toure that March.

Over the following decade, armed rebellion expanded across parts of the Sahel, particularly Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger.

Since 2012, those three countries alone have experienced six military coups: three in Mali, two in Burkina Faso and one in Niger.

Many of the coups unfolded against a backdrop of deteriorating security, with military leaders accusing civilian governments of failing to contain increasingly powerful armed groups.

But insecurity was not the only factor. Political grievances, governance failures and rivalries within armed forces also contributed to the coups.

Who else is operating in the Sahel?

Another factor shaping Algeria’s calculations is the changing presence of foreign military forces across the region.

For more than a decade, France was a central player in counterterrorism operations in the Sahel, deploying thousands of troops to combat armed groups linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS).

But that military presence has largely unravelled.

Following successive coups and deteriorating diplomatic relations, France withdrew its troops from Mali in August 2022, Burkina Faso in February 2023 and Niger in December 2023.

The withdrawals were accompanied by growing anti-French sentiment and demands from military governments for greater control over their security policies.

Niger demanded the departure of approximately 1,500 French soldiers following its July 2023 coup.

Just months later, in April 2024, approximately 100 Russian military personnel arrived in Niamey, bringing equipment and providing training to Nigerien forces.

The personnel were associated with Africa Corps, a Russian paramilitary group close to the Kremlin.

Moscow has also expanded its military cooperation with Mali and Burkina Faso, where Russian personnel have undertaken training, advisory and security roles, including combat support in Mali.

The United States has also seen its military footprint shrink.

In 2024, Washington withdrew approximately 1,000 soldiers from Niger after the military government terminated their security cooperation agreement. The withdrawal included personnel stationed at an important US drone base near Agadez.

The result has been a significant realignment of the Sahel’s security partnerships, with Western military forces departing and Russia assuming a more prominent role.

What does Algeria stand to gain?

For Algiers, the proposed deployment to Niger carries immediate security and wider strategic implications.

At the most practical level, protecting Algerian energy investments would help safeguard the country’s economic interests in a region affected by armed rebellions and political instability, including the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP), which would transport Nigerian gas to Europe and traverse Niger and Algeria.



It could also deepen cooperation with Niger, whose military government has sought new security partners since taking power in 2023.

More broadly, the move would allow Algeria to establish a direct military presence in a neighbouring country at a time when the Sahel’s security architecture is being reshaped.

“We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure,” Senator Boulghiti told reporters after the vote. “It is simply an adaptation of our doctrine to evolving circumstances so we can rise to the new challenges imposed by the situation in the Sahel region.”

World.title: Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron
World.content:
Israel’s assault on the West Bank city has forced thousands of people to flee their homes.

Share Palestinians are opening their doors to the displaced of besieged Hebron on social media

The Farsh Al-Hawa area in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank is unrecognisable after Israeli forces demolished a three-story building and industrial facilities there. Israel’s Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also holds the West Bank portfolio in the Ministry of Defence, said he ordered their destruction.

It all started on Friday, when two Palestinians attacked an Israeli military checkpoint in Farsh Al-Hawa, killing two soldiers and injuring others.

Since then, Hebron, the West Bank’s economic capital, has been attacked and put under lockdown by Israeli forces.

Israel has announced a sweeping military assault in the city, targeting the neighbourhood of the gunmen, who were killed on Friday. Israeli forces have already forcibly displaced more than 2,000 Palestinians. City officials say almost half of the displaced are babies and children under 18, along with 81 pregnant women and 204 elderly.

Fahd Ahmaro was forced to leave his home, along with his family. He told Al Jazeera that he planned to stay but felt compelled to seek shelter outside his neighbourhood because the women and children were terrified.

“We left with nothing but the clothes on our backs. Our savings, belongings and documents are all in the house,” he said. “I tried to go back after I got my family out safely, but I couldn’t. It’s not safe any more.”

Palestinian authorities in Hebron have declared a state of emergency and created a crisis group, bringing together government agencies, the private sector and civil society, to respond after thousands of people in the city were forced to flee their homes.

Riyadh Khamis, who serves on the committee, told Al Jazeera that philanthropists who could not bear the thought of fellow Palestinians staying in temporary shelters opened their homes to the displaced.



“Hebron is known for its social solidarity and generosity. Our city was the first to provide aid during the COVID lockdown and during the genocide,” Khamis told Al Jazeera. “Today, our neighbours needed help so we all rallied.”

Real estate developer Mohamed Al-Rujoob is one of the philanthropists who sprang to action at the start of the assault on the city.

Al-Rujoob, who owns several apartments in Dura, a town close to Hebron, announced that the properties would be made available for displaced families, prompting other owners to do the same. He now hosts three extended families in his apartments, including 30 children.

“We must preserve people’s dignity. Today, we host these good people. Tomorrow, who knows? It might be us who need shelter. We’re all under the same occupation and we’re all vulnerable,” he said.

The Israeli army says Hebron is on lockdown, which affects nearly 1 million Palestinians who live in the city and the rest of the district.

Restrictions on movement have had a severe impact on the West Bank’s largest district. Schools have moved to online classes, while Hebron’s universities have made similar arrangements for their 18,000 students until the Israeli operation ends.

The measures are essential for Palestinian students who are stuck in their homes and neighbourhoods, including the besieged Fawwar refugee camp in Hebron, home to nearly 8,000 Palestinians. Israeli soldiers closed the camp’s entrance gate on Saturday, barring residents from entering or leaving, even on foot.

Abdel Fattah Al-Ttitti, a school teacher who lives in the camp and works in a Hebron school, said “we are locked in”.

“If, God forbid, somebody needs medical attention, we may be able to get them to the clinic in Masafer Yatta, but that clinic is poorly equipped. If there’s a medical emergency, they can’t help,” Al-Ttitti told Al Jazeera.

He is glad that schools announced online classes. “Until this campaign is over, there’s no other way,” he said.

Many in Hebron believe that Israel’s military campaign in the city has a political dimension, with Israelis heading to the polls on Tuesday for a general election.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing coalition is vying for every right-wing vote. Violence against Palestinians has proved an expedient campaign tactic for politicians such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Minister of Settlement Affairs, Orit Strook.

Both right-wing ministers have homes in illegal settlements in the Hebron area and support the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank and Gaza, which they refer to as “encouraging voluntary migration”.

World.title: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
World.content:
Serbia's long-standing leader Aleksandar VuÄiÄ has admitted defeat to a student-led protest movement in snap parliamentary elections.

Celebrations erupted as crowds descended on the centre of Belgrade, Novi Sad and other cities.

The student movement was formed less than two years ago in response to a railway station disaster blamed on corruption and negligence, but fought the election with candidates from a cross-section of Serbian society.

"It is clear we have lost these elections," right-wing populist leader VuÄiÄ said as he conceded. With 96% of polling stations counted, Serbia's election commission said the students had won 2.24 million votes and the former ruling party 1.67 million.

The students had secured 52.65% of the vote, while VuÄiÄ's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) was on 39.2%, according to its preliminary figures late on Monday morning.

VuÄiÄ had spent two terms as president and could not seek a third term, so was leading his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.

He called the snap elections after two years of protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy in front of Novi Sad station which killed 16 people.

World.title: Venezuelan opposition leader María Machado returns after months in exile
World.content:
Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃ­a Corina Machado has returned home to a fraught political landscape after more than 10 months in exile.

"I am here. With you," Machado wrote on X on Sunday. Her return comes after repeated prior efforts to re-enter the country came to no avail.

In January, a month after Machado left Venezuela on a speedboat under cover of darkness to accept the Nobel Peace Prize in Norway, the US seized her opponent, President NicolÃ¡s Maduro.

The Trump administration then backed his deputy, Delcy RodrÃ­guez, as leader and she was sworn in as interim president, later signing an oil deal which granted very favourable terms to the US.

Machado was photographed on Sunday attending Mass at a church in the Venezuelan state of Lara, surrounded by supporters hugging her and clasping her hands.

She then began travelling to the capital Caracas in a caravan of cheering supporters. More supporters have lined the route of her journey to the capital.

She was photographed smiling as she leaned out of the sunroof of a car as she entered Caracas late on Sunday night.

"Night of reunion in our Caracas. For the reunion of each family, for the Freedom of each political prisoner, for the Freedom of Venezuela," she wrote on X.

World.title: Australian murderer loses bid to eat Vegemite in prison
World.content:
A convicted murderer serving a life sentence in Australia has lost his bid to overturn a ban on prisoners consuming Vegemite - the salty yeast-based spread that has become a national symbol.

Andre McKechnie argued that the ban, in place since 2006, denied him the right to "enjoy his culture as an Australian".

Authorities in the state of Victoria say inmates may use the strong-smelling paste to disguise contraband substances or to brew alcohol behind bars.

And on Monday, a Supreme Court judge rejected McKechnie's appeal, saying the prisoner's "cultural rights are limited primarily by the fact he has been sentenced to a term of imprisonment".

In his lawsuit against Victoria's Department of Justice and Corrections, the agency which manages the state's prisons, McKechnie, 54, said the ban on the spread breached law requiring prisons to provide food that allowed inmates to maintain their health and well-being but the judge said that had not been proven.

McKechnie was handed a life sentence for stabbing a property developer to death in Queensland in the 1990s. He served part of his sentence in Queensland before being transferred to Victoria.

During the hearing, the court heard evidence from Corrections Victoria that the smell of vegemite can distract sniffer dogs trying to detect drugs being brought into prison.

The product is also banned in jails in Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania.

A much-loved breakfast spread for some, Vegemite has acquired controversial accolades since it first hit shop shelves in Australia in 1923.

The thick, brown spread was invented in the Victorian capital of Melbourne more than a century ago as an alternative to the British spread Marmite.

It sparked an international dispute in April last year when an Australian cafe owner in Canada was told to remove jars of the condiment from his shelves as it did not comply with local health regulations.

Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese intervened in the row, saying it was "rather odd" that Canada allowed the sale of Vegemite's "rubbish" rival product Marmite. The cafe owner was later allowed to continue selling the spread.

World.title: Eric Bauza, voice of Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, dies aged 46
World.content:
Eric Bauza, the voice artist behind Looney Tunes characters including Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, has died aged 46.

A statement from the Emmy award-winning star's family posted on Instagram, external said he had died "suddenly".

Bauza had voiced a number of characters in this summer's animated hit Coyote vs. Acme, and appeared in the recent release Forgotten Island.

Variety reports that the cause of death was hypertensive cardiovascular disease and that Bauza died at home on Sunday.

In a 2021 interview with NBC News, Bauza, who was born in Ontario and was of Filipino descent, said he grew up a huge fan of the Looney Tunes characters and used to copy the voices as a child.

"Looney Tunes transcends all languages and all cultures," he said, external. "It doesn't matter what part of the planet you're from. You get the comedy."

He voiced Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Elmer Fudd and Foghorn Leghorn in 2021's Space Jam: A New Legacy before reprising those roles and that of Road Runner in Coyote vs. Acme.

He also played the part of Toad General in 2023's The Super Mario Bros. Movie and its sequel The Super Mario Galaxy Movie, the fifth highest-grossing film internationally this year.

Between 2022 and 2025, he won three Emmy awards for outstanding voice performance in a number of TV series.

In a statement reported by the Hollywood Reporter, external, Channing Dungey, the chairman of Warner Bros. Television Group and US Networks, said: "Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world.

"He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc. Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life."

World.title: Rapper Nicki Minaj joins Trump onstage at Michigan rally
World.content:
Rapper Nicki Minaj said US President Donald Trump has "changed the energy of the country" as she joined him at a Michigan rally to stump for Republicans ahead of the nationwide midterm elections.

"He's given us a future to look forward to," she said, after Trump praised her figure and called her on stage to speak.

Minaj has called herself Trump's "number one fan" despite criticising some of his policies in his first term.

In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is locked in a tight race with Republican Mike Rogers with just over a week to go before the midterms. Former President Barack Obama held a rally - one of the first in this cycle - with the Democrat on Saturday.

Democrats are also aggressively hitting the campaign trail, with close elections taking place on 3 November which will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency.

In his remarks on Sunday, Trump focused on El-Sayed's Muslim faith and background, alleging that he will "invite jihadists" into America if he wins.

El-Sayed has criticised similar remarks by Trump as Islamophobic, saying in an ad to voters last week that the US president "thinks he can use my name and my faith to distract us from the suffering his policies are inflicting on us at the pump, at the grocery store, and at the doctor's office".

In Port Huron on Sunday, Minaj, wearing a gold-coloured Gucci-branded suit, led the crowd in chanting Trump's name, and the names of Republican candidates in Michigan.

"We really need all these great people to be elected, because this is a major turning point for our country," she said.

"She never looked more beautiful," Trump said as she left the stage. "She gets it. She's smart," he added.

Earlier in his speech, Trump praised the rear end of one male Republican candidate before turning the crowd's attention to Minaj.

"By the way, I looked at a beautiful ass before," he segued. "Nicki Minaj. That's hard to miss."

He then asked her to "stand up" as the crowd cheered, and added that he hoped she was not "insulted" by his remark.

World.title: Uganda imposes 21-day quarantine on citizens returning from DR Congo
World.content:
Ugandans returning from neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo will be quarantined for 21 days, the health ministry has said, as the country tightens restrictions to contain the spread of Ebola virus.

More than 4,800 people have died in DR Congo since May - the country's deadliest outbreak of the disease - and has since spread to several other countries.

Uganda's restrictions follow questions after two people who had travelled through the country tested positive for Ebola, in Kenya and Nigeria.

The health ministry on Sunday said the 60 people who were being monitored after coming into contact with the Kenyan Ebola patient had all been discharged.

Announcing the new measures on Sunday, the health ministry said travellers who had been to DR Congo would not be allowed to transit through Uganda.

It said returning Ugandans would "undergo 21 days of quarantine at their own cost".

Uganda has also "intensified traveller screening at Entebbe International Airport and all land border crossings, supported by screening at designated road checkpoints", it added.

Uganda's Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi told the BBC's Newsday programme that only essential travellers from DR Congo would be allowed in but would be subjected to "intense public health measures".

"All these are measures to ensure that we keep Uganda free of Ebola," he said.

Since the two cases were reported in Kenya and Nigeria this month, Uganda has repeatedly stressed that no cases have been reported within its borders. Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases and two people died shortly after the outbreak started in DR Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country free of the disease in August.

Concerns have however persisted after the two passengers tested positive after passing through Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day.

The patient in Nigeria is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat who had travelled to the Ugandan capital for a holiday, according to the head of Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention Jean Kaseya, while the Kenyan had travelled from the DR Congo where he had business interests.

Diana Atwine, the health ministry's permanent secretary, said CCTV camera footage showed no physical interaction between the two patients.

The Kenyan businessman died two days after arriving in Nairobi, and the country has since confirmed eight other cases of Ebola. A second woman, related to the businessman died over the weekend.

World.title: Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
World.content:
The prime minister has traditionally relied on a stable base of right-wing voters, but is projected to see a thinning of support in this election. Some voters may be slipping away to opposition parties like Eisenkot's. Others, including some die-hard Likud voters we spoke to, said the 7 October attacks had pushed them towards parties further on the right.

Lt Col (Res) Eyal Hajbi, head of the regional civil defence unit in the Netanyahu stronghold of Sderot, right on the Gaza border, lost several friends and colleagues in the attacks. He lights candles for them every day in his office, and told me he would be thinking about them when he cast his ballot on Tuesday.

Standing on a ridge overlooking the ruins of northern Gaza, he gestured to the wasteland where Israel's army has completely flattened the neighbourhoods of Beit Lahia and Beit Hanoun.

"As far as I'm concerned, after 7 October, we should wipe them all out," he said. "I've changed my understanding of Gaza. Before, I wouldn't have said we should destroy it."

He told me he and his family had always voted Likud, but that now he was voting for the far-right party of Itamar Ben Gvir, Jewish Power.

"My family has become more extreme than it ever was before," he said. "If once we deliberated over it, today we don't think twice; we vote."

Polls suggest that less than 10% of Israelis are undecided and that very few of those are considering switching between government parties and opposition ones.

Ben Gvir, National Security minister in Netanyahu's coalition, has been reaching out to younger voters through headline-grabbing social media campaigns.

A poll for one of Israel's leading newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth, published on 9 October, suggested that more than 16% of first-time voters in Israel would choose far-right parties like his.

In Sderot, a group of 18 year olds from a nearby Jewish religious college told me their political views had been affected by the 7 October attacks far more than their parents. All four teenagers were planning to vote for another far-right party, Religious Zionism, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"Today, the whole younger generation understands that peaceful paths will not work," Aviad Elmahach, one of the teenagers, told me. "Older adults, who are set in a fixed mindset, find [it] harder to change, but the youth understand that we need to be here with strength and an iron fist, which is the only way to win."

The lesson of 7 October, he said, was that Israel needed to be as forceful as possible in its relations with the Palestinians, more than 74,000 of whom have been killed by Israel in Gaza since then, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

"The youth have a fresh new perspective that has not yet become entrenched in politics, and they understand very well why we're voting for Smotrich - it means holding the land with strength and giving [the Palestinians] nothing through peaceful gestures."

World.title: Suspect in deadly Paris suburb shooting sent for psychiatric observation
World.content:
The lawyer for Pengo Bossio Wangi, the one person killed during the attack, told French media the move to place the suspect under observation was "very rare".

He alleged that it was being used to portray the suspect as criminally irresponsible rather than having acted deliberately.

Wangi, a 26-year-old French-Congolese martial artist, was named as the one fatality on Saturday.

The mixed martial arts club where he trained paid tribute to him, saying: "On the mats as off them, he was one of those who lead by example: present, respectful, always ready to lift others up.

"His smile, his energy and his generosity will remain etched in our walls and in our hearts."

Three of those injured in the attack were taken to hospital in a serious condition - including a 12-year-old girl who remains in a critical condition.

The mayor of La VerriÃ¨re, Nicolas Dainville, told French radio network France Info on Sunday that he had spoken to the girl's mother over the phone and confirmed she was "doing better".

Another injured resident was recovering while a third remained in a critical condition, he said.

The suspect had been known to police prior to the attack but not to France's intelligence services, local media report. PNAT previously said he had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".

He is thought to have used an old semi-automatic weapon during the attack, firing in bursts from his car window.

World.title: Otti rewards Abia world debate champions with N1m each
World.content:
Governor Alex Otti of Abia State has rewarded five students who represented Nigeria at the 2026 International Schools Debate Championship in Doha, Qatar, with N1 million each.

Mr Otti announced the rewards on Saturday at a welcome ceremony in the Michael Okpara Auditorium, Umuahia, for the contingent made up of students from Abia Model Junior Secondary School.

The team won four major awards: Best International School Debate Team, Overall Best Team in the junior category, Best Debater Award, and Best Leadership Award, alongside 12 medals for outstanding individual performances.

The governor approved the team’s request to participate in the 2027 competition, announcing financial rewards for the school and the officials who facilitated the team’s participation.

Mr Otti announced N750,000 each for three education officials involved in the students’ participation and N1 million for the Executive Chairman of the Abia State Universal Basic Education Board (ASUBEB), Lydia Onuoha.

He also approved N1.75 million for Abia Model Junior Secondary School, which produced the debating team.

Mr Otti announced another N1 million reward for Okonkwo Onyinyechi, winner of the 2026 National Essay Championship.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Scholarship for orphaned girl

Mr Otti also directed the Alex Otti Foundation to sponsor 15-year-old Esther Christian, captain of the debate team, making an exception to its usual undergraduate scholarship programme.

“Because you lost your dad when you were four, today you have another dad. So, the Alex Otti Foundation takes over your sponsorship,” Mr Otti said.

The governor said that the decision was an exception to the foundation’s usual practice of supporting undergraduates.

He said the girl would be admitted into its scholarship programme before university.

Mr Otti congratulated the students and commended their coaches, school authorities and other stakeholders, urging the team to sustain its commitment to excellence.

He said that his administration was renovating public schools and improving teaching and learning facilities across the state.

The governor disclosed that the government had approved 21 smart schools, with two completed and handed over, while a third was expected before the end of the year.

He urged individuals, community leaders and other stakeholders to adopt schools in their communities to complement government efforts.

Mr Otti said the government was working to deploy armed personnel of the Homeland Security outfit to schools to protect pupils and school property.

Commendation for Abia government

Earlier, the Executive Secretary of the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC), Aisha Garba, commended the state government’s investment in education.

Ms Garba, represented by the commission’s Abia Coordinator, Unyime Umoetti, urged political office holders and other stakeholders to support grassroots development by visiting their communities and adopting local schools.

She encouraged the students to remain focused and pursue greater achievements.

In her remarks, the ASUBEB chairman, Ms Onuoha, said the team won four trophies and 12 medals at the international championship, competing against teams from Jordan, Pakistan, India, Kenya and Ghana.

She said that Chukwuemeka Akamnonu won the Best Speaker Award in the final, adding that the team’s success reflected ongoing investments in school renovations, teacher training and free, compulsory basic education.

ALSO READ: Otti flags off reconstruction of two key Aba roads after years of neglect

Speaking on behalf of the parents of the debate team members, Christopher Akamnonu, thanked the government for its efforts in enhancing the standard of education in the state.

Mr Akamnonu said Abia’s investment in education was transforming the school system in the state and creating opportunities for students to excel.

Speaking on behalf of the team, Miss Christian said the team competed against 84 teams and 168 debaters, with all five members ranking among the world’s top 10 speakers.

She thanked the governor, the team’s coach, Emmanuel Chigozie, and other stakeholders for supporting the team, pledging that the students would continue to strive for excellence.

The ceremony featured the presentation of certificates and trophies to the champions and education officials, as well as a demonstration of the British Parliamentary debating format by the students.

The names of the debaters are Simon Nduoma, aged 18; Chikodi Nmesooma, aged 15; Akamnonu, aged 16; and Ifeanyichukwu Cherechukwu, aged 16.

(NAN)

World.title: NASS Roundup: Ebola, fuel import, unity college funding, other top Senate stories
World.content:
Bill seeks increased funding for unity colleges, armed forces schools

The Senate on Tuesday debated and passed for second reading a bill seeking to amend the National Senior Secondary Education Commission Act to strengthen the administration and funding of federal unity colleges and Armed Forces senior secondary schools.

The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, announced the passage after the bill received majority support in a voice vote.

The bill was subsequently referred to the Senate Committee on Primary and Secondary Education for further legislative scrutiny and a public hearing.

Sponsored by the Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, the bill seeks to strengthen the administration, coordination and funding of public senior secondary schools across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

It also proposes a legal framework for direct government intervention to address infrastructure deficits and shortages of learning resources in public senior secondary schools.

Senate seeks emergency funds to fight Ebola

The Senate on Wednesday rejected a proposal for lawmakers to visit the entry points through which a woman infected with Ebola reportedly entered Nigeria before she was isolated at a private hospital in Abuja.

Instead, the upper chamber urged the federal government to immediately release emergency funds from the Service Wide Vote to prevent the spread of the virus.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The lawmakers adopted the resolution while debating a motion on the need to enforce mandatory health screening at all international airports and other entry points to prevent the spread of Ebola and other epidemic-prone diseases.

The motion was sponsored by Francis Faduyile, the senator representing Ondo South Senatorial District.

Senate moves to review Nigeria’s century-old Quarantine Act

On Wednesday, the upper chamber of the National Assembly resolved to engage the presidency on reviewing Nigeria’s Quarantine Act to bring it in line with modern public health legislation and the International Health Regulations.

Mr Akpabio directed the Senate Committee on Judiciary to liaise with the executive arm of government and relevant health agencies to develop proposals for amending the law.

He gave the directive during plenary while lawmakers debated a motion on the need to enforce mandatory health screening at all international airports and other entry points to prevent the spread of Ebola and other epidemic-prone diseases.

The Senate president said the proposed amendment should be treated as urgent to strengthen Nigeria’s public health response to the Ebola outbreak and prevent further spread of the disease.

Bill to empower NUC to update university accreditation processes

A bill seeking to repeal and re-enact the National Universities Commission (NUC) Act to strengthen the commission’s regulatory powers and modernise university accreditation processes passed second reading in the Senate on Thursday.

The bill was subsequently referred to the Senate Committee on Tertiary Education and TETFund for further legislative scrutiny and a public hearing.

The executive-sponsored bill seeks to strengthen the NUC’s regulatory framework, promote global best practices in university education, and encourage innovation and research.

It also proposes stronger enforcement measures against universities that violate the commission’s guidelines and procedures. In addition, it seeks to reinforce the NUC’s role as the apex regulatory body responsible for accrediting academic programmes in Nigerian universities.

Senate panel summons NNPC, NEITI, others over discrepancies in PMS import records

The Senate Committee on Public Accounts on Tuesday resolved to summon the heads of the Nigerian Midstream and Downstream Petroleum Regulatory Authority (NMDPRA), the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI) over discrepancies in records of Premium Motor Spirit (PMS) imports into Nigeria between 2021 and 2023.

The committee’s chairperson, Ibrahim Dankwambo, announced the resolution on Tuesday after the NMDPRA appeared before the panel to respond to queries raised in NEITI’s Oil and Gas Industry Audit Report covering the period.

Mr Dankwambo, who represents Gombe North Senatorial District, said the heads of the three agencies would be required to explain the discrepancies and work towards reconciling the conflicting figures.

Senate seeks international climate financing to protect coastal communities

On Thursday, the Senate on urged the federal government to explore appropriate budgetary provisions and international climate adaptation financing to protect coastal communities threatened by ocean surges and sea incursion.

The upper chamber also directed the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) and relevant state authorities to provide immediate humanitarian assistance, including safe water, healthcare services and temporary shelter, to residents whose homes and livelihoods have been destroyed by ocean surges.

The lawmakers adopted the resolutions during plenary while debating a motion on the urgent need to construct shoreline protection infrastructure to save Ayetoro community in Ondo State from sea incursion.

The motion was sponsored by Francis Faduyile (APC, Ondo South).

World.title: Anambra govt seeks NMA support in fight against illegal health facilities
World.content:
The Anambra State Government has called on the Nigeria Medical Association (NMA) to support its efforts to eradicate quack and unregistered health facilities in the state.

Adam Obidike, the commissioner for health in Anambra made the appeal during the closing ceremony of the 2026 Physicians Week and Scientific Conference of the Nigerian Medical Association, Awka Zone in Awka on Sunday.

The theme of the Week, Luncheon and Award Presentation Ceremony was “Securing the Future of Medicine in Nigeria and Sub-Saharan Africa”.

Mr Obidike, a medical doctor, said the NMA was a critical partner and that the government would collaborate with the association to track fake and unregistered facilities.

According to him, “Anambra is going to work with the NMA because they will help us to identify people who are not medical personnel practicing in Anambra.”

“We are determined to shut all of them down because when people go there, they receive treatment that is not proper for their ailment.

“We have a checklist and anybody who wants to set up a facility should go to the department of medical services and get the conditions, including the design of the building,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In his welcome address, Tim-Uzoma Mbaeri, chairman of NMA, Awka Zone, said this year’s Physicians Week and Scientific Conference was a time to celebrate the profession and reconnect members with each other.

Mr Mbaeri, a professor, said the association used the event to visit sick colleagues, provide free laboratory tests including prostate specific antigens testing, urinalysis among others.

He thanked members and partners of the NMA, Awka branch, whose contributions ensured the success of the physicians’ week.

“We also enjoyed a novelty football match, had an opportunity for friendship, recreation, and strong inter-agency relationships.

“We find satisfaction not merely in the event we organised, but in the lives we have touched, the colleagues we have encouraged, the relationships we have strengthened and the visibility we have given to our profession,” he said.

Mr Mbaeri said three personalities were honoured with awards of meritorious service to the medical profession and the NMA, including Ifeoma Njelita, Emmanuel Umenweke and Amaka Ezeno.

Njelita is an associate professor and a consultant in community medicine at the Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu University Teaching Hospital.

Umenweke is a medical doctor with the Nnamdi Azikiwe University Medical Center, Awka while Ezeno, the third awardee is a lawyer, Notary Public and member of the Body of Benchers.

(NAN)

World.title: From vision to abandonment: Nigeria’s unfinished development, By Dipo Baruwa
World.content:
…addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments.

The drive for socio-economic development has seen Nigeria embark on several developmental projects, ranging from physical infrastructure to economic programmes. These initiatives, on the face value, were often well articulated; designed to address strategic gaps in the country’s socio-economic landscape or to deepen the capacity for growth through new opportunities.

Unfortunately, a significant number of these projects have never seen the light of day. Some were abandoned before completion, while others have been left in a state of prolonged inactivity; effectively maintained in a form of ‘suspended animation’. As a result, unfinished structures dot the landscape across the country; some are completed facilities that never became commercially viable, while others remain trapped indefinitely between conception and construction. Several continue to receive annual budgetary allocations, even though they produce little or no public value.

The true cost of these projects, therefore, extends far beyond what was originally budgeted or already spent. It includes the recurring expenses of maintaining dormant institutions, the escalating cost of eventual completion, and the lost productive capacity, employment opportunities, and private investment that these projects were intended, but failed, to generate. Nigeria’s abandoned projects cannot, therefore, be understood through a single headline figure. They represent monumental undertakings that have continued to drain the economy both financially and psychologically, denying the country the benefits of a healthy, prosperous, and development-driven socio-economic environment.

Importantly, this challenge is not limited to physical infrastructure alone. A number of non-physical initiatives – economic programmes, policy interventions, and reform agendas – have also suffered similar fates. Many of these programmes were designed to stimulate growth, enhance productivity, or support vulnerable sectors, but were either prematurely discontinued, inconsistently implemented, or allowed to fade without achieving scale. The consequence is a significant loss of economic gains that could have been realised through scaling effects and multiplier impacts across sectors. In many cases, these abandoned or under-implemented programmes represent missed opportunities for sustained economic transformation, as their intended ripple effects across employment, income generation, and private sector development were never fully realised.

To fully grasp the scale and implications of this challenge, it is important to examine not only the financial outlays but also the systemic issues that have contributed to the persistence of these unfinished ambitions. Weak project planning, inconsistent policy direction, inadequate funding structures, corruption, and poor accountability mechanisms have all played significant roles. In many cases, changes in political leadership have led to shifts in priorities, resulting in the discontinuation or neglect of ongoing projects. A question that naturally arises is: why does the continued allocation of funds to such projects persist? While some may argue that allocation does not necessarily translate to disbursement, it nonetheless represents a diversion of scarce resources from other initiatives that could better align with the objectives of the incumbent administration and may have contributed to the high rate of budget non-completion recently experienced.

… strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate.

Addressing this issue requires a deliberate and coordinated approach, one that is devoid of political bias. First, there is a need for a comprehensive audit of all abandoned projects undertaken by the government, federal or state, within the last two decades, to determine their current status, viability, and potential for completion or repurposing. This audit should also extend to major economic programmes and policy initiatives that have been discontinued or under-implemented, in order to capture the full spectrum of lost economic value. Projects and programmes that remain economically and socially relevant should be prioritised for completion or revival, while those that are no longer viable should be formally discontinued to prevent further waste of public resources.

Second, strengthening institutional frameworks for project planning, execution, and monitoring is essential. Here lies the responsibility of the Federal Ministry of Budget and Economic Planning, with the National Infrastructure Integrated Master Plan serving as a central institutional instrument. Transparent procurement processes, clear accountability structures, and consistent policy implementation remain critical to ensuring that future projects and programmes are not subjected to the same fate. By adopting a more disciplined and strategic approach to development planning, Nigeria can begin to reverse the trend of abandoned initiatives and unlock the economic potential that these investments were originally intended to deliver.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

To better illustrate the scale, diversity, and implications of these unfinished ambitions, the table below presents a selection of notable projects across different sectors. It highlights their intended purpose, estimated costs, current status, and the economic opportunities that have been lost or deferred as a result of their prolonged inactivity.

Project Vision Estimated Cost Current Status What Nigeria Lost Governance Lesson Ajaokuta Steel Complex Build the foundation for Nigeria’s industrialisation US$8–$10bn invested Non-operational after four decades Steel production, industrial jobs, manufacturing capability Continuity without completion Mambilla Hydroelectric Project Add electricity generation capacity to power industrial growth US$5.8bn Yet to commence full construction Reliable power, industrial competitiveness Planning without execution Brass LNG Transform Nigeria into a global gas industrial hub ~US$16.5bn Long delayed after repeated announcements Export earnings, petrochemical industries, jobs Decisions without commitment Tinapa Business Resort Complement existing facilities to position Nigeria as a regional trade and tourism destination >US$350m Commercially dormant Trade, tourism, SME growth Investment without sustainability National Library Headquarters Build a national knowledge and innovation institution >₦100bn to complete Unfinished Research, innovation, national knowledge assets Construction without delivery

Beyond the financial and sectoral overview provided above, it is also important to recognise that not all “abandoned” projects are the same. They differ in form, stage of development, and the nature of their failure. The classification below provides a framework for analysing these projects which could help in identifying appropriate policy responses.

At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion.

Category Meaning Illustrative example Physically incomplete Construction began but was never completed National Library Headquarters Substantially built but non-operational Major assets exist but do not deliver their intended output Ajaokuta Steel Company Permanently pre-construction Repeated announcements and preliminary spending without full construction Mambilla Hydroelectric Project Commercially stranded Facility completed but unable to achieve economic viability Tinapa Business and Leisure Resort Investment decision repeatedly deferred Preparatory work was done, but the final investment commitment was never secured Brass LNG Project

This classification underscores that each category of project failure requires a distinct policy response; while some projects may require renewed funding and completion, others may need restructuring, concessioning, or outright discontinuation. Without such differentiation, policy interventions risk being ineffective or misdirected.

From the tables above, it is apparent that the inglorious act of project abandonment has no boundary or sectoral limitation; it cuts across the fabric of the economy, with no sector or region spared. This reality extends beyond physical infrastructure to include economic programmes whose discontinuation has equally deprived the economy of growth momentum and multiplier benefits. While the figures cited are indicative and based on publicly accessible information at the time of writing, what remains undeniable is the continued accumulation of these colossal costs while the country grapples with severe socio-economic infrastructure deficits. It is also important to note that the projects highlighted exclude the thousands of educational, health, and social infrastructure facilities that have deteriorated due to poor maintenance and inadequate resource allocation, further compounding the scale of the challenge.

At its core, the persistence of abandoned projects in Nigeria reflects deeper governance failures that can be understood through the lenses of authority, coordination, incentives, and commitment. The tragedy of Nigeria’s development is not that it lacks vision, but that it has not built the political and institutional capability to consistently translate vision into completion. In this context, authority speaks to the clarity of institutional mandates and the ability of designated agencies to make and enforce decisions without undue political interference. Coordination highlights the need for alignment across ministries, departments, and agencies, as well as between federal and state governments, to ensure continuity and coherence in project execution. Incentives must be redesigned so that public officials are rewarded for completing projects efficiently and held accountable for delays, cost overruns, or abandonment. Finally, commitment requires a long-term policy orientation that transcends electoral cycles, ensuring that projects and programmes are seen through to completion regardless of changes in political leadership.

In conclusion, addressing Nigeria’s challenge of abandoned projects demands more than increased funding or renewed political rhetoric. It requires systemic reform anchored in strong authority, effective coordination, well-aligned incentives, and unwavering commitment. By embedding these principles into the country’s development framework, Nigeria stands a better chance of breaking the cycle of unfinished ambitions, both physical and programmatic, and beginning the process of realising the full economic and social value of its investments. Development is ultimately about state capability.

Dipo Baruwa is a business climate development analyst.

World.title: NASS Roundup: Ebola, corps member’s death, Abuja rent, other stories from the House of Reps
World.content:
Reps demand action against fake, adulterated food and drinks

On Tuesday, House of Representatives urged the federal government to intensify efforts to stop the production and circulation of fake, adulterated, counterfeit and substandard food and drinks in Nigeria.

The resolution followed an urgent motion sponsored by Makki Yalleman (APC, Jigawa) who said unsafe food and beverages posed serious risks to public health, particularly to children, elderly people and other vulnerable groups.

Mr Yalleman cited recent enforcement operations, including the dismantling of an illegal alcohol counterfeiting syndicate at Zamfara Plaza on Lagos Island by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) in April and the discovery of an illegal fruit juice factory in Badagry, Lagos State, in September.

The lawmaker said some manufacturers and distributors were falsifying production and expiry dates, batch numbers, manufacturer details and ingredient information, while others allegedly used contaminated raw materials or illegally refilled containers.

The House consequently urged NAFDAC, the Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) and the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC), alongside the police, the Nigeria Customs Service, state governments and other agencies, to strengthen surveillance, inspection, sampling, laboratory testing and enforcement.

Relevant House committees were also mandated to examine the scale of the problem and the effectiveness of existing enforcement measures and report their findings within four weeks.

Lawmakers order probe into corps member’s death at NYSC camp

The House also ordered an investigation into the death of a National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) member, Etimbuk Sunday, at the NYSC Orientation Camp in Awgu, Enugu State.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The motion, sponsored by Unyime Idem (APC, Akwa Ibom) on Tuesday, followed concerns about the treatment Mr Sunday received after falling ill during his orientation programme.

Mr Sunday, a former president of the Students’ Union Government of Akwa Ibom State University, reportedly visited the camp clinic on 7 October with symptoms suggestive of malaria or typhoid. He was treated and discharged with oral medication, but his condition later deteriorated. He died on 11 October.

Mr Idem raised questions about the treatment administered to the corps member, the delay allegedly involved in referring him to a hospital and the circumstances surrounding the handling of his remains.

He also raised concerns over reports that the body was handed over to the family naked and with visible bruises, saying the allegations required investigation.

The House thereafter mandated its Committees on Youth Development, Health Care Services, Police Affairs and Human Rights to conduct a joint investigation and report within four weeks.

The development came after the Senate had also called for an investigation, while NAFDAC said it had begun investigating the death, including allegations concerning medicines administered to the deceased.

Ebola: Reps demand release of outstanding health funds

Following the confirmation of an imported Ebola case in Abuja, the House called for the immediate release of outstanding funds appropriated for health agencies to strengthen the country’s preparedness and response.

The motion, sponsored by Amobi Ogah (LP, Abia), was considered against the backdrop of the confirmed case involving a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria from Uganda.

Health authorities had identified 44 close contacts linked to the case, including healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and travel contacts, for monitoring.

Mr Ogah warned that delays in detecting suspected cases, conducting laboratory tests, isolating confirmed cases and tracing contacts could increase the risk of transmission.

He also raised concerns about gaps in public awareness, infection prevention and control supplies, healthcare workers’ preparedness and emergency response capacity.

The House, therefore, urged the Ministry of Finance to release outstanding appropriated funds to relevant health agencies. It also asked the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare and the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to assess additional resources required for the response.

The House further called for stronger surveillance involving federal and state health authorities, port health officials, the agriculture ministry and private healthcare providers, while urging collaboration with the World Health Organisation and other international health institutions.

Its Committee on Infectious Diseases was mandated to obtain updates from relevant agencies on the Ebola situation and Nigeria’s preparedness and report back to the House.

Reps demand review of Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway realignment

The House asked the federal government to review the proposed realignment of sections of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and retain the originally conceptualised route through parts of Ondo State and the Escravos–Ogheye–Ugborodo corridor in Delta State.

The motion was sponsored by Thomas Ereyitomi (APC, Delta), who argued that diverting the highway away from coastal communities could undermine the project’s original objective of improving connectivity and unlocking economic opportunities in the region.

The federal government has defended proposed changes to sections of the route on grounds including difficult terrain, flooding, weak subsoil conditions and climate-related risks. Works Minister Dave Umahi has said portions of the existing East-West Road would be used in the affected areas.

Mr Ereyitomi, however, argued that the government should first conduct an independent assessment of the engineering requirements, environmental consequences, socioeconomic impact and lifecycle costs of the alternative routes.

Lawmakers consider bill to regulate advance rent in FCT

The House has begun consideration of a bill seeking to restrict landlords and agents in the Federal Capital Territory from demanding more than one year’s rent in advance from tenants.

The proposed legislation which passed first reading on Thursday seeks to regulate rent payments for both residential and commercial properties in the FCT. It would also prevent landlords and agents from circumventing the restriction through compulsory service charges, additional payments, artificial tenancy renewals or other arrangements designed to force tenants to pay more than a year upfront.

The Federal Capital Territory Advance Rent Regulation and Tenants’ Protection Bill, 2026 (HB.2839), sponsored by Paul Nnamchi (APC, Enugu), with Ahmed Doro (PDP, Katsina) as co-sponsor, proposes the establishment of mechanisms for registering letting agents, receiving complaints and monitoring rental practices across the FCT, including the satellite towns.

It would also empower the proposed authority to order landlords or agents to refund unlawful payments within 30 days where violations are established.

Individuals who knowingly demand or receive rent above the permitted period could face fines ranging from N500,000 to N5 million, while corporate bodies could face fines between N5 million and N20 million. Courts could also order refunds and compensation for proven losses.

The proposal comes amid rising accommodation costs in Abuja, where tenants have complained of high rents alongside agency, agreement and caution fees.

World.title: APC defends Tinubu’s poverty claim, blames PDP’s 16 years in power
World.content:
The All Progressives Congress (APC) has defended President Bola Tinubu’s claim that opposition politicians caused the hunger and poverty confronting Nigerians, blaming previous administrations, particularly the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), for failing to address the country’s longstanding economic problems.

The party’s National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the foundations of Nigeria’s current poverty crisis were laid before Mr Tinubu assumed office in May 2023, arguing that former leaders should not portray the hardship as a problem that emerged under the current administration.

Mr Morka spoke on Monday during an appearance on News Central Television’s Breakfast Central programme, where he responded to questions about Mr Tinubu’s remarks at the APC’s 2027 presidential campaign flag-off in Kaduna on Saturday.

At the rally, Mr Tinubu accused opposition politicians of creating hunger and poverty, insisting that his administration was working to eradicate both problems.

“I have heard the opposition talking about hunger and poverty. Who created them? They did. They created the hunger; they created the poverty. We are trying to eradicate it,” the president said.

Defending the statement, Mr Morka said former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, now an opposition figure, had been part of a political establishment that governed Nigeria for 16 years under the PDP between 1999 and 2015 but failed to eliminate poverty.

“Poverty has been with us. As a matter of fact, the foundations for the endemic poverty we’re dealing with today were laid in that era,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He argued that Atiku, who served as vice president from 1999 to 2007, should explain why successive administrations failed to address poverty before criticising the current government over the economic hardship Nigerians are experiencing.

Mr Morka maintained that Mr Tinubu was referring to the historical roots of poverty rather than suggesting that the current administration had no responsibility for the conditions Nigerians face today.

However, the defence comes amid persistent concerns about the cost of living, declining purchasing power and the impact of the Tinubu administration’s economic reforms on households.

The World Bank estimated that 69.6 per cent of Nigerians lived below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day in 2025, while 50.8 per cent, or about 123 million people, were living in extreme poverty. The figures underscore the scale of the challenge facing the government, even as it argues that its reforms are necessary to stabilise the economy.

Mr Morka disputed the way poverty figures are sometimes presented in public discussions, arguing that currency depreciation and changes in the exchange-rate system must be considered when assessing incomes and living standards.

He said the government’s decision to harmonise the exchange rate was intended to correct distortions in the economy and that assessing the policy only through its immediate effects on purchasing power would give an incomplete picture.

The APC spokesperson acknowledged that the reforms had reduced Nigerians’ purchasing power and contributed to the high cost of living but argued that the government had little alternative to addressing what he described as deep-rooted economic distortions.

He also defended the removal of petrol subsidy, saying the policy was necessary to reduce the burden on public finances and end a system that successive governments had struggled to reform.

Mr Morka argued that the government should be assessed not only by whether Nigerians have immediately felt improvements in their living conditions but also by whether its policies are producing measurable progress towards economic recovery.

He said economic transformation could not be achieved overnight, citing countries such as China, Malaysia and Singapore as examples of economies whose development took time.

“We didn’t tell you we had a magic wand to correct Nigeria’s generational problems in one day or in two weeks or in one year,” he said.

According to him, the Tinubu administration has introduced several measures to cushion the effects of its reforms, including cash transfers to vulnerable households and initiatives aimed at reducing transportation costs and improving access to financing.

He said the government was not denying the hardship caused by the reforms but argued that the effects of removing long-standing economic support systems would inevitably be felt by households.

Mr Morka also defended the administration’s electricity-sector reforms, saying the changes had empowered states and other actors to develop power-generation capacity, although the results would take time to materialise.

He maintained that the reforms would eventually improve electricity supply and support economic growth.

The APC’s defence comes as Mr Tinubu begins his campaign for a second term amid public concerns over the cost of living and the effects of his administration’s economic policies.

While the government argues that the reforms are necessary to restore economic stability, the immediate impact on household incomes and the persistence of widespread poverty remain central issues in the debate over its economic record.

Morka defends vehicles for campaign mobilisation

Mr Morka also defended the provision of vehicles for political campaigns by First Lady Remi Tinubu, amid the controversy surrounding the presentation of seven new Toyota Land Cruiser Prado sport utility vehicles (SUVs) to selected APC youth leaders.

The party’s National Youth Leader, Dayo Israel, had said the vehicles were intended to support election mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections, prompting criticism over the reported cost of the fleet amid the economic hardship facing Nigerians.

Responding to questions about campaign vehicles, Mr Morka argued that such provisions were part of the logistics required for electioneering and should not be interpreted as rewards for party loyalists.

“During the campaign, every campaign season, people brand vehicles to move because it’s an activity. It’s not as if they were given as a reward,” he said.

He added that vehicles provided for campaign purposes should be understood within the context of preparations for the 2027 elections.

World.title: Algerian upper house of parliament approves troop deployment to Niger
World.content:
Algeria’s upper house of parliament has approved deploying troops to Niger to protect its energy facilities.

The country’s Council of Nations approved the deployment during an emergency session on Sunday, while the lower house is expected to hold a session on Monday.

If the deployment is approved in the lower parliament, it means the country is highly likely to deploy troops to protect its facilities located along the border area in the north of Niger, particularly the Kafra oil region and other energy facilities linked to Algeria’s state-owned energy company Sonatrach.

If approved, it would also be the first mission outside Algeria’s borders since the 1973 War between Israel and several Arab countries.

The vote came after Niger’s Defence Minister, Salifou Modi, visited Algeria. Mr Modi met with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and the Chief of Staff of the People’s National Army, Said Chanegriha, last week. Both countries signed a military cooperation protocol during the meeting. But the details of the cooperation were not made public.

Mr Tebboune had also earlier disclosed that Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger in late August to help thwart a “coup attempt” that shook the capital, Niamey.

The Algerian Ministry of Defence previously said it had sent four jets to Niger following the unrest. It said two patrols of four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft had landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an air-to-air refuelling plane.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The ministry said the warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilise the brotherly state of Niger.”

Niger’s defence minister, Salifou Mody, said a group of soldiers, in August, detained some of their comrades and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the capital.

Fighting between the group and Niger forces lasted for several hours, during which the state broadcaster was temporarily taken off air, while gunfire and explosions were reported around the airport and presidential palace.

ALSO READ: Algeria severs ties with UAE

Niger faces persistent attacks by armed groups, including in areas near the border with Algeria.

The country has also grown increasingly isolated since the democratic government was overthrown in 2023. The military junta cut off relations with France, leading to the complete withdrawal of French and US troops.

It withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 2025, alongside Burkina Faso and Mali.

This vacuum has forced Niger to seek alternative regional and Western allies.

World.title: Police detain 28-year-old for robbing POS operator at gunpoint
World.content:
The Police Command in Enugu State has detained a 28-year-old suspect for allegedly robbing a female Point-of-Sale (POS) operator of N200,000 at gunpoint in Obollo-Afor within Udenu Local Government Area of the state.

This is contained in a statement issued by the command’s spokesperson, SP Daniel Ndukwe, on Sunday in Enugu.

Mr Ndukwe, a superintendent of police, said that on 18 October at about 12:26 p.m., police operatives attached to Udenu Division, supported by members of the Neighbourhood Watch Group, arrested and detained the suspect.

He said the detention of the suspect followed a report that he had robbed the victim at her shop along Old Orba Road, Uhulor, Obollo-Afor, on 17 October at about 9 a.m.

“Preliminary investigations indicate that the victim raised the alarm as the suspect fled and was allegedly threatening to shoot anyone pursuing him.

“A Beretta-like pistol and an expended 9mm ammunition shell were recovered from him, while the suspect has confessed to the crime during interrogation.

“The suspect will be arraigned in court upon conclusion of investigations,” Mr Ndukwe said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Ndukwe quoted the Commissioner of Police in Enugu State, Mamman Giwa, as commending the operatives for the successful operation and acknowledged the complementary support provided by the neighbourhood watch group.

The commissioner reiterated the command’s commitment to combating crime and urged residents to promptly report suspicious activities to the police and other recognised security agencies.

(NAN)

World.title: Nigeria has no Ebola case after patient’s evacuation to Switzerland – WHO
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, says Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases following the medical evacuation of the patient and her husband to Switzerland.

Janabi disclosed this in a statement on his official X handle on Monday, adding that Nigeria would continue monitoring 52 contacts, while Switzerland would manage the patient and follow up with her husband.

He said the evacuation took place earlier in the morning, noting that both the patient and her husband were Swiss citizens.

According to him, the patient was clinically stable after Nigerian medical teams successfully managed her through the acute phase of the illness and stabilised her condition.

Janabi congratulated the Federal Government, health workers, clinicians, emergency responders and other partners involved in the Ebola response, describing the development as a remarkable achievement.

He said the successful management of the patient demonstrated Africa’s expertise, resilience and leadership in public health, particularly when countries worked together to respond to health emergencies.

However, the WHO regional director stressed that vigilance remained critical despite the evacuation, urging continued attention to contact monitoring and other response measures.

He said Nigeria would maintain close follow-up of 52 contacts, while Switzerland would assume responsibility for the continued management of the patient and monitoring of contact number 53, her husband.

(NAN)

World.title: AY apologises after payment dispute disrupts UK comedy show
World.content:
JEDDAH, SAUDI ARABIA – DECEMBER 06: Ayo Makun attends the “Kamla” screening at the Red Sea International Film Festival on December 06, 2022 in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. (Photo by Tim P. Whitby/Getty Images for The Red Sea International Film Festival)

By Wasiu Rokibat

Nigerian comedian and actor Ayo Makun, popularly known as AY, has apologised to fans disappointed that the Cardiff leg of his “AY Live: Single and Not Searching” UK tour failed to go ahead as expected.

The event, scheduled for Sunday, October 25, 2026, at Valegate Retail Park in Cardiff, Wales, reportedly saw hours of delays and confusion, leaving many ticket holders unable to see any of the advertised performers.

AY, in a statement shared on Monday on Instagram, said he and the other comedians on the bill had travelled to Cardiff and arrived at the venue but could not perform because of unresolved payment commitments with the organisers.

“My fellow comedians and I travelled to Cardiff to perform and eventually entered the venue. Unfortunately, unresolved payment commitments delayed our appearance, and by the time we arrived at the hall, most of the audience had left,” he said.

The comedian expressed regret over the experience, acknowledging that fans who paid to attend the show deserved better treatment.

“You deserved a properly organised show and timely information. You should never have been caught in the middle of a payment dispute,” AY stated.

He also appealed to fans to hear his account of the incident before reaching conclusions about what transpired, saying he had explained the circumstances in a video.

Addressing the issue of compensation, AY called on the organisers and the UK tour management to provide a clear resolution for affected ticket holders, including information on refunds.

“I am calling on the organisers and our UK tour management to provide a clear resolution for ticket holders, including refund information,” he said, adding that verified updates would be communicated through his official channels.

The incident had triggered complaints from attendees on social media, with reports of prolonged waiting, heated exchanges and police presence at the venue.

As of the time of filing this report, the organisers had yet to publicly explain the circumstances surrounding the disruption or announce refund arrangements.

World.title: Trade Pathways launches Nigeria coverage as US tariffs weigh on small business exporters
World.content:
New US import tax falls hardest on processed goods, the core of Nigeria’s small-business export economy.

For Nigeria’s small businesses, selling to the United States has become a moving target. Tariff costs for buyers have changed four times in the last 18 months, and the latest change brings new challenges for entrepreneurs and business owners.

The recent volatility began in April 2025, when the US placed a 14 per cent tax on most Nigerian goods. Four months later, the tariff rate rose to 15 per cent. Then, in February 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled these taxes unlawful, and a temporary 10 per cent tax was put in their place. For many exporters, it became difficult to know which rate applied, or for how long.

That temporary tax expired in July 2026 and was replaced by the one in place today: a 12.5 per cent tax on goods from countries that, according to the US government, have not banned imports made with forced labour. Nigeria is one of the few African countries on that list.

A key concern with the latest tariff is that it falls hardest on small businesses. Nigeria’s largest exports to the US, such as crude oil, gas and fertiliser, are exempt, and those are mostly handled by large enterprises. Beyond these exports, the dividing line tends to fall between raw and finished goods. Most raw commodities, like cocoa beans and raw cashews, are exempt, while finished goods such as roasted cashews, chocolate, shea butter, leather goods, cosmetics, packaged foods and crafts are taxed. These finished goods tend to be items that Nigeria’s small and medium-sized businesses most commonly export.

“The greater challenge lies not in the immediate loss of export opportunities, but in navigating an increasingly fragmented and protectionist global trading environment,” Dr Muda Yusuf, Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise (CPPE), said in a policy brief issued after the tax was announced.

This growing challenge for small and medium-sized businesses is why Trade Pathways, a US-based, student-run organisation, was founded. Its goal is to create opportunities for small businesses in Africa by giving them free access to the same clear, up-to-date picture of US trade policy that multinationals and large enterprises get from legal teams and policy experts.

The platform tracks every US trade policy change and explains the structure in simple terms, so business owners can keep up with the constant shifts and understand buyer behaviour. Having initially served businesses in Kenya and Ghana, Trade Pathways is now launching full coverage for Nigeria, driven by recent trade policy changes and the potential adverse impacts on Nigerian business owners.

“Small business owners should be spending their time making and selling great products, not on interpreting US government trade notices,” noted Keshav Suman, the platform’s founder. “The information is public, but it changes constantly and is written for lawyers and policy experts, not for the business owners it affects most.”

The timing reflects growing activity among smaller Nigerian exporters. Non-oil exports reached a record $6.1 billion in 2025, and the Nigerian Export Promotion Council (NEPC) registered 1,129 new exporters during the year. NEPC’s Executive Director, Nonye Ayeni, has said the council is focused on “reducing dependence on large exporters by supporting small and medium-scale enterprises.”

What Nigerian exporting businesses should know now

Which party pays the tariff. The US import tax is paid by the American buyer when the goods arrive, not by the Nigerian supplier. Suppliers are still impacted indirectly, however, as buyers ask for lower prices, order smaller quantities, or move part of their orders to suppliers in countries that pay less. The exception is when a seller agrees to deliver goods with all import duties already paid, an arrangement that is common when shipping parcels directly to US customers. In that case, the seller would be responsible for the tax.

Product classification. Exemptions from the new tax are set based on product and further classified by process, so two closely related goods can be treated very differently. Raw cashews, for example, are exempt, while roasted cashews are not. Before agreeing on a price, exporters should confirm exactly how their product is classified, so a buyer is not surprised by a higher cost after the order is placed.

Refunds of the 2025 tariffs. The emergency tariffs the US charged on imports from around the world in 2025, including the 14 and 15 per cent rates on Nigerian goods, were ruled unlawful by the US Supreme Court in February 2026. US Customs has been refunding importers since April 2026, and on October 8, a US court ruled that importers who have not filed their own lawsuits are covered under a single group claim. Although refunds benefit US buyers, Nigerian export businesses that lowered prices to help buyers absorb the tariff can reasonably negotiate in future pricing discussions.

AGOA and duty-free entry. The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a US programme that removes the standard import tax on qualifying goods from sub-Saharan Africa, was extended in September 2026 and now runs until December 2028. It covers thousands of products, including several forms of clothing, footwear, leather goods, processed foods and wooden crafts. Nigeria has also been certified since 2005 to export handloomed and ethnic printed fabrics such as aso oke, Akwete cloth and Ankara prints under AGOA, a benefit that many business owners are not aware of. AGOA does not, however, cancel the new 12.5 per cent tax rate in place for Nigeria.

US travel restrictions. Since January 2026, the US government has suspended new business and tourist visas for Nigerian nationals, which makes US trade shows difficult to attend. Video meetings, product samples sent ahead of a call, and US-based sales representatives or partners in the Nigerian diaspora can all help maintain buyer relationships through the absence of physical visits to the US.

Alternative markets and customers. Selling to more than one market reduces the risk of depending on a single country’s trade rules. Europe is already Nigeria’s largest buyer of non-oil goods, and many Nigerian products receive reduced import taxes there. Since May 2026, China has charged no import tax on Nigerian goods, an arrangement that runs until April 2028, though food and agricultural exporters must still register with Chinese customs and meet its product standards. Closer to home, the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is gradually lowering import taxes between African countries, opening regional markets that are often easier to reach than the US.

What comes next

Several US developments could change the picture in the coming months. American importers and 25 US states are challenging the current 12.5 per cent tariff in a US trade court, which heard the case on September 30. A potential ruling could reduce or remove the tax entirely, though an appeal is expected on either side. The US government is also expected to announce its annual decisions on which countries remain eligible for AGOA near the end of the year. Trade Pathways noted it is currently tracking each of these policy movements and will update guidance as announcements come.

Trade Pathways’ resources for small business owners

Trade Pathways provides tools and services that are free for business owners in Kenya, Ghana, and now Nigeria.
