One such tool is a cost estimator, which calculates what a US buyer would pay at the border for a given product and shipment by country. On a $10,000 shipment, for example, Nigerian cocoa butter costs the buyer about $47 in customs fees, because it is exempt from the current tariff. The same shipment of wooden carvings costs about $1,297, almost all of it the 12.5 per cent tax. This allows sellers to anticipate how a buyer might respond to the tax, and to go into pricing conversations better prepared.

The platform also offers guidance on labour management, an area where US buyers are paying closer attention than ever. Because US law bans imports made with forced labour, American buyers increasingly ask their suppliers for proof of fair employment, such as written contracts, payroll records and confirmation that workers keep their own identity documents. Trade Pathways provides a checklist of these records so businesses can respond to buyer requests quickly.

Suman, a US-based high school student, started Trade Pathways in 2025. For years, he had bought home decor from sellers in Africa through platforms such as Etsy and TikTok Shop. When US tariffs took effect, he noticed several of those sellers begin to raise prices, pause shipments to the US, or announce closures of their operations. Realising that small businesses had limited ability to absorb or ride out sudden policy changes, he built Trade Pathways to give them clearer information to make informed decisions.

US trade policy is likely to remain unpredictable, and the businesses best placed to adapt will be those that understand the rules early. With its launch in Nigeria, Trade Pathways aims to make sure that knowledge base is available to every small business owner.

World.title: Plateau motorcycle rider killed, mutilated body found
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa

A motorcycle rider has been killed by unknown assailants, with his mutilated body reportedly discovered along Longvel Road in Shendam Local Government Area of Plateau State.

The victim’s motorcycle was also reportedly stolen, while the circumstances surrounding the killing remained unclear as of the time of filing this report.

A resident of the community, Henry Homsuk, told newsmen that “Residents woke up on Monday to the disturbing news of the incident.”

“It is sad that someone would be killed and his motorcycle carted away. We woke up to the news this morning, and it was disturbing,” Homsuk said.

“It is painful that somebody would lose his life in such circumstances. We are worried about what happened and hope the authorities will take the matter seriously,” he added.

” The issue has been reported to security operatives,” he added

“We appeal to the security agencies to investigate this matter thoroughly and ensure that those responsible are arrested.”

” People should be able to go about their lawful activities without fear,” Homsuk said.

“Security should be strengthened along Longvel Road and in other vulnerable communities to protect lives and property and prevent a recurrence,” he added.

Efforts to reach security operatives for confirmation of the incident were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Military clears air on troops’ clash with police personnel in Plateau
World.content:
The Special Task Force Operation Enduring Peace (JTF-OPEP) has cleared the air on the recent encounter between its troops and personnel of the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) in Bassa Local Government Area (LGA) of Plateau.

The media officer of the operation, Capt. Polycarp Oteh, in a statement on Monday in Jos, said that the encounter between the two security agencies was misconstrued to be a clash.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that videos and photographs of an alleged clash between the military and police personnel went viral on social media a few days ago.

It was alleged that troops had prevented the police personnel from going after some criminals in the area.

But Oteh said that troops only responded to a distress call, following a sporadic shooting at Mai Farin Moto, Maraban Dere and adjoining communities of the area.

“On Oct. 20, troops of our Sector 3 responded to a distress call reporting sporadic gunfire in Mai Farin Moto, Maraban Dere and adjoining communities. This is alongside reports of the suspected killing of a resident, Mr Adamu Suleiman.

“The troops were deployed to the affected area to assess the security situation, establish the circumstances of the incident, prevent escalation and protect lives and property.

“On arrival, the troops sought to engage the police personnel operating in the area to clarify the situation and facilitate a coordinated security response.

“Regrettably, the interaction was characterised by a lack of cooperation from some personnel in spite of efforts to de-escalate tensions and maintain operational discipline,” he said.

Oteh emphasised that troops’ intervention was prompted by an operational distress call, adding that it was undertaken in the interest of public safety.

“JTF-OPEP remains committed to impartiality, professionalism and the protection of lives and property.

“As a joint security arrangement, our operational effectiveness depends on inter-agency coordination, mutual respect, adherence to established procedures and unity of effort.

“Issues arising from the incident are being addressed through appropriate command and inter-agency channels to establish the facts, sustain operational cohesion and prevent recurrence,” he explained.

The media officer advised members of the public and reporters to verify information before going to the press, adding that such move would ensure credibility and professionalism.

He assured residents of Plateau of its resolve to maintain law and order, protect innocent residents and consolidate peace and security across its joint operations area. (NAN)

World.title: Phone-tapping charge: Court rejects El-Rufai’s no-case submission
World.content:
Nasir El-Rufai

…orders him to open his defence

By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

The Federal High Court in Abuja on Monday held that the detained former Kaduna State governor, Nasir El-Rufai, has a case to answer over an allegation that he unlawfully intercepted the phone communications of the National Security Adviser (NSA), Nuhu Ribadu.

The court, in a ruling delivered by Justice Joyce Abdulmalik, dismissed as lacking in merit a no-case submission that the embattled former governor filed to be discharged and acquitted of the charge against him.

El-Rufai, who was governor between 2015 and 2023 and also served as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) under former President Olusegun Obasanjo’s administration, is facing trial over comments he made when he appeared as a guest on Arise Television on February 13.

He is answering to a five-count amended charge that the Federal Government preferred against him through the Department of State Services (DSS).

It was alleged that the defendant, during his appearance on Arise TV’s Prime Time programme in Abuja, admitted that he knew and was associated with an individual who had illegally intercepted the NSA’s telephone communications.

Aside from the allegation that his action breached national security and public safety, an offence punishable under Section 12(1) of the Cybercrimes (Prohibition, Prevention, etc.) (Amendment) Act, 2024, the former governor was also charged with failing to report the crime to the relevant security agencies.

The defendant had, during the TV interview, reacted to what he described as an attempt by DSS operatives to “abduct” him at Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport in Abuja on February 12, 2026, upon his return from Cairo.

He insisted that the security agency was being instigated by the ICPC, which he said had received a directive from the NSA, Ribadu, to detain him.

The former governor claimed the information reached him through someone who had listened in on the NSA’s telephone conversations.

Meanwhile, after the prosecution closed its case with the evidence of two witnesses who testified before the court, the defendant applied to be discharged and acquitted.

El-Rufai, through his team of lawyers led by Mr. Paul Erokoro, SAN, insisted that the prosecution had failed to establish a prima facie case to warrant the court compelling him to enter a defence to the charge, which he described as incompetent.

However, the prosecution counsel, Mr. Oluwole Aladedoye, SAN, urged the court to dismiss the application and order the defendant to open his defence to the charge.

Aladedoye, SAN, maintained that the oral and documentary evidence laid before the court was sufficient to tie the defendant to the allegations against him.

In her ruling on the matter, Justice Abdulmalik said the court was satisfied that the evidence laid by the prosecution was strong enough to warrant explanations from the defendant.

Even though the court had yet to ascertain the defendant’s culpability or otherwise, it dismissed the no-case submission and ordered him to open his defence to the charge.

It will be recalled that shortly after being accused of admitting that he used “technical equipment” to illegally intercept the NSA’s calls, El-Rufai filed a motion to stop his trial.

He gave 17 reasons why the charge, marked FHC/ABJ/CR/99/2026, should be quashed by the court.

He argued that the charge was incompetent and legally defective, insisting that the DSS had no legal basis to elevate a “casual remark” he made during a television interview into “a confession” that he had indeed tapped the NSA’s telephone line, as alleged.

He argued that the statement he made on Arise TV did not constitute a confessional statement in law, saying that for a statement to be admissible as a confession, it must be made under caution, voluntarily, and in circumstances that satisfy the Judges’ Rules.

El-Rufai maintained that the statements he made during his television interview were made without caution or warning, in a voluntary public discussion, and without the protections afforded to suspects in custody.

“A casual remark on a television programme cannot be elevated to a judicial confession,” he further argued.

However, the court declined to quash the charge and ordered an accelerated hearing of the case.

El-Rufai who has been in detention since February is standing trial before courts in both Abuja and Kaduna state.

Justice Abdulmalik had, on July 23, dismissed as lacking in merit an application that the former governor filed for the variation of his bail conditions, which he described as very stringent and difficult to fulfil.

According to El-Rufai’s lawyer, the bail conditions sought to be varied included the requirement that the defendant produce level 17 civil servants with properties in Maitama or Asokoro, as well as verification and attestation letters from the Kaduna State traditional council.

However, the prosecution opposed the variation request, insisting that qualified public officers who could meet the conditions existed and could easily be secured by the defendant.

It persuaded the court to reject the application.

World.title: No rift between Netanyahu, army chief on Iran – Israel defence minister
World.content:
Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz

Defence Minister Israel Katz said Monday that reports of a rift between Israel’s army and its civilian leaders over fresh action in the war with Iran were “entirely baseless”.

Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Sunday, citing unnamed sources, that there had been a confrontation between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and army chief Eyal Zamir over an unspecified new directive.

The premier dismissed the report as “rubbish” during a TV appearance, and Katz characterised it as an effort to cast doubt on the Netanyahu bloc’s judgement on the eve of close elections.

“The reports about gaps between the political echelon and the IDF (army) on the Iran issue are entirely baseless and false,” Katz said on X, insisting there was “complete” coordination between the two.

In its report, Channel 12 said Zamir had demanded a detailed discussion as well as legal guarantees and the signatures of the political leadership before carrying out the directive he had received.

The outlet did not offer details of the directive, but cited sources saying there were concerns within the army that the war might be exploited for political gain.

Katz stated “unequivocally that there was no intention on Israel’s part to initiate an attack on Iran before the elections”.

Opposition leader Yair Lapid referenced the report in a post on X Sunday, accusing Netanyahu of seeking to put off the vote.

“Tonight it was published that he wants to set off an escalation and a confrontation with Iran, just to postpone the elections,” he said.

“This man has lost his grip. We absolutely must send him home.”

Netanyahu has campaigned heavily on his security credentials, arguing that only he can finish the job in the US-Israeli war against Iran.

AFP

World.title: Iran says outcome of Israeli elections ‘makes no difference’
World.content:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi

Iran’s foreign ministry said Monday that the outcome of the Israeli elections in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing a tight race will make “no difference”.

“It makes no difference to us who, in these elections, takes the helm of a regime that has brought nothing but violence and massacres to our region,” said ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei in a weekly press briefing.

Tuesday’s legislative elections will take place amid mounting threats by Israel and the United States to renew attacks on Iran after they launched their war in late February.

Netanyahu has in recent days repeatedly said the only way to remove the threat posed by Iran is to topple its government.

On Sunday, he told Israel’s Channel 14 that he had “instructed the Mossad and the IDF to overthrow the Iranian regime”.

Baqaei dismissed Netanyahu’s remarks as “empty threats” and a “sign of desperation”.

World.title: Anambra Student Wins 2026 National Head Girl Competition
World.content:
Jane-Frances Chiamaka Gabriel of Queen of the Rosary College Onitsha has emerged champion of the 2026 National Head Girl Competition, organised by the Women in Leadership Advancement Network (WILAN Global).

She won a cash prize of ₦1 million and a brand-new laptop at the grand finale held on Tuesday, October 13, at Alliance Française in Ikoyi, Lagos.

Jane-Frances, who represented her school in the competition, clinched the top prize with an innovation that uses plantable pencils made from recycled paper to teach children about climate change.

Her victory followed a multi-stage selection process that saw her advance from an initial pool of applicants to the top 16 contestants, then the top eight, before securing a place among the final three. Her progression earned her an all-expenses-paid trip to Lagos, which she undertook alongside the school’s principal, Reverend Sister Maria Chijioke Nwankwo, for the grand finale.

At the final, Jane-Frances competed against some of Nigeria’s most promising young female student leaders while presenting her innovation as a practical way to introduce environmental awareness to children while encouraging sustainable habits from an early age.

The competition concluded with Fetuga Ameerah of the International School, University of Lagos, taking second place, while Oritsematosan Jackson of Royal Family Academy, Abuja, finished third.

Organised by WILAN Global, the National Head Girl Competition is an innovation and leadership platform for head girls across Nigeria. It provides participants with an opportunity to demonstrate their leadership abilities, develop innovative solutions to real-world challenges and showcase their capacity to contribute meaningfully to their communities.

Speaking on the school’s achievement, the school’s principal, Rev. Sr. Maria Chijioke Nwankwo, said the victory reflected the school’s sustained commitment to preparing young girls for leadership, entrepreneurship and the future of work.

“Wins like this are not entirely new to QRC. At QRC, we take entrepreneurship education and digital skills training seriously because we believe that girls must be equipped not just to participate in the future economy but to shape it,” she said.

The principal also acknowledged the contributions of teachers and the school’s proprietor, Archbishop Valerian Maduka Okeke, whose support continues to strengthen the school’s commitment to nurturing confident and socially responsible young leaders.

For Gabriel, the victory provided an opportunity to put her creativity to practical use and demonstrate how young people can contribute to addressing challenges in their communities.

“I am incredibly excited and grateful for this opportunity from WILAN Global. I am also deeply grateful to my entrepreneurship education coach and mentor, Mr John Onuigbo, who has helped me understand what is possible and encouraged me to turn my ideas into solutions that can make an impact,” she said.

World.title: Nigeria’s Ebola Patient Evacuated to Switzerland
World.content:
The Federal Government has confirmed the evacuation of Nigeria’s first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) to Switzerland following significant clinical improvement.

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Pate, said this on Monday in a post on his official X handle.

Pate said the evacuation was approved by him and carried out early on Monday, with the patient accompanied by her spouse, who remained asymptomatic.

He said the patient was stable, conscious and communicating, while her laboratory test results were approaching baseline levels.

“The index patient was clinically much improved, stable, conscious, communicating, and her clinical laboratory test results closing towards baseline.

“This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” he said.

Pate commended the clinical staff for providing quality care and public health personnel for ensuring that the evacuation complied with appropriate public health measures.

He said the government would provide further updates after the patient and her spouse arrived safely at their destination.

The minister said public health measures remained in place to ensure that the imported virus was contained, urging Nigerians to remain vigilant and rely on credible information sources.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Nigeria confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease on Oct. 20, following laboratory confirmation of infection in a woman with recent travel history to Uganda.

The patient developed symptoms on Oct. 7, four days after arriving in Nigeria, and sought medical care in Abuja on Oct. 11, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) activated its incident management system, while health authorities commenced contact tracing, laboratory investigations and infection prevention measures.

The NCDC’s Oct. 24 situation report identified 53 contacts linked to the case, including healthcare workers, domestic staff and the patient’s spouse.

None had tested positive at the time of the report.

On Oct. 23, Pate said genomic analysis showed that the virus isolated from the Nigerian patient appeared closely related to that identified in the index case in Kenya.

He, however, cautioned that the genetic relationship did not establish a direct transmission link between the two cases.

The Federal Government has also intensified surveillance at points of entry, strengthened infection prevention and control in health facilities, and urged healthcare workers to promptly report suspected cases.

Bundibugyo virus disease is caused by a species of Ebola virus. Transmission occurs through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials.

The government has urged Nigerians to observe basic preventive measures, cooperate with public health officials and avoid spreading unverified information about the disease.(NAN)

World.title: Customer Outcomes Define Service Excellence, Says Remita MD
World.content:
The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Remita Payment Services Limited, ’DeRemi Atanda, has called on businesses and public institutions to measure digital transformation by the outcomes customers achieve, rather than the sophistication of deployed technology.

He made the call at the 2026 Service Excellence Conference held in Lagos recently, where business executives, regulators and public sector leaders discussed how technology and human interaction could improve service delivery.

Speaking on the conference theme, ‘Tech-Enabled. Human-Powered,’ Atanda said organisations often invest heavily in digital platforms and automation without addressing the delays, uncertainty and difficulties customers encounter when accessing services.

He urged service providers to understand customer expectations before adopting new technologies, noting that automation cannot compensate for poorly designed processes or unclear service standards.

“Technology has been, and will continue to be, a means to an end, not the end itself. Customers are not looking for technology; they are looking for outcomes. Technology cannot deliver service excellence if it is optimising for the wrong expectations. The journey begins with how we understand what customers want, which ultimately comes down to less effort and greater certainty,” he said.

During a panel discussion, Atanda said speed alone was insufficient to guarantee customer satisfaction, adding that a transaction could be completed quickly without meeting customer expectations.

“Speed is just one attribute of service delivery. Fast service is not always pleasant, nor does it always meet customer expectations. To deliver true service excellence, you must combine speed with smart solutions and human connection. That is what builds consistency and trust,” he explained.

He also stressed the importance of retaining empathy and responsiveness in digital service delivery, saying technology should not prevent customers from receiving appropriate support when problems arise.

“When we speak of human connection in technology, ‘human’ does not mean manual processes. It is about the emotional component of service delivery and how people relate to your brand. As we deploy technology as an invisible layer, we must ensure that it does not remove the human touch, because technology that remembers is technology that feels human,” he added.

On accountability in financial services, Atanda said businesses must take responsibility for the promises they make to customers, even when transactions depend on multiple networks and service providers.

“You don’t prepare for war in the time of war; you prepare for war in the time of peace. Service providers must design for failure as seriously as they design for success. In a complex financial ecosystem, reliability is shared across multiple partners, but accountability is never shared. It is entirely yours to deliver on your promise to the customer,” he emphasised.

He recommended that business leaders understand customer expectations before choosing technology, map the customer journey, incorporate empathy into service processes, prepare for service failures and assess performance using actual customer experiences rather than system uptime alone.

The conference highlighted the need for organisations to evaluate digital investments based on their impact on customers.

World.title: Access Holdings Has Built Scale: Now Comes The Test Of Creating Value
World.content:
After two decades of acquisition-led growth, one of Africa’s most widely spread banking groups has made returns, not reach, its measure of success. The early numbers are encouraging. The real test is whether the discipline lasts.

For most of its history, Access Bank measured progress by size. Acquisitions, entry into new markets, repeated capital raises and steady diversification turned a mid-sized Nigerian lender into one of Africa’s most extensive financial services groups, with total assets of ₦51.56 trillion at the end of 2025.

That strategy worked. But it has limits. Beyond a certain point, getting bigger stops being the best measure of a business, and does not necessarily translate into stronger returns

Access Holdings appears to have reached that point. More notably, it has said so itself. The Group now describes its strategy as a move “from scale to value,” and management has told shareholders that its central aim is to deliver stronger earnings per share and generate returns on equity that consistently exceed the cost of capital. After a period of heavy acquisition activity, the stated priority is to get more from the businesses it already owns.

That is the right ambition. Whether the Group can deliver it consistently is what will determine how investors value it over the next few years.

Why size alone is no longer enough

Scale matters in banking. A larger bank attracts more deposits, can serve bigger corporate clients, can spread the cost of technology and compliance across more customers, and is less exposed to any single economy.

But scale has costs, and they tend to arrive later than the benefits. Every acquisition brings new systems, staff, regulators, and risks. Every new country demands management time and capital. A bigger balance sheet produces more income, but also more credit exposure, larger funding needs, and heavier capital requirements.

During rapid expansion, these costs are easy to miss. Assets, deposits, and customer numbers keep rising, and the headline story is one of success, even where parts of the business earn less than the capital they consume.

Access Holdings’ 2025 results show both sides of this picture. Group profit before tax passed ₦1 trillion, and the cost-to-income ratio improved from 56.7% to 51.7%, a sign that the enlarged group is starting to run more efficiently. Yet return on average equity fell from 21.6% to 18.4%, reflecting higher impairment charges during the year, as the Group accelerated provisions on legacy loans and on exposures previously covered by regulatory forbearance.

Addressing these credit exposures, through appropriate provisioning, rather than carrying them forward, is the kind of decision that tends to pay off later. A cleaner balance sheet is a stronger base for the next phase than a flattering short-term profit figure. It also makes clear that future growth must come from better returns, not wider reach.

Every subsidiary needs a clear job

Access Holdings operates in markets with very different economies, competitors, and regulators. Some of its subsidiaries are mature and highly profitable. Others are newly acquired, being restructured, or still building a customer base.

Holding them all to the same short-term targets would be a mistake. An established bank, a recently acquired franchise, and a young payments business are at different stages and should be judged accordingly.

But those differences must have limits. Each significant subsidiary should have a clear economic purpose, a target return, and a timetable for reaching it. Where a business falls short, investors should be able to tell whether the cause is temporary, such as currency weakness or a one-off clean-up, or structural.

There is early evidence that the approach can work. Pre-tax profit from the Group’s subsidiaries elsewhere in Africa grew double-digit to about N284 billion in 2025 from ₦201 billion in the previous year, with Access Bank DR Congo alone doubling its net profit. Operations outside Nigeria now account for close to half of the Group’s pre-tax profit by segment.

The same discipline has to apply in the other direction. Where a business cannot reach acceptable returns within a reasonable period, the options should include restructuring it, bringing in partners, or reducing exposure. The goal is not to abandon every subsidiary that is struggling. It is to ensure that every naira of capital has a clear commercial reason to be where it is.

Nigeria: the biggest opportunity is at home

Nigeria remains the core of the Group, and it is where the most work remains. Pre-tax profit from the Nigerian business increased year on year by 8% in 2025, despite higher provisions and pressure on interest margins, which weighed on earnings.

The answer is unlikely to be another large acquisition or a wave of new branches. It is more likely to come from deepening existing customer relationships.

For individuals, that means bringing salary payments, savings, transfers, cards, and credit into one relationship. For businesses, it means handling collections, payroll, supplier payments, trade finance, and cash management. The more of a customer’s financial life a bank handles, the more stable and recurring its income becomes.

The Group’s non-banking businesses strengthen this case. Access Pensions, Access Insurance Brokers, and Hydrogen Payments provide the opportunities to grow fee-based income, while Oxygen X Finance focuses on digital consumer lending. Together, these businesses can broaden the Group’s earnings base, deepen customer relationships, and support stronger returns.

The economics still have to add up. Adding customers creates little value if serving them costs more than they bring in. Growing the loan book does little for profitability if credit losses and funding costs absorb the margin. The Nigerian business is where investors will see most clearly whether the strategy is working.

Making the international network pay

The Group’s international footprint is a genuine strategic asset. A Nigerian company that imports equipment, exports goods, or expands into other African countries needs banking services in several markets at once. A group present in those markets, and in financial centres such as London, can build deeper relationships and earn income from trade finance, payments, and foreign exchange.

Presence alone, however, does not guarantee returns. Some international subsidiaries add to the Group’s reach and reputation, while earning modest profits. That can be justified for a period where the long-term opportunity is clear, but investors should be able to see the reasoning and the timetable. Currency movements add a further layer of risk: gains earned in local currencies can shrink when translated into naira, as the Group’s 2025 accounts showed.

A diversified group creates value when its businesses, taken together, produce stronger and steadier earnings than they would on their own. Owning banks in many countries does not prove that. Consistent results do.

How investors can assess progress

For shareholders, the move from scale to value means using a different scorecard. Assets, customer numbers, and country count matter less. Profitability, efficiency, asset quality, and return on capital matter more. Over the next two to three years, a credible delivery of this strategy will show:

return on equity held consistently above the cost of equity;

further improvement in the cost-to-income ratio;

loan-loss charges returning to normal levels once the legacy clean-up is complete;

a rising share of earnings from fee-based and non-bank businesses;

clear disclosure of returns by subsidiary and by region; and

improved capacity for sustainable shareholder distributions from subsidiaries to the holding company, and from the holding company to shareholders.

That last point deserves attention. Consolidated profit and cash available to shareholders are not the same thing. Subsidiaries often have to retain capital for regulatory or commercial reasons, which limits what they can pass up to the parent. Access Holdings did not declare dividends for FY2025 amid outstanding regulatory requirements, and its Board has said the decision does not reflect weaker performance and that payments could resume once those conditions are met.

How quickly that happens will be an important indicator of progress in restoring dividend capacity.

More broadly, the holding company must show that capital retained in a subsidiary earns more there than it would elsewhere in the Group. The clearer the link between each business and the Group’s overall returns, the stronger the investment case becomes.

The harder phase

Access has shown that it can build. Running a large multinational portfolio well is a different skill. Acquisitions and market entries come with visible milestones. Strong returns, efficient use of capital and dependable shareholder payouts require consistent delivery, year after year.

The early signs are encouraging: better efficiency, stronger profits from the African subsidiaries, a willingness to take provisions early, and a clearly stated focus on returns. They suggest that management understands the nature of the task. What remains is to sustain that discipline long enough for the results to speak for themselves.

Scale has given Access Holdings a platform few African financial groups can match. The task now is to show that this platform can earn returns that justify the capital, complexity, and management attention it demands.

World.title: Campaign Council: Of NDC’s Authority, O-K Movement and Race against Time
World.content:
As the January 16, 2027 presidential poll approaches, the Nigerian Democratic Congress faces a defining test: reconcile competing campaign structures, resolve support-group tensions and translate political enthusiasm into coordinated electoral strength, writes Sunday Aborisade.

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) is approaching a critical moment in its preparations for the January 16, 2027 general election. With Peter Obi as its presidential candidate and Senator Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso as his running mate, the party has assembled a ticket with potential cross-regional appeal. Yet, beneath the enthusiasm surrounding the alliance lies an organisational challenge that could determine whether its electoral promise translates into success: who controls the campaign, how competing interests are accommodated and how quickly a coherent national structure can emerge.

The delayed inauguration of the National Campaign Council (NCC), uncertainty surrounding the party’s manifesto and friction with support groups, particularly the Obi-Kwankwaso movement that established a Presidential Campaign Council (PCC) outside the party’s approved framework, have raised questions about NDC’s preparedness.

These are more than administrative disagreements. They concern the relationship between political parties and the movements supporting their candidates, the balance between institutional authority and grassroots mobilisation, and the ability of an opposition platform to manage competing expectations under a demanding electoral timetable.

The central question is whether the NDC can resolve these differences or allow disputes over recognition, appointments and authority to consume valuable campaign time.

The NDC leadership has attributed the delay in constituting its campaign council to consultations, due diligence and the need to involve its presidential candidates in selecting key officials.

Following a two-day meeting of the National Working Committee (NWC), National Chairman, Senator Moses Cleopas announced October 20 as the proposed inauguration date, explaining that the party had been developing its campaign blueprint since August.

“The constitution and inauguration of the presidential campaign council is a responsibility of the party at the highest level. But the party itself cannot do that without recourse to the presidential candidate and the vice-presidential candidate,” Cleopas said.

He disclosed that Obi and Kwankwaso were consulting on appointments to strategic positions, including director-general, deputy director-general, finance director, mobilisation director and media director.

“It is better to get it right. It is a sensitive election that we are going into, and we must check characters,” he added.

The October 20 inauguration was subsequently postponed to October 26, with the party citing Obi’s overseas engagement. National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director attributed the decision to “the very tight schedule of our presidential candidate” and an important overseas engagement.

The party later announced that its third National Executive Committee (NEC) meeting, scheduled for October 26 in Abuja, would feature the unveiling of the NCC, presentation of certificates of return to candidates and disclosure of its financial accounts.

Although consultation and scrutiny are legitimate, repeated adjustments to the inauguration timetable risk creating an impression of uncertainty. The leadership must demonstrate that consultation has a definite endpoint and will not become an obstacle to implementation.

The candidates deserve meaningful input into the composition of their campaign council. They will defend the party’s policies, lead public engagements and bear the greatest political responsibility for the election.

However, consultation must not translate into the indefinite concentration of campaign decisions in the hands of two individuals.

A presidential campaign council is the operational machinery through which a party coordinates communications, finances, policy, state organisations, mobilisation and electoral protection. The NDC must therefore reconcile the candidates’ preferences with its institutional responsibilities.

Cleopas has warned against appointing officials whose loyalty is uncertain, arguing that divided political commitments could undermine the campaign. While understandable, such screening must not become an open-ended exercise or reduce appointments to questions of personal loyalty rather than competence and clearly defined responsibilities.

The party needs transparent appointment criteria, firm deadlines and a mechanism for resolving disagreements. If the candidates and leadership cannot agree on every position, they should settle essential appointments first and establish a deadline for completing the remaining arrangements.

In an election campaign, the cost of prolonged vacancies may exceed the benefits of pursuing ideal appointments.

The more complicated issue concerns the relationship between the party and the support groups associated with its candidates.

Obi’s political appeal has been sustained by the Obidient Movement and networks of volunteers, professionals, young people, diaspora supporters and community organisers. Kwankwaso also brings an established political constituency and mobilisation networks that the NDC needs to incorporate into its national strategy.

These groups can provide campaign resources, grassroots contacts, volunteers and visibility beyond conventional party structures.

However, the Obi-Kwankwaso movement’s creation of a separate PCC raises a fundamental question: can a support group establish a parallel campaign structure while the party is constituting its own NCC?

Cleopas has insisted that the NDC welcomes support groups but expects them to operate within its approved framework.

“Why wouldn’t we be here and love an OK Movement? Why wouldn’t we be here and love an obedient movement?” he asked.

He added: “We are not against support groups. We know their relevance. We need them, we love them, and we see them as our helpmates.”

The chairman identified the Directorate of Mobilisation under the Office of the National Organisation Secretary as the channel through which support groups should register and coordinate their activities.

His position reflects a legitimate concern about accountability. Multiple bodies issuing competing directives, organising overlapping programmes or claiming authority over the same resources could undermine campaign coordination.

Nevertheless, support groups also have legitimate interests in preserving their identities, networks and operational independence. Many volunteers have invested personal resources and spent years mobilising supporters before the emergence of the NDC as their preferred political platform.

The solution is neither unrestricted parallel authority nor the wholesale absorption of every group into the party hierarchy. It is a negotiated division of responsibilities.

At the heart of the disagreement is whether the campaign belongs primarily to the party, its candidates or the movements mobilising support for them.

The party must retain authority over its official electoral machinery, compliance with electoral requirements and formal campaign coordination. The candidates must exercise substantial influence over political messaging, public engagements and strategic direction. Support groups should retain room to mobilise volunteers, organise community outreach, engage professional associations and develop innovative ways of reaching voters.

These responsibilities are complementary, not mutually exclusive.

A group’s ability to attract thousands of supporters does not automatically confer authority to appoint national campaign officials. Equally, the party’s formal control of its structures does not justify disregarding the experience, resources and grassroots relationships of its supporters.

The NDC should establish a joint coordination mechanism involving party leaders, representatives of Obi and Kwankwaso, and recognised support groups. The body should meet regularly, document decisions and resolve disagreements before they escalate publicly.

The leadership should also review the existing Obi-Kwankwaso PCC, examining its personnel, activities and objectives to determine which elements can be incorporated into the official campaign.

Where appointments or responsibilities conflict with the party’s constitution, the leadership should explain the problem and propose an acceptable alternative. This would defend institutional authority without unnecessarily alienating supporters whose contributions could prove decisive.

Parallel campaign structures can produce conflicting instructions to state coordinators, contradictory media statements, overlapping fundraising activities and competing demands for candidates, venues and volunteers.

Disputes could become particularly damaging if separate groups claim authority over campaign appointments, polling agents or official communications.

Beyond administrative inconvenience, public disagreements could undermine voter confidence, reinforce perceptions of unpreparedness and distract the candidates from communicating their policies.o

However, the leadership must not assume that every disagreement represents disloyalty. In a coalition involving established politicians, newer party officials and independent movements, disagreements are inevitable. What matters is whether credible mechanisms exist to manage them.

Cleopas has maintained that elected party officers cannot be removed arbitrarily and that disputes must be handled in accordance with the party’s constitution. The same commitment to rules should guide relations with support groups.

Procedures must be clear, consistently applied and flexible enough to accommodate legitimate differences. A party demanding discipline from supporters must demonstrate fairness in exercising its authority.

The campaign council is not the only outstanding issue. According to statements from the party leadership, the NDC has yet to establish a firm timeline for releasing its manifesto.

Osa Director previously explained that the candidates and party were conducting due diligence to ensure that the campaign reflected competence, unity and the national interest.

However, organisational preparation and policy communication should proceed simultaneously.

A manifesto should explain the party’s priorities, how its proposals would be implemented and how voters can assess its candidates. The Obi-Kwankwaso ticket must articulate credible plans for addressing economic hardship, insecurity, education, healthcare, employment and institutional reform.

It must also demonstrate how the candidates’ different political experiences and constituencies translate into a coherent governing programme.

The NDC should establish a policy committee comprising professionals, researchers, sectoral specialists and representatives of relevant support groups to consolidate the candidates’ positions into a clear, cost-conscious and measurable manifesto.

The document should be published within an announced timeframe, with accessible summaries for young people, traders, workers, farmers, professionals and other constituencies.

The campaign cannot afford to spend its limited time debating appointments while leaving voters uncertain about what the party intends to accomplish.

The NDC chairman’s emphasis on recruiting polling agents early offers another important lesson from Nigeria’s recent electoral experience.

Cleopas has argued that winning votes is insufficient unless parties ensure that results are accurately recorded and transmitted through the collation process.

“It is vote protection. It is vote protection legitimately, and the vote protection starts from awareness that must be created among our voters,” he said.

The party has begun preparations to recruit polling agents through its state structures rather than wait until the final stages of the electoral process.

This should be expanded into a comprehensive electoral-readiness programme involving trained agents, reliable communication channels, legal support, incident-reporting procedures and a central system for collating polling-unit results.

Support groups could help recruit volunteers, identify training needs and educate voters about participation and lawful vote protection. However, the party must retain responsibility for official nominations, compliance with Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) requirements and coordination of electoral agents.

Vote protection must mean lawful observation, accurate documentation, prompt reporting and appropriate legal action, not intimidation, obstruction or vigilantism.

The objective should be a single, accountable electoral system supported by multiple mobilisation networks.

The campaign council dispute also reflects the NDC’s wider challenge of managing internal disagreements.

Cleopas has disclosed efforts to reconcile prominent Adamawa politicians, including former Secretary to the Government of the Federation, Babachir Lawal, and the party’s governorship candidate, Aishatu Binani.

“Even as you have mentioned Babachir and Binani, the party will not allow them to disintegrate. We need one another,” he said.

The proposed reconciliation recognises that a national campaign cannot succeed if its constituent political interests remain divided.

The same approach should govern disputes involving support groups, state executives and campaign appointments. The leadership should establish a rapid dispute-resolution mechanism with clear timelines for complaints, mediation and decisions.

Where disagreements involve the presidential candidates, the chairman and designated representatives should convene structured consultations rather than allow grievances to escalate through the media.

Party officials must avoid using disciplinary procedures to silence legitimate criticism, while support-group leaders should not interpret every disagreement as evidence that their contributions are being disregarded.

Both sides must distinguish genuine organisational concerns from struggles for influence.

With January 16, 2027, designated as election day, the NDC cannot afford prolonged uncertainty over its campaign machinery. The October 26, 2026 unveiling should be treated as a critical operational milestone rather than a ceremonial event.

First, the party should publish the names and responsibilities of campaign officials, clarify reporting lines and establish a timetable for operations across the states.

Second, Obi and Kwankwaso should jointly endorse the agreed structure to reassure supporters that the ticket is united.

Third, the party should register support groups under transparent criteria, distinguishing independent mobilisation from official campaign responsibilities and constitutional party functions.

Fourth, representatives of the Obi-Kwankwaso movement should negotiate the future of its existing PCC, with the aim of integrating useful personnel and programmes without unnecessarily destroying its identity or grassroots capacity.

Fifth, a campaign coordination committee comprising the party, candidates and recognised support groups should harmonise communications, schedules and mobilisation activities.

Sixth, the manifesto should be released on a definite date, accompanied by policy engagements and public consultations.

Seventh, the NDC should accelerate polling-agent recruitment, voter education, financial transparency and legal preparedness.

Finally, all parties should commit to internal dispute resolution and regular progress reviews to identify bottlenecks before they threaten the campaign.

The NDC’s difficulties present both a risk and an opportunity.

If the leadership insists on control without consultation, it could alienate the support networks needed to expand its electoral reach. If support groups operate independently of agreed structures, they could create competing centres of authority. If the candidates delay decisions while awaiting perfect agreement, the campaign could lose valuable preparation time. Conversely, rushing appointments without adequate scrutiny could create avoidable problems.

The way forward requires a balance between institutional discipline, political inclusion and administrative urgency.

The leadership must recognise that consultation and transparent procedures strengthen party authority. Obi and Kwankwaso must demonstrate that their alliance extends beyond sharing a presidential ticket to a common commitment to organisational success.

Support groups, in turn, must understand that enthusiasm, personal sacrifice and grassroots influence confer political value but do not automatically supersede the party’s formal responsibilities.

Their greatest contribution would be to bring their organisational strengths into a coordinated campaign capable of reaching communities where conventional party structures may be weak.

Ultimately, the contest is about whether the NDC can demonstrate the competence required to compete for national power. Its promises of transparency, internal discipline and early electoral preparation will carry greater weight if reflected in how it manages its affairs.

The coming weeks should therefore be a period of consolidation rather than confrontation. The campaign council must be inaugurated, the manifesto published, support groups accommodated within a clear framework and electoral preparations accelerated.

The election will ultimately be decided by voters, not the number of meetings held or titles assigned to campaign officials. But voters must first have compelling reasons to believe that the party is organised, prepared and capable of translating promises into action.

The real test of the Obi-Kwankwaso alliance is not simply whether supporters can mobilise crowds or the NDC can announce a campaign council. It is whether both can convert political enthusiasm into a disciplined, inclusive and credible national campaign.

The NDC still has an opportunity to get this right. Whether it succeeds will depend on its ability to replace uncertainty with decisions, rivalry with cooperation and parallel structures with a shared electoral purpose.

World.title: FG: Era of Holding Nigeria’s Oil, Gas Assets as Souvenirs Over
World.content:
*Drill-or-drop policy: Operators returning assets voluntarily, says Lokpobiri

*Explains how exit of EPC firms pushed up project costs

*Kachikwu: How govt interference delayed decisions as NNPC GMD

*Ekpo: Nigeria’s 215TCF gas reserves must lead to higher domestic supply

*NEITI: NUPRC has brought greater openness to oil bid rounds

Emmanuel Addeh in Abuja

The federal government has declared an end to the era of oil companies holding petroleum assets without developing them, insisting that operators must either invest in production or relinquish their licences under the drill-or-drop provisions of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA).



Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Oil), Senator Heineken Lokpobiri, said the policy has empowered the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission (NUPRC) to recover undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and able to develop them.



Also, a former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, and Group Managing Director of the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), Prof. Ibe Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company.



In the same vein, Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekperikpe Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 Trillion Cubic Feet (TCF) of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years.

Similarly, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, has maintained that the PIA has brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs).

They all spoke in a series of interviews published in ‘Upstream Gaze’, a special edition of a quarterly magazine by the NUPRC to mark its fifth anniversary.



Lokpobiri said the policy had helped make petroleum assets available for fresh investment, with 50 assets recently offered for bidding and another licensing round in the offing.

The drill-or-drop policy, provided for under the PIA requires oil and gas companies to develop their licensed petroleum assets within the stipulated period or risk losing them to the government. The policy empowers the regulator to revoke or recover licences for undeveloped assets and make them available to investors willing and capable of putting them into production.

Essentially, it is designed to discourage speculative ownership and the hoarding of oil blocks which has been the norm, accelerate exploration and development, attract fresh investment, increase crude oil and gas production, and help Nigeria achieve its production targets.



Lokpobiri said: “The drill-or-drop provision is one of the most consequential provisions of the PIA. It has kept operators on their toes. If you do not develop your assets within the provisions of the law, the NUPRC has the authority to recover those assets and make them available to investors that are willing and able to develop them.



“The era of holding assets as souvenirs or symbols of wealth is gone: you either drill or drop. Some operators are now willing to relinquish assets voluntarily because that may be preferable to regulatory recovery. Others are reassessing their portfolios and recognising that certain assets no longer fit their development plans.”

He also attributed the increase in active drilling rigs to reforms and improved regulatory activity, saying the number had risen from between 10 and 14 in 2023 to more than 60 currently.

However, the minister said the departure of major Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contractors, deep-offshore contractors and other service providers had contributed to higher project costs in Nigeria, following prolonged uncertainty before the passage of the PIA.



According to him, inadequate project activity had made it difficult for contractors to sustain their operations, prompting some to leave the country and reducing competition in critical areas of the industry.

“The cost of our projects became higher than in some other jurisdictions because there was limited competition and insufficient project activity. Contractors can only survive where there are projects to execute. If the project pipeline dries up, they will leave,” he said.

“Many contractors therefore left the country, leaving only one or two providers in some areas and contributing to prohibitive costs. That was a major challenge, but we are now working to bring them back.”



Lokpobiri said the government was engaging contractors in Europe and America to encourage their return, while pursuing fiscal, operational and regulatory reforms to improve Nigeria’s competitiveness.

He added that a recent presidential executive order was expected to help unlock almost $50 billion in deep-offshore investments, while the re-entry of shut-in wells following recent divestments was contributing to production growth.



He cited developments following Seplat Energy’s acquisition of ExxonMobil’s assets and Renaissance Africa Energy’s acquisition of Shell’s onshore assets as examples of efforts to revive previously inactive wells.

Looking ahead, Lokpobiri said Nigeria could significantly increase crude oil production over the next five years if investment commitments and development programmes materialised, projecting a potential output range of 3 million to 5 million barrels per day.

Kachikwu: Govt Interference Hobbled My Work as Minister

Also, former Group Managing Director of the NNPC and former Minister of State for Petroleum Resources, Prof. Kachikwu, has recalled how government interference and cumbersome approval processes delayed decisions and constrained investment during his tenure at the national oil company.



Kachikwu said the petroleum industry had suffered from excessive government control, which restricted managerial independence and made it difficult to implement decisions quickly, even when the commercial case for action was clear.

“The oil sector could be very frustrating because there was a great deal of government interference. In my case, I had the rare privilege of serving as both GMD of NNPC and Minister of State. Dealing with the investment process at NNPC was difficult because you could hardly do anything without government approval.



“The lack of independence constrained decision-making. The oil sector was run almost like a conventional government agency, which limited creativity. One of the things I tried to do when I came in was to bring more of a private-sector orientation into NNPC and the Ministry. It took quite a while for the system to adjust to new ways of doing things,” he explained.

He said the absence of clearly defined institutional powers under the old Petroleum Act meant investment decisions often depended on the initiative of individual officeholders, while the PIA had introduced greater clarity on responsibilities and institutional independence.

However, Kachikwu expressed concern that significant government control remained and that the new law had yet to deliver the scale of investment anticipated.



He noted that much of the investment recorded since the PIA’s passage involved domestic acquisitions, mergers and takeovers of existing assets, rather than the development of major new production platforms and floating production facilities at the expected pace.

Kachikwu also argued that Nigeria needed to raise its production ambitions beyond the federal government’s 3 million barrels per day target, saying the country had the potential to produce 4 million barrels daily by 2030.



“I think Nigeria could do four million barrels per day by 2030; targeting three million barrels may be underestimating our potential. We have to recognise that oil will not simply remain in the ground waiting for us indefinitely,” he said.

“The world is changing. Electric vehicles are expanding, solar power is growing, alternative energy systems are developing and new producing countries are entering the market. The world will not wait while we increase production gradually. We need a significant volumetric shift and we should sit down and ask what would it take to reach four million barrels per day,” he added.



He said Nigeria needed to identify the investments, projects, infrastructure and timelines required to achieve the higher target, warning that the country was competing with emerging oil producers, including Guyana and Namibia, for international capital.

Predictable fiscal terms, transparency, competitive project economics and timely government decisions, he stressed, were essential to attracting the investments required to increase production.

Ekpo: Enormous Gas Resources Must Benefit Nigerians

In the gas sector, the Minister of State for Petroleum Resources (Gas), Ekpo, said Nigeria must translate its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into higher domestic supply, stronger infrastructure and industrial growth over the next five years.

He reiterated that the country was targeting gas production of 10 billion standard cubic feet per day by 2027 and 12 billion standard cubic feet daily by 2030, but achieving the goals would require faster development of non-associated gas resources and sustained investment in processing and pipeline infrastructure.



“Over the next five years, Nigeria must convert its 215 trillion cubic feet of proven gas reserves into increased production, stronger infrastructure and sustainable industrial growth. Success must ultimately translate into reliable gas supply for power generation, fertiliser production, petrochemicals, manufacturing, Liquefied Petroleum Gas and Compressed Natural Gas, alongside sustained regional gas supply projects and Liquefied Natural Gas exports,” he said.



On the Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) initiative, introduced to provide a cheaper transport alternative following the removal of the petrol subsidy, Ekpo said the planned national network of refuelling stations was being expanded from 500 to 1,000.

He repeated that more than $2 billion had been catalysed in the CNG ecosystem since 2023, supporting 120,000 vehicle conversions, more than 400 certified conversion centres and over 90 operational refuelling stations.

He said the priority was to extend access beyond major cities and ensure that the lower cost of CNG translated into reduced transport expenses for Nigerians.

NEITI: NUPRC Has Improved Licensing Processes

Speaking on transparency in the upstream sector, the Executive Secretary of the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI), Musa Adar, commended the NUPRC for improving licensing procedures, disclosure and regulatory oversight since its establishment under the PIA.



Adar, who chaired the House Committee on Petroleum Resources (Upstream) in the Ninth National Assembly, said the law had created a clearer institutional and regulatory framework after years of concerns over transparency, accountability and disclosure.

“The NUPRC, as one of the institutions established under the Act, has helped to improve the licensing process, strengthen disclosure and provide more structured oversight of upstream operations. These are commendable developments,” he said.



On the 2025 licensing round monitored by NEITI, Adar said the organisation was awaiting its final report and would not pre-empt its conclusions, although preliminary feedback from field officers had not identified any material misalignment in the process.

He called for further improvements in disclosure, accountability and regulatory responsiveness, noting that investors valued regulators that were firm, fair, transparent and predictable.

Adar also argued that Nigeria’s ambitions should extend beyond crude oil production to greater domestic refining and petrochemical processing to retain more value within the economy and reduce exposure to imported refined products.

Olu of Warri: Indigenes Now Have Clearer Stake in Oil Sector

For his part, the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, said the PIA had brought greater calm and responsibility to oil-producing communities by giving them a clearer stake in petroleum operations through Host Communities Development Trusts (HCDTs).

He said the framework had improved communities’ understanding of their entitlements and created incentives to protect petroleum infrastructure, although official data would be needed to establish the extent of any reduction in sabotage.

The PIA requires oil companies to contribute 3 per cent of their actual operating expenditure for the preceding financial year to the applicable HCDT.



“As someone who is on the ground, I would say that it has brought a sense of calm. There is also a clearer sense of direction and consideration. Before the PIA, these obligations were not set out in law in the same way. Today, the framework is captured in black and white and stakeholders have greater clarity about what is expected.

“When people know that a defined percentage is available, there can be better planning and consideration of development priorities. That goes a long way towards giving communities a sense of ownership and belonging,” he posited.

World.title: Nigeria’s Index Ebola Case Set for Medical Evacuation Abroad Today, Two Contacts Test Negative
World.content:
Quarantined persons may get N100,000 weekly upkeep

Ebola, brain drain top agenda as doctors in W/Africa meet in Abuja

Emmanuel Addeh and Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja

Nigeria’s index case of the Ebola virus disease is expected to be evacuated abroad for further medical treatment early Monday (today), a source familiar with the development told THISDAY last night.

The source said arrangements had been made to fly the 42-year-old woman out of the country by 6am, adding that a medical evacuation aircraft was already at the airport awaiting her arrival.

The fresh development came as the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said two suspected Ebola cases from the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) and Rivers State have tested negative, while 53 primary contacts of the confirmed index case have been identified and are being monitored.

The agency also said that based on complaints by the contacts in quarantine, the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week.

However, NCDC said that the welfare arrangement was in the interim, as states were expected to take over maintenance of the contacts cases in their domain subsequently.

“The medivac plane is already at the airport waiting to evacuate her,” the source said, adding that the federal government was expected to announce the development after the patient had departed Nigeria.

The proposed evacuation is coming amid heightened surveillance and contact-tracing efforts by Nigerian health authorities to prevent further transmission of the disease.

Earlier, the Director General of the NCDC, Dr. Jide Idris, spoke at a press briefing in Abuja to provide an update on Nigeria’s Ebola disease response.

Idris said the search for other secondary contacts was ongoing, assuring Nigerians that the federal government through Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, NCDC, FCT health authorities and partners was fully committed to containing the outbreak.

“As previously announced, Nigeria has confirmed one case of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The patient is currently receiving medical care under isolation, with infection prevention and control measures in place. Clinical teams continue to monitor and manage patient’s condition,” he said.

According to him, the 53 primary contacts comprise 44 personnel from the hospital where the index case is receiving treatment, while nine additional contacts from the index, three from Julius Berger office where she visited before coming down with symptoms, and three health workers who attended to index case.

He said samples collected from the husband of the index case tested negative, adding that two suspected cases in FCT and Rivers also tested negative, but will have more follow up.

Responding to a question about the true identity of the index case, the DG said she is from Uganda and married to a Swiss national, and the government is carrying out further investigations to establish her exact travel details. He said Nigerian officials will meet with Ugandan officials online to exchange information.

Idris explained that the case was detected through event-based surveillance after vigilant healthcare workers recognised clinical features that raised concern.

He said the response was being implemented through a structured Incident Management System coordinated by the Emergency Operations Centre under the leadership of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Ali Pate, and Presidential Task Force on EVD.

Idris listed critical components as identifying and monitoring contacts for 21 days, ensuring safe clinical care, strengthening infection prevention and control across facilities, boosting surveillance and laboratory capacity, and community engagement.

The DG said the centre is being assisted by the Department of State Services (DSS) in tracking contacts, has expanded case definition for community surveillance, and is boosting genomic capabilities of 12 laboratories to test for Ebola.

He said the government has designated the University of Abuja Teaching Hospital as a special isolation centre and has fumigated premises of the index case.

On the welfare of contacts, Idris said the federal government was considering the payment of N100,000 per week for feeding and upkeep of each quarantined contact, while states are expected to take responsibility for contacts in their domain.

He appealed to Nigerians to cooperate with contact tracing teams, provide accurate information and adhere to public health advisories.

“An identified contact does not mean you have Ebola. It means public health teams need to assess and monitor your health,” he said, urging hand hygiene, avoiding contact with blood or body fluids of suspected cases and prompt reporting.

Idris commended healthcare workers whose vigilance led to detection and called on all public and private facilities to strengthen screening, triage and availability of personal protective equipment.

He recalled leading Lagos State response in 2014 as Commissioner for Health, saying experience taught lessons on leadership, coordination and public trust which are being deployed.

He warned against misinformation and stigmatisation, urging reliance on verified information from NCDC and Federal Ministry of Health.

“The government has worked hard to strengthen the surveillance system and boost capacities of disease testing laboratories. Success depends on the whole of society,” he said, noting that the patient is improving.

Meanwhile, to find solutions to major healthcare challenges facing West Africa, issues such as brain drain, infrastructure deficit and Ebola threat will be among key issues for deliberation as West African College of Physicians (WACP) marks 50 years anniversary with a summit in Abuja beginning on Monday.

The body had earlier visited President Bola Tinubu at State House Presidential Villa in Abuja where the president urged them to help find solutions to some of the daunting healthcare challenges facing the region.

Speaking at a press conference on Saturday, President of WACP, Dr. Mamadou Mourtalla, said the College will appraise developments in the health sector as it relates to new scientific discoveries, manpower training, infrastructure and infectious disease control.

“We’ll be discussing various perspectives, how to deal with the pandemic, an epidemic coming up in Africa which puts a lot of stress on our health system. We have over 70 scientific papers based on this theme. At the end, we usually issue a communique,” Mourtalla said.

He said implementation of resolutions is key, adding that the President of ECOWAS Commission, Director General of West African Health Organisation and President Tinubu who promised to send the Minister of Health will be present to make recommendations to leaders.

Assistant Secretary General of WACP, Dr. Habibu Galadanci, said the conference has scheduled deliberations on several key areas including brain drain, infrastructure deficit, rise in non-communicable diseases like kidney disease, hypertension, and infectious disease epidemics including current spread of Ebola.

“The scientific content will touch on several aspects of medicine, including disease conditions, health policies and contemporary medical issues,” he said.

On brain drain, he said the conference has a whole session that will look at push and pull dynamics.

“There are pull dynamics, push dynamics, and we are going to look at that and find solutions. When we saw President Tinubu, that was one main thing he charged us with, that we should discuss Japa syndrome and find solutions,” Galadanci said.

He said the conference will also look at use of artificial intelligence in medicine and ethical concerns in managing patients, maternal and reproductive health, access to safe healthcare for women and children, mental health priorities and development of balanced scorecards for improving performance of public sector hospitals.

Galadanci said the conference will be a landmark event that offers opportunity for stakeholders to pause and look at where College has come from in 50 years, achievements and pending issues.

“We still have a lot of problems, but we have come a long way, at least we can train our doctors. We have specialists, so many doctors that they poach them from outside because of how good we are,” he said.

Other areas include kidney disease epidemic, dementia which is creeping into society as population ages, and mental health often stigmatised and downplayed.

As part of its corporate social responsibility, members of College organised a medical outreach programme in Waru community, a suburb in Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Abuja on Saturday, attracting a large crowd of men, women and children who benefited from free healthcare services.

The week-long summit in Abuja is expected to bring over 1,300 experts from across West Africa to propose solutions for the next 50 years.

World.title: FirstHoldCo Reports N911bn Profit Before Tax in 9 Months 2026; Reinforcing Profitability and Resilience
World.content:
First HoldCo Plc’s 9 months 2026 performance marks an important transition: the Group is moving from balance sheet repair toward a more resilient, capital-supported growth phase. The headline is compelling — profit before tax rose 60.8% year on year to N911.2 billion, while profit after tax advanced 65.1% to N744.5 billion; importantly, the quality of this growth is also improving.

First, earnings have broadened year on year and beyond the traditional interest income. Second, operating discipline has improved efficiency. Third, stronger capital and better asset-quality indicators are increasing the Group’s capacity to absorb risk and pursue selective growth. These factors support a more durable earnings profile and a stronger long-term shareholder proposition.

Profitability continues to strengthen

Gross earnings increased 8.8% to N2.87 trillion, but profitability expanded faster: profit before tax reached N911.2 billion and profit after tax reached N744.5 billion. Post-tax return on average equity improved to 27.7% from 24.7% in the previous year, while return on average assets rose to 3.3% from 2.6% in 9M 2025 showing that balance sheet growth is generating stronger returns.

This growth was supported by a more diversified revenue mix. Non-interest income surged 143.5% to N722.9 billion, supported by a 48.1% increase in net fee and commission income to N316.4 billion. Transaction-led revenues, including electronic banking, funds transfers and credit-related services and other non-interest income contributions are giving the Group more diversified avenues for earnings growth.

Operating leverage is becoming visible

Operating income rose 10.3% even as operating expenses declined 8.1% to N866.6 billion. The resulting cost-to-income ratio of 43.7%, down from 52.4%, is a strong indicator of improving operating leverage and cost discipline particularly in a 15.39% inflationary environment. The result suggests that management is not relying on balance-sheet expansion alone; it is extracting more value from the franchise while containing the cost base.



Core margins present a compelling earnings-upside opportunity. Although net interest income moderated by 16.0% to N1.26 trillion and net interest margin adjusted to 8.7% from 11.3% amid softer asset yields, the improvement in cost of funds to 4.5% from 4.9% demonstrates effective funding discipline and provides a strong foundation for margin recovery. Enhanced risk-adjusted pricing and a more efficient funding mix offer credible levers for margin expansion and sustainable returns, while maintaining rigorous credit standards and asset quality.



A balance sheet with greater strategic capacity

The balance sheet provides greater capacity for disciplined growth. Total assets increased 18.1% from year-end 2025 to N32.20 trillion, while customer deposits grew 21.3% to N22.91 trillion. Group equity rose 17.0% to N3.86 trillion. In contrast, net customer loans expanded by a deliberate and measured 4.8% to N9.39 trillion. This combination of strong funding growth, firmer equity and selective lending reflects disciplined capital deployment rather than indiscriminate risk-taking.

FirstBank’s capital adequacy ratio improved to 18.6% at September 2026 from 16.7% at half-year. The stronger capital buffer increases resilience supports regulatory confidence and provides greater flexibility to finance attractive opportunities. Importantly, capital is strengthening while profitability is accelerating, improving the Group’s capacity to compound value internally.

Asset-quality repair is gaining traction

Asset-quality repair is also advancing. The Group’s non-performing loan ratio declined to 10.4% from 13.9% at H1 2026 while NPL coverage, including regulatory reserves, increased to 98.8%. Impairment charges declined 28.3% to N207.1 billion and recoveries reached N94.3 billion.

These figures show broad-based progress: stronger coverage, reduced impairment charges and meaningful recoveries to date. Although the NPL ratio remains above management’s desired level, the downward trajectory improves protection and loss-absorption capacity.

To further strengthen asset quality by year-end, management could combine targeted restructuring of viable exposures, negotiated settlements and intensified recoveries with ongoing legal actions. These asset-quality measures are supported by more than N850 billion already held in regulatory risk reserves, providing a substantial prudential buffer against identified credit risks. Accordingly, subject to applicable accounting and regulatory treatment, additional impairment charges recognised in the books would be broadly capital-neutral, enabling management to accelerate the resolution or write-off of fully provided loans with limited recovery prospects without materially weakening regulatory capital, while recovery efforts continue. These measures should further reduce the NPL ratio, reinforce coverage and underscore the strength of the balance sheet.

Diversification strengthens the earnings growth outlook

Commercial Banking remains the Group’s principal earnings subsidiary, generating gross earnings of N2.70 trillion and profit before tax of N784.7 billion. Its scale, deposit franchise and broad customer relationships underpin recurring revenue.

Alongside this core franchise, Investment Banking and Asset Management is becoming more significant. The segment generated gross earnings of N120.1 billion, up 85.5%, and profit before tax of N85.7 billion, up 133.6%.
