World.title: LIVESTREAM | Eugene de Kock testifies before TRC inquiry
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Former apartheid police commander Eugene de Kock, known as “Prime Evil”, is testifying before the TRC Cases Inquiry on Monday.

De Kock headed the notorious Vlakplaas unit near Pretoria, which was used to plan attacks on anti-apartheid activists. The unit was also linked to the torture, interrogation and killing of freedom fighters.

In 1996, De Kock was sentenced to two life terms in prison, plus 212 years, for six murders. His victims included askari Goodwill Sikhakane, members of the Nelspruit Five and ANC lawyer Bheki Mlangeni.

READ | De Kock says activists were not seen as terrorists

In 1997, De Kock applied for amnesty through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC).

The commission granted him amnesty for some offences but rejected applications for most others, finding insufficient political motivation.

De Kock was released on parole in 2015 after serving 19 years in prison.

World.title: Who's who at your voting station? Your guide to the IEC election team
World.content:
Who checks whether you are registered to vote?

The voters’ roll officer or voter management device (VMD) operator helps verify voters’ details against the voters’ roll.

Voters must be checked against the relevant records before proceeding through the voting process. The VMD is used to support voter verification and the administration of the voters’ roll.

If there is a problem with a voter’s details or the device, the matter can be referred to the relevant election official for assistance.

Who gives you your ballot papers?

The ballot paper issuer is responsible for issuing ballot papers to eligible voters at the appropriate stage of the voting process.

Voters should follow the instructions provided by election officials and make sure they understand how to mark their ballot papers correctly.

Who controls the ballot box?

The ballot box controller helps oversee the ballot box and supports procedures intended to protect the integrity of the voting process.

Election officials are responsible for following the prescribed procedures for handling election materials and ensuring ballot boxes are managed appropriately.

What does an inker do?

The inker is responsible for applying the prescribed electoral ink as part of the voting process.

The procedure helps election officials administer voting in accordance with the applicable rules and safeguards.

World.title: Tshwane poll: DA leads, but Brink trails Moya
World.content:
PRETORIA - The Democratic Alliance is leading the race in Tshwane, while the African National Congress is losing support to several rival parties, according to the latest eNCA-MarkData survey projections.

The projections put the DA in first place ahead of the upcoming local government elections, with the ANC in second position, followed by the Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), ActionSA and the Freedom Front Plus.

However, the DA remains short of an outright majority, meaning it could need coalition partners to govern the capital.

Elections analyst Wayne Sussman says the survey points to a significant shift in Tshwane’s political landscape, with the ANC losing support to competing parties.

While the DA can take encouragement from leading the race, Sussman says it may struggle to form a stable coalition without the ANC.

The projections suggest that no single party is likely to secure an outright majority, making coalition negotiations potentially decisive in determining the city’s next government.

World.title: Why Utumishi Girls murder suspects are seeking plea bargain deal with DPP
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nine students linked to the Utumishi Girls Academy dormitory fire that claimed the lives of 16 learners appear before Chief Magistrate Ramadhan Abdulqadir at the Naivasha Law Courts, on June 3, 2026. [Kipsang Joseph, Standard]

Two of the eight minors charged over the deaths of 16 Utumishi Girls Academy students have initiated plea-bargaining requests with the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), weeks after being denied bail.

The new twist emerged before Kibera High Court Judge Diana Kavedza on Monday, when lawyers for two of the minors told the court they had formally approached the prosecution to seek plea-bargaining negotiations.

Lawyer Odiero Osiemo, representing Subject Minor 3, told the court he had submitted the request through his office, prompting the state prosecutor to confirm it had formally received the application.

“We do confirm that indeed we have formally received a plea bargain request from accused 3 here through his lawyer Osiemo,” State Counsel Linda Ndambiri told the court.

Ndambiri said the office of the DPP had held an initial engagement with the minor's lawyer and parents, who indicated that they needed more time to obtain proper instructions from the child before proceeding with a plea deal.

Lawyer PK Nganga, representing Subject Minor 7, separately informed the court that he had written to the ODPP seeking a plea bargain after consulting the child's parents.

“I have been contacted by the parents of the student, Subject 7 and we have formally written to the ODPP requesting a plea bargain in the murder case and we have channelled the letter this morning,” Nganga said.

He sought permission for two enhanced visits to Kamae Borstal Institution to enable him to discuss the request with his client and communicate the outcome of the prosecution's engagement.

However, Ndambiri told the court that the prosecution had not formally received Nganga's request.

“We are yet to formally receive the request for the plea bargaining,” she said.

The lawyers representing the other six minors said they were yet to receive instructions on whether their clients would pursue similar negotiations.

Lawyer Kipcoech, representing Subjects 1, 5, 6 and 8, said they were still consulting their clients and parents but urged the court to set a hearing date to fast-track the trial because it involved children.

Lawyer Nelson Omagwa, representing Subject Minor 2, said he had only recently been hired and had not discussed any intention to pursue a plea bargain with his client.

The lawyer representing Subject Minor 4 also said he had not received instructions to pursue the plea deal negotiations and sought a hearing date.

Plea bargaining is a legal process through which the prosecution and an accused person negotiate a possible resolution of a criminal case under the law, subject to the court's approval.

In a murder case, the process may involve an admission of guilt to an agreed charge or other legally permissible terms.

However, submitting a request does not amount to pleading guilty, and negotiations do not guarantee an agreement or a particular sentence.

Justice Kavedza urged the parties seeking plea bargains to move swiftly, saying the court needed to establish whether the negotiations would proceed or whether the case should move to trial.

The judge also declined to fix the matter for hearing, noting that her diary was full for the remainder of the year and directed that the lawyers for the other six minors also pursue plea bargaining if they do so.

The court also allowed parents of all eight minors to have two enhanced visits per month at the institution where the children are being held to facilitate the negotiations.

The parents were directed to liaise with the institution to arrange the visits.

The judge further directed Kamae Borstal children's officer Hilda Mbatha to provide details supporting a request by the lawyer representing Subject Minor 4 for monthly dental appointments for braces.

The court sought clear appointment dates every month, the hospital to be visited and an explanation of the medical need.

On the education status of the eight students, officer Mbatha told the court that the minors were continuing with their education while in custody and were expected to sit their second-term examinations next week.

Justice Kavedza directed that the children continue with their studies and ordered that the matter be mentioned on November 11, 2026, for an update on the progress of the plea-bargaining negotiations.

The developments come weeks after the court declined to release the eight minors on bail, ordering that they remain in custody pending trial.

The minors face 16 counts of murder contrary to Section 203 as read with Section 204 of the Penal Code over the deaths of 16 students in a dormitory fire at Utumishi Girls Academy in Gilgil, Nakuru County, on the night of May 27 and 28, 2026.

They pleaded not guilty to the charges when they were arraigned in July.

The fire also left 79 students injured.

World.title: Sakaja protests release of 14 suspects linked to Eastleigh collapsed building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has protested the release of suspects linked to the collapsed building in Eastleigh.

While pushing for the county to have prosecutorial powers, Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court.

Sakaja in statement posted on his X account (formerly Twitter) said City Hall had taken enforcement action against those involved after establishing change of user from a residential property to a commercial had been approved.

According to Sakaja, architectural plans required to authorise construction had not been approved.

The Governor said County officers arrested the suspects and handed them over to Kamukunji Police Station because county governments no longer hold prosecutorial powers they previously held.

“We enforced the law and arrested those involved. However, because we do not have prosecutorial powers, the suspects were handed over to Kamukunji Police Station. They were reportedly released on a cash bail of Sh50,000 without being taken to court,” Sakaja said.

“We want the police to explain why the suspects were released without being presented in court and why construction was allowed to continue. These are serious questions that must be answered,” he added.

A police occurrence book entry from Kamukunji Police Station indicates that 14 suspects were booked into custody on June 17, 2026, over the alleged offences relating to contravention of city planning laws.

Enforcement action and arrests were made severally by the county officials and most recently in July after failing to comply with the enforcement order below. However the suspects were released on a 50k bail at Kamukunji police on the very same day. Prosecution of the same was also denied. We have repeatedly asked for the resumption of the power to prosecute such violations of such county and county related laws after this was taken away from County governments in 2024 (one such letter to the office of the DPP is attached). Meanwhile, several such cases have either been rejected by prosecutors (who are independent of the County), dismissed by the justice system or have had minimal fines imposed. Fining a developer 50k for an illegal development with hundreds of millions without orders to stop and remove the offensive development is completely unreasonable. I raised this in the Senate a fortnight ago and we shall keep pushing for a review of this position. All of these instances, where enforcement action has been curtailed, blocked or interfered with, will be published to the public. October 25, 2026

The entry, recorded under OB No. 98/17/06/2026, names the suspects and states that they were booked by Nairobi City County officers before being placed in police cells.

A separate Kenya Police Service record indicates that 10 suspects were subsequently released on a cash bail of Sh50,000.

The entry, recorded at 9.44pm, states that the release was carried out on the instructions of the Officer Commanding Station (OCS), identified in the record as C.I. Onyapidi, through Corporal Awadh.

The record references receipt number 2039434 and states that the suspects left the station without complaints.

However, the documents do not, on their own, establish the specific charges against the suspects, the legal basis for the bail arrangement or whether they were subsequently presented in court.

The discrepancy between the 14 suspects recorded as booked into custody and the 10 named in the release entry also raises questions about the subsequent status of the other suspects. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Sakaja said a June 2025 enforcement notice adds another dimension to the questions surrounding the property and the enforcement of planning regulations.

The notice, issued by Nairobi City County over alleged construction works undertaken without the required development permission, cited the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, 2019, and county by-laws.

It directed the recipient to stop the works and remove the development described as illegal, warning that the County could undertake the required action and recover the costs if the directives were not followed.

The notice also provided for an appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee.

Sakaja clarified that approval to change a property’s use from private to commercial-cum-residential does not amount to approval of architectural plans authorising construction.

He said the County approved the change of use but did not approve the architectural plans, yet construction proceeded.

I have seen some people peddling a fake approval document alleging that the Eastleigh development was approved. It is telling that this is the same document that the Eastleigh developer used to get NCA approval. They allege that the development was approved in January of 2024. This is not true. The application for development as shown below was made in November of 2024, it could not have been approved in February of the same year. Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: Pregnant woman rescued from collapsed Eastleigh building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya Red Cross workers after rescuing a man who trapped in the rubble.

A pregnant woman was on Saturday evening rescued from the multi-storey building that collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh estate on Friday, October 23 and rushed to the Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) for treatment.

She is the second person to rescued as earlier in the afternoon the Kenya Red Cross society announced the rescue of a man from the ill-fated building.

The man was also taken to KNH for treatment with the society saying that the rescue followed hours of work put in by the search and rescue multi-agency team.

“After hours of painstaking work alongside multi-agency partners, our search and rescue teams in Eastleigh brought a trapped man out of the rubble,” said Red Cross.

The rescue comes even as the fate of six people who were reported missing on Friuday remains unknown with rescue teams still continuing with the search at the site of the collapsed building along Yusuf Haji Avenue.

The society said that 66 of the 67 construction workers who were at the site had been traced and accounted for but the search continues for people who may have been near the site of the collapsed building.

The development comes as police announced that they had launched a manhunt for the for the owner and contractor of a building.

Police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said that officers had launched a probe in collaboration with relevant bodies to establish the cause of the collapse and determine criminal liability.

“Any individual or entity found culpable of negligence or of violating building regulations will face the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.

Nyaga called on members of public to stay completely clear of Yusuf Haji Avenue and 9th Street to give access to heavy excavators, specialised canine units and rescue personnel to perform their duties.

Earlier Saturday, at least 31 families reported their relatives missing as coordinated rescue efforts entered their second day.

No deaths have been reported so far.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) on Friday evening identified the developer, contractor, architect and structural engineer listed for the collapsed building.

The Authority has faced scrutiny over its oversight role, as Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the project had failed to comply with construction guidelines.

He said the county had forwarded relevant information to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations for further investigation.

In a statement, the NCA said the building was registered on July 30, 2025, as a proposed development on 9th Street in Eastleigh.

It identified 9th Street Plaza Limited as the developer and Stromax Holdings E.A. Limited as the contractor.

Emmanuel Mwangi Maina was listed as the project architect, while Joseph Muturi Mugu was named as the structural engineer.

World.title: Several feared trapped in Eastleigh building collapse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

What was supposed to be a usually busy Friday afternoon in Eastleigh's 9th Street turned chaotic after an 18-floor building that was under construction came down, tumbling.

By Friday evening, rescue operations were still ongoing, with cries from people believed to have been trapped being heard from a distance as bulldozers and rescuers continued the search operation.

Two victims, a man and a woman, who were injured in the building had been rescued and rushed to hospital as the search continued.

Asha Jilo, one of the witnesses, said the building collapsed around 1:09 pm just after the afternoon prayers.

"Immediately after the building collapsed, we started contacting some people we know who work there, one of them was still available on the phone until around 3 pm, when his phone went offline," Jilo shared

On Fridays, Eastleigh is usually a hive of activities, being the main market day, but all the businesses were shut as police were battling rowdy youths, some of them believed to be opportunists.

The building, whose height was said to be about 15 floors, had not been cleared for occupation as required, raising questions about why the investors had allowed it to be taken.

It is said that the ground and first floors were already occupied by businesses, raising fears that the number of victims could be high. Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

At the time of the collapse, it is said that some construction workers were busy on the upper floors.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, who visited the scene after the collapse, was still gathering information about the building. The first priority was about saving lives.

“The building that collapsed is around 16 floors, and we have got information about the building, but what is more concerned right now is for us to save lives,” said Sakaja

Adding, “Equipment has already been mobilized, excavators and breakers, so we can be able to remove the big debris and save lives,’

The Governor said some developers engage qualified professionals to secure construction approvals before dismissing them and disregarding approved plans and safety standards.

He urged professional bodies to strengthen oversight, investigate such cases and take appropriate disciplinary action, stressing that developers must comply with approved designs, engage qualified personnel and obtain occupation certificates after safety inspections.

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud, who was at the scene, said that, according to reliable information, several people were trapped inside the debris, inside the big boulders, and the rescue effort is ongoing.

The city police boss said investigations will be carried out to ascertain who is responsible for any negligence.

“If there will be any death, that is negligence by murder. Whoever is the owner, whoever authorized the building, all of them will be charged properly. But that will come after thorough investigation is done,” he warned

Adding, “We will not excuse anybody on this matter. This has become now and then, and we will make sure that people face the law accordingly for any criminal negligence,”

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Kenya confirms third Ebola case
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya has confirmed a third case of Ebola involving a 65-year-old woman who is a close relative of the first two patients.

The Ministry of Health, in a statement, said the woman developed a fever, sore throat and malaise while in quarantine, prompting her isolation and testing.

Her samples tested positive for Ebola at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute (KEMRI).

According to the Health Director-General Patrick Amoth, the patient has been transferred to an infectious disease unit, where she is receiving supportive care and being monitored.

“Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease,” the statement read.

The second patient, on the other hand, is in stable condition and responding well to supportive care.

The latest case brings the number of confirmed Ebola infections in Kenya to three.

According to the Ministry, of the 130 contacts identified so far, 127 had been traced and placed in quarantine, with efforts ongoing to trace the remaining three.

World.title: Motorists, households face fresh fuel price hikes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

EPRA attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East. [FIle, Standard]

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) has increased fuel prices, raising the cost of super petrol by Sh12.93 per litre, diesel by Sh9.90, and kerosene by Sh28.49.

The new prices, effective from October 15 to November 14, 2026, will see motorists in Nairobi pay up to Sh226.96 per litre for super petrol, Sh227.76 for diesel, and Sh219.85 for kerosene.

EPRA Director-General Edward Mwirigi Kinyua attributed the price increases to the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has disrupted petroleum supply chains and driven up the cost of importing fuel.

The rise in kerosene prices is likely to hit low-income households that rely on the fuel for cooking and lighting.

Meanwhile, higher diesel prices could raise the cost of transporting goods and operating public service vehicles, potentially driving up fares and commodity prices.

Diesel is a key fuel for the country's freight transport sector and a significant portion of public service vehicle operations, meaning the increase could have a ripple effect across the economy.

The latest review comes after EPRA maintained pump prices during the September 15 to October 14 pricing period, despite a decline in the cost of importing petrol.

World.title: Spiritual leader Sri Sri Ravi Shankar guides meditation and cultural program across Egypt
World.content:
World-renowned Indian spiritual leader and humanitarian Sri Sri Ravi Shankar—affectionately known to millions as Gurudev—embarks on a four-day cultural and spiritual journey across Egypt from October 25 to 28.

Titled “A Journey to Egypt with Gurudev,” this unique retreat weaves together historical exploration and inner reflection, guiding participants through the awe-inspiring Pyramids of Giza, the historic temples of Luxor, and a scenic voyage along the Nile.

Beyond admiring Egypt’s ancient heritage, the program offers a sanctuary for deep meditation, music, and thought-provoking discussions focused on cultivating daily tranquility and fostering deep human connection.

As the founder of the Art of Living Foundation, established in 1981, Ravi Shankar has spent over four decades championing global peace and self-discovery.

What began as a singular vision has expanded into an international educational and non-profit powerhouse active across more than 180 countries.

The foundation pairs breathwork and meditation courses with wide-reaching community development and humanitarian relief.

Its extensive scope includes expanding access to children’s education, supporting women’s empowerment, rehabilitating prison inmates, and delivering crucial aid to regions ravaged by natural disasters and armed conflict.

Environmental stewardship forms another core pillar of its mission, driving major initiatives in river restoration and sustainable agricultural practices.

Beyond his educational endeavors, Ravi Shankar’s personal commitment to peace-building has positioned him as a vital mediator in conflict zones worldwide – foremost being facilitating peace and reconciliation dialogues in Colombia.

In recognition of his distinguished service to humanity, he was awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 2016, India’s second-highest civilian honor.

His official biography reflects the vast reach of his work: he has personally designed over 50 meditation and self-development programs, trained upwards of 41,000 certified instructors, and touched the lives of more than one billion people globally, backed by an online community exceeding 26 million followers.

Following his four days in Egypt, the global spiritual figure heads to Munich, Germany, from October 30 to November 3 to host a series of live breathing and meditation workshops culminating in a Happiness Festival.

World.title: Prime Minister attends opening of IWWI 2026 International Water, Waste and Infrastructure Exhibition & Conference
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly took part on Monday, October 26, 2026, in the opening of the IWWI 2026 International Water, Waste and Infrastructure Exhibition & Conference.

The exhibition and conference serve as a specialized platform for showcasing the latest technologies and solutions in water and wastewater management, desalination and water reuse, as well as waste treatment and recycling.

The event also provides an opportunity to exchange expertise and explore technological advances in water resource management and improving water-use efficiency.

A number of organizations and companies operating in the water, wastewater and environmental technology sectors are participating in the conference to showcase solutions and technologies aimed at developing infrastructure and improving water services, amid challenges related to rationalizing consumption and promoting sustainability.

World.title: Egyptian, Algerian and Tunisian Foreign Ministers reject all forms of foreign interference in Libya’s internal affairs
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty participated in a ministerial meeting of the Tripartite Mechanism of Libya’s Neighboring Countries, held in Algeria on Sunday, October 25, 2026.

Algerian Minister of State and Minister of Foreign Affairs, National Community Abroad and African Affairs Ahmed Attaf and Tunisian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Migration and Tunisians Abroad Mohamed Ali Nafti also took part in the meeting.

The meeting was held as part of the ongoing work of the tripartite mechanism and aimed to strengthen consultations among the three countries on developments in Libya.

Foreign Ministry Spokesman Nader Zaki said on Monday, October 26, 2026, that the meeting focused on coordinating the positions of Libya’s immediate neighbors regarding developments in the country.

During the meeting, Abdelatty reaffirmed the fundamental principles underpinning Egypt’s position, particularly the need to preserve Libya’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.

He stressed that Libya’s security is an integral part of Egyptian and Arab national security.

In this regard, Abdelatty categorically rejected any external dictates, emphasizing that a Libyan-led and Libyan-owned solution is the only foundation for ensuring lasting stability and achieving a comprehensive settlement.

He underscored the importance of reaching a Libyan-owned political settlement that would preserve the country’s unity, ensure the unification of its institutions, and create favorable conditions for holding simultaneous presidential and parliamentary elections as soon as possible.

He also stressed the need for the immediate withdrawal of all foreign forces, mercenaries and foreign fighters from Libyan territory, in accordance with relevant international resolutions.

The three Foreign Ministers emphasized the importance of adopting a comprehensive approach that addresses not only the security and political dimensions of the crisis but also its economic and social aspects, with a view to tackling its root causes.

The meeting’s final communiqué stated that the gathering was held within the framework of the tripartite mechanism to follow up on developments in the Libyan crisis and explore prospects for resolving it.

In the communiqué, the Foreign Ministers reaffirmed the historical responsibility and central role of the neighboring countries’ mechanism, under United Nations auspices, in supporting Libya’s political process and backing all serious efforts aimed at ending the crisis.

They stressed the importance of recognizing the mechanism’s pivotal role, noting that its member states are more directly concerned than others with developments in their neighboring and brotherly country, have a deeper understanding of the crisis’s complexities and repercussions, and are particularly committed to accelerating efforts to achieve a comprehensive and lasting settlement.

The Foreign Ministers also expressed their full support for United Nations (UN) efforts and international initiatives aimed at facilitating the political process and organizing simultaneous, free and fair presidential and parliamentary elections under an agreed constitutional and legal framework.

They said the elections should bring an end to the successive transitional phases that have become entrenched and contributed to the deepening of the crisis. They added that the elections should lead to the establishment of legitimate, unified, strong and stable constitutional institutions capable of ending the current institutional division.

The Foreign Ministers stressed the need to coordinate and integrate regional and international efforts in support of an inclusive Libyan political process facilitated by the United Nations Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL).

They further emphasized that the political process must be Libyan-led and Libyan-owned, and that a political solution must reflect the will of the Libyan people and their national consensus while guaranteeing the unity, sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Libyan state.

They stressed the need for mercenaries, foreign fighters and foreign forces to withdraw from all Libyan territory to preserve the gains achieved under the ceasefire agreement and accelerate the unification of all Libyan institutions, including military and security institutions.

The Foreign Ministers underscored the importance of safeguarding Libya’s resources and using them to serve the interests of its people and promote development and prosperity.

They also highlighted the need to protect Libya’s financial assets frozen abroad, preserve their value, and ensure their proper management by the international financial institutions holding them, in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions.

The Foreign Ministers agreed that the next meeting of the tripartite mechanism would be held in Tunisia on a date to be agreed upon later.

World.title: GUEA-USA: Egypt Forum recommendations open new horizons for strengthening Egyptians’ ties with their homeland
World.content:
Vice President of the General Union of Egyptians Abroad in the United States (GUEA-USA) Essam Eddin Bassiouni said on Monday, October 26, 2026, that the outcomes of the Egypt Forum 2026 and the initiatives proposed during the event represent an opportunity to deepen ties between Egyptians living abroad and their homeland, translate their demands and proposals into practical steps, facilitate their lives, and strengthen their participation in development efforts.

In an exclusive interview with Nile News TV, the union’s Vice President noted that issues concerning Egyptians abroad received considerable attention during the five-day forum. Participants’ demands and proposals were heard and documented, helping shape a number of outcomes and recommendations aimed at improving the services provided to them and strengthening their ties with Egypt.

Bassiouni explained that the forum’s sessions addressed a number of important issues affecting Egyptians abroad and resulted in decisions concerning consular and housing initiatives, including the “Beit Al-Watan” and “Housing for All Egyptians” programs, alongside other issues that will undergo further study and discussion in the coming period.

He said the proposed initiatives include the “Speak Arabic” initiative, which seeks to preserve the Arabic language and national identity among the children of Egyptians living abroad, particularly those residing in European countries. Other initiatives include programs related to “Your Insurance in Egypt.”

Bassiouni stressed the importance of continuing to develop initiatives and services for Egyptians abroad in ways that respond to their needs, strengthen their ties with their homeland, and create greater opportunities for their participation in development efforts.

World.title: Al-Azhar renews condemnation of Houthi attacks near Mecca and Medina
World.content:
Al-Azhar Grand Imam Ahmed al-Tayeb on Monday, October 26, 2026, renewed his strong condemnation of continued Houthi attacks targeting Mecca, Medina and surrounding areas, as well as civilian facilities in Saudi Arabia. The latest attacks, directed toward the two holy cities, were intercepted by Saudi air defenses near the holy sites.

The Grand Imam reaffirmed his categorical rejection of any actions that violate the sanctity of the holy sites or endanger Saudi Arabia’s security and the safety of its citizens and visitors.

Al-Azhar reiterated its condemnation of the Houthi attack, which came dangerously close to the precincts of the Two Holy Mosques and the surrounding sacred sites. It stressed that God has forbidden aggression against these areas and guaranteed the safety of all living beings there, including humans, animals and plants, as well as pilgrims, visitors, residents and workers.

Al-Azhar warned that such attacks are sinful acts that offend the sentiments of nearly two billion Muslims worldwide. It added that they also constitute an assault on the country responsible for overseeing the holy sites, which hold a special place in the heart of every Muslim.

Al-Azhar expressed hope that an urgent mediation and de-escalation committee would be formed, comprising respected and level-headed figures from across the Muslim world who are committed to promoting peace and stability. The committee would work swiftly to defuse escalating crises and conflicts and resolve disputes among members of the same faith and nation that threaten the security and stability of their countries.

Such efforts would help preserve the strength and sovereignty of Arab and Muslim nations, protect lives, and safeguard their peoples’ resources and those of future generations.

World.title: Israel is holding its most important election in years. Here’s what’s at stake
World.content:
Tel Aviv —

When Israelis go the polls on October 27, they will face a familiar question: Should Benjamin Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, stay in power?

Nearly every recent election has been a referendum on Netanyahu. This time, many Israelis say the choice is more consequential than ever: not only about who will lead the country, but about where it is heading.

It is the first national vote since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, the deadliest security failure in Israel’s history, and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, which have mobilized much of the country and subsequently deepened Israel’s international isolation.

For many voters, this is the first chance to pass judgment on the leadership that presided over October 7 failures, to decide who should lead the country in conflict and who should carry the burden of increased military service.

Netanyahu’s outgoing government – the first in decades to conclude a full four-year term – relied on far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners, who pushed Israel in a more nationalist and religious direction than ever before. He became the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial on corruption charges as his government pursued a judicial overhaul aimed at weakening the supreme court and other checks on power. The overhaul effort sparked massive protests in 2023.

At stake in Tuesday’s election is whether Israel keeps moving in the nationalistic, conservative and religious direction – or changes course. The answer might not be clear for weeks, because of the way Israeli coalitions are built. Polls suggest neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition is likely to win a majority alone, meaning the vote may launch Israel’s next political crisis rather than settle it.

Who is running and who is ahead?

Israelis vote for party lists, not individual candidates. In a society divided by nationality, religion, ethnicity and ideology, that produces a crowded field.

Dozens of lists register each cycle – 37 this time around – but only those that pass a 3.25% vote threshold win seats and enter the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament. Polls suggest 11 to 13 parties will meet the bar; seats are allocated through a proportional representation system.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to local residents and supporters during a campaign stop at HaTikva Market in Tel Aviv on Thursday. Erik Marmor/Getty Images

The two largest parties are Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and Yashar, a new centrist party led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who has emerged as his principal challenger.

The latest Channel 12 opinion poll puts Eisenkot first with 23 seats, ahead of the Likud with 21, though other pollsters differ. On the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, Likud is projected to take 30 seats and Eisenkot about 20. In head-to-head matchups about who is better suited to be prime minister, Eisenkot has led Netanyahu by a steady margin.

But coming out as the largest party is not enough to win. A prime minister needs 61 seats to form a government, and no party has ever won that majority alone. So, election night usually settles very little. The real contest is the coalition calculus that follows, which can take days, weeks, and even months.

Most polls put Netanyahu’s bloc, made up of Likud, two far-right parties led by Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, and two ultra-Orthodox parties, at 49 to 55 seats, short of the 61-seat majority.

The opposition, which looks strong on paper, is deeply fragmented: Eisenkot has parties led by former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett and former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman to his right, and the Democrats party led by Yair Golan on his left. Bennett and Liberman have not endorsed Eisenkot and both have their own premiership aspirations.

Leader of the Yashar party Gadi Eisenkot visits the Western Wall in Jerusalem’s Old City on Thursday. Mahmoud Illean/AP

According to the opinion polls, any alternative government would probably need the support or the abstention of the Arab parties, and several opposition leaders have ruled out any cooperation.

With no side holding a clear majority, a deadlock, a minority government, a unity government – or another election – are all plausible outcomes.

What could swing the result?

With neither bloc projected to win comfortably, the outcome may hinge on the margins: which small parties clear the 3.25% threshold and how many votes go to parties that miss it, effectively sending them down the drain.

Turnout matters, since a few thousand votes can determine whether a party disappears entirely or enters parliament, or even becomes the kingmaker that breaks the deadlock between the blocs and reshapes the political map.

Arab voter turnout could be pivotal. Palestinian citizens of Israel – who make up roughly 20% of the Israeli population – have traditionally voted at lower rates than the national average. In the 2022 election, the Arab turnout was 53.2%, while the general turnout was 70.6%. This time, pollsters expect it to exceed 60%. That would raise the threshold and make it harder for small parties to survive.

Mansour Abbas, head of Israel’s conservative Islamic Ra’am party, speaks at a campaign rally in the Arab-Israeli village of Abu Gosh on Wednesday. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

Netanyahu’s coalition has several small parties at potential risk, including Smotrich’s Religious Zionism and a new right- wing party led by Ofer Winter, a prominent retired military general.

While most opposition parties sit safely above the line, another new, uncommitted small party, connecting a reservist and economic agenda, is polling close to the 3.25% threshold.

Another factor drawing attention is Israelis living abroad. Israel does not allow overseas voting, except for diplomatic staff, and official data suggests more than 11% of the 7.3 million eligible voters, about 810,000 people, live outside the country. Thousands plan to fly to Israel to vote in person, a number that could potentially impact the election.

What do Israelis vote about?

In a country that has been through years of war, security and accountability are powerful electoral forces. But opinion polls suggest the cost of living is also a leading concern for many voters – particularly for younger ones.

According to the latest Channel 12 poll, 21% of Israelis rank the economy and the cost of living as their top priority in the coming election – ahead of the ultra-Orthodox conscription with 17%, the October 7 failure at 14% and the war with Iran at 10%.

The picture differs sharply by political bloc: among voters of Netanyahu’s coalition – the war with Iran ranks first at 21%, while among opposition voters, the October 7 failure leads at 28%.

A September survey by the Achord research center at Hebrew University found that 58% of voters aged 22-34 year olds said cost of living and housing prices would drive their vote, while 36% cited security issues.

Despite these figures, the economy has not been a central theme in the campaign topic – until this weekend, when Netanyahu moved it to the top of the agenda. In an interview to Channel 10 focused on the economy, Netanyahu addressed the wave of international condemnation of Israeli settlements in the West Bank and said Israel should prepare for possible international banking sanctions by developing “an economy that can circumvent them.” He said crypto currency and blockchain are being considered, and he had requested a plan to deal with it.

The interview sparked harsh criticism of Netanyahu by economists, including a rare rebuke from the Bank of Israel, who publicly rejected the idea, which said that “cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means of circumventing sanctions.”

Netanyahu’s main rivals portrayed his proposal as evidence he expects Israel to become more isolated. Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger, mocked the idea as “BibiCoin” and called it a “threat to national security,” accusing Netanyahu of planning to “dismantle the Israeli economy for generations ahead.”

How might October 7 and the war in Gaza shape the vote?

Netanyahu built his political career as a security hawk, yet he was prime minister on October 7, when Hamas infiltrated the Israeli border, killing more than 1,200 Israelis and taking 251 hostages into Gaza.

He has resisted taking personal responsibility and has rejected demands to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the security failures. His opponents have made that lack of accountability a central campaign theme.

Israeli soldiers look across to northern Gaza from a viewpoint on the Israeli side of the border on August 13, 2025. Amir Levy/Getty Images

The war has also shaped Eisenkot’s personal story. His son Gal, 25, was killed fighting in Gaza in December 2023, a loss that reinforces his appeal to voters focused on security. Other party lists have recruited bereaved families and relatives of former Israeli hostages as candidates. Opposition parties have also added new reservist candidates, fresh from fighting in Gaza and Lebanon, pushing the issue of military service to the top of the election agenda.

Most Jewish Israelis over 18 are subject to conscription, but ultra-Orthodox men have long enjoyed a blanket exemption for religious study. Netanyahu’s ultra-Orthodox coalition partners have sought to preserve and expand the exemption, even as the Israeli military says it is missing more than 12,000 personnel while being stretched by multi-front fighting. Reservists fill the gap, serving up to hundreds of days a year on repeated deployments.

All the opposition parties have made universal service a central campaign pledge.

What does the election mean for the Palestinians?

The outgoing government was among the most hardline on Palestinian issues in Israel’s history, driven largely by two far-right nationalist party leaders.

Smotrich, the finance minister, who also oversees civil administration in the occupied West Bank, pushed to expand settlements dramatically, while withholding tax revenues to the Palestinian Authority (PA), which critics say could bring its economic collapse.

Ben-Gvir, the national security minister, championed a death penalty law in the Knesset, toughened conditions for Palestinian prisoners, and weakened police enforcement against Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Both opposed ending the Gaza war, both are advocating for Israeli settlements in Gaza, and both envision full annexation of and Jewish control over the West Bank.

Members of Israeli forces block a road, preventing Palestinians from harvesting olives in the West Bank village of Deir Jarir on Wednesday. Leo Correa/AP

If Netanyahu returns to power with his current partners, that approach is likely to continue and intensify. Smotrich wants to cancel the Oslo Accords, dismantle the Palestinian Authority, and go to war in the West Bank. Ben-Gvir, who has said he will demand the defense ministry in a new government, has called for Palestinian emigration from Gaza and the West Bank.

An opposition government would probably not represent a radical ideological reversal, and would change the tone more than the substance. Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has rejected Palestinian statehood, and any opposition coalition would include right-wing parties resistant to any concession.

Still, a government not dependent on Ben- Gvir and Smotrich would likely act more forcefully against settler violence, drop open advocacy of emigration and PA collapse, and be more responsive and receptive to US and regional initiatives in Gaza and elsewhere.

But it would inherit the same unresolved questions: how to disarm Hamas, who rebuilds Gaza, and who restores law and order in the West Bank.

What does it mean for the rest of the world?

The wars in Gaza and Lebanon, the conflict with Iran and the surge in settler violence have left Israel’s diplomatic standing at its weakest point in decades. Netanyahu faces an International Criminal Court warrant alleging war crimes in Gaza, and he avoids traveling to most European countries because of the risk of being arrested. US President Donald Trump endorsed him ahead of the vote, but the picture in the wider American public is much less friendly.

A March 2026 Pew Research Center poll found 60% of US adults surveyed held an unfavorable view of Israel, and 59% had little or no confidence in Netanyahu to do the right thing regarding global affairs. Pew’s Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey pointed the same way, with majorities in most of the 36 countries it covered holding unfavorable views of Israel and its prime minister.

A road sign stands in front of a large billboard featuring Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and Gadi Eisenkot, in Ramat Gan on Tuesday. Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images

The shift has been sharpest in Western Europe, where several countries – including the United Kingdom, France and Canada – have recognized a Palestinian state and imposed sanctions and trade restrictions on Israeli settlements and individuals and entities linked to settler violence. Ben-Gvir and Smotrich have been personally sanctioned and are facing travel bans from multiple Western countries.

If Netanyahu’s government is re-elected, that international pressure will likely grow. A government led by Eisenkot or another opposition figure might see some easing of tensions, at least at first. Firmer action on settler violence could open a window to restore warmer ties with some European governments and the US Democratic party.

But it is not likely to reverse the broader trend. The main opposition contenders are not expected to overhaul Israel’s security and foreign policy, so a new government would regain some diplomatic breathing room, but not a clean slate.

World.title: Musk accuses Ukraine of violating Starlink’s terms of service following dispute over coverage
World.content:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk has accused Ukraine’s military of violating Starlink’s terms of service, after Kyiv said that access to the service had been restored.

In a post on X Saturday, Musk said that Ukraine’s armed forces had “violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people.”

“That loophole was closed last week,” he added, referring to the restrictions temporarily placed on the service last week which limited speeds to 100 miles per hour. Musk also maintained that Starshield is a separate system controlled by the US government.

Musk also underscored Ukraine’s reliance on the service, saying it “remains critical to the defense of Ukraine” and claimed that if Starlink were turned off, “the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately.”

Zelensky’s adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov disputed Musk’s accusation that Ukraine is using the commercial service to kill people, saying speed restrictions and the service’s unavailability over Russian territory made Ukraine “physically unable to use commercial Starlink” for medium- and long-range strikes into Russia.

Serhiy Sternenko, a former Ukrainian Ministry of Defense adviser, also denied Musk’s claims. “As someone who was involved in the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true,” Sternenko said.

Echoing Beskrestnov’s claims, he said, “It was technically impossible to use the civilian Starlink system for drone missions. All drone missions requiring satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”

Ukraine’s defense ministry said Saturday that full access to Starlink and Starshield was restored. It came after US President Donald Trump said he asked Musk to lift restrictions on Kyiv’s use of the military grade version of the Musk-owned Starlink internet service.

“The Ministry of Defense’s monitoring systems are recording a recovery in Starlink/Starshield speeds,” Ukrainian Minister of Defense Yevheniy Khmara said in a statement, adding that restored speeds exceeding 400 kilometers per hour were being recorded.

An artilleryman sets up Starlink satellite internet system near the frontline in Ukraine’s Donetsk region on October 16. Stringer/Reuters

For more than a week, Ukraine had faced a speed limit on the Starshield satellite terminals used by its military, hindering its ability to intercept fast-moving Russian drones.

Trump and his top officials have denied making the call to throttle Ukraine’s use of Starshield, which limited speeds to 100 mph, according to Ukrainian officials.

Musk said the Trump administration was behind the ban in a post to social media last week.

It comes as Russia’s attacks on Ukraine continued overnight. According to Ukrainian authorities, over 153 Russian Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) were launched at Ukraine from Russia, mainly targeting large department stores and warehouses. At least three people were killed in the UAV strikes and 25 others were injured.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said at least two were killed and 22 injured in Ukrainian attacks. 532 UAVs fired from Ukraine were intercepted, the MoD said, adding that industrial sites were hit in multiple regions.

World.title: Brazil’s Lula wins reelection with victory over Trump ally Bolsonaro, who rejects result
World.content:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was reelected to a historic fourth term Sunday, but his defeated rival and Trump ally Senator Flávio Bolsonaro said he would not accept the results and would mount a legal challenge.

The 80-year-old leftist leader won more than 51 percent of votes, securing a runoff victory that bucks a broader rightward political shift across Latin America and comes after a campaign dominated by concerns over the cost of living, crime and corruption.

Bolsonaro, who trailed Lula by about 4.4 million votes, said his team would challenge the result after the Supreme Court’s last-minute ruling to extend voting by two hours.

“It is impossible to recognize the election result given how these events unfolded,” Bolsonaro told supporters in the capital Brasilia after Lula’s victory was declared.

“We will take legal action. We will ask for this election to be annulled.”

The vote marks the first time since the return of direct presidential elections in 1989 that a candidate has won the presidency after finishing second in the first round.

“I can assure you that we are going to change the way we govern this country. We are going to give the people a greater role in our decisions,” Lula said after his reelection.

Lula thanked the Brazilian people for their “generosity,” especially the country’s youth who “took to the streets to defend democracy.”

In Rio de Janeiro, Lula’s supporters were seen hugging, beeping their car horns and raising the “L” sign. And in Belo Horizonte, capital of the key swing state Minas Gerais, supporters could be seen chanting and singing following Lula’s victory.

Lula’s win is a major setback for the Bolsonaro political movement, with Flávio failing to accomplish what his father, imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, also couldn’t to do in 2022: defeat Lula at the ballot box.

But the results came after a turbulent election day, with voting being extended by two hours following last-minute pleas from both candidates to electoral authorities.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin granted a request from Lula’s campaign, which asked for an extension citing “incidents” affecting buses that provide transportation to polling venues in several states.

Bolsonaro’s campaign had also requested an extension in some areas, citing difficulties voters faced reaching polling stations because of heavy rain. The extension order came around 5 p.m. in Brasilia, just as polls were scheduled to be closing, and many stations had already shut down.

It is unclear how successful Bolsonaro’s challenge of the results will be.

Paulo Sotero, of the Brazil Institute at the Wilson Center, told CNN that the voting extension “was not an irregularity.”

“It was authorized by the Supreme Court of Brazil because there were some localized problems,” Sotero said, adding that Bolsonaro’s “chances of winning a recount or having a new election are very very slim.”

“The Senator has very little space to contest the elections. I think this is a done deal,” he said.

The election outcome will have repercussions beyond Brazil, keeping Latin America’s largest country on a more independent foreign-policy path under Lula, who has emphasized Brazil’s sovereignty and closer ties with the Global South and China amid tensions with the US administration.

Before polls closed on Sunday, US President Donald Trump said that he was “monitoring” Brazil’s presidential runoff. Although he declined to endorse either candidate, he previously praised Flávio’s first-round performance and described the election as “very important.”

Here’s what to know about Sunday’s high-stakes election:

People queue to cast their votes during the presidential runoff election, in Salvador, Brazil, October 25, 2026. Rafael Martins/Reuters

A first-round upset for Lula

According to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Bolsonaro secured 2.2 million votes more than Lula in the first round of voting. Neither candidate reached the majority needed to win outright, forcing both campaigns to compete for a shrinking pool of undecided voters while trying to mobilize their supporters in a country deeply divided over its political future.

The result exposed vulnerabilities in Lula’s reelection bid, from frustration over the cost of living and crime to difficulties mobilizing parts of his traditional base. It also showed that Jair Bolsonaro’s movement remained strong, even as the former president served a prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 defeat.

The shift in the first round of the election reflected a broader electoral trend across Latin America, where several presidential elections since April 2025 — in Ecuador, Bolivia, Honduras, Chile, Costa Rica, Colombia and Peru — have resulted in victories for right-wing or center-right candidates.

A July Datafolha survey found 44 percent of Brazilians leaning right or center-right in their political values, compared with 39 percent on the left or center-left, reversing the balance measured in 2022.

Despite this, leftist Lula prevailed in the second round.

Crime, the economy and last-minute shifts

Public safety emerged as one of the defining issues of the election. A September Quaest/Pax survey found that 28 percent of Brazilians saw violence as the country’s biggest problem, followed by corruption at 22 percent and the economy at 19 percent.

Bolsonaro promised to designate major criminal factions as terrorist groups, expand prisons and lower the age of criminal responsibility. “Those who think I’m radical on public security haven’t seen anything yet,” he said October 13, adding that even El Salvador’s infamous hardline approach under President Nayib Bukele was not enough.

Lula struggled to reconcile his party’s traditional positions with demands for tougher action. A widely circulated clip of him saying last year that drug traffickers were also victims of drug users reinforced what Brian Winter, editor-in-chief of Americas Quarterly, called a “longstanding perception that the Brazilian left is soft on crime.” Lula later acknowledged that he had expressed himself poorly.

Women walk as army soldiers provide security at Ipanema Beach in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, during the presidential election on October 4. Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images

Lula faced criticism about the state of the economy and affordability. During his first two terms, a commodities boom helped lift millions of Brazilians out of poverty and into the middle class.

This time, many voters had said they felt little progress. Lula can point to low unemployment and easing inflation, but those indicators had not changed perceptions for households struggling with everyday prices.

Winter compared the dynamic to the 2024 US presidential election, when favorable statistics failed to overcome frustration with prices under President Joe Biden and then-Vice President Kamala Harris.

Lawmakers celebrate after voting in favor of a constitutional amendment to reduce Brazil’s workweek from six days to five days, during a session of the Brazilian Federal Senate, in Brasilia, Brazil, October 14. Adriano Machado/Reuters

Still, many voters have remained loyal to Lula because of the social gains made during his first two terms, while fearing that a Bolsonaro presidency could roll back social rights. Flávio sought to counter those concerns by distancing himself from some traditionally conservative positions.

Part of the shift to the right in Brazil is due to the association of the left with corruption, although scandals have shadowed both campaigns. During last Sunday’s debate, Lula challenged Bolsonaro to open his financial records and pressed him over his ties to Daniel Vorcaro, the former head of the collapsed Banco Master, whose alleged connections to powerful figures have embroiled Brazil’s political and judicial establishment, including the Supreme Court. Flávio, meanwhile, accused Lula of corruption and raised allegations involving the president’s eldest son, known as Lulinha. Lula’s previous corruption convictions were annulled in 2021.

The corruption allegations are deepening political fatigue in Brazil, say experts. “It reinforces the disgust and apathy that Brazilians feel with their political system as a whole,” Winter told CNN.

Women and religion: two crucial divides

But if there was one key group the candidates needed to win over, both experts and campaigns agreed it was women.

Women account for nearly 53 percent of registered voters and had been more resistant to Bolsonaro-aligned candidates than men. An Oct. 15 Datafolha survey put Lula ahead among women by 49 percent to 40 percent, while Flávio led among men by 52 percent to 40 percent.

Malu Gatto, an associate professor of Latin American politics at University College London, said the gender gap widened after Jair Bolsonaro emerged in 2018, as men gravitated toward the right and women became more supportive of the Workers’ Party.

Both campaigns addressed violence against women, particularly femicide, after several brutal cases drew national attention. Brazil recorded 1,571 femicides in 2025, the highest number since the crime was defined in law in 2015, according to the Brazilian Forum on Public Safety.

A woman prays as evangelicals gather to sing and give praise at dawn on Paulista Avenue in Sao Paulo, Brazil, on October 11. Fraga Alves/Reuters

Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL), Douglas Ruas and pastor Silas Malafaia attend the official celebration of the 100th anniversary of the Assembly of God, Madureira Ministry, in Rio de Janeiro on October 10. Tita Barros/Reuters Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva kisses an image of Our Lady of Aparecida, Brazil’s patron saint, next to his wife Rosangela “Janja” da Silva, on the day of a Mass marking the Day of Our Lady of Aparecida, outside Alvorada Palace in Brasilia, Brazil, on October 12. Adriano Machado/Reuters

According to Gatto, the right traditionally emphasizes tougher criminal penalties for aggressors, while the left places greater emphasis on protection and support for victims, including shelters and specialized services.

Evangelicals, a growing demographic in the predominately Catholic country, have also turned into an important voting bloc for the right. Datafolha found Bolsonaro leading among evangelicals by 62 percent to 29 percent, while Lula led among Catholics by 52 percent to 42 percent.

President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva waves a Brazilian flag during a campaign rally in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, on October 21, 2026. Douglas Magno/AFP/Getty Images

Beyond Brazil

Trump praised Flávio Bolsonaro’s electoral performance following the first round but stopped short of formally endorsing him, even as his administration’s tariffs on Brazil and pressure over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution have strained relations with Lula.

The tensions surfaced again during last week’s TV debate. Lula accused the Bolsonaro family of aligning itself with US interests at Brazil’s expense, while Flávio rejected the charge and criticized Lula’s foreign policy.

A Bolsonaro victory could have brought Latin America’s largest economy closer to the US, particularly on security and organized crime, and strengthen a wave of conservative governments elected across the region. Lula has instead emphasized multilateralism, ties with the Global South and China — Brazil’s largest export market — and his resistance to Trump’s tariff measures as a defense of national sovereignty.

The narrow result could also test the country’s stability after Jair Bolsonaro’s attempts to overturn his 2022 defeat led to the January 8, 2023, attacks on government institutions. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.

Lula has secured an unprecedented fourth term as Brazil’s president, but with a more conservative Congress and a razor-thin margin of victory, he faces governing a country that remains deeply divided.

Helen Regan contributed reporting.

World.title: Liberia: Low Inflation, High Cost of Living: Senator Konneh Raises Alarm Over Rising Fuel and Commodity Prices, High Interest Rates Squeezing Liberian Small Businesses
World.content:
Monrovia- The Chairman of the Senate Committee on Public Accounts and Audit Amara Konneh has observed that the increase in macro-economic stability in Liberia, low inflation and the execution of the over US$1billion budget have not positively impacted the lives of ordinary Liberians across the country.

By Obediah Johnson

Senator Konneh is representing the people of Gbarpolu county in the 55th National Legislature. He previously served as a Minister of Finance and Development Planning during the administration of ex-Liberian President Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf.



According to him, the decline in the exchange rate between the United States and Liberian dollars is not bringing any relieve to ordinary Liberians.

He made these comments during the confirmation hearing of the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) Deputy Governor for Economic Policy-designate Euphemia Sweh Monmia

Senator Konneh stressed that despite Liberia’s current low inflation rate of 4.6%, the prices of basic commodities, including rice, cement remain high across the country.

He put the cost of a 25kg bag of rice in some parts of Gbarpolu county at US$22, US$15 for a bag of cement, which are far above the US$17 and US$8 they are being sold in Monrovia.

Currently, Senator Konneh claimed that the cost of a gallon of fuel in the county is also sold for L$1,500.

He maintained that the more than 87% increment in the prices of basic commodities in western Liberia cannot easily transition citizens from mud to bricks houses.

He said present hike in the cost of petroleum products are negatively contributing to the increase in basic commodities citizens need for survival.

Growth inflation dynamics

Senator Konneh noted that despite efforts being applied by the economic management team of Liberia to improve the country’s economy, inflation remains higher than growth.

“The economy is more stable now; the interest is that macro environment is stable and growth is expected to be more than 5% this year. We’ve worked hard from December 2024 to present to bring down inflation. However, inflation is still higher than growth. So, that dynamics is contributing to the legitimate noise amongst citizens.”

He said Liberians are not feeling the impact of the decline in inflation as the prices of goods and tuition fees for students continue to increase.

“Our money, the Liberian dollars is stronger here today against the US dollar. But with all of that we should see some relieve (on our people) technically. Eventhough inflation is 4.6% real on paper, but in Bopolu, Gbarpolu county, Kinjor in Cape Mount closed to where the biggest mining company in our country is operating today, and Tubmanburg, the prices are still high. The people are not feeling the impact of this impressive number. Prices are rising higher on top of an already price flow.”

He observed that the current situation is strangulating growth in real income.

Senator Konneh wondered why the prices of major goods are not reducing, despite the appreciation of the local currency.

He further alarmed over the unproductive capacity of both the mining and agriculture sectors, with manufacturing only contributing to 8% growth in the economy.

He maintained that though 87% of Liberians are in the informal sector, they are not captured in the Liberian economy.

Senator Konneh said government should intensify efforts to accelerate growth and decelerate inflation.

On US$1billion budget

He further observed that despite the passage of the US$1.25billion national budget, students of the Monrovia Consolidated School System (MCSS) were constrained to stage protests for the return of their teachers to the classrooms over unpaid salaries.

He added that many public schools are in deplorable conditions, while the University of Liberia remains closed.

Senator Konneh indicated that citizens would only celebrate the execution of the US$1.25billion budget, if it impact their lives positively.

“We keep announcing low inflation, but inflation should be reflected in the consumer price index on the ground.This US$1billion budget should be celebrated because it is felt.”

High importation of fuel

Senator Konneh disclosed that 30% of Liberia’s economy runs on imported fuel.

He accused the Liberia Petroleum and Refining Company (LPRC) and the Ministry of Commerce of using March last year exchange rate circular to set the price of petroleum products for May without consulting the CBL.

He added that consumers were unknowingly paying the price at various filling stations as a result of the blunder from the two agencies.

Meanwhile, Senator Konneh has underscored the need for the executive to regulate and supervise price control to help alleviate some of the constraints citizens are experiencing.

He stressed that inter-agency coordination would address most of the problems confronting Liberians.

High petroleum Taxes

Senator Konneh pointed out that additional two levy fees being charged petroleum importers to the already existing including Goods and Services Tax (GST) and road fund are contributing to the increase in the prices of petroleum and diesel on the Liberian market.

He said the Economic Management Team (EMT) must sit with the relevant authorities to address the situation as lawmakers do not intend to take arbitrary actions to affect the smooth execution of the national budget.

“Our people are paying for the price at the pump through the transportation cost and the prices rice they eat. The importers are getting wealthier; the government is getting fatter US$1.3billion budget-about 80% goes to recurrent cost and we in the government are getting fatter everyday and the skinning man out there is paying for the price.”

He maintained that government should consider providing a “tax holiday” to importers to alleviate sufferings they are encountering on a daily basis.

Senator Konneh observed that Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are the engine of growth of the Liberian economy.

He said CBL monetary policy alone cannot fix the supply and pricing.

He noted that a shorter pay-back period for loan credited from commercial banks is strangulating the growth of many SMEs in Liberia.

Senator Konneh called on the CBL to be intentional towards ensuring low interest rate for SMEs and the reduction of risks to the sustenance of their businesses.

He said steps should be taken by the bank towards the publication of the daily exchange rate and the setting of a variation interest rate for both SMEs and large businesses.

He observed that despite the passage of the Small Business Empowerment Act of 2016, no single Liberian company has benefited.

Amongst other things, the Act calls for at least 25% of public procurement and contracts for goods and services to be allocated to Liberian owned Micro, Small and Medium-sized (MSMEs),

Senator Konneh said government must be deliberate to provide support to MSMEs operating in the country, adding that, “the interest rate is killing our people.”
