World.title: Liberia: The New Era of DStv Starts Now
World.content:
Monrovia – The completion of CANAL+’s acquisition of MultiChoice last year marks the beginning of a new era for African entertainment, creating greater opportunities to invest in content, innovation, and customer experiences across the continent. Reflecting this ambition, MultiChoice Group, a CANAL+ Company, introduces its most significant product update in years, bringing more of Africa’s greatest entertainment live to subscribers from 5 November.

The new package line-up is designed around how customers watch today, with clearer choices, more accessible content, and greater value across the portfolio.

With a focus on giving subscribers better value and access to the entertainment they love, DStv is focusing on its strength with African entertainment, leading international content and unrivalled live sport in one place. Our new packages are reimagined to reflect how customers watch today, with tailored options specifically for general entertainment and sports fans.



More Entertainment for More Subscribers

For the first time, some of DStv’s biggest channels will be available at significantly more accessible price points.

• DStv Access becomes DStv Starter ($7/month): Adding more channels than its predecessor, including the brand-new SuperSport KICKOFF channel, Premier League Match of the Week, La Liga, M-Net Legends, and Star Life.

• DStv Family becomes DStv Select ($13/month): Offering a wide variety of entertainment for the whole family across a broad selection of channels. Subscribers will enjoy all movie channels (including M-Net Movies+), African and international series (Novelas+, Telemundo, Serie A, Betway PSL), as well as top kids’ channels like Nickelodeon.

• Refreshed Movie Line-up: Refreshed with M-Net Movies+, M-Net Stars, and M-Net Legends, bringing more blockbuster movies, faster access to new releases, and fewer repeats.

More Sport Across the Line-Up

• DStv Compact becomes DStv Sports ($24/month): DStv’s first package built specifically for sports fans, covering every Premier League and UEFA Champions League match, cricket, selected international club rugby, WWE, and UFC.

Alongside this extensive sporting offering, DStv Sports includes all the general entertainment channels available on DStv Select, proving that Expect More is not simply a new brand tagline, but a tangible promise delivered through DStv’s refreshed content offering.

• DStv Compact Plus & Premium become DStv Ultimate ($37/month): DStv’s most comprehensive all-in-one package, combining everything available on DStv Sports with additional premium sport—including Formula 1, MotoGP, ATP Tennis, and PGA Golf majors—as well as flagship M-Net entertainment.

More African Stories, Backed by CANAL+

As part of the MultiChoice Group’s integration with CANAL+, the business is able to draw on CANAL+’s global scale, content relationships, and more than 30 years of experience across Africa to further enhance its offering to customers.

At the same time, MultiChoice remains firmly committed to investing in local content and telling authentic African stories. The business continues to expand its portfolio of original productions across markets, ensuring audiences can enjoy a rich mix of locally relevant entertainment alongside the very best international content. Over the next few months, viewers in Liberia can look forward to rich West African storytelling, hit Nollywood blockbusters, and flagship regional productions across MultiChoice’s local channels.

“MultiChoice has built an extraordinary connection with African audiences and a deep understanding of the stories they love to watch,” said Nomsa Philiso, EVP Content, CANAL+ Africa. “Not only does CANAL+ share that passion and commitment, but it is also investing in African storytelling through increased production and global distribution opportunities.”

Get Connected for Less

To make premium entertainment and sport more accessible to households across Liberia, DStv will launch a special hardware promotion. During this period, customers will be able to purchase selected decoders and hardware bundles at promotional prices, making it easier and more affordable to get connected and enjoy an unmatched range of local and international content.

The promotion reinforces MultiChoice’s commitment to delivering greater value, wider access to quality entertainment, and more opportunities for customers to experience the very best of DStv.

For more information on the new packages, migration, and local decoder promotions:

• Visit: www.dstv.com

• Customer Support: call 0886 510 000 / 0777 510 753

• Office: Consolidated Group Incorporated, Monrovia, Liberia

World.title: Liberia: LMTI and LiMA Strengthen Maritime Regulatory Capacity Through Port State Control Training
World.content:
MARSHALL, Margibi County – The Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI), in collaboration with the Liberia Maritime Authority (LiMA), today concluded a five-day Basic Port State Control (PSC) Training Course aimed at strengthening Liberia’s maritime regulatory capacity and enhancing the professional competencies of maritime personnel.

Held from October 19 to 23, 2026, at LMTI’s campus in Marshall, the training brought together 25 participants nominated by the Liberia Maritime Authority and provided them with foundational knowledge of Port State Control principles, vessel inspection procedures, and international maritime regulatory requirements. Participants were awarded certificates during a formal certification ceremony marking the successful completion of the program.

Port State Control is a critical component of the international maritime safety and environmental protection framework. It enables competent authorities to inspect foreign-flagged vessels calling at national ports and assess their compliance with international conventions relating to vessel safety, seafarer welfare, security standards, and environmental protection.



The training forms part of ongoing efforts to strengthen Liberia’s maritime administration, improve regulatory oversight, and support compliance with international maritime standards.

LiMA Reaffirms Commitment to Professional Development

Representing the Liberia Maritime Authority at the certification ceremony was Mr. Joel O. Dickerson, Director of Training, who underscored the importance of continuous capacity building and professional development within Liberia’s maritime sector.

Speaking during the program, Mr. Dickerson commended the partnership between LiMA and LMTI and emphasized the value of investing in human capital as a cornerstone of maritime development.

“The continued development of maritime professionals is essential to maintaining Liberia’s reputation and effectiveness as a leading maritime nation. Port State Control is a vital regulatory tool that helps safeguard maritime safety, protect the marine environment, and ensure compliance with international standards. We are pleased to see participants successfully complete this training and acquire knowledge that will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of the maritime sector.”

Mr. Dickerson further encouraged the participants to remain focused, disciplined, and determined as they continue their professional development journeys. He reminded them that the knowledge and skills gained through the training come with a significant responsibility, noting that they are not only representing their respective institutions but also representing Liberia on the international maritime stage.

“As maritime professionals, you carry the responsibility of upholding the highest standards of professionalism and competence. Stay focused and determined in your pursuit of excellence, because the work you do reflects not only on yourselves but on Liberia as a maritime nation. You represent your country, and your commitment to quality and integrity will help strengthen Liberia’s standing within the global maritime community.”

Mr. Dickerson also noted that collaboration between LiMA and LMTI remains important in building a skilled workforce capable of meeting the evolving demands of the global maritime industry.

Building National Maritime Expertise

As one of the world’s foremost maritime registries, Liberia recognizes the importance of strengthening local maritime expertise to support safer shipping operations, identify substandard vessels, and promote compliance with international maritime conventions.

The Basic Port State Control Training Course provided participants with practical exposure to internationally recognized inspection procedures and regulatory frameworks, establishing a solid foundation for continued professional growth in this specialized field.

By investing in maritime education and training, Liberia continues to strengthen its institutional capacity, enhance regulatory effectiveness, and support the sustainable development of the maritime sector.

Advancing Maritime Education and Institutional Cooperation

For LMTI, the successful delivery of the training reflects its commitment to providing industry-relevant maritime education and professional development opportunities that contribute to the growth of a highly skilled Liberian maritime workforce.

The Institute remains committed to working closely with national and international partners to advance maritime knowledge, foster professional excellence, and support a safer, more secure, and environmentally responsible maritime industry.

About the Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI)

The Liberia Maritime Training Institute (LMTI) is Liberia’s premier maritime education and training institution dedicated to developing competent maritime professionals through quality education, practical training, and industry-focused capacity-building programs that support national and international maritime development.

World.title: Liberia: How One President Could Shape Liberia’s Supreme Court for a Generation
World.content:
Monrovia – Few Liberian presidents have been in a position to remake the Supreme Court from top to bottom. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai is on course to do exactly that. If the justices retire as the Constitution requires, every seat on the five-member bench will have been filled by Mr. Boakai by the time Liberians vote in the October 2029 general elections, or shortly after.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The arithmetic is set by Article 72(b) of the 1986 Constitution, which requires the Chief Justice and Associate Justices to retire at 70. They may stay on only to finish cases they began hearing before that birthday. Justices are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.



Three down, two to go

Mr. Boakai, who took office in January 2024, has already made three appointments.

In July 2024, the Senate unanimously confirmed Judge Ceaineh D. Clinton-Johnson, his nominee, to replace the late Associate Justice Joseph Nagbe. She was the first nominee confirmed under a new Senate rule requiring a two-thirds vote, or 20 senators, for tenured presidential nominees.

A year later, Chief Justice Sie-A-Nyene Yuoh reached the mandatory retirement age. Mr. Boakai nominated Associate Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay, Sr. to succeed her. Mr. Gbeisay had joined the Court as an associate justice in October 2022, under former President George Weah. He was confirmed as Chief Justice in July 2025.

To fill Mr. Gbeisay’s former seat, the President nominated Cllr. Boakai N. Kanneh, chairman of the Law Reform Commission. Mr. Kanneh is a former deputy foreign minister for legal affairs and public defender, and has taught at the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law. He is also the brother of Gbarpolu County Senator Botoe Kanneh, a family tie that has drawn political attention.

The retirement calendar

The remaining seats will open on a predictable schedule:

• 2027: Associate Justice Jamesetta Howard Wolokolie, the longest-serving member of the bench, appointed in 2007 under President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

• 2028: Associate Justice Yussif D. Kaba, born July 19, 1958, appointed under President Weah in 2019.

• 2029: Chief Justice Yarmin Quiqui Gbeisay, born May 3, 1959, turns 70 in May 2029, five months before the election.

• 2029: Associate Justice Clinton-Johnson, a Boakai appointee, is also due to retire in 2029.

• 2041: Associate Justice Kanneh, the youngest member of the Court.

By 2028, the last two justices appointed by earlier presidents, Ms. Wolokolie and Mr. Kaba, will have left. Mr. Boakai will then fill the Chief Justice’s seat and Ms. Clinton-Johnson’s seat in 2029, in the middle of an election year. If all of these appointments are made and confirmed, the full bench will be his.

Why it matters

In most democracies, the makeup of the highest court is decided gradually, by several presidents. That spread is one of the quiet protections of judicial independence. No single administration owns the bench, and justices are less likely to be seen as one leader’s choices.

Liberia’s fixed retirement age makes turnover predictable, but it can also cluster vacancies. That is what is happening now. A Court made up entirely of one president’s nominees is not illegal or improper by itself. Whether it becomes a problem depends on who is chosen and how they rule.

Concerns have already been raised. When Mr. Gbeisay was nominated as Chief Justice in 2025, a veteran lawyer told allAfrica that three Supreme Court appointments in less than two years signaled growing executive influence over the judiciary. The lawyer also questioned Mr. Gbeisay’s firmness, pointing to his lone dissent in the Court’s December 6, 2024 ruling on the House speakership crisis.

That crisis shows why the Court’s independence matters. In November 2024, a majority bloc of lawmakers declared the Speaker’s seat vacant and elected Rep. Richard Koon outside a formal session. Speaker J. Fonati Koffa refused to step down. The Executive began recognizing Mr. Koon after a Ministry of Justice opinion in favor of the bloc. In April 2025, the Supreme Court declared Mr. Koffa the constitutional Speaker, but he resigned weeks later and Mr. Koon took the gavel.

The tension has not gone away. This week the Court reserved its ruling in former Rep. Yekeh Kolubah’s appeal against his April 2026 expulsion. The House voted to expel him a day after Justice Kaba ordered it to halt the proceedings. These cases put the Court at the center of disputes between the Legislature, the Executive and individual lawmakers. A future bench will decide many more.

The 2029 election

The timing of the final vacancies raises its own questions. Two seats are due to open in 2029, the year Liberians choose a president. A bench appointed entirely by the sitting president could be asked to rule on election disputes, including challenges involving that president or his party. Liberia’s Supreme Court is the final arbiter of electoral disputes. Its rulings in 2017 and 2023 helped settle contested results peacefully.

The Senate’s two-thirds confirmation rule gives senators a real check. Nominees now need broad support, not just a governing majority. How the Senate uses that power in 2028 and 2029, in the heat of a campaign, will be closely watched.

There is also a longer-term effect. Justices appointed in their fifties will serve into the 2040s. The next president, whether it is Mr. Boakai in a second term or someone else, may inherit a bench with few scheduled vacancies. Mr. Kanneh alone is set to serve until 2041. Unless justices die, resign, or are removed through impeachment, a new president could serve a full six-year term without appointing anyone.

Is there room for young lawyers?

The Constitution sets a low floor. Under Article 68 and Section 2.4 of the Judiciary Law, a justice must be a Liberian citizen for at least 10 years, at least 30 years old, a Counsellor-at-Law of the Supreme Court Bar, and engaged in active practice of law for at least seven years before appointment.

In practice, the path is long. A Liberian lawyer usually earns an undergraduate degree before law school, then a law degree, typically from the Louis Arthur Grimes School of Law. After passing the bar, the graduate is admitted as an Attorney-at-Law. Only after years of active practice can an attorney petition the Supreme Court to be admitted as a Counsellor-at-Law. The Court has cited a five-year practice requirement for that petition. Candidates are then examined by committees of senior lawyers.

Can someone be a Counsellor-at-Law at 30? On paper, yes, but only with an unusually early start. A lawyer who finishes a first degree at 21, completes law school by 24 and is admitted to the bar at 25 could, after five years of practice, petition at about 30. Most Liberian lawyers reach that point in their mid-thirties or later.

Because of the seven-year practice requirement, the earliest realistic age for appointment to the Supreme Court is the early-to-mid thirties. No Liberian president has come close. Liberia’s justices have generally been appointed in their fifties or sixties, after long careers as judges, government lawyers or senior practitioners. Mr. Kanneh, the youngest on the current bench, will serve until 2041, which suggests he was appointed in his early fifties.

So for lawyers aged 30 to 45, the honest answer is: not soon. With the bench likely to be filled by 2029, the next wave of scheduled vacancies may not come until the late 2030s and 2040s. Today’s young counsellors who build strong careers as judges, scholars or advocates may be the leading candidates then. A president could choose to appoint a younger justice sooner, but that would break with long practice, and the Senate would have to agree.

A test of institutions, not just appointments

Mr. Boakai did not create this calendar; the Constitution and the birthdates of sitting justices did. How he uses it is a choice. He can pick nominees known for independence and legal skill, from a range of backgrounds and regions, and give the Senate time for real scrutiny. Or the appointments can be seen as political rewards. The first path would strengthen a Court that Liberians and Liberia’s international partners increasingly rely on to settle political disputes.

For a country that rebuilt its institutions after 14 years of civil war, the Supreme Court is one of its most important achievements. The next five appointments, more than any single ruling, will decide whether the Court stays a check on power or becomes an extension of it.

World.title: Liberia: Inside the Peter Bon Jallah verdict, and the questions Criminal Court “E” has yet to answer
World.content:
MONROVIA – A 63-year-old resident of Monrovia’s Airfield area will spend the coming weeks in the Monrovia Central Prison awaiting sentence. On Friday, Criminal Court “E” found him guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping of a 16-year-old boy who, according to the indictment, ran errands and did domestic work at his home.

By Rodney D. Sieh

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh, Sr., sitting without a jury at the defendant’s own request, found Peter Bon Jallah guilty of statutory rape and kidnapping. He acquitted Jallah of gang rape, the most serious-sounding charge in the three-count indictment. The court ordered the Bureau of Probation Services at the Ministry of Justice to prepare a pre-sentence report “as soon as possible,” and suspended the matter until then.



The verdict closes one chapter of a case that has moved slowly through the system since the boy was found by the roadside in Sinkor on the night of January 3, 2026. It also raises questions about how such cases are prosecuted, what the split verdict means, and why a ruling of this weight was issued with its legal reasoning still unwritten.

What the State Alleged

According to the indictment returned by the Montserrado County Grand Jury in its February 2026 term, the abuse began in late 2025. Prosecutors alleged that on November 29 and December 24, 2025, Jallah lured the boy to his residence and sexually abused him there.

The indictment says the most serious episode began on New Year’s Day. Prosecutors alleged that after the boy played in a community football match, Jallah met him outside his fence and offered to take him to buy football boots. He told the boy to go home, bathe and come back. The boy returned and got into Jallah’s car.

Instead of a shopping trip, the indictment alleges, the boy was taken to a building in the Camp Johnson Road area. He was held there for three days, given noodles that made him dizzy, and abused repeatedly. Prosecutors alleged that two unidentified men took part.

On the night of January 3, the indictment says, the boy was hidden in the back of Jallah’s vehicle and left on the roadside on 15th Street, Sinkor. Private security guards found him and alerted his family. His mother and relatives took him to the John F. Kennedy Medical Center for examination.

Why Gang Rape Fell Away

The court’s ruling does not explain why Jallah was acquitted of gang rape. The two men named alongside him in the indictment were never identified, never arrested and never brought before the court. Jallah was severed from them and tried alone.

Gang rape by definition requires proof that more than one person took part. With the alleged accomplices still unknown, the prosecution may simply have been unable to prove their involvement to the court’s satisfaction. That is an inference, not a finding. The court has not yet said why. Each of the three findings ends with the same note: “legal citations are pending.”

That phrase matters. The public, the defense and any appellate court now have the outcome without the reasoning. Until the full opinion is filed, it is impossible to say which evidence the judge found credible and which he set aside.

A Long Road to Trial

The case was first filed before Criminal Assizes Court “A” before being transferred to Court “E.” Court “E” is Liberia’s specialized court for sexual and gender-based violence. Jallah was arraigned on June 18, 2026, pleaded not guilty, and chose a bench trial.

The trial then stalled. The prosecution’s motion for a change of venue was denied. Prosecutors went to the Supreme Court seeking a writ of certiorari, which the Justice in Chambers also denied, and the case was ordered to proceed. It stalled again when the court’s regular term expired before evidence could be taken. Hearings finally began on August 5 under a reassigned judge.

The record shows a heavily contested trial. The prosecution called 13 witnesses, including the boy himself and police officers, plus six rebuttal witnesses. The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah himself. It also subpoenaed three institutions: the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the mobile operator Orange, and the JFK Medical Center. The Orange subpoena suggests phone records were part of the defense’s case.

The Wider Picture

The case is unusual in one important way: the victim is a boy. Liberia’s 2005 rape law amendment made rape gender-neutral. Advocates nonetheless say sexual abuse of boys remains heavily under-reported, shadowed by stigma and the assumption that only girls are at risk. A conviction in a case involving a male child, especially one in which the accused held a position of trust and patronage over the victim, is rare in Liberia’s courts.

It also shows a familiar pattern. Prosecutors alleged that Jallah had small, everyday power over the boy, as an employer for errands and the man who could buy him football boots. Child-protection workers say that kind of power is often the doorway to abuse.

What Comes Next

Jallah is remanded until the probation report is ready, after which the court will hand down its sentence. Under Liberian law, rape of a minor by an adult is a first-degree felony that can carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment. The defense is expected to have the right to appeal to the Supreme Court once judgment is entered.

For now, the boy’s family has a verdict. What it does not yet have, and what the public is owed, is the court’s written explanation of how it got there.

World.title: Liberia: New executive order prepares the ground for a permanent railway regulator, four years after the idea was first launched by decree
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has issued a new executive order setting out how the country’s interim railway office will finish its work and hand over to a permanent, legally established railway authority. The move comes as two global mining companies prepare to share the country’s only major rail line to export iron ore.

By Rodney D Sieh

Executive Order No. 169, signed on October 22, 2026, renews the Liaison Office for the Establishment of the Liberia National Railway Authority (LNRA). For the first time, it also sets out a timetable for winding the office down. Once the Legislature passes a law creating the authority, the office will have 90 days to hand over its records, studies, staff and equipment. It will then be dissolved.



The order matters well beyond Liberia’s borders. The railway between the Nimba mountains and the port of Buchanan is becoming one of West Africa’s most important export routes for iron ore. It carries ore from Liberia and, soon, from neighbouring Guinea, to steel mills in Europe, Asia and the United States.

The order also comes as Liberia hosts the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Exhibition (LIMEC 2026) in Monrovia this week. The conference is organised by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, the Liberia Chamber of Mines and AME Trade Ltd., and will bring together investors, mining companies and government officials. Its agenda includes iron ore expansion and the planned rail and port corridor linking Guinea’s Nimba region to Buchanan. Organisers expect current and planned projects to attract more than $3 billion in new investment.

One Track, Two Giants

The line is currently operated by ArcelorMittal Liberia, a subsidiary of the world’s second-largest steelmaker. In January, the company and the government extended their mineral development agreement to 2050, with a right to renew for another 25 years. ArcelorMittal agreed to pay $200 million for the extension and for reserved rail capacity. It is completing a $1.8 billion expansion expected to lift its shipments from about 5 million tonnes a year to 20 million.

Under that deal, President Boakai said the railway would become independently operated from October 2030.

The second user is Ivanhoe Atlantic, a company linked to mining billionaire Robert Friedland. In December 2025, the Legislature ratified its $1.8 billion rail access and concession agreement. The deal allows Ivanhoe to move high-grade ore from its Kon Kweni mines in Guinea across the border and down the Liberian line to Buchanan. It is the first project carried out under a 2019 treaty between Liberia and Guinea. Liberia is expected to earn more than $1 billion in rail access fees over the life of the project.

Until now, there has been no independent body to referee the arrangement. That is the gap the LNRA is meant to fill.

What the Order Does

Executive Order 169 keeps the Liaison Office under the supervision of the Minister of State for Presidential Affairs. It directs the office to complete a U.S. Trade and Development Agency-funded study of the condition and capacity of the Tokadeh–Buchanan corridor. The office must also finalise a draft LNRA Act with the Law Reform Commission and submit it to the Legislature through the Ministry of State.

The office is further tasked with preparing staffing plans, budgets and funding models for the future authority, including public-private partnerships, along with draft safety and regulatory rules. It must continue engaging mining companies, local communities, ECOWAS and neighbouring countries on regional rail development.

The order is careful about the limits of its own power. It bars the Liaison Office from adopting any regulations or commitments that must await the law. Any rules the office drafts for the future authority will take effect only after the Act is in force. The order’s preamble says the aim is to wind down the office “without creating gaps or extending executive powers beyond the lawful transition period.”

Four Years of Decrees

That caution reflects a long-standing criticism. That caution reflects a long-standing criticism. Liberia’s railway authority has existed only through a chain of executive orders since October 2022, when former President George Weah first created it. President Boakai renewed it in 2024 and again in October 2025 with Executive Order 153, which brought in international technical advisers and provided for a liaison officer.

Rail workers have grown impatient. In February, the National Association for Railway Workers of Liberia petitioned the Legislature to pass a law creating an autonomous authority, separate from the Ministry of Transport. The workers also asked that rail assets left behind by defunct mining companies be placed under the authority’s control.

The new order does not set a deadline for introducing the bill. Instead, it says the bill’s introduction will trigger the transition, and that the office will continue until the law passes or the President revokes the order. Any extension beyond “a reasonable transition period” must be justified in writing and approved by a separate executive order. The order does not define how long that period is.

What It Could Mean for the Sector

For investors, a statutory regulator would offer something executive orders cannot: permanence. An executive order can be amended or revoked by any president. A law passed by the Legislature carries more weight with lenders and with companies making 25-year commitments.

A permanent authority could also settle questions that remain open as traffic on the line grows. These include who sets and enforces the terms on which new users gain access to the track, who inspects a railway carrying heavier and more frequent trains, who decides when the line needs new capacity and who pays for it, and who resolves disputes between companies sharing the track.

The order commits the government to “multi-user, open-access” governance that is fair and transparent to all users. It does not say how disputes between users would be settled. Those details are likely to sit in the draft Act, which has not been made public.

Timing is also a factor. If the railway is to be independently operated by October 2030, as the government has said, a regulator will need to be in place well before then, with staff, rules and a budget of its own.

The Road Ahead

The order lays out a path from preparation through legislative consideration to handover. It requires the liaison officer to submit a final report to both the President and the Legislature before the office is dissolved. Staff will move into the new authority unless they choose to return to their previous posts.

What the order cannot do is pass the law. That decision now rests with the Legislature. Lawmakers moved quickly to ratify the Ivanhoe deal last year. Whether they move as quickly on the body meant to regulate such deals may shape how well Liberia manages its rail boom.

As investors gather in Monrovia this week, the question of who will regulate Liberia’s busiest railway, and when, is likely to be on many of their minds.

World.title: A Former Security Chief’s Vision for Liberia’s Immigration Service Finally Plays
World.content:
MONROVIA – C. Clarence Massaquoi once commanded Liberia’s national police and led the unit that guarded the head of state. On Friday, he stood before a group of young cadets holding trumpets and drums and described himself as something else: a father who had come home.

By Jaheim T Tumu

“I stand before you today not just as a Guest Speaker, but as a proud father returning home,” Massaquoi told the pioneer graduating class of the Liberia Immigration Service (LIS) Basic Military Band Training. The Armed Forces of Liberia Band Unit ran the program.



For Massaquoi, the day closed something he had left unfinished. He had first proposed a marching band for the immigration service years earlier, when he was Commissioner of what was then the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization (BIN).

A Vision Interrupted

Massaquoi has held several of the most sensitive security jobs in Liberia. He directed the Special Security Service, the presidential protection detail now called the Executive Protection Service (EPS). He was Commissioner of BIN. He later led the Liberia National Police, and served as its Inspector General until September 2016, when President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf named Col. Gregory Coleman to replace him. Sirleaf said at the time that the government still had confidence in him and would need his skills in another role. Massaquoi has also served as National Security Advisor.

He said his goal at BIN had been to turn the agency “from a checkpoint institution into a full-fledged, disciplined, paramilitary service worthy of its place in the Joint Security Architecture of Liberia.” That is the framework of agencies, led by the army and police, that has protected the country since its civil wars ended in 2003.

He considered a marching band central to that plan. “We started the process; we identified talent, we began consultations,” he said. “But before the first drum could be beaten, I was reappointed by the President to head the Liberia National Police Service. I left with an unfinished agenda in my heart.”

He told the cadets they had finished that work. He thanked the current leadership of the service for “keeping the dream alive.”

More Than Music

A brass band may look like ceremony with little to do with protecting a border. Massaquoi made the opposite case. He said the band training holds lessons a security officer needs in the field.

“You did not just learn music. You went through basic military training. You learned discipline, endurance, teamwork, and precision,” he said. “In a band, if one man is out of step, the whole parade is spoiled. If one trumpet is out of tune, the whole melody is lost. You have learned the greatest lesson of our profession: We succeed together, or we fail together.”

Bands have been part of military life for centuries, and he placed the new unit in that tradition. “The world over, the band is the commander’s voice,” he said. “It sets the pace, it announces his arrival, it comforts troops on long patrols.”

He said the habits learned on the band square, “punctuality, practice, perfection,” would follow the graduates to border posts in Lofa, Grand Cape Mount, Ganta and Maryland. Liberia shares these frontiers with Sierra Leone, Guinea and Côte d’Ivoire, and they are long and porous.

Ending the Silence

He also spoke about the agency’s pride. The LIS is part of the Joint Security, but he said that “for too long, at national parades and state functions, we marched in silence, or to the drums of another institution.”

He said that ends now. The LIS will march to its own music on July 26, Liberia’s Independence Day. It will greet visiting heads of state at Roberts International Airport with its own band, and honor fallen colleagues the same way. “That builds esprit de corps that money cannot buy,” he said.

He listed five benefits of the band:

• Identity and morale

• Discipline and command

• A stronger place in the Joint Security alongside the army and police

• Community trust

• Recruitment for the future

Soft Power at the Border

His strongest argument was about how the public sees the service. He described the band as a tool of soft power.

“An immigration officer is the first and last Liberian a visitor meets,” he said. When the band plays in schools, border towns and county programs, he said, it changes how people see the LIS, “from an enforcement body to a people’s institution. And in modern border management, community trust is our best intelligence.”

Many border agencies around the world have learned the same thing: people living near a frontier are often the first to notice smuggling, trafficking or unusual movement. Massaquoi said that kind of trust “is more powerful than any fence.”

He also pointed to the next generation. “You are the First Notes of a new LIS anthem,” he told the graduates. “The child who hears you play in Bo Waterside today will want to wear this uniform tomorrow.” Bo Waterside is the main crossing into Sierra Leone.

Arms and Accountability

Massaquoi also spoke about a more sensitive reform he had pushed: arming immigration officers.

He said many Liberians had worried about giving guns to a semi-military service in a country still recovering from years of civil war. He said the service has since answered those fears. He cited Bo Waterside, Roberts International Airport, the Ganta border and central Monrovia, and said “there have been no reports of misuse, intimidation, accidental discharge, or harassment of citizens with LIS weapons anywhere.”

He praised officers for “discipline and restraint in carrying arms,” courtesy toward travelers and residents, and professionalism at checkpoints. He warned that being armed brings “a heightened responsibility.” Officers who carry weapons, he said, must “consistently demonstrate professionalism and humility.”

He asked the service to use the new band to build ties with communities at every border point.

A Charge and an Appeal

He gave the graduates a direct charge: “Guard this legacy jealously. Practice every day. Respect your instruments. Teach others. Never let these drums gather dust.”

He then asked LIS Commissioner General Elijah F. Rufus to make the band a permanent unit, with a bandmaster, its own budget line, a home and a mandate to train future classes.

“Instruments are expensive, but discipline is priceless,” he said. “Let this not be a one-time project.”

His closing line summed up why he came. “I came as the man who planted the seed,” he said. “I leave today as the proudest father of the harvest.”

World.title: Liberia: PUL Boss Uses Governance Commission Platform to Accuse Boakai Gov’t of ‘Dismantling’ FOI Law, Demands End to Civil Service Gag Order
World.content:
Monrovia – The President of the Press Union of Liberia (PUL), Julius Kanubah, has accused the administration of President Joseph Boakai of carrying out “ongoing, systematic actions” to dismantle the Freedom of Information (FOI) Act and do away with open-data practices across government. He demanded that the government unconditionally rescind a new confidentiality agreement being imposed on civil servants.

Kanubah made the charge Friday, October 23, at the EJS Ministerial Complex in Congo Town. He was speaking at a two-day policy dialogue organized by the Governance Commission (GC) to mark October as the Month of Good Governance. The theme of the dialogue was “Promoting Good Governance through Accountability, Transparency, and Citizens’ Participation for Inclusive Development.”

The PUL had been invited to speak on the “Implementation of the Freedom of Information Act and Open-Data Practices Across Government.” Kanubah told participants the topic was urgent “not from the PUL’s expertise to lecture on it, but from a deeply troubling reality.”



‘It upends the FOI Act entirely’

At the center of the PUL’s complaint is a new Confidentiality and Non-Disclosure Agreement. Kanubah said the Executive is “forcing” it on all civil servants through the Civil Service Agency (CSA), which is headed by Dr. Josiah Joekai.

“This non-disclosure policy does not merely chip away at our democratic gains; it upends the FOI Act entirely,” Kanubah said.

He argued that the policy undermines the lawmaking functions of the Legislature and strips the Independent Information Commission (IIC) of its statutory authority. He also said it “reintroduces state secrecy, and effectively recriminalizes the disclosure of public information by government workers.”

Kanubah noted that the IIC opposed the policy. The IIC is the state body legally mandated to enforce the FOI Act.

“As one of the foundational stakeholders that championed the enactment of the FOI Act and the creation of the IIC, the Press Union of Liberia is profoundly saddened by the Boakai administration’s decision to weaponize confidentiality agreements against the public interest,” he said.

“The PUL categorically calls on the Boakai administration to unconditionally rescind this policy. If this government is genuinely committed to its stated theme of promoting accountability, transparency, and inclusive development, it must align its actions with its rhetoric.”

GC’s ‘conspicuous’ silence

Kanubah also criticized the host institution, saying the Governance Commission should “break its silence.”

“The GC cannot afford to stand by passively while landmark transparency laws are hollowed out,” he said. “In the face of this policy, the Commission’s silence is conspicuous and self-defeating.”

He did, however, commend the Commission for bringing together a diverse group of stakeholders. He also praised President Boakai for issuing the proclamation that declared October the Month of Good Governance.

78 of 103 agencies without information officers

The PUL president said the confidentiality policy comes at a “precarious moment.” He noted that the FOI Act was passed more than 15 years ago but has long faced structural, financial and institutional obstacles.

He cited a recent IIC audit which found that 78 of 103 ministries and agencies assessed had not appointed designated Public Information Officers.

Under a USAID-supported program, he said, journalists filed 104 FOI requests, and fewer than five received responses within 90 days.

Kanubah described the IIC as chronically underfunded. He said the Commission had at one point been evicted from its office over unpaid rent and had operated from a basement without electricity.

He also pointed to other problems:

• poor record-keeping, with no central systems for tracking information requests

• a “default administrative culture of secrecy”

• inconsistent political will

• low public awareness of the law, especially among rural communities, women and marginalized groups

Open data stalled

On open data, Kanubah said Liberia still does not have an enforced data protection and privacy law. A draft was validated in late 2024, but the national Data Authority has yet to be formally established.

Most government agencies have working websites, he said, but almost none regularly publish key data such as budgets and expenditure reports. He named the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning as a rare exception.

He also cited high internet costs, poor rural connectivity and digital illiteracy. He warned that open-government reforms depend heavily on donor programs such as the Open Government Partnership (OGP) and USAID rather than national budget allocations, which leaves their future “fragile.”

“To actively introduce policies that roll back these hard-won freedoms is a step backward we cannot afford,” Kanubah said.

World.title: 2026 National Child Health Week Campaign launched
World.content:
Minister of Health, Professor Roma Chilengi, has called for a shift from annual child health campaigns to the routine delivery of essential healthcare services to ensure that no child is left behind.

Professor Chilengi says interventions such as immunisation, vitamin A supplementation, deworming and nutritional screening should become part of daily healthcare delivery rather than being concentrated during Child Health Week.

Speaking during the launch of the 2026 Child Health Week Campaign, Professor Chilengi said the Ministry of Health was targeting 4.5 million children under the age of five with essential health and nutrition services.

He said the campaign provided an opportunity to reach children who had missed scheduled health interventions, particularly those in rural and remote communities.

Professor Chilengi noted that despite progress in reducing under-five mortality to 42 deaths per 1,000 live births, Zambia still faced challenges in ensuring universal access to essential child health services.

He said the Ministry of Health estimated that one in every five children missed a critical, life-saving vaccine before their first birthday, highlighting the need to strengthen community health systems.

Professor Chilengi said the campaign would provide vitamin A supplementation to children aged six to 59 months, deworming services to those aged 12 to 59 months, and nutritional screening for children aged six to 59 months.

He added that eligible girls aged nine years and above would also receive routine human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination to help prevent cervical cancer.

Meanwhile, UNICEF Country Representative, Saja Abdullah, said the organisation would continue working with the Government and other partners to strengthen healthcare delivery through immunisation, breastfeeding promotion, nutrition support and vitamin A supplementation.

Dr Abdullah said the initiative also provided an opportunity to implement the Integrated Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn, Child and Nutrition Outreach Package, which aims to improve the delivery of essential health services.

And World Vision Zambia has disclosed that it has successfully transported approximately 900,000 vitamin A supplements and nearly four million deworming tablets to all provincial centres across the country ahead of their distribution to health facilities.

World Vision Zambia Strategy, Impact and Learning Director, Ekwase Msoni, said the supplies were intended to improve child health and nutrition, particularly among vulnerable children.

World.title: Fire destroys makeshift shop in Chipata
World.content:
A-52-year-old woman of Mthilasembe Compound in Chipata District has lost her makeshift shop worth K2,000 after it was destroyed by fire in the early hours of today.

Zambia Police Service Eastern Province Commanding Officer, Robertson Mweemba said the incident occurred around 02:00 hours.

Mr Mweemba said the matter was reported at Nabvutika Police Post, under Chipata Central Police Station, by the shop owner, Beatrice Chulu.

He said Ms Chulu was sleeping at her residence when she heard a noise outside and went to investigate.

Mr Mweemba said she discovered that her shop, locally known as a kanthemba, was on fire, while neighbours had already started pouring water in an attempt to extinguish the flames.

However, their efforts failed to contain the fire, resulting in the shop being completely burnt to ashes.

He said police officers visited the scene and confirmed that the shop had been destroyed.

Mr Mweemba said investigations into the incident were ongoing.

World.title: SDA donates 110 wheelchairs worth K250,000 to UTH
World.content:
The Seventh Day Adventist church (SDA) has donated 110 wheelchairs worth K250,000 to the University Teaching Hospital (UTH) aimed at easing mobility challenges among patients.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, SDA Woodlands Conference President, Daniel Chunga says the donation reflects the church’s commitment to Christian Service and Compassion by helping the vulnerable members of the Society.

Dr Chunga highlighted that improving health care requires collective efforts from Government, churches, the private sector and other stakeholders.

“The Gesture highlights the need for continued efforts to ensure that patients with mobility challenges can access health care facilities and services without unnecessary mobility barriers” he added.

Dr Chunga explained that wheelchairs are expected to assist patients who have difficulties with walking, helping them move between hospital departments and access medical services more conveniently.

Speaking at the same event, SDA Woodlands Conference Dorcas President Melody Mudenda reaffirmed the Dorcas Societ’s commitment to reaching out to communities through Charitable works and supporting people in need.

Miss Mudenda said the donation was part of the Dorcas society’s efforts to reach out to people in need and improve their quality of life, particularly those facing mobility challenges.

She encouraged continued acts of generosity and community service, noting that collective efforts can make a meaningful difference in the lives of the vulnerable people.

In receiving the donation, University Teaching Hospital Head Clinical Care Humphrey Kunda expressed appreciation for the Gesture.

Dr Kunda commended the church for complementing Government’s efforts in health care delivery, noting that partnerships with faith based organisations play an important role in addressing the needs of patients.

He has further encouraged other organisations to emulate the church’s example by supporting health care institutions and vulnerable members of society.

World.title: Freedom fighter champions free education policy
World.content:
A freedom fighter in Milenge District, Bernard Chishimba, has urged pupils to remain focused on their education and take advantage of the Free Education Policy, saying they are privileged as compared to the challenges faced by learners during the colonial era.

Speaking in Milenge, Mr Chishimba pointed out that access to education was difficult during colonial rule, making the opportunities available to pupils today something they should value.

He said pupils should not take their education for granted, as the government has created opportunities for them to attend school without paying tuition fees.

Mr Chishimba urged pupils to avoid absenteeism during the current mopani worm(caterpillar harvest season), warning that some learners could be tempted to miss classes to go and collect caterpillars at the expense of their education.

“Pupils should not abandon their lessons to go and pick caterpillars. This is a season that comes and goes, but education is important for their future,” Mr Chishimba said.

He said the difficulties experienced by learners during the colonial era should serve as a reminder to pupils to appreciate the educational opportunities available to them today.

“During our time, it was difficult to go to school and learn. Today, children have the opportunity to learn under the Free Education Policy, and they should make good use of it,” he said.

Meanwhile, Milenge District Commissioner, Kayula Mulenga said education was essential to the development of the district and the country, as it equipped learners with the knowledge and skills needed to contribute to national development.

Mr Mulenga said pupils should remain committed to their studies and make effective use of the learning opportunities provided by the government.

“Education is key to the future of our children and the development of our country. Pupils must take their studies seriously and ensure that they attend classes consistently,” Mr Mulenga said.

He urged parents and guardians to support their children’s education by encouraging regular school attendance and ensuring that seasonal activities such as caterpillar collection did not interfere with learning.

World.title: Konkola humble Nkana
World.content:
Record 13-time Super League champions Nkana’s perfect start to the transitional season has ended after a 2-0 loss to Konkola Blades on Sunday in Chililabombwe.

Kalampa had won their opening three matches ahead of the visit to Chililabombwe.

Konkola Blades reignited their title challenge in Stream A with an impressive 2-0 victory over Nkana on Matchday 5.

Blades took the lead in the 34th minute through Emmanuel Kunda before Congolese striker Idrissa Ilunga Mbombo doubled the advantage three minutes after the restart to seal all three points for the Chililabombwe side.

The defeat sees Nkana remain second on the log with 9 points from four games, level with Konkola Blades who move to third on goal difference, while FC MUZA continue to lead Stream A with 10 points after Saturday’s 1-0 win over Power Dynamos.

In Stream B, Green Buffaloes beat Kabwe Warriors 2-1 at Godfrey Ucar Chitalu Stadium.

Charles Majapa had given Warriors hope with a stoppage time goal in the 91st minute, but earlier strikes from Paul Mbuyi in the 65th minute and Golden Mashata in the 74th minute were enough to hand the Army side maximum points.

The win moves Buffaloes to second place in Stream B with 8 points, two behind leaders Green Eagles.

At Shinde Stadium, Mufulira Wanderers’ woes continued after suffering a 0-1 home defeat to Chirundu United.

Andrew Simumba scored the only goal of the game in the 27th minute.

The result leaves Mighty in the relegation zone with 2 points from four games, while Chirundu United climb to third with 7 points.

World.title: President Hicilema honours fisherman, Chalala Hero, other medal recipients
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has awarded Medal of Gallantry to Namwala fisherman who wrestled a crocodile to save a fellow fisherman and a civilian who risked his life to guide security agencies to rescue 13 young women abducted in Chalala.

President Hakainde Hichilema conferred the honours during the Investiture Ceremony held at State House where Newton Nalumino was honoured for exceptional courage and bravery on the night of April 2023 at around 04:00 hours while fishing in the Namwala River.

He said Mr Nalumino witnessed a crocodile attack in which a crocodile captured another fisherman, Without hesitation and at great personal risk, he confronted the reptile and repeatedly struck it with his paddling stick, forcing it to release the victim who he then pulled to safety.

“The injured fisherman was rushed to Namwala District Hospital and later referred to Livingstone Teaching Hospital, he survived but sustained permanent disability, he said

The second recipient of the Gallantry Medal was Robby Chitambo, who was recognised for compassion and selflessness during the 2022 abduction case that shook Lusaka, where young women were held captive in Chalala, causing widespread fear and anxiety.

Mr Chitambo, who was a civilian then, displayed remarkable bravery by assisting authorities and guiding them to the location where 13 young women were being held captive.

His courageous actions contributed to the successful rescue of the victims and subsequent apprehension of the perpetrators.

Mr Chitambo has since been employed in Government by Zambia Airforce.

President Hichilema also conferred others for their distinguished service among them is Chandra Desai and Lata Desai who received honours for significant contributions to education, healthcare, job creation and community development in Luanshya district where they settled in 1960.

“As a business couple, they established several enterprises including Desai Discount Centre, Quality Furniture, GMMI Limited and Gaurav Zambia Limited, creating over 500 employment opportunities,” he added.

Mr Hichilema added that their philanthropy has supported school infrastructure, computer laboratories, water and sanitation facilities and feeding programmes benefiting over 500 learners, as well as healthcare infrastructure at Thompson District Hospital and the Zambia Combined Staff Clinic, including assistive devices for children with special needs and tuition for over 600 vulnerable students.

A personal secretary by profession and early childhood education consultant born on 13th June 1953 in Mongu District, was awarded the President’s Insignia of Merit for outstanding contributions to education, youth empowerment and community development.

She personally financed the construction of a 1×3 classroom block and a fully equipped computer laboratory in Mongu District and through her Foundation has empowered women with sewing machines, provided housing support and assisted the elderly. Her initiatives have benefited over 2,000 people.

Meanwhile, Patrick Chinyemba, popularly known as Bado, the highly distinguished Zambian flyweight boxer born on 3rd January 2001 in Lusaka, was honoured for his consistent performance at national and international level, including representing Zambia at the Olympic Games, including Paris 2024, and winning several senior national titles.

Further, Carol Kanyemba, Head Coach of Zambia’s Under-17 Women’s National Football Team, the Copper Princesses, born on 23rd January 1988 in Kabwe, was honoured for exceptional commitment to youth development and advancement of women’s football, leading the team to major regional and international competitions including FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup qualifiers.

Moreover, Ashious Melu, the Zambian footballer, national team captain and coach, popularly known as Super Ash, was honoured posthumously.

Born on 16th June 1957 in Zambezi District, Melu began his career with Konkola Blades before joining Mufulira Wanderers in the late 1970s, became Zambian Footballer of the Year in 1983 after scoring 43 goals.

He again in 1987, captained Zambia from 1988 to 1992 leading the team to the 1988 Seoul Olympics quarterfinals with memorable wins over Italy and Guatemala, and later coached Wanderers to consecutive league titles in 1995 and 1996.

President Hichilema also conferred other national honours for distinguished service which include Trade Kings limited, Patel Iqbal, Wonderful group Limited Chief Executive Officer, Yaochi Huang and ambassador Cox Sikumba who was awarded posthumously.

The President said the honorees’ generosity, courage and exceptional service have advanced socio-economic development and elevated the Zambian flag, making them worthy of national recognition.

World.title: Government prioritises social sectors for economic independence-Bwalya
World.content:
Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya says Government is working hard to improve social sectors to achieve economic independence and ensure that citizens live dignified lives.

‎Dr Bwalya, who made the remarks during the commemoration of the 62nd anniversary of independence, said the government wants to transform the economy in a sustainable manner in line with the growing Zambia agenda.

The Province Permanent Secretary said the government is fully committed to boosting the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) with a sharp focus on sustainable job creation and rural industrialization.

‎Dr Bwalya emphasized that the ultimate goal of the province and the country’s economic expansion is to uplift ordinary citizens by revitalizing key social sectors.

‎”We want to improve social sectors so that we can improve the lives of the people.” he said

Dr Bwalya stressed that economic growth will not come at the expense of the environment.

‎He assured residents that the government is strictly pursuing green policies to ensure natural ecosystems are preserved for future generations.

‎”Government wants to ensure the environment is not damaged and will grow the economy in a sustainable manner,” he noted.

‎Dr Bwalya, who outlined the specific trajectory for Muchinga Province, said the region will no longer rely solely on exporting raw materials.

‎He indicated that the government will instead be pivoting toward value addition and the creation of local manufacturing enterprises to aggressively drive national development.

‎Dr Bwalya further underscored that true economic independence is impossible without local ownership.

‎He linked economic success directly to quality education, noting that an empowered workforce is the engine of development.

‎”Economic independence requires the involvement of the people. Hence, quality education is important so we can give skills to our people so we can develop,” he explained.

‎Dr Bwalya has since reiterated the government’s unwavering commitment to inclusive development, promising that no district or chiefdom in Muchinga Province or the wider nation will be left behind.

‎”We will ensure that development reaches all corners of the country,” he said.

‎‎Meanwhile, Dr Bwalya, who was responding to the concerns from freedom fighters, said the government has put up interventions to support them.

‎Dr Bwalya stated that all freedom fighters have been put on social cash transfer, and encouraged those who are not there to visit the relevant department for them to receive the support.

‎He also said that the freedom fighters have been encouraged to form cooperatives so that they can be supported with farming inputs such as fertilizer.

Meanwhile, Chinsali District Commissioner Brenda Silwembe said Chinsali is witnessing massive development facilitated through governmental development agenda and the increased Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

‎Ms Silwembe cited infrastructure development such as the construction of health facilities and schools and the delivery of youth and women empowerment, among others.

‎She added that as the Independence journey continues, President Hakainde Hichilema remains committed to fostering development in the district and the country at large.

‎”As we celebrated this year’s independence, I implore everyone to renew our commitment to hard work for us to honor the dreams of our founding fathers who fought for the nation to gain independence,” she said.

‎Ms Silwembe stated that with chinsali being a sacred place in the story of Zambia’s struggle for independence, there is a deliberate need to embrace unity, resilience, and the spirit of togetherness.

‎”As we gather to honor the liberation of Mother Zambia, the theme Zambia @62 Our Journey, Our Growth, Our Future challenges us to reflect deeply on where we are coming from and where we are heading to,” she said

‎Chinsali District Freedom Fighters Association Gremson Katongo said Zambia is enjoying freedom and unity today because of the founding fathers of mother Zambia who fought for the country’s liberty.

‎Mr Katongo said currently there are a few surviving freedom fighters who need to be taken care of.

‎Mr Katongo therefore, has called on the Government to look into the plight of freedom fighters and care for them.

World.title: Serenje DC calls for unity to boost Agriculture
World.content:
Serenje District Commissioner (DC), Ellen Mibenge has called on agricultural stakeholders to work together to unlock the district’s agricultural potential and contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ms Mibenge says farmers, cooperatives, agricultural institutions, agro-dealers and private investors should strengthen collaboration to boost agricultural production and support the Government’s Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking during the commemoration of Zambia’s 62nd Independence Anniversary in Serenje, Ms Mibenge said the Government cannot not achieve its sector targets without the active participation of all stakeholders.

“The Government cannot realise this transformation alone. We need to contribute to the national agricultural targets under the Grow Zambia Agenda, which the Government, under the leadership of President Hakainde Hichilema, is implementing over the next five years,” Ms Mibenge said.

She said as the Government pursued national production targets for maize, soya beans, wheat and sugar, agricultural stakeholders in Serenje should ensure that agriculture remained a key driver of economic transformation and contribute meaningfully to national production.

Ms Mibenge added that all stakeholders have a responsibility to facilitate collaboration and ensure that national development priorities translate into tangible benefits for the people of Serenje.

On decentralisation, the DC emphasised the need to strengthen coordination between central and local government to ensure that district development priorities aligned with provincial and national objectives.

She also called on residents to uphold peace, unity and national values, saying these were essential to achieving the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ms Mibenge further urged Serenje Town Council to manage public resources transparently and efficiently to ensure that development projects responded to the needs of local communities.

World.title: Kenya: Police, Protesters Clash During Cost-of-Living, Fuel Demonstrations
World.content:
Cape Town — Nairobi police arrested several protesters on Monday as officers and demonstrators clashed in running battles across the CBD over rising fuel prices and the cost of living, The Eastleigh Voice reports.

Protesters gathered on Moi Avenue and Kimathi Street despite a heavy police deployment, carrying placards reading 'Remove taxes on fuel'. The protests followed the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority's latest pricing review for the October-November cycle, which pushed petrol in Nairobi to Sh226.96 per litre, diesel to Sh227.76, and kerosene to Sh219.87.

In a letter dated October 22 and received at police headquarters the same day, the Coalition of Human Rights Defenders said the demonstration aimed to highlight the burden of fuel costs on households and businesses. Organisers estimated 500 to 900 participants, and pledged to keep the march orderly and respect the rights of other members of the public.

World.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia's Transitional Justice Should Resume, but Not Where It Left Off
World.content:
analysis

Public consultations on transitional justice laws should start only after National Dialogue recommendations, gaps and new developments have been considered.

Ethiopia's Ministry of Justice launched a government-civil society platform on transitional justice on 23 October, signalling the resumption of the process that stalled in April 2025. The transitional justice website is now active, and public consultations on draft transitional justice laws are reportedly expected to begin soon.

The interruption came just as the draft laws were about to be opened for consultations. The pause, which had no official explanation, weakened momentum and created uncertainty. To rebuild public and donor confidence, reasons for the resumption should be made public - along with next steps and timelines.



Four priorities should guide the resumed process: the National Dialogue's recommendations, existing gaps, outstanding commitments and developments during the pause.

The first priority is the National Dialogue Commission's recommendations, which were submitted to Parliament on 3 October. They are yet to be made public. Since transitional justice was allegedly paused to make way for the dialogue, proceeding without considering its recommendations would miss the point and the chance to strengthen transitional justice.

The Ministry of Justice should establish a committee to review the dialogue's implications for the Transitional Justice Policy, draft legislation and implementation. The recommendations may affect transitional justice in three ways: through explicit proposals affecting its scope and mandates; through relevant recommendations in other thematic areas; and through broader reforms that may overlap or interact with its implementation. The review should therefore extend beyond recommendations explicitly labelled as transitional justice.

Addressing these implications requires two complementary approaches. Targeted adjustments to the legal frameworks should incorporate relevant recommendations without reopening the entire legal and policy basis for public debate. A separate strategy could coordinate with other institutions or reforms mentioned in the dialogue's recommendations to prevent institutional confusion or another pause.

Beyond its specific recommendations, the dialogue could help give Parliament a more prominent role in transitional justice. It may also contribute to establishing a shared, officially recognised account of victimhood and suffering across communities, laying the groundwork for official acknowledgement of and apology for the violence and harm suffered. These contributions should be reflected in the revised transitional justice framework.

The second priority is to address unresolved weaknesses in the policy. The existing framework had shortcomings concerning which institution could resolve legal disputes arising between transitional justice bodies. The proposed Special Bench could do this.

Accountability for crimes allegedly committed by foreign perpetrators, particularly Eritrean forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, also remains insufficiently addressed.

Mental health and psychosocial support are hidden under the reparations pillar. The revised framework should recognise them as cross-cutting priorities with clear institutional responsibilities - if not as a standalone pillar whose implementation should begin immediately. Currently, just a few civil society organisations offer support to victims and survivors in their struggle to heal and be recognised.

Economic, social and cultural rights violations also require greater attention, not only in reparations but across other pillars such as criminal accountability and institutional reform. Reform should extend beyond vetting security and justice institutions to government offices responsible for economic governance and development, whose policies and practices may have contributed to historical grievances and systemic violations.

The process also had procedural gaps regarding participation. Dedicated consultations with youth, diaspora communities and other vulnerable groups and underrepresented constituencies did not take place. This should not be repeated in the forthcoming consultations. For communities excluded by continuing conflicts, the resumed process should provide opportunities for later participation and targeted adjustments.

The third priority is fulfilling outstanding commitments. The coordination mechanism envisaged in the policy is yet to be established. Its absence led to failure to resolve misunderstandings between the National Dialogue and transitional justice processes, ultimately contributing to the pause.

The urgent need for such a mechanism was also recognised in the 2024 transitional justice implementation roadmap. This called for an interim, multi-stakeholder body to guide and monitor progress until formal transitional justice institutions were established. Establishing this mechanism is now even more important to coordinate transitional justice with institutions and reforms emerging from the dialogue.

The fourth priority is to consider how the institutional landscape has evolved during the pause. Regional transitional justice initiatives, including the Commission for Investigation of Violence and Reconciliation and Reparation of Victims in the Somali Region, have advanced their work. During the break, the Commission of Inquiry on Tigray Genocide also released its findings.

The national transitional justice framework must clarify its relationship with these initiatives, particularly in recognising and using their findings, institutional cooperation and avoiding duplication.

Ethiopia has also established thousands of customary courts across several regions, with the new criminal procedure and evidence code allowing for complementarity between formal and traditional justice mechanisms in criminal cases. But the Transitional Justice Policy addresses traditional justice largely in abstract terms. Its practical integration within each transitional justice pillar, and principles and safeguards governing this relationship, require clarification.

To strengthen the independence, transparency and credibility of the forthcoming consultation process, two measures are essential.

First, independent experts involved in drafting the laws should participate alongside Ministry of Justice experts to ensure independent scrutiny and preserve the coherence and rationale of the legal frameworks. Second, the draft laws should be shared in advance to allow stakeholders to prepare informed contributions.

Close 

Resumption should kick off with independent monitoring, parliamentary oversight, African Union engagement and meaningful civil society participation.

Civil society's contribution should not be confined to structures controlled by the Justice Ministry or other government institutions. It must retain the space to organise independently, contribute to implementation and exercise critical oversight. Its access to credible information and opportunities for meaningful engagement should not be conditional on membership in a Ministry of Justice-led civil society coordination platform.

Overall, the conclusion of the National Dialogue appears to have offered an opportunity to end the uncertainty surrounding transitional justice. The immediate priorities are to review and incorporate those recommendations, address outstanding legal and institutional gaps and commitments, update the roadmap and proceed with consultations on revised legislation.

Rather than restarting transitional justice from where the process left off, the task should be to recalibrate and resume.
