World.title: Air Canada blamed maintenance issues to deny compensation. Records show it wanted planes for other routes
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Air Canada denied Juan Rojas compensation for a cancelled flight after it swapped the aircraft assigned to his flight with one that needed safety-related maintenance.

The Gatineau man challenged the airline through the Canadian Transportation Agency and won — and the evidence raises questions about the information Air Canada provided to justify denying him compensation.

"I felt like they were trying to cheat the system," Rojas told Go Public.

Under Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations, passengers can be entitled to up to $1,000 for delayed flights, but only if the delay is within the airline's control and not required for safety.

Rojas's case is not the only one raising questions about airlines' use of the safety exemption.

Got a story you want investigated? Contact Erica and the Go Public team gopublic@cbc.ca

Go Public has uncovered three other instances in which Air Canada told passengers their flights were cancelled because of safety-related maintenance while flight records show the aircraft they were scheduled to fly on were subsequently used on other routes. In all three cases, Air Canada maintains it does not owe compensation.

What is the maintenance 'loophole'?

The maintenance "loophole" is a simple way for airlines to potentially deny compensation for countless passengers every year, said Montreal lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille.

"It's a huge duffel bag in which they can put anything and everything," said De Bellefeuille, director of legal services for Option consommateurs, a Montreal non-profit that advocates for consumer rights.

"Most passengers do not have enough information to counter whatever is said by the airline."

Lawyer Sylvie De Bellefeuille says Ottawa should close a maintenance 'loophole' airlines use to deny paying compensation for delayed or cancelled flights. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

Air Canada declined Go Public's request for an interview.

But in a written statement, it acknowledged that in all four cases, it made a commercial decision: reassigning a functioning aircraft to another route where the scheduled plane required safety-related maintenance, leaving passengers on the original route without their scheduled flight.

Air Canada argued that an aircraft's schedule is fluid, and it must be able to make "operational adjustments" to "minimize the overall impact on passengers." The airline said it was within its rights to deny compensation.

Gabor Lukacs, founder of Air Passenger Rights, strongly disputes that interpretation. He points to a 2022 CTA decision, which said mechanical issues must be "a direct cause" of a cancelled flight and cannot be considered a "knock-on effect."

"I am finding it stunning that Air Canada continues to pretend as if the law has not been settled," said Lukacs.

Air Canada 'misrepresents' info to federal regulator

When Rojas's September 2022 flight to Bogotá from Montreal was cancelled, Air Canada denied his request for compensation, citing safety-related maintenance.

When Rojas challenged the airline before the Canadian Transportation Agency, Air Canada submitted documents claiming a catering truck had struck his plane, damaging it.

A complaints resolution officer with the CTA found that Air Canada's claim it cancelled a flight due to safety issues was unfounded and ordered the airline to pay $1,000 in compensation. (CBC)

It wasn't until a friend suggested he check the public Civil Aviation Daily Reporting System , that he realized the Air Canada plane struck by a catering truck was not the same one assigned to Rojas's cancelled flight.

In other words, the incident Air Canada cited to justify denying Rojas compensation involved a different aircraft.

It's "outrageous," said De Bellefeuille, the lawyer.

"They were clearly misrepresenting the information," said Rojas, who submitted his discovery to the CTA.

Air Canada told Go Public Rojas's aircraft was moved to cover for the one that had been damaged.

This past January, a complaint resolution officer ruled in the case, ordering Air Canada to pay Rojas $1,000 for the "inconvenience."

"The decision to swap aircraft to avoid or minimize delays for one group of passengers at the expense of another is a commercial decision," the officer wrote. The airline could make that decision, per the ruling, but it was required to compensate affected passengers.

'A real black mark on Air Canada'

Michael Bociurkiw was flying from Bangkok to Vancouver last February when he received an email from Air Canada mid-flight. His connecting flight from Vancouver to Newark had been cancelled because of safety-related maintenance, the airline said.

But the plane with supposed safety concerns had the exact registration number of the very aircraft Bociurkiw was seated on.

"I wasn't too concerned about a safety issue," said Bociurkiw. "I was more concerned about what the hell is going on? And why is Air Canada giving me this story?"

Michael Bociurkiw had his flight cancelled for safety-related maintenance. He found out the plane assigned to his flight was perfectly fine, but the airline needed it for another flight. (Submitted by Michael Bociurkiw)

Go Public found two more cases in which Air Canada cited safety-related maintenance to deny passengers compensation, while flight records showed the aircraft originally assigned to their flights were perfectly fine and used on other routes.

Carlos Fernandez accuses Air Canada of "blatantly lying" after his May flight from Las Vegas to Toronto was cancelled 10 minutes after his aircraft was swapped for one needing safety-related maintenance. Alison Monaghan's July flight from Toronto to Vancouver was similarly impacted.

"It's a real black mark on Air Canada as far as ethics and integrity go," said Monaghan.

Alison Monaghan's flight to Vancouver was cancelled after Air Canada used the plane to replace an aircraft on a different route that had developed maintenance issues. (Submitted by Alison Monaghan)

How often does this happen?

Go Public has previously reported on WestJet using the safety-related maintenance exemption to deny passengers compensation. But the full extent of the practice among Canada's two largest airlines remains unclear.

The CTA, which launched an investigation in the WestJet cases, does not publish its decisions on air passenger disputes — despite a recent court order requiring them to be made public. The agency declined Go Public's request for past decisions.

A CTA spokesperson cited privacy concerns and said the agency planned to begin publishing decisions early next year, once those had been addressed.

But Lukacs said airlines have little financial incentive to comply with passenger protection rules if they face no meaningful consequences for violating them.

"Right now, it is just more economical for an airline to deceive passengers than to actually comply with the law."

The CTA said no fine has been issued in Rojas's case, nor has it ever issued a penalty against Air Canada "for incorrectly characterizing a flight cancellation as safety-related maintenance."

It should have issued a "hefty" fine in Rojas's case, Lukacs said, "because Air Canada was not only mistreating the passenger, it was also maintaining the same fraudulent falsehood even when it came before a decision-maker."

Feds need to do more to protect air passengers, advocates say

De Bellefeuille says Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations need to change so passengers are not left to rely on airlines' own explanations when flights are cancelled or delayed.

"It's really David against Goliath," said the Montreal lawyer and consumer advocate.

In the European Union , airlines can only avoid paying compensation for a qualifying disruption caused by a mechanical problem in limited situations, such as extraordinary circumstances that could not have been avoided, such as an act of terrorism.

But Lukacs – who has also called for an overhaul of air passenger protections – said the government has shown little appetite for reform.

Documents obtained by Go Public through an Access to Information request show previous transport ministers telling the CTA to maintain the airlines' ability to deny compensation for safety-related maintenance.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon declined an interview request.

Rojas says he's angry that the current rules can leave air passengers in the dark when airlines cite mechanical problems to deny compensation. He's now been compensated, but wonders about the other people who were booked for the same flight?

"The least the government can do is ensure that our rights are protected."

World.title: U.S. officials accuse Canada of midterm meddling — but Trump has endorsed foreign candidates
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Despite U.S. officials repeatedly warning Canada not to get involved in the upcoming U.S. midterms, President Donald Trump has his own track record of weighing in on foreign elections.

Trump has endorsed about half a dozen candidates across the globe since he returned to the White House in early 2025 and even boasted earlier this year that he has "a very good record of endorsing candidates in the U.S.," before touting a number of foreign candidates he backed.

"I'm not supposed to be endorsing people," Trump said during the February inaugural meeting of his Board of Peace. "As long as it works, it's OK with me."

Since early 2025, Trump has backed presidential or prime ministerial candidates in Poland, Honduras, Colombia and Japan.

Most recently, he voiced support for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is facing an election on Tuesday.

The U.S. president also put his support behind former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán's failed re-election bid, which included Vice-President JD Vance appearing at a rally in Budapest.

Trump also weighed in to last year's midterms in Argentina, suggesting that a financial support package would hinge on a good result for President Javier Milei's party.

WATCH | The Power Panel on U.S. meddling claims: U.S. election meddling fears just 'distraction politics': ex-AG | Duration closed caption 18:48 Global Affairs Canada instructed Canadian diplomats in the U.S. on Tuesday to avoid meeting with, attending events with or appearing in photos or promotional materials alongside U.S. midterm election candidates. The memo came after U.S. President Donald Trump accused Canadian politicians of interfering in American elections. The Power Panel stops by Power & Politics to unpack the election interference concerns.

Daniel Drezner, a professor of international politics at Tufts University in Massachusetts, said U.S. officials suggesting Canada is interfering in the midterms is a situation of the "pot calling the kettle black," given Trump's track record.

"The truth is that this administration has had a long track record of intervening directly into the elections of official allies," he told CBC News in an interview.

The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa released a "fact sheet" on Wednesday pointing to instances that could amount to "potential interference in U.S. elections" after Prime Minister Mark Carney and other Canadian politicians dismissed previous suggestions that Canadian officials are trying to influence the vote outcome on Nov. 3.

WATCH | 'No merit' to U.S. claims, Carney says: 'No merit' to suggestion Canadian politicians interfering in U.S. election, Carney says | Duration closed caption 3:37 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from Istanbul on Friday, says there are deep diplomatic ties between Canada and the U.S., and engagement happens no matter the timing, including during elections. 'We have no intention to interfere' with their democratic processes, Carney said.

The embassy's release pointed to Liberal MP Anthony Housefather canvassing for a Florida Democrat, whom he's said is a friend, during a primary vote earlier this year and comments made by Industry Minister Mélanie Joly regarding Canada's counter-tariff strategy, some going back to March 2025 when she was in charge of foreign affairs.

The embassy's list also included the Ontario government's now infamous Ronald Reagan ad that ran in the U.S. last year and a federal government billboard campaign from early 2025.

In an exclusive interview with Rosemary Barton Live airing on Sunday, former U.S. ambassador to Canada James Blanchard said the administration has "no credibility" given Trump's list of public endorsements.

"If this accusation had come from the Reagan administration or the Bush administration or the Obama administration, the Clinton administration, I would take it seriously," Blanchard said. "But I can't from this current administration."

Embassy declines to comment

CBC News reached out to the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa and pointed out Trump's track record of endorsing foreign candidates. The embassy declined to comment when asked if a Canadian official offering a similar endorsement to a midterm candidate would amount to potential election interference.

Trump also jumped into the Canadian political fray during the 2025 campaign, writing on social media that he'd "rather deal with a liberal than a conservative."

The current president is not the only notable U.S. politician to talk Canadian electoral politics during a campaign. Former president Barack Obama publicly endorsed former prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2019 and 2021, albeit after he had left the White House. Sen. Bernie Sanders also backed former NDP leader Jagmeet Singh in the 2021 campaign.

Drezner said those examples are different from Trump's endorsements because neither were a part of the executive branch at the time. He pointed out that typically it's the norm for heads of states or heads of government not to weigh in on foreign elections.

"The idea was that surely you can do business with whoever wins and you might have to do business with whichever party wins. So therefore you shouldn't be seen as campaigning overtly for one side or another," he said.

Trump officials also appeared to take an interest in the recent Alberta referendum. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in January that Alberta would make a "natural partner" for the U.S. while discussing the possibility of a separation referendum.

WATCH | Canadian diplomats told to be cautious during midterms: Canadian diplomats told to avoid appearances with U.S. midterm candidates | Duration closed caption 2:04 Global Affairs Canada has advised Canadian diplomats in the U.S. to be careful on social media and to avoid appearances with midterm candidates as American warnings about election interference ramp up.

The Globe and Mail reported recently that Republican political operatives were on the ground in Alberta earlier this year to help the separatist campaign. CBC News previously reported that Alberta separatists also attended meetings in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

The U.S. Embassy's list came after Ambassador Pete Hoekstra and Trump adviser Peter Navarro warned against Canada getting involved in the midterms.

Carney and other government officials have pushed back on the suggestion that Canada is looking to interfere.

"There is no merit to these claims, so I'll call it out that way," Carney told reporters during a news conference in Istanbul on Friday.

"I'm disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions," the prime minister said of Hoekstra in particular.

WATCH | Joly denies U.S. election interference claims: Joly denies U.S. election interference claims by Trump administration | Duration 0:54 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters on Thursday that she regularly meets with both Democratic and Republican politicians, after the Trump administration accused her of planning to 'influence American politics.'

While Drezner said Housefather's canvassing for a candidate might be "slightly unusual," other instances the embassy mentioned — like Joly and Bernadette Jordan, Canada's consul general in Boston, meeting with American politicians — amounts to "garden variety diplomacy."

Joly herself has pushed back against the accusations saying she has met with Republicans and Democrats in recent months.

The trade war has become a pressure point on Republican candidates in border states like Michigan and Maine.

Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who has represented Maine since 1997 and has tried to distance herself from Trump's tariffs, said Friday that she "secured" some exemptions to those levies.

"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," she said in a social media post.

WATCH | Trade war a major issue in midterms: Canada-U.S. trade war emerges as key issue ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:18 The Canada-U.S. trade war is solidifying itself as a major ballot-box issue in pivotal states ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

The Republican candidate for Michigan's open Senate seat released a 30-second ad criticizing tariffs earlier this month.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Mike Rogers says in the ad.

Drezner said he could "easily see" a situation where the Trump administration blames bad midterm results on Canada.

"They're going to blame anyone and everyone. That is the modus operandi of this White House," he said.

When asked on Friday if the Trump administration might blame Canada for a poor midterm result and slap more tariffs on Canadian exports, the prime minister said he doesn't "see that coming to pass."

World.title: The Bank of Canada's inflation dilemma
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of Mind Your Business, a weekly analysis of the biggest business stories emailed to subscribers on Monday mornings. If you haven't subscribed yet, you can do that by clicking here.

The Canadian economy is facing two very distinct problems right now.

On the one hand, inflation is high and rising. So far, at least, price increases have been contained to energy. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent last month, but core measures (which strip out more volatile components) remained subdued.

But as we saw in the U.S., the containment doesn't hold forever — and once price increases spill over into other sectors, it can be tough to rein them back in.

On the other hand, the economy is weak. And we haven't even really started to get a measure of the impact of the latest tranche of tariffs.

Those two duelling crises pose a difficult riddle for the Bank of Canada.

Weak growth would usually prompt the central bank to cut interest rates to spur some economic growth. But rising inflation makes the bank want to raise rates to slow the economy and keep prices from increasing too quickly.

Two problems — with two solutions in complete contradiction to one another.

WATCH | Bank has held interest rates 7 times in a row: 'We have to be realistic' about Canada-U.S. situation, Bank of Canada governor says | Duration closed caption 1:52 Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says while he hopes for a return to a 'more normal' Canada-U.S. relationship, he doesn't anticipate getting back to 'where we were' when dealing with an American administration that favours tariffs and protectionism.

One by one, most of the major economic outfits in the country have switched their forecasts. Most now believe that on Wednesday the Bank of Canada will increase its key overnight lending rate.

They all lay out the economics of the matter, but as Frances Donald and Nathan Janzen from RBC Economics remind us, the bank is seeing this year's surge in inflation through the prism of the last surge — the pandemic shock of 2022 to 2023.

"The cautionary lessons of the post-pandemic inflation surge ... demonstrated how supply-side shocks and persistent cost pressures can overwhelm an economy surprisingly quickly," wrote Donald and Janzen in a note to clients last week.

So, most economists now believe the bank will increase rates, even though they don't all feel the bank should make such a move.

Donald and Janzen say a quarter-point increase won't materially move the needle on where they think the economy is headed. (They had, after all, built their forecast on the assumption that rates were going to rise next year.)

"Ultimately, the signal of a rate hike on Oct. 28 has a larger meaning we shouldn’t ignore: Central banks do not have the same patience for inflation they might have had in the past, and are willing to act pre-emptively to guard against it," they wrote.

If we could wave a magic wand, we would probably like the economic data this week to come in opposite order. We have the interest rate decision on Wednesday and GDP numbers on Friday.

GDP stalled in July (zero per cent growth) and the economy is expected to have grown by 0.1 per cent in August. But new tariffs kicked in that month, so the risks to the forecast remain firmly planted on the downside.

Uncertainty is the new ... everything.

The Canadian economy and the Canadian consumer have both proven themselves to be far more resilient than expected. But each new obstacle takes a fresh swipe out of the Canada's potential growth.

On the upside, we will also get an update on the Bank of Canada's forecasts this week. The Monetary Policy Report is the central bank's deep dive into where it sees the economy headed.

World.title: A new cancer drug costs as much as a home down payment each month. Doctors say that's greed, not health care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

James Howard thinks most people would say they're willing to pay any price to stay alive — until they're asked to put a dollar figure on it.

"The question that nobody's ever prepared to ask themselves is how much is your life worth ... and how long does that decision take for you," he said.

For Howard, the answer is $90,000 a month for a new pancreatic cancer drug he hopes will extend his life.

Doctors in Vancouver diagnosed Howard with pancreatic cancer in November 2025. He underwent chemotherapy, but the cancer has since metastasized and is now Stage 4.

Earlier this year, he learned about daraxonrasib, a treatment approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in August but not yet in Canada. At three doses a day, it costs him about $63,000 US — roughly $90,000 Cdn — a month.

Howard is far from the only Canadian confronting the soaring cost of new cancer treatments. Oncologists across the country say increasingly expensive drugs — particularly treatments not yet approved or publicly funded in Canada — are forcing some patients to choose between paying enormous sums themselves and going without potentially life-extending medication.

James Howard, seen in his Vancouver home, takes three doses per day of the new pancreatic cancer drug daraxonrasib, which isn't approved in Canada and that he has to get from the U.S. at a cost of about $90,000 Cdn. a month. (Glen Kugelstadt/CBC News)

More than two dozen cancer specialists who spoke with CBC News said the trend is putting growing pressure on patients and the public health-care system.

It's not that pharmaceutical companies don't deserve to make money from their products, says Dr. Christopher Booth, a medical oncologist in Kingston, Ont.

But he says prices have reached a point where profit can come at the expense of patients.

"Corporate greed is gonna harm patients and health systems," he said.

An ecosystem that forbids negotiation

Booth, who is also a health-services researcher at Queen's University in Kingston, Ont., has been treating patients with pancreatic cancer — one of the most lethal forms of the disease — for more than 20 years.

He says U.S. drugs like daraxonrasib are approved and funded in an "ecosystem that essentially forbids" negotiation.

In Canada, Health Canada will give regulatory approval for doctors and hospitals to use a drug and then health authorities will work with the drug companies to determine a price.

But in the U.S., he says, it's illegal for the government to negotiate with the pharmaceutical companies when they launch most new drugs — a rule that was eased slightly in the 2022 Inflation Reduction Act — allowing the manufacturers to set their own price.

The median net price for new drugs launched in the U.S. was more than $250,000 US last year, according to a new report from the Boston-based Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER), up more than 35 per cent from the $190,000 US median three years earlier.

California-based drug maker Revolution Medicines set its launch price for daraxonrasib at $480,000 US ($675,000 Cdn) annually, or $40,000 for a 30-day supply at wholesale cost.

WATCH | Trump administration's deals with drug companies could push up prices for Canadians: Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada | Duration closed caption 2:00 New documents reveal the Trump administration is striking deals with pharmaceutical companies to lower drug costs in the U.S. But that could drive up prices in Canada, warn experts.

Profits over patients

Booth recalls how he and many of his colleagues were "thrilled" to see a treatment like daraxonrasib, a pill targeting a specific mutation in pancreatic cancer cells, prove effective in clinical trials.

The research found daraxonrasib halted or reversed tumour progression in nearly a third of patients, compared with about 10 per cent of those given chemotherapy, and increased survival from less than seven months to roughly 13.

"It was a signal of hope that we finally started to see some progress in this very difficult disease," Booth told CBC News.

But the excitement faded when Revolution Medicines announced the price of the drug, marketed as Rasonque.

LISTEN | Is Canada too reliant on the global supply chain for pharmaceuticals: Cost of Living 9:13 Why is Canada so vulnerable to drug shortages?

In a statement emailed to CBC News, Revolution Medicines said how much a patient pays out of pocket depends on factors including treatment duration and insurance coverage.

"Our goal is to establish a price that reflects meaningful therapeutic advancement while supporting patient access and continued scientific innovation," a spokesperson wrote.

But doctors whose patients may benefit from daraxonrasib question the price.

"Sometimes the prices they quote make absolutely no sense," said Dr. Ramy Saleh, an associate professor of oncology at McGill University who researches early-stage clinical trials.

"I'm not convinced as an oncologist or a researcher that when a drug is approved that it will cost half a million a year, he said. "I'm pretty sure to produce it is, you know, a fraction of that cost."

A Revolution Medicines facility in Redwood City, Calif. The company developed daraxonrasib, a new pancreatic cancer drug that has been approved in the U.S. but not yet in Canada. (Revolution Medicines)

Dr. Ralph Wong, a senior medical oncologist at CancerCare Manitoba, accuses the company of profiting off the backs of patients like his.

"I've had multiple patients in my practice crying because they can't access the drug," he said.

Wong says it's "particularly galling" that Revolution Medicines set such a high benchmark price based on its clinical-trial results rather than what he considers a price that would support patient access.

He and other doctors say they do everything they can to get patients free access through clinical trials or compassionate-access programs.

But if a drug isn't approved by Health Canada or covered by public or private insurance, patients can be left to pay for it themselves.

Revolution Medicines has yet to apply for Canadian approval of daraxonrasib.

WATCH | Could this medicine help pancreatic cancer patients double their life expectancy: Drug doubles survival time for pancreatic cancer patients, trial shows | Duration closed caption 2:37 An experimental drug, Daraxonrasib, is being hailed as a potential game changer after trial results published in the New England Journal of Medicine found it helped pancreatic cancer patients live twice as long as standard chemotherapy patients.

'Crippling' cost of longer life

While wealthy patients may be able to manage the price of a drug like daraxonrasib, Booth said it would be financially "crippling" for many.

Data from the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board (PMBRB), the arms-length federal agency that regulates patented drug prices, show Canadians are spending more on medications.

Sales of patented drugs reached $22.1 billion in 2024, up nearly 11 percent in a year, according to the PMPRB's most recent annual report. Patented medicines accounted for 47 per cent of all spending on medicines. There were 1,137 patented medicines approved for human use in Canada that year.

And that doesn't include what some patients pay for medications that aren't available in Canada.

For Howard, paying for daraxonrasib is like making a "down payment for a condo every month" for the hope of prolonging his life.

"It's not sustainable long term," he said, especially with all of the hurdles involved in getting the drug, including crossing the border to pick up the prescription at a U.S. postal address.

"[But] if I can gain a quality of life which allows you to spend more time with family, that's a significant bonus for me."

World.title: First Nations want tangible results as 'historic' first ministers' meeting opens
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The warning 43 years ago was about good talk without action.

It's why Indigenous leaders approached prime minister Pierre Trudeau's 1983 first ministers conference on constitutional rights with caution — concerned about holding negotiations to hold more negotiations, and about skeptical premiers primed to listen but not understand.

On Monday, First Nations leaders and Canada's first ministers will meet again in Ottawa to discuss Indigenous rights, the first such meeting in two decades, with those same warnings looming over what the Assembly of First Nations is calling an "historic gathering."

"First Nations and Canada and the provinces are at a crossroads," Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, national chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) told CBC Indigenous. "Many chiefs have told us that they see this meeting as a chance to chart maybe a path forward, a new path forward."

At an AFN-organized ceremony on Sunday few would speculate on what the meeting's outcome will be, but for chiefs the mantra going in is "tangible results." They stressed it can't be a "one-and-done" event.

"We're a minority in our own country," said Kelsey Jacko, chief of Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta, "and everybody's living off the milk and honey of our lands, but we're being left out, so we need a seat at the table."

WATCH | Indigenous leaders debate PM, premiers: Indigenous leaders meet to amend the Canadian Constitution in 1982 | Duration 5:36 Canada addresses and enshrines the issue of rights for Indigenous people. Aired March 16, 1982 on CBC's The National.

AFN, a national advocacy organization, has circulated several discussion papers suggesting it might seek commitments on building economic prosperity, policing, constitutional rights, health and education.

Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty on Sunday declined to speculate on potential outcomes, saying the federal government's top priority is "to listen, to learn and to discuss how we can move forward."

The AFN also circulated among First Nations a draft of a "Declaration of a Shared Path Forward" to be considered at the meeting that, if agreed to, would commit the parties to continue these meetings on an annual basis.

"If this goes well, then maybe that's what's in the future," New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt told reporters walking into the ceremony on Sunday.

However Woodhouse Nepinak said Friday "you will not see a declaration" following the meeting because the AFN needs more time to consult its chiefs, with negotiations continuing on potential outcomes all weekend.

First such meeting since 2005

The last Indigenous-focused first ministers meeting was held in 2005 in Kelowna, B.C., seeking solutions to close the gap in living standards and yielding an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

To prepare for this meeting, Woodhouse Nepinak was thinking back to the 1983 Indigenous rights conference and its famous moments, beginning with Pierre Trudeau interrupting the chiefs' ceremonial opening prayer then answering it with prayer of his own, which she called "hard to watch."

Several premiers or their ministers attended the AFN's day of ceremony on Sunday. Prime Minister Mark Carney didn't attend but sent Alty in his place.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew and Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak at the AFN's Day of Ceremony on Sunday. (Brett Forester/CBC News)

The closed-door meeting comes as fundamental issues of Indigenous land title, self-determination and place in confederation remain fractious.

In Alberta last week, First Nations celebrated the decisive defeat of a separation referendum called by Premier Danielle Smith. Quebec just elected a new sovereigntist Parti Québécois government.

The B.C. Conservative Party, which campaigned on repealing the province's legislation on the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, won a majority government on Saturday.

Federally, Carney proposed the meeting while facing backlash for his hyperfocus on fast-tracking development of major infrastructure and energy projects, pipelines in particular.

"Of course they want major projects," Woodhouse Nepinak reiterated,"but they're not going to get there without First Nations."

Speaking in French with Radio-Canada's Espaces autochtones, AFN's Quebec/Labrador Regional Chief Francis Verreault-Paul likened the situation facing First Nations to the one Canada faces, according to Carney, as a middle power on the world stage.

Verreault-Paul quoted Carney's headline-grabbing speech earlier this year in Davos, where he said,"if you are not at the table, you are on the menu."

“Right now, First Nations are not at the table for these major projects, " Verreault-Paul said.

Does that mean they're on the menu? Russ Diabo would probably say yes.

'Recipe for conflict'?

A member of the Mohawk Nation of Kahnawà:ke and a spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, Diabo helped organize a grassroots rally outside the meeting.

"We're challenging their mandate," he said, meaning AFN, "saying they don't have one to represent rights-holders, the inherent and treaty-rights holders."

AFN's national chief position is elected by chiefs and not popular vote among First Nations people. It also has no Alberta regional chief and sometimes faces questions about its relevance.

"It's a recipe for conflict, I think, because First Nations rights-holders weren't involved in this. It was just with chiefs — and select chiefs," Diabo said.

Three First Nations also raised those concerns in an open letter, warning about the meeting becoming "political cover" for the federal agenda. One signatory, Onion Lake Cree Nation on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border, also sent AFN a formal cease-and-desist notice.

"I'll be outside with the grassroots people," Onion Lake Chief Darwin Peter Chief said in an interview. "We're standing alongside First Nations in defence of our inherent treaty rights and independence and our right to determine our own future."

His community has serious and long-standing concerns about representation, transparency, meaningful consultation and the protection of treaty rights, he said, and wrote. Woodhouse Nepinak said she welcomes the peaceful protest.

World.title: Who is B.C.'s new premier Lorne Doerkson?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson struck political gold Saturday night.

The former small-town newspaper publisher delivered a stunning defeat to David Eby's NDP and led the B.C. Conservatives to a commanding majority government.

Early Sunday morning, Doerkson's Conservatives were leading in 64 ridings, reducing the NDP to just 27 seats and toppling several cabinet ministers.

It's a remarkable turnaround for a political party that was in disarray just five weeks ago, days before a snap election was called.

But where his political opponents may have seen weakness, Doerkson said British Columbians chose instead to seize an opportunity.

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," Doerkson told a throng of more than 1,000 supporters at the Rocky Mountaineer Station in Vancouver.

"But tonight the whole map counts."

WATCH | Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson gives victory speech: FULL SPEECH: Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson's victory speech | Duration closed caption 17:01

Rodeos to newspapers to politics

Born in New Westminster, Doerkson grew up in Surrey and the B.C. Interior, before settling in Williams Lake, where he raised a family. In his early 20s, he was a rodeo rider.

He then spent 20 years publishing community newspapers and volunteering with local business and community service groups before entering politics.

"That was a very good education for me," he told supporters. "You learn what’s really going on in a town: who’s hiring, who’s closing, who’s hoping."

Doerkson was first elected in Cariboo-Chilcotin as a B.C. Liberal in 2020, and later joined John Rustad's fledgling Conservative caucus.

His victory makes him the first premier from B.C.'s Interior since Bill Bennett left office in 1986.

Doerkson was on his way home from South Africa last month when he learned his Conservative caucus colleagues wanted him to take over the party as interim leader.

Kerry-Lynne Findlay had just resigned after months of scandals that led to the departure or expulsion of more than a dozen MLAs.

Doerkson admitted he needed convincing.

"Of course, it was a little bit of a short notice," he said in a pre-election interview with CBC News.

Lorne Doerkson speaks to supporters in the crowd during provincial election night Saturday. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Promises to cut income taxes, red tape

Doerkson spent his victory speech Saturday night introducing himself to British Columbians at the same time as celebrating the "trailblazers" who came to the province searching for gold and a better life.

It's a spirit he told supporters that still animates the province, where people want to build something big, from resource communities through to the big metro areas.

"That is the trailblazing spirit of British Columbia and it never left, it just needs government that’s on its side," he said.

WATCH | CBC News projects a Conservative government: CBC News projects a B.C. Conservative majority government | Duration closed caption 1:59

Doerkson reiterated promises to cut red tape "like it’s never been cut before," speed up forestry and mining permits, and triple natural gas production by 2035.

"A province only works if all of it works," he said.

"A mill running in Quesnel keeps a trucker working in Surrey. A mine opening in the north keeps the port busy in Delta. It’s one economy and it runs through every town on our map."

Doerkson also pledged no new taxes and health care that is "fully and publicly funded."

Still, questions remain about how he'll pay for everything, including a promise to cut income taxes by $1,000 a year.

The province is already on track to see a $13.8-billion deficit in 2026-27.

The NDP spent their campaign warning that the Conservatives' platform could mean cuts to health care and education.

Speaking in Vancouver Saturday, Doerkson reiterated election promises, including to cut red tape 'like it’s never been cut before.' (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

Overcoming divisions

As premier-designate, Doerkson now faces the challenge of not only governing but keeping together a coalition that includes social conservatives and more centrist, fiscal conservatives.

WATCH | B.C. 'chose change,' Doerkson says: Doerkson vows to boost B.C. economy as next premier | Duration closed caption 3:45 B.C. Conservative interim Leader Lorne Doerkson is the province's next premier after a historic victory, earning him a majority government. He laid out his priorities including boosting the economy, repealing the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA) and keeping hospital emergency rooms open.

And though he has promised to repeal B.C.’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous People’s Act, he appealed to First Nations communities as partners in the province’s development.

"This future is one we build together as partners with the certainty that all of us need," he said.

One source of division Doerkson won't need to deal with immediately will be the NDP.

With preliminary results showing New Democrats reduced to fewer than 30 seats, the Official Opposition's first priority will be choosing a new leader to replace David Eby who announced Saturday that he will step down.

World.title: Historic lawsuit challenging government over climate inaction begins trial hearings
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

After a seven-year wait and a circuitous path through the justice system, a climate lawsuit against the federal government is finally getting its trial hearings this week in Vancouver.

The lawsuit, launched by 15 youth applicants who claim their Charter rights to life, liberty and security of the person have been violated because of the government’s inadequate action on fighting climate change, was first filed in 2019. It was initially dismissed by the Federal Court, then sent back for a full hearing by the Federal Court of Appeal.

It is the most prominent of several legal challenges based on climate policy across Canada, and has gotten further than any others. This is the first time such a lawsuit will receive a full hearing in court, with the potential for a precedent-setting judgment that could influence Canadian law and inspire other climate lawsuits around the world.

Nine of the 15 youth plaintiffs in the case in Vancouver when it was first filed in 2019. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

What do the applicants want?

The applicants want the court to declare that not doing enough on climate action is, in fact, a violation of Canadians’ rights.

Their key argument is that the federal government’s landmark climate law, the Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act , puts the country on an emissions trajectory that is inconsistent with a safe and livable future.

Essentially, the lawsuit argues that despite the government’s emissions targets and current policies to decarbonize, it still is not aligned with what scientists say is required to stave off the worst impacts of climate change.

“It's hard to see how our governments aren't taking the proper stand needed to combat this crisis because it seems so urgent to me,” said Sadie Vipond, one of the applicants in the case.

Vipond was seven years old when she remembers her grandmother waking her up in the middle of the night, telling her they needed to flee from rising waters during the 2013 Calgary floods. She was 13 when she joined the climate lawsuit, and has experienced many more climate-related disasters since then — wildfire smoke, extreme heat waves and a near-repeat of those Calgary floods. She’s now a student at the University of British Columbia studying environmental science.

As a remedy, Vipond and her fellow applicants want the government to develop a new climate plan that’s backed by the latest scientific evidence on avoiding climate impacts, and open to further judicial review to make sure it remains strong.



"I would like to see my country be able to take a stand for what I know is right," said Vipond.

How will the trial unfold?

The hearings begin on Monday, and the applicants and their expert witnesses will be testifying in the first two weeks. Vipond and other applicants will speak about the climate harms they have experienced — which have piled up in the past seven years as extreme heat, wildfires and flooding have touched the lives and millions of Canadians.

The applicants will have eight expert witnesses, including prominent climate scientists and experts in health, international law, clean energy and Indigenous rights. Two of their witnesses have been lead authors for the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the premier global climate science agency that advises the UN.

The government is expected to present their side in the third week, with four witnesses who are experts in climate science, law and economics.

The government is not disputing that climate science is real and causing harm. But it is expected to argue that Canada's laws are not directly harming the youth plaintiffs, according to Columbia University's Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, which studies climate-related litigation worldwide.

A key legal debate in this case is whether Section 7 of the Charter, which guarantees life, liberty and security, imposes what's known as a "positive obligation" on the government. In other words: is the government constitutionally required to proactively protect Canadians from climate harms by enacting laws or other actions?

A court ruling on this question “would constitute a major development in Canadian constitutional law,” wrote human rights lawyer Catherine Savard, Canadian expert for the Sabin Center in New York City.

After the government witnesses, the hearings will take a break and both sides will return in February to make closing arguments.

The outcome will be closely watched around the world. The Canadian case is the first major climate trial since a landmark opinion from the International Court of Justice last year.

The global court found that countries could be in violation of international law if they didn’t take steps to reduce emissions, and countries that are suffering the impacts of climate disasters could seek compensation from the countries causing climate change.

“I think there is a very important role for the courts here in terms of protecting constitutional rights,” said David Wu, partner at the law firm Arvay Finlay who is representing the applicants.

“Are we going to allow governments to do what they want in terms of climate policy or targets or does our Constitution have something to say about it?”

World.title: Lula re-elected in Brazil as Bolsonaro rejects results
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a vocal critic of U.S. President Donald Trump, was re-elected Sunday in a result that provides relief to critics of widening U.S. influence in Latin America.

With 100 per cent of the vote counted, Brazil's electoral court announced that Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, had a lead of nearly 4.4 million votes — 51.8 per cent of the total vote — over opponent Flávio Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro quickly refused to concede defeat and asked for the election results to be annulled after an evening of chaos at some polling places that followed a last-minute decision to extend voting by two hours.

Bolsonaro is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated to take the presidency in 2022.

Lula's triumph bucks a regional trend of victories for right-of-centre presidential candidates allied with Trump. It also means Latin America's largest economy, with a GDP of $2.6 trillion US per year, will likely continue defying Trump's demands, despite the pressure of increased tariffs.

Lula supporters celebrate election results in São Paulo on Sunday. (Amanda Perobelli/Reuters)

A video published by Lula's campaign shows the veteran leader celebrating with his wife Rosângela da Silva and allies after his run-off victory was confirmed by Brazil's electoral court. Wearing star-shaped red glasses, he kissed his wife.

Speaking to his supporters, thousands of whom gathered on São Paulo's main artery and in Rio de Janeiro's Cinelândia Square, Lula expressed his gratitude to the Brazilian people and pledged to respect all Brazilians, regardless of gender or religion. He also attacked Bolsonaro.

"This was a defeat for denialism and lies. I must confess that every time I attended a debate, I felt embarrassed," he said.

Lula also doubled down on his commitment to Brazil's sovereignty.

"Either the homeland remains free or we die for Brazil," he said. "This country will not accept being anyone's backyard."

Lula supporters celebrate

In Rio de Janeiro, cars beeped their horns and a woman dressed in red — the colour of Lula supporters — shouted "You lost! Cry harder!" to four men in yellow and green sipping beers, Bolsonaro's signature colours. A huge roar echoed in the street as the result was confirmed.

Rodrigo Valentim, a 51-year-old businessman and supporter of Bolsonaro, said that another Lula government would harm the economy. He pointed to financial markets' positive reaction to the result of the first round, when Bolsonaro bested Lula.

"I don't understand how people can vote for Lula," he said. "The country is collapsing."

Lula is set to begin his fourth non-consecutive term as president on Jan. 5, 2027.

Lula's supporters celebrate in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Lucas Landau/The Associated Press)

Last-minute polling station confusion

The electoral court's announcement ended an evening of confusion at polling places after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled three minutes before the scheduled end of voting to keep polls open for two more hours, following requests by both candidates.

Lula's request came after issues with buses that provide transportation to polls in São Paulo and Salvador, two cities that tend to favour the incumbent. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south, where he is favoured.

The decision delayed tallying the votes by two hours. It was unclear how many polling stations stayed open after the scheduled closing time. Polling stations in Brasilia and Rio de Janeiro closed shortly after the original 5 p.m. local time deadline, reporters for The Associated Press observed.

People line up outside a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Agustin Marcarian/Reuters)

Bolsonaro, whose father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after he lost the 2022 presidential election to Lula, pointed out that Zanin is Lula's former lawyer and criticized him for "changing the rules of the game in the middle of the game."

"It's impossible to recognize the results of the election in the context of these things that happened," he said.

It's not clear if Bolsonaro's complaint could meet the legal threshold to annul the results. Bolsonaro also has the right to request a recount if he has evidence of fraud, but that might not change the results.

Cost of living, security top of mind for voters

Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. Sunday night's apparent victory by Lula marked the first time since Brazil's military dictatorship ended in 1985 that the second-highest vote-getter in the first-round elections won the presidency.

Lula faced a tough re-election battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs, while Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives.

Presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro walks toward a voting booth at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro on Sunday. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

This will likely be the last victory of the veteran leader's political career. Lula began his political career in the 1970s as a union leader. He then helped found the Workers' Party, which he represented as a presidential candidate three times until he finally won in 2002. He was re-elected four years later and was succeeded by one of his cabinet ministers, Dilma Rousseff, in 2010. She was re-elected in 2014.

Rousseff was impeached for accounting manoeuvring in 2016 amid a sprawling corruption probe, which also ensnared Lula. He tried to run for president again in 2018 but was jailed in March after being convicted.

Members of the military police stand guard as people gather to watch election results in São Paulo on Sunday. (Jean Carniel/Reuters)

Lula was released from prison after 580 days and saw Brazil's Supreme Court annul his sentence after police found messages that showed the judge who convicted him was biased. He quickly became one of former president Jair Bolsonaro's biggest critics and narrowly beat him in 2022.

Since he lost the first round, Lula reorganized his campaign, appealed to young voters, put millions of Brazilians on the streets to defend democratic values and his legacy, raised fears of another Bolsonaro administration and boosted several government initiatives.

He joins Trump and Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega — all aged 80 — as the oldest presidents in the Americas.
