World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

World.title: LatAm and Africa Prediction Markets, Week of 26 Oct
World.content:
Prediction Markets: Latin America and Africa

Key Facts —Prediction markets. Polymarket, a crypto prediction exchange, gave President Lula 18.5% on voting day; he won with 51.79% (26 October, 7:04 am ET). —Brazil’s rate. Bets on a central bank cut on 4 November fell from 90.5% to 24.5%; a pause rose from 8.6% to 57.8%. —Brazil in 2026. Bets on exactly five central bank cuts this year, meaning no more, rose from 10% to 71% in one day. —Mexico. Bets on third-quarter growth of 3.5% or more rose from 12% to 32%, on small volume. —Most traded. Venezuela’s year-end leader market drew about US$355,000 in a week, the most among Latin America and Africa markets we track.

Brazil’s voters surprised the bettors: Lula won a fourth term after prediction markets had given him about a one-in-five chance.

Polymarket priced President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva at 18.5% at 3 pm Brasília time on Sunday 25 October, two hours before polls were due to close. He won 51.79% of valid votes, which exclude blank and spoiled ballots, against 48.21% for Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the count of every polling station by the Superior Electoral Court (TSE).

Bets on Brazil’s interest rate swung in the same days, and traders now give 58% to a pause in the Selic, Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, on 4 November, up from 9% a week ago. It matters to US readers because the rate helps set what Brazilian bonds and loans pay.

This report covers 19 to 26 October across Latin America and Africa. It shows what moved, what comes next and how far to trust each price.

What Prediction Markets Say

Prediction markets are exchanges where people buy and sell contracts on future events, and a price of 60 cents means the crowd gives that outcome roughly a 60% chance. The prices below are bets, not polls, and we read them on 26 October 2026, 7:04 am ET.

Brazil presidency (Polymarket, US$249.1 million total volume, now settled): Lula 100%. A week earlier Flávio Bolsonaro stood at 76.8% and Lula at 22.5%.

Brazil central bank, 4 November (Polymarket, US$93,781): no change 57.8%, quarter-point (25 basis point) cut 24.5%, increase of 50 basis points or more 9.4%.

Brazil rate cuts in 2026 (Kalshi, last trades, more than 170,000 contracts): exactly five 71%, exactly six 15%, seven or more 23%. Each line is a separate contract, and last trades need not add to 100%.

Mexico central bank, 5 November (Polymarket, US$105,052): no change 90.5%, 25 basis point cut 8.6%.

Colombia central bank, 30 October (Polymarket, US$59,134): no change 51.5%, 25 basis point rise 39.5%.

Mexico third-quarter growth against a year earlier, 30 October release (Polymarket, US$69,956): 3.0% to 3.5% 33.6%, 3.5% or more 32.1%, 2.0% to 2.5% 14.0%, 2.5% to 3.0% 6.5%; other brackets not shown.

Argentina 2027 presidency (Polymarket, US$1.1 million): President Javier Milei 46.5%, Buenos Aires Governor Axel Kicillof 29.5%, former minister Sergio Massa 14.0%.

Venezuela’s leader on 31 December (Polymarket, US$98.9 million): Nicolás Maduro 75.8%, Delcy Rodríguez 20.5%.

Kalshi is a US exchange regulated in the United States by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), while Polymarket is a crypto-based platform. Both publish prices that anyone can read for free.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

In Plain English Basis point (bps): one hundredth of a percentage point, so 25 bps is a quarter of a point. Selic and Copom: the Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, and Copom is the central bank committee that sets it. Banxico: Mexico’s central bank. Banrep: Colombia’s central bank, the Banco de la República. INEGI: Mexico’s national statistics office. TSE: Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which runs and counts elections.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa & Latin America Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Week’s Biggest Moves

Brazil: the bettors backed the wrong winner

Polymarket’s price for a Flávio Bolsonaro win stayed at or near 75% or higher in the week before the vote, and Lula’s stayed at or near 25% or lower. Flávio, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, had led the first round on 4 October with 47.03% to Lula’s 45.16%.

A late poll by CNT/MDA, a Brazilian polling firm, had him at 50.5% of valid votes to 49.5%. The TSE count instead gave Lula 64,256,232 votes to 59,826,041, a lead of 4,430,191 votes or about 3.6 points.

A price of 80% never meant certainty, because an outcome priced at 20% happens one time in five. Flávio Bolsonaro said on 25 October that he would ask to annul the result, citing the extension of voting hours in some places.

The Central Bank of Brazil headquarters in Brasília. File photo.

Brazil: rate-cut bets flip to a pause

Polymarket’s price for a quarter-point cut at the central bank’s 4 November meeting fell from 90.5% to 24.5% in a week, while “no change” rose from 8.6% to 57.8%. Kalshi shows the same turn: “exactly five cuts in 2026” rose from 10% on Sunday to 71%, and “seven or more” fell from 60% to 23%.

The central bank has already cut its benchmark Selic rate five times this year, by 25 bps at each of five meetings between March and September, taking it from 15.00% to 13.75%. Our reading is that “exactly five” is a bet that nothing more happens at the meetings on 4 November and 9 December.

The bank’s weekly Focus survey of economists, with answers collected to 16 October, still pointed the other way, with a median Selic of 13.25% at the end of 2026. We found no central bank statement or data release behind the repricing, so we cannot name a trigger.

Mexico: growth bets jump, rate bets harden

Polymarket traders now give 32.1% to Mexico’s third-quarter economy growing 3.5% or more from a year earlier, up from 12.2%, while the 2.5% to 3.0% bracket fell from 33.5% to 6.5%. These small brackets can swing on a few trades.

INEGI reported 1.9% annual growth for the second quarter, after seasonal adjustment, so these bets imply a sharp pickup. INEGI publishes its first third-quarter estimate on Friday 30 October, and this market has only US$69,956 in volume.

On rates, Polymarket gives 90.5% to no change at Banxico on Thursday 5 November, up from 76.5%, after the bank held at 6.50% on 24 September. Banxico is Mexico’s central bank, and we found no data release or statement behind either move this week.

Brazil’s Supreme Court: bets on Moraes leaving fade

Polymarket’s price that Justice Alexandre de Moraes leaves Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court for any reason by 31 December fell from 21.0% to 4.5%, on US$252,631 in volume. A separate market on any justice being removed by impeachment before 2027 stands at 5.0%, up from 1.5%.

We found no resignation, impeachment motion or ruling behind the drop. It came in the week of the runoff, but we cannot link the two.

Two thin markets: El Salvador’s bitcoin and a three-election combo

Polymarket’s “31 December 2026” outcome for El Salvador’s government holding at least US$1 billion in bitcoin rose from 15.5% to 48.5%. Only US$10,879 has ever traded on that outcome, and almost none of it this week, so a handful of trades can explain the move, and we found no government announcement behind it.

A Polymarket combination bet pays only if Lula wins Brazil, Gadi Eizenkot, Israel’s former army chief, is the first prime minister sworn in after Israel’s vote, and Democrats control the US Senate. It jumped from 8.7% to 46.4%, and our reading is that Lula’s win settled the first leg, leaving Israel’s vote on Tuesday 27 October and the US midterm elections on Tuesday 3 November.

Latin America

Venezuela’s market for who leads the country on 31 December was the most traded among the Latin America and Africa markets on our board, with about US$355,000 changing hands in seven days by Polymarket’s own count. Nicolás Maduro, captured by US forces in January, is priced at 75.8%, and Delcy Rodríguez, acting president since January, at 20.5%.

The market resolves to whoever officially holds the office on 31 December, and we cannot explain why bettors rate Maduro so far ahead. Our earlier report covers the push for an election date.

On Cuba, Polymarket gives 9.5% to US military action by 31 December (US$5.5 million traded on that outcome) and 13.0% to the regime falling in 2026, up from 9.5%. For Colombia, the price for a US strike by 31 December is 20.5% (US$1.2 million), and for Mexico 3.5% (US$0.8 million).

Colombia’s central bank, Banrep, decides on Friday 30 October, and Polymarket gives 51.5% to no change and 39.5% to a quarter-point rise, against 56.0% and 38.0% a week ago. The bank raised its rate by 25 bps to 12.25% on 30 September.

Argentina’s 2027 presidency is the main long-range market. Milei leads at 46.5% on Polymarket, with Kicillof second at 29.5%.

Africa

No African outcome with more than US$50,000 traded moved 10 points this week, and all are small beside Brazil’s. Nigeria’s presidency is the biggest, with US$136,293 traded in the market: President Bola Tinubu is at 68.5%, down from 72.0%, and opposition politician Peter Obi at 24.0%, before the vote on Saturday 16 January 2027.

For Sudan, 12.5% is the price of a civil-war ceasefire by 31 December, thinly traded at US$15,050. For Ethiopia, the price of Eritrea invading by 31 December rose from 10.5% to 14.5% (US$59,820), while the 31 October date fell from 9.8% to 4.3%.

For South Africa, 79.3% is the price that 2026 inflation ends above 5.0%, down from 86.0%, thinly traded at US$27,899. The statistics office Stats SA reported 4.5% for September, up from 4.4% in August.

Mali’s market on junta leader Assimi Goïta leaving office by 30 June 2027 rose from 23.0% to 29.5% (US$51,652). It is a small market, so a few trades can move it.

Decisions Ahead

Tuesday 27 October: Israel votes, one leg of the three-election combination bet.

Friday 30 October: Mexico’s first third-quarter growth estimate from INEGI, and Colombia’s central bank decision.

Tuesday 3 November: US midterm elections, which decide control of the US Senate, the third part of the combination bet.

Wednesday 4 November: Brazil’s central bank announces its decision after a two-day meeting, and South Africa holds local elections.

Thursday 5 November: Mexico’s central bank decision.

Wednesday 9 December: Brazil’s central bank decides again, after the November meeting.

Saturday 16 January 2027: Nigeria’s presidential election.

What It Means for US Readers

Investors in Brazilian bonds, the Brazilian real and US-listed Brazilian shares should watch 4 November. A pause would keep the Selic at 13.75%, while bettors a week ago expected a cut.

The runoff also shows the limit of these prices, because a market that says 80% can still be wrong. For the trade side of the story, see our report Brazil Awaits US Tariff Offer After Lula Win.

What Is Not Known

We do not know why Brazil’s rate odds, the Moraes market or the Mexico growth bracket moved, because we found no official event behind them. Each could reflect a handful of traders, since most of these markets hold under US$150,000.

We have not seen Flávio Bolsonaro’s annulment request filed or any court response. We also cannot explain why Venezuela’s market prices Maduro as the likeliest leader at year end.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did prediction markets say before Brazil’s runoff?

Polymarket priced Flávio Bolsonaro near 80% and Lula at 18.5% on voting day, 25 October. Lula won with 51.79% of valid votes, so the market was wrong.

What are bettors expecting from Brazil’s central bank?

Polymarket gives 57.8% to no change on 4 November and 24.5% to a quarter-point cut. A week earlier the cut stood at 90.5%.

Which Latin America bets moved most this week?

Polymarket’s price for a Brazil rate cut on 4 November fell from 90.5% to 24.5%, and Kalshi’s “exactly five cuts” rose from 10% to 71% in a day. Mexico growth and El Salvador bitcoin bets also jumped, on small volume.

What do prediction markets say about Africa?

Polymarket gives Bola Tinubu 68.5% to win Nigeria’s presidency, Eritrea 14.5% to invade Ethiopia by 31 December and a Sudan ceasefire 12.5%. All three are small markets, so a few traders can move them.

Are prediction market prices reliable?

They are bets, not polls, and a 20% outcome happens one time in five. Thin markets can be moved by a few traders, so we label them and show them next to official data.

World.title: France Keeps Curfews After 1,435 Arrests
World.content:
File photo: Laurent Nuñez, France’s interior minister. Credit: Ministère de l’Intérieur, Licence Ouverte, via Wikimedia Commons.

France in Turmoil

Published Monday, 26 October, 6:46 a.m. ET (11:46 a.m. Paris) · Source: French Interior Ministry, Élysée Palace

France woke up on Monday to the news that the night-time curfews are not over. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, the government’s top police official, said they will continue, while President Emmanuel Macron is due in Marseille to talk about the “return of order”.

The curfews follow two weekends of France protests over the cost of living, with riots and looting on 17 October and another tense day on 24 October. The numbers from Saturday explain why the government is not backing off.

Key Facts —Curfews: Nuñez says the local night curfews will continue in the coming days. —Arrests: 1,435 people were arrested on Saturday, 24 October, more than 100 of them for carrying weapons. —Injuries: 267 police officers and gendarmes (military police) and 150 protesters were hurt, three protesters seriously. —Next test: Saturday, 31 October, when the minister expects another difficult day.

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: French Shop Lobby Asks for Protest Pause

In plain English A curfew here means people may not be on certain streets at night, and only in the areas the local authorities pick. France has not declared a state of emergency, so these are targeted limits, not a national lockdown.

Why the Curfews Stay

Nuñez described Saturday as a “controlled” day, yet the figures he gave are heavy. He also acknowledged a very high level of violence against officers.

That is the reasoning for keeping the night limits for now. The government prefers narrow, local rules to a nationwide emergency decree.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How We Got Here

After the riots of 17 October, Nuñez offered to resign on 18 October. Macron refused on 19 October and asked him for new ways to stop the vandals.

The same day Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu asked regional prefects, the state’s local representatives, to impose partial and very localised curfews. In Paris the restrictions cover the Place de la République area and the Les Halles shopping district in the centre of the city from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m., according to the rules set on 19 October

Macron Goes to Marseille

Macron’s trip to Marseille, France’s second city, is framed around restoring order after the unrest. The 17 October riots hit several French cities.

The Élysée has not published a detailed programme in the sources we could confirm, so the exact timing of his visit is not known.

What Comes Next

Nuñez warned that Saturday 31 October, Halloween, could again be complicated and said police would deploy an “extremely robust” force. Yellow Vest protest groups, a loose movement named after the high-visibility jackets worn at its demonstrations, have called for action that day.

A bigger test follows on Thursday 5 November, when the main trade unions (CFDT, CGT, FO, UNSA and FSU) have called a national strike over budget cuts. The government has not said whether the curfews will still be in force by then.

What It Means for US Readers

Travellers should expect local night restrictions in affected city centres this week, and check city and prefecture notices before going out after dark. Our guide to why France is protesting explains the background in plain terms.

For investors, the unrest adds to political risk ahead of the 2027 presidential race. We will update this story as the numbers change.

What Is Not Known

Officials have not published, in the sources we could confirm, the exact number of curfews, their hours or their boundaries in every city. The orders differ from town to town.

The injury and arrest tallies may still change, and there is no split of the 1,435 arrests by city yet. Whether the curfews will still apply on 5 November is open.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will the curfews in France continue?

Yes for now. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said on Monday 26 October that the local curfews will continue in the coming days.

How many people were arrested on 24 October?

The interior minister gave 1,435 arrests, with more than 100 for carrying weapons. He also reported 267 injured police officers and gendarmes and 150 injured protesters.

Sources French Interior Ministry statements (26 October 2026), Élysée Palace, Prime Minister’s Office, Marseille city authorities, Prefecture of Police of Paris.

World.title: French Shop Lobby Asks for Protest Pause
World.content:
File photo: a shop on the rue de Rivoli in central Paris, 2011. Photo: Bob Hall, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Published Monday, 26 October, 6:33 a.m. ET (11:33 a.m. Paris) · Source: CCI France, French Interior Ministry

Key Facts What happened: The head of CCI France, a network of chambers of commerce, asked on 26 October for a pause in protests.

The numbers: Interior Ministry: 410,000 marched on 24 October, with 1,435 arrests. The CGT, a major trade union, claimed 800,000.

What happens next: A national strike day is set for Thursday, 5 November. Police plan a strong deployment on 31 October.

Prediction markets: Traders on Polymarket and Kalshi put a French state of emergency by year-end near 16% (as of 6:33 a.m. ET).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: France Arrests 1,314 at Latest Protests

French shopkeepers are tired of sweeping up broken glass, and their top lobbyist now wants the street marches to pause before the holidays. Alain Di Crescenzo, president of CCI France, the national network of chambers of commerce, made the plea on Radio Classique, a French national radio station, on Monday, 26 October.

It lands after two Saturdays of national protests over living costs and public services, which we track in our guide to France protests.

In plain English CCI France speaks for French business owners. It says weekly street protests over living costs are hurting shops just before their busiest season, and it wants a break.

Why Shopkeepers Say Enough

“We have shopkeepers who are tired, who are dejected, and we are in the process of killing local commerce,” Di Crescenzo said. It was his second appeal in a week.

On 20 October, on Sud Radio, he had urged “no protests next week,” saying more marches would “add suffering to suffering.” He then put the damage from the violence of 17 October at close to 3,000 looted or vandalised shops.

The timing is what hurts. Shops earn about 40% of their annual sales in November and December, and he said summer sales were already down about 20%.

How Big Were the Marches?

The Interior Ministry counted 410,000 marchers across France on Saturday, 24 October, down from 550,000 a week earlier. The CGT, a major French trade union, claimed 800,000.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, called the day “controlled”. Even so, police made 1,435 arrests nationwide, and 267 police and gendarmes (France’s paramilitary police) were hurt, most of them lightly and three seriously.

In Paris, between 110,000 and 250,000 people marched, depending on who counted.

What Comes Next

Nuñez said curfews will continue where local officials want them. He also promised an “extremely robust” police deployment next Saturday, 31 October, noting that Halloween weekend invites trouble. Unions have called a national day of strikes and marches for Thursday, 5 November.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a global prediction exchange: France declares a state of emergency by 31 December 2026, about 16%; by 31 October, about 2%. Volume: about US$1.1 million traded.

Kalshi, a US exchange regulated in the US by the CFTC (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission): before 1 January 2027, 16%; before 1 November 2026, 4%. Volume: 98,461 contracts.

Prices as of 6:33 a.m. ET.

These prices are real-money bets, not polls. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Americans planning trips to France should expect more marches and heavy policing on 31 October and 5 November, with possible strike disruption.

For investors, the damage to small shops is a drag on French consumer spending going into the holidays.

What Is Not Known

Turnout is disputed, with a gap of 390,000 between the ministry and the CGT. The shop figures come from business groups, not from a government count.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did CCI France ask for?

Its president, Alain Di Crescenzo, asked on 26 October for a pause in the street marches before the holidays. He says shops earn about 40% of their year in November and December.

When is the next big French protest day?

Unions have called a national day of strikes and marches for Thursday, 5 November. Police plan a very strong deployment on Saturday, 31 October.

Sources: CCI France (cci.fr); French Interior Ministry (interieur.gouv.fr); Polymarket and Kalshi price data.

World.title: Mexico City Borough Guards Day of the Dead
World.content:
A family ofrenda, or Day of the Dead altar, in the state of Puebla, with marigolds, candles and food, pictured on 1 November 2019. Photo: Pablo Ignacio Osorio Torres / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Key Facts Who: Azcapotzalco’s mayor, Nancy Núñez, launched a Day of the Dead security operation with Navy, National Guard and city police.

Where: Azcapotzalco, a north-western Mexico City borough; cemeteries, processions and public spaces are covered.

Next: “Entre Xolos y Catrinas” festival runs 26 October–1 November; the parade is Sunday, 1 November, about 7:00 p.m. ET.

Unknown: Personnel numbers, arrests and the exact start date of the operation have not been published.

Published Monday, 26 October 2026 · Source: Azcapotzalco borough announcements, INAH, Mexico City Historic Center Authority, Oaxaca and León governments

Marigolds are going up at the cemetery gates in Azcapotzalco, a borough in north-western Mexico City, and this year the Navy is helping to guard the crowds. The borough has opened a security operation for Day of the Dead, the holiday on 1 and 2 November when Mexican families welcome the souls of their dead home.

Families build altars with candles, photographs and food, then visit cemeteries day and night. Cemeteries fill with visitors, which is the setting for the borough’s operation.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Who Is Guarding Azcapotzalco’s Cemeteries?

Mayor Nancy Núñez led the launch of the operation in recent days. It brings together the Navy (the Secretaría de Marina, or Semar), the National Guard (Mexico’s federal security force) and the Secretariat of Citizen Security (SSC), the Mexico City police.

The borough says the teams cover cemeteries, processions and public spaces around its cultural events. They also warn temporary businesses about Ley Seca, the “Dry Law” that restricts alcohol sales around the holiday.

The operation runs alongside the borough’s third Festival Tlalmanalli Azcatl, a local Day of the Dead festival with an altar contest. The reports we reviewed give no personnel numbers, arrests or hours of deployment.

File photo: a giant skeleton figure at Mexico City’s Day of the Dead parade in 2018.

Where Can Visitors See an Indigenous Altar?

At the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City, an offering from Santa Rosa Xochiac opened at noon on Sunday, 25 October (2:00 p.m. ET). Santa Rosa Xochiac is an Indigenous community in the Álvaro Obregón borough, and the display is titled “Aromas y sabores en los altares de Santa Rosa Xochiac”, or aromas and flavours on the altars.

It stays open through Sunday, 1 November. The museum is run by INAH, Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History, a federal body under the Culture Ministry.

What Happens in the Historic Center?

The festival “Entre Xolos y Catrinas” runs from 26 October to 1 November in Mexico City’s Historic Center. Xolos are Mexico’s hairless dogs, and catrinas are elegantly dressed skeleton figures that became the holiday’s best-known symbol.

A night bicycle ride, “Leyendas sobre ruedas”, leaves at 6:00 p.m. on Thursday, 29 October (8:00 p.m. ET). A fair selling cempasúchil, the orange marigold of the holiday, and crafts follows on Friday, 30 and Saturday, 31 October.

The festival ends with a parade of catrinas and catrines starting at about 6:00 p.m. on Sunday, 1 November (7:00 p.m. ET, after US clocks go back that morning). Mexico City does not observe daylight saving time, so its clocks stay at UTC−6.

How Are Other States Preparing?

Oaxaca’s governor, Salomón Jara Cruz, announced more than 100 cultural and tourism activities between 26 October and 3 November. Oaxaca, in southern Mexico, is among the best-known places to see the holiday.

In León, a city in the central state of Guanajuato, police, firefighters, civil protection and a C4 centre (a command room fed by video cameras) are covering cemetery events. That operation also covers the Caminata del Despertar de las Ánimas, a walk of the “awakening spirits”, on 1 November.

What It Means for US Readers

Visitors flying in from the United States should expect uniformed security at cemeteries and festival sites in Azcapotzalco. Alcohol sales may be restricted under Ley Seca, although the reports we reviewed do not give the dates.

Check borough and city notices for route and traffic changes before you travel, because event schedules can shift at short notice. The Historic Center dates above are the ones to plan around.

What We Don’t Know Yet

The number of Navy, National Guard and city police officers in Azcapotzalco has not been published. Reports differ by a day or two on the exact start date, and we could not find the borough’s own release.

The reports we reviewed mention no arrests, injuries or incidents. No prediction market on the holiday exists, so there are no odds to show.

Related: what to do in Mexico City in November and why Janitzio cemetery is closed to tourists. More at Mexico news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Day of the Dead 2026?

Day of the Dead is observed on 1 and 2 November 2026. Events across Mexico City run from late October into early November.

What security is in place in Azcapotzalco?

A borough operation brings the Navy, National Guard and city police to cemeteries, processions and public spaces. Businesses are also warned about Ley Seca alcohol rules.

World.title: Brazil Rate Pause Odds Jump to 67%
World.content:
The Finance Ministry building on Brasília’s Esplanada dos Ministérios, in a file photo. The photo does not show this week’s events. Photo: Agência Senado / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

BRAZIL · INTEREST RATES · PREDICTION MARKETS

Published Monday, 26 October 2026, 5:30 a.m. ET · Source: Central Bank of Brazil, Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Kalshi market data

US-regulated traders now bet that Brazil’s central bank has finished cutting interest rates this year, a sharp turn in one day.

Key Facts — Prediction markets Kalshi (US exchange): exactly 5 Brazil rate cuts in 2026 at 67%, up 57 points in 24 hours (26 October, 5:25 a.m. ET).

— Trigger No single trigger reported; one economist expects a pause after President Lula’s runoff win.

— Next date Brazil’s rate-setting committee decides on 4 November.

— Volume About 20,800 contracts traded in 24 hours, so the market is thinly traded.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro – · Lula – (US$249 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 0.4% · Lula 99.6% As of 25 October, 11:40 pm ET (03:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

Brazil woke up to a re-elected president and a new bet on its interest rates. Overnight, traders on Kalshi flipped from expecting more rate cuts to expecting none.

Kalshi is a US exchange regulated by the CFTC (the US derivatives regulator). It prices exactly five Brazilian rate cuts in 2026 at 67%, up 57 points in 24 hours from about 10%.

It matters in the United States because the rate drives what Brazilian bonds, the Brazilian real and business loans pay. The central bank’s benchmark rate, the Selic, is 13.75% a year, and a pause would keep it there into 2027.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In plain English The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark interest rate, set by the central bank. Copom is the central bank committee that votes on the Selic about every six weeks. A prediction market is an exchange where people bet real money on events, and the price shows the crowd’s implied chance.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi asks how many times the Central Bank of Brazil will cut its rate in 2026. Each line pays US$1 per contract if its count is right, and the rules count the cuts for the whole year.

Exactly 5 cuts: 67%, up 57 points in 24 hours; about 7,160 contracts traded in 24 hours.

67%, up 57 points in 24 hours; about 7,160 contracts traded in 24 hours. 7 or more cuts: 26%, down 34 points; about 5,790 contracts traded in 24 hours.

26%, down 34 points; about 5,790 contracts traded in 24 hours. Exactly 6 cuts: 11%, down 14 points; about 7,860 contracts traded in 24 hours.

The three live lines have traded 172,034 contracts in total, about 20,800 of them in the past 24 hours. That is thinly traded, and the three prices add up to 104%, so no single figure should be read as exact.

Copom’s 16 September decision was its fifth cut in a row. If five cuts are already counted, “exactly 5” means no cut at the November or December meeting, “6” means one more and “7 or more” means two.

Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, did not respond when we read its data, so this report uses Kalshi alone. These prices are bets, not polls and not a forecast by this newsroom.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Live prices are on our Prediction Markets page.

File photo: the Central Bank of Brazil headquarters in Brasília. Photo: Banco Central do Brasil / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0).

Why the Odds Moved

No single trigger was reported, and the traders have not said what drove the move. We can document the timing and one economist’s view.

On Sunday, 25 October, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Brazil’s official vote counter, announced that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected. He won 64,256,232 votes, 51.79% of valid votes, against 48.21% for senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. Our report on what the result means covers the vote.

Copom had already sounded careful. Its 16 September statement said the external environment remained uncertain because of undefined armed conflicts in the Middle East.

A survey of economists run by the central bank, called Focus, pointed the other way on 13 October. It had them expecting a 0.25-point cut on 4 November and another in December, which would be seven cuts for the year.

On 26 October, economist Bruno Corano said he sees a “high probability” that the central bank interrupts its cutting cycle on 4 November. He cited a weaker Brazilian real, the currency, and inflation pressure.

That is one voice, and we found no second source. Our reading, not a claim from any source: a few large orders in a small market could also have moved the price.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, the Selic decides how much Brazilian government bonds pay and how costly credit is for Brazilian companies. A pause would keep borrowing costs high for Brazilian companies that carry debt.

The Brazilian real tends to hold up when rates stay high. That is our analysis, and it is one reason a pause bet matters to anyone who travels to Brazil or holds Brazilian assets.

The test comes soon. Copom meets on 3 and 4 November and announces its decision on 4 November. See also our Brazil page and the Latin America odds page.

What Is Not Known

It is not known why the price moved so far in one day. It is also not known whether Copom will cut on 4 November, since the committee has not said so.

We do not yet have the Focus survey due on 26 October, which may show whether economists have changed their view. A thin market can reverse as quickly as it jumped.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are prediction markets saying about Brazil’s interest rates?

Kalshi prices exactly five Brazilian rate cuts in 2026 at 67% as of 26 October, 5:25 a.m. ET, up 57 points in 24 hours. Copom has already cut five times, so that is a bet on no further cut.

Will Brazil’s central bank cut rates on 4 November?

That is not decided. Copom announces its decision on 4 November, and economists surveyed on 13 October expected a 0.25-point cut, while one economist now expects a pause.

Sources: Central Bank of Brazil, Copom statements · Superior Electoral Court, 2026 runoff result · statements by economist Bruno Corano, 26 October 2026 · Kalshi public market data (read 26 October 2026, 5:25 a.m. ET).

World.title: What to Do in Santiago in November 2026: Ed Sheeran, Creamfields
World.content:
SANTIAGO · Culture

Iron Maiden plays the Estadio Nacional on 1 November, Ed Sheeran plays two stadium nights in La Florida, and Creamfields Chile takes over Club Hípico on 14 and 15 November. The month, day by day.

The Centro Cultural Estación Mapocho in Santiago, pictured in February 2020. (Photo: Carlos Figueroa / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0)

SANTIAGO — This is the monthly culture and events guide for people who live in the city or are staying for weeks, with things to do in santiago november 2026 arranged by date.November is late spring in Santiago, so expect warm, dry days and cooler evenings.

The month is heavy with international rock and pop, from Iron Maiden and Def Leppard to Ed Sheeran, plus the big Creamfields electronic weekend in the middle of the month. Local art fairs and smaller cultural events fill the gaps, and the city feels busy but not yet in summer holiday mode.

1 to 4 November: Metal and R&B Open the Month

Sunday 1 November (second night; the first is Saturday 31 October) Iron Maiden Estadio Nacional, Ñuñoa · Tickets available The British heavy metal institution brings its theatrical stage show to the national stadium as part of the Run For Your Lives World tour. This is a rare stadium-scale rock production in Santiago and worth the trip to Ñuñoa even if you are not a diehard fan. Check the official stadium and promoter channels for ticket details.

Sunday 1 November Opeth – The Last Will and Testament Movistar Arena, Santiago · CLP 35,000–79,000 (about US$35–79) · Puntoticket Swedish progressive metal band Opeth plays Movistar Arena, which is easy to reach by metro. Its long, complex compositions suit an attentive crowd. Tickets are sold through Puntoticket.

Tuesday 3 and Wednesday 4 November, 21:00 Jorja Smith Teatro Caupolicán, Santiago Centro · Puntoticket The British R&B singer plays two nights at one of Santiago’s most atmospheric mid-size venues. Teatro Caupolicán has a standing floor and balcony seating, so choose your ticket according to how close you want to be. The area around the theatre is busy at night, so use the metro or a ride app.

7 to 11 November: Art Week and Arena Rock

Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November Art Week Chile Centro Cultural Estación Mapocho, Santiago Centro Art Week Chile fills the Centro Cultural Estación Mapocho, a former railway station turned arts centre, for a weekend of contemporary art. Check the organisers’ programme for entry details before you go.

Sunday 8 November Def Leppard with Extreme Movistar Arena, Santiago · From CLP 44,800 (about US$45) · Puntoticket The British rock band plays Movistar Arena with Extreme in support. It is one of the month’s big arena nights. Check the Puntoticket listing for the start time and seat categories.

Wednesday 11 November, 21:00 Cypress Hill Teatro Caupolicán, Santiago Centro · Puntoticket The hip-hop group plays the Teatro Caupolicán, a mid-size theatre with a standing floor. It is a good night out for fans of 1990s rap. Use the metro or a ride app afterwards.

14 and 15 November: Creamfields Weekend

Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November Creamfields Chile Club Hípico de Santiago, Santiago Centro · Puntoticket Santiago’s biggest electronic-music festival takes over the historic racecourse for two days of DJs and large-scale stage production. It is a full-day event, so bring sun protection and a refillable water bottle if the rules allow. Tickets are sold through Puntoticket.

Saturday 14 and Sunday 15 November Los Tres – Unplugged 30 años Movistar Arena, Santiago · Both shows sold out One of Chile’s most influential rock bands marks three decades of its famous acoustic album. Both nights have sold out, so look for official resale only. Spanish-language lyrics dominate, but the musicianship carries the evening.

21 and 22 November: Ed Sheeran and Argentine Rock

Saturday 21 and Sunday 22 November Ed Sheeran Estadio Bicentenario de La Florida, La Florida · From CLP 54,040 (about US$54) · Ticketmaster Chile The British singer-songwriter plays two stadium nights in the south of the city, with FINNEAS as guest. The stadium is far from the centre, so leave early and use the metro to avoid traffic.

Saturday 21 November, 21:00 Babasónicos Movistar Arena, Santiago The long-running Argentine rock band plays on the same night as the first Ed Sheeran show. If you prefer a smaller, Spanish-language rock show, this is the alternative.

26 to 29 November: The Month Closes With More Live Music

Thursday 26 November, 21:00 Eros Ramazzotti Movistar Arena, Santiago · CLP 30,000–120,000 (about US$30–121) · Puntoticket The Italian singer-songwriter brings his romantic pop catalogue to Movistar Arena. Seats are priced by section, so compare categories before buying. Tickets are sold through Puntoticket.

Sunday 29 November, 20:00 A Perfect Circle + Puscifer Hipódromo Chile, Independencia · Puntoticket The American alternative-rock band plays the Hipódromo Chile with Puscifer. It is an open-air racecourse venue, so bring a light jacket for the evening.

Planning Your Santiago in November

November is late spring in Santiago. Days are typically warm and dry, with strong sun in the middle of the day, while mornings and evenings stay cool enough for a light layer.

The only public holiday in November 2026 is Sunday 1 November (All Saints’ Day), which falls on a weekend.Most large concerts sell through Puntoticket, while Ed Sheeran uses Ticketmaster Chile.

Prices here are converted at about CLP 995 per US$ (RT, 26 October 2026).The metro is the most reliable way to reach the big venues, especially Estadio Nacional, Estadio Bicentenario de La Florida and Movistar Arena.

After late shows, use a ride app or arrange transport in advance, as metro services wind down before midnight.For weekly listings, follow the cultural agendas in La Tercera and the social media accounts of Teatro Municipal, Centro Cultural CEINA and the venues named above.

Many smaller events are announced only a week or two ahead.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where can I buy tickets for concerts in Santiago?

Most large concerts in Santiago sell through Puntoticket, while Ed Sheeran uses Ticketmaster Chile.

Is November a good time to be outdoors in Santiago?

Yes, November is late spring with warm, dry days and cooler evenings, ideal for parks, fairs and open-air events.

Are there any public holidays in Santiago in November 2026?

The only public holiday is Sunday 1 November, All Saints’ Day, which falls on a weekend.

Which big concerts are in Santiago in November 2026?

Iron Maiden and Opeth play on 1 November, Def Leppard on 8 November, Creamfields on 14 and 15 November, and Ed Sheeran on 21 and 22 November.

World.content:
MÉRIDA · Culture

The Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil runs through 29 November, and the Festival de Jazz Mérida runs from 18 to 22 November. The month, day by day.

Paseo de Montejo in Mérida, Yucatán, pictured in April 2021. (Photo: Sharon Hahn Darlin / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0)

MÉRIDA — This guide is for people who live here or are staying for weeks, not for a weekend dash. It lists things to do in Mérida November 2026 day by day, with venues, prices where confirmed, and practical notes for getting there.

November in Mérida is shaped by one enormous event: the Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, which fills most of the month with concerts, rodeo, comedy and regional traditions in the south of the city. Around it sit the Festival de Jazz and a public holiday on Monday 16 November.

Expect warm, humid days with strong sun and the chance of heavy showers, so plan for both heat and rain.

1 to 5 November: Día de Muertos Closes, the Fair Begins

Monday 2 November Festival de las Ánimas, final day Mérida and its comisarías · Free It is a cultural observance rather than a nationwide statutory holiday, so many businesses stay open while altars and commemorations continue. Check the Ayuntamiento de Mérida agenda for specific locations on the final day.

Thursday 5 to Sunday 15 November 29ª Exposición Nacional Brahman Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil, south Mérida · Price not specified The Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil 2026 will host the 29ª Exposición Nacional Brahman and the 29º Congreso Mundial de Ganado Brahman. It draws breeders and rural families from across Mexico and gives city residents a direct look at Yucatán’s agricultural life. Go early in the day to avoid the strongest heat and the largest evening crowds.

6 to 8 November: The Fair Opens With Vaquería and Electronic Music

Friday 6 November, registration 18:30, dance from 19:00 Gran Vaquería Regional Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · Price not specified It is the most rooted cultural event of the fair’s first weekend and a good reason to cross the city south. Arrive for the registration window if you want to join the dance rather than watch from the edge.

Saturday 7 November, 21:00 Deorro and Tribal Monterrey Centro de Espectáculos Montejo, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$440, or MX$660 for VIP (about US$24 and US$35) Deorro and Tribal Monterrey play the Centro de Espectáculos Montejo on the fair’s first Saturday. It is a late-night draw for a younger crowd and a contrast to the traditional vaquería the night before. Check the fair’s official channels for ticket details.

12 to 15 November: Comedy, Carín León and Marco Antonio Solís

Thursday 12 November, 22:00 Guerra de Chistes Palenque, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$460 (about US$25) · TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices A touring Mexican comedy show takes the Palenque stage with a rotating cast of stand-up performers. It is a good midweek option if you want the fair’s atmosphere without the biggest weekend crowds. Buy through TusBoletos.mx or the listed box offices before the night, as Palenque shows often sell in advance.

Friday 13 November Carín León Centro de Espectáculos Montejo, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · Price not specified One of the fair’s principal ticketed regional-Mexican concerts brings Carín León to the Centro de Espectáculos Montejo. It is a major draw for fans of the genre and likely to be one of the busiest nights of the fair. Check the fair’s official ticket channels early if you plan to attend.

Saturday 14 November Marco Antonio Solís Centro de Espectáculos Montejo, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · Price not specified Marco Antonio Solís brings his show to the fair’s main concert venue. The show spans decades of Mexican pop and regional music and will draw a broad, multi-generational audience. Plan transport in advance, as the Xmatkuil area becomes congested on major concert nights.

Sunday 15 November, 22:00 Kika Edgar Palenque, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$690 (about US$37) · TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices Kika Edgar performs on Sunday 15 November 2026 at the Palenque de la Feria Xmatkuil. It closes the second weekend with a strong theatrical and musical presence. Tickets are available through TusBoletos.mx and the listed box offices.

16 to 22 November: Public Holiday, Jazz Festival and Nodal

Monday 16 November Mexican Revolution Day public holiday Citywide · Free The legal holiday is observed on the third Monday of November, so many government offices, banks and schools close. Tourist businesses generally remain open on reduced or normal schedules. Use the quieter daytime streets for errands or a long lunch, and check individual venue hours before heading out.

Wednesday 18 to Sunday 22 November Festival de Jazz 2026 Multiple Mérida venues · Price not specified The Festival de Jazz Mérida runs from 18 to 22 November, with local, national and international jazz spread across multiple venues in Mérida, plus food, workshops, conferences and talks. It is the month’s main counterpoint to the fair and a good reason to stay in the centre rather than head south. Check the Ayuntamiento de Mérida agenda and Diario de Yucatán for the daily venue list once it is published.

Friday 20 November Carlos Cuevas and Ricardo Caballero — Brindemos por ella Palenque, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$660–MX$1,430 (about US$35–77) · TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices Two established voices in Mexican romantic music share the Palenque stage for Brindemos por ella. It is a strong option if you prefer bolero and ballad traditions over the fair’s bigger pop nights. Tickets are sold through TusBoletos.mx and the listed box offices.

Saturday 21 November, 22:00 Christian Nodal Centro de Espectáculos Montejo, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$550–MX$2,750 (about US$29–147) Christian Nodal performs at the fair’s main concert venue. It is one of the biggest regional-Mexican nights of the month and will draw a large crowd. If you are going, arrange transport early and expect heavy traffic around Xmatkuil.

Saturday 21 November, 22:30 Leonardo Aguilar y la Emoción del Jaripeo Plaza de Toros, Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$403–MX$690 (about US$22–37) It is a more folk-rooted alternative to Nodal on the same evening. The event sits inside the general fair programme, so check whether fair admission covers it or a separate ticket is needed.

27 to 29 November: Tributes, Rodeo and Ozuna Close the Fair

Friday 27 November Pablo Marentes and Julio Ponze — El Mejor Tributo a El Príncipe y El Divo Palenque, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$660–MX$1,430 · TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices A tribute to José José and Juan Gabriel, two defining figures in Mexican popular music, fills the Palenque on the fair’s final Friday. It is a sentimental, singalong night aimed at a devoted local audience. Book through TusBoletos.mx or the listed box offices.

Friday 27 November Santos Bravos Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · Free show A free contemporary-pop performance sits inside the fair programme on the same Friday night. It is a low-cost way to experience the fair’s music offering without a Palenque ticket. Arrive early to secure a good spot near the stage.

Saturday 28 November, doors 19:00, show 21:00 Cuernos Chuecos rodeo Plaza de Toros, Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · Price not specified It is a loud, physical show that draws families and rodeo fans from across the region. Doors open at 19:00, so arrive before the 21:00 start to settle in.

Saturday 28 November, 21:00 Ozuna Centro de Espectáculos Montejo, Feria Xmatkuil, Xmatkuil · MX$770–MX$2,090 (about US$41–112) · TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices Ozuna closes the fair’s principal concert programme with an urban-music set at the Centro de Espectáculos Montejo. Tickets range from MX$770 to MX$2,090 depending on section and are sold through TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices. This is likely to be the busiest concert night of the month, so plan your route south well in advance.

Planning Your Mérida in November

November is warm and humid, with the chance of heavy showers even as the wet season fades. Carry water, use sun protection, and keep a light rain layer with you, especially if you are walking between venues in the centre.

Monday 16 November is the Mexican Revolution Day public holiday, observed on the third Monday of the month. Banks, government offices and schools generally close, while tourist businesses and many restaurants stay open on reduced or normal schedules.

The Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil is in the south of the city, and traffic builds heavily on major concert nights. If you are going to Xmatkuil, leave early, agree a meeting point with your group, and consider using a rideshare or taxi rather than driving yourself.

For Palenque and Centro de Espectáculos Montejo shows, buy through TusBoletos.mx or the listed box offices where prices are confirmed. Conversions use about MX$18.7 per US$ (RT, 26 October 2026).

For weekly listings and last-minute changes, check the Ayuntamiento de Mérida agenda and Diario de Yucatán. The Festival de Jazz venues are announced closer to the dates, so watch those sources from mid-November.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest event in Mérida in November 2026?

The Feria Yucatán Xmatkuil runs through Sunday 29 November 2026 in Xmatkuil, south Mérida, with concerts, rodeo, comedy, livestock exhibitions and traditional dance.

When is the Festival de Jazz in Mérida in November 2026?

The Festival de Jazz Mérida runs from 18 to 22 November 2026 across multiple venues in Mérida, with concerts, workshops, conferences and food events.

Is there a public holiday in Mérida in November 2026?

Monday 16 November 2026 is the Mexican Revolution Day public holiday, observed on the third Monday of November, when many government offices, banks and schools close.

How do I buy tickets for Feria Xmatkuil concerts in Mérida?

For confirmed Palenque and concert shows such as Ozuna, Guerra de Chistes and Kika Edgar, tickets are sold through TusBoletos.mx and listed box offices, with prices varying by section.
