World.title: French presidential hopeful Philippe slips in new poll
World.content:
Edouard Philippe listens during a meeting between the Alliance for General News Press and several presidential candidates in Paris on October 14, 2026. | Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP via Getty Images

The former PM lost three points compared to Cluster 17’s survey from last month.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Edouard Philippe is losing ground to far-left challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon in the French presidential race, according to polling conducted exclusively for POLITICO.

The survey, carried out by Cluster 17 between Oct. 19 and Oct. 22, showed Philippe with 16% trailing Mélenchon on 18.5%. Cluster 17’s poll on the presidential election last month had the two tied at 19% apiece.

Both leaders are significantly behind far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, who held her first presidential campaign rally on Sunday. Le Pen’s candidacy does not appear to have been significantly affected by allegations that her protégé Jordan Bardella made antisemitic comments in private as a teenager. Bardella, who was reelected as president of the National Rally at the far-right party’s conference this past weekend, has repeatedly denied the accusations.

World.title: 4 reasons Andy Burnham’s MPs are feeling more cheerful — and the pitfalls ahead
World.content:
Disgruntled Labour MPs warned their new leader must show up, listen to them and accept some disagreement to avoid repeating his predecessor’s mistakes.

POLITICO sets out the four reasons Labour MPs are feeling more chipper under Burnham — but they still see potential pitfalls ahead.

Some of the dozen parliamentarians interviewed by POLITICO for this piece were granted anonymity to speak candidly about the internal party matters.

1) Disagreement is tolerated

MPs reckon Burnham’s administration is more willing to recognize different views within the broad church Labour Party.

Burnham himself told a Parliamentary Labour Party meeting that disagreement is fine as long as MPs speak to him about it, according to Simon Opher — a 2024-intake MP and member of Mainstream, the soft-left faction supported by Burnham when he was Greater Manchester mayor.

“It sounds weird, but that is a remarkable difference from what they had before,” Opher said, claiming he felt a “slight climate of fear” early in his political career.

World.title: SONDAGE EXCLUSIF 2027. La chute de Philippe, relégué derrière Mélenchon
World.content:
La candidate du RN, elle, ne pâtit manifestement pas de la révélation par Mediapart fin septembre d’anciens écrits antisémites attribués à Jordan Bardella, et reste hyperfavorite du premier tour, avec 33% d’intentions de vote lorsque Philippe représente le bloc central, contre 31% dans notre dernière enquête.

A noter : fraîchement auréolé de sa victoire dès le premier round à la primaire du PS et de Place publique, Raphaël Glucksmann, lui, passe de 12% à 13% des intentions de vote, en légère dynamique. Dans le détail, selon Cluster 17, le social-démocrate récolterait 29% des voix des électeurs d’Emmanuel Macron en 2022, ce qui explique en partie pourquoi seuls 49% d’entre eux voteraient Philippe.

“Glucksmann progresse parce que Philippe ne s’adresse pas assez à l’aile sociale-démocrate de l’espace modéré”, note Jean-Yves Dormagen, président de Cluster 17.

Retailleau doublé par Lisnard

Quant au candidat des Républicains, Bruno Retailleau, il ne décolle toujours pas, mais se maintient avec 7,5%-8% des intentions de vote. Il a toutefois une nouvelle raison de s’inquiéter : lorsque David Lisnard, étiqueté Nouvelle Energie, est testé lui aussi, il atteint les 8%, grappillant des points à Le Pen (30,5%), Retailleau (7%), ainsi qu’Eric Zemmour (qui passe de 4% à 3,5%).

La cote du maire de Cannes, pourtant encore méconnu d’une partie des Français, s’explique parce qu’il “répond à une forte demande de libéralisme du centre et même de miléisme des très conservateurs”, commente Jean-Yves Dormagen, en référence au président argentin Javier Milei.

Testée également par Cluster 17, l’hypothèse d’une candidature de Gabriel Attal à la place de celle d’Edouard Philippe ne donnera guère plus d’espoir aux partisans du bloc central : le secrétaire général de Renaissance recueillerait 12% des voix aujourd’hui, contre 13,5% selon le même institut au mois de septembre. Dans ce scénario, Jean-Luc Mélenchon grimperait lui à 19,5% et Raphaël Glucksmann à 14%.



(*) Sondage réalisé du 19 au 22 octobre auprès d’un échantillon de 3 000 personnes, représentatif de la population française âgée de 18 ans et plus grâce à la méthode des quotas. L’enquête a été réalisée via un questionnaire autoadministré en ligne. La marge d’erreur est comprise entre 0,8 et 1,8 point.

World.title: Galp and Moeve fail to agree merger of refining and distribution operations
World.content:
Galp issued a statement on Monday confirming that, after several months of negotiations, "it was not possible to reach an agreement" on the proposed combination of its downstream, refining and distribution activities with those of the Spanish company Moeve, whose shareholders are Mubadala Investment Company (Abu Dhabi) and the US group Carlyle.

 

The Portuguese oil and gas company stressed, however, that this outcome has no impact on its operations or on confidence in the company.

"Galp holds an exceptionally strong position, with one of the most attractive upstream growth profiles in the sector, robust industrial and commercial businesses and a diversified portfolio that includes renewables and significant trading activities. This business mix, combined with a solid balance sheet and strong cash-flow generation capacity, gives Galp a firm foundation to continue growing, investing and creating value," wrote Paula Amorim, chair of Galp’s Board of Directors.

Maarten Wetselaar, CEO of Moeve, also wrote in a statement that the combination with Galp "represented an opportunity to accelerate value creation", but that its strategy was never dependent on that deal going ahead. "After extensive discussions, it was not possible to reach a commercial agreement with Galp. We remain focused on executing our transformation with financial discipline and on generating sustainable long-term value."

The Portuguese online newspaper ECO (source in Portuguese) had reported on Sunday night that the deal had fallen through because Paula Amorim had not agreed to the Spanish company’s demands, according to sources familiar with the talks.

Galp’s downstream business is underpinned by "a leading retail network" in Portugal and by "a significant portfolio of energy transition projects in Sines", the statement adds. These include one of Europe’s largest green hydrogen production projects using electrolysis and a biofuels production unit.

The company also revealed on Monday, in its quarterly results and financial disclosure, that its net profit jumped 68% year on year in the third quarter, to 682 million euros. "The increase in oil and natural gas production in Brazil to a new record, the strong performance of exports and oil and gas trading activities in international markets" are said to have driven the result.

World.title: Trump officials back Orbán bid for UN secretary-general, WSJ reports
World.content:
Officials in the Trump administration are advocating the nomination of former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán for the post of UN secretary-general, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal.

 

The newspaper reports that Orbán could be a joint American, Russian and Chinese candidate, and that sources in all three countries have confirmed the Trump administration is backing his bid.

Orbán lost power in Hungary’s parliamentary election in April, when Péter Magyar’s Tisza party defeated him after 16 years of governing with an absolute majority.

His hard-right, fiercely anti-migration and eurosceptic policies, together with the rule of law backsliding in Hungary, strained relations with Western allies, including the European Union and NATO. Nevertheless, Orbán maintained close ties with Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Since the election, Hungarian authorities have launched fraud and corruption investigations into several members of Orbán’s former government. Two former ministers and the former governor of Hungary’s National Bank are under arrest, and authorities could also examine Orbán’s potential involvement in those cases.

According to the WSJ, no final decision has been taken on the plan. A US State Department official admitted that the idea sounds crazy at first, but said previous talks with Washington suggest Russia and China also support it. The aim is for Orbán to be the joint candidate of the three countries.

“If the United States, Russia and China want the same thing in the UN Security Council, they usually achieve it,” officials from the United States and another country told the newspaper. The second five-year term of the current secretary-general, António Guterres, ends on 31 December.

The White House, Moscow and Beijing have not confirmed the information.

Euronews has contacted Orbán’s spokesperson for comment but has not yet received a response. The spokesperson previously dismissed press reports about Orbán’s candidacy for the post of deputy secretary-general as “fake news”.

In May, the VSquare investigative newsletter reported that a UN position could be important for the former prime minister because of the diplomatic immunity attached to the role.

According to the WSJ, Orbán would only run if his victory were assured, a scenario that currently seems unlikely. A candidate must secure the support of at least nine of the 15 Security Council members, while any of the five permanent members can veto the nomination. Besides the US, Russia and China, France and the United Kingdom are also permanent members.

World.title: Why Israel’s wartime election isn’t just about the battle with Iran and Hamas
World.content:
Israelis head to the polls on Tuesday in the country’s first national election since Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack, a vote that is shaping up as a verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

 

Yet for a country that has spent three years fighting on several fronts, the campaign has been strikingly quiet on how those wars were fought.

Israel’s conduct in Gaza, which led to an international arrest warrant for Netanyahu, has barely been debated. Nor have its occupation of much of southern Lebanon and parts of Syria, or the two wars it launched against Iran. All enjoy broad support among Jewish Israelis.

The main contenders have instead argued over Netanyahu himself: his character, his responsibility for the security failures of 7 October, military exemptions for ultra-Orthodox men and his 2023 attempt to overhaul the judiciary.

There is also little to separate the two main blocs on the Palestinian question. Both are dominated by parties that back Jewish settlement in the occupied West Bank and oppose a Palestinian state, and no leading candidate is calling for a revival of the peace process.

The shadow of 7 October

Reminders of the war are everywhere. Stickers bearing the faces of fallen soldiers line train stations, alongside fading yellow ribbons for the hostages, the last of whom came home under a ceasefire deal last year.

According to the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI), a Jerusalem-based think tank, around 68% of Jewish Israelis say their views on 7 October are central to how they will vote. Among Arab citizens, the figure is 32%, with most naming crime as their main concern.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government faced criticism over his support for Donald Trump and failure to expedite an inquiry into the events of 7 October, 2023. AP Photo

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, has pointed to military gains against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran while placing blame for the 7 October failures on the security establishment.

His critics say he has dodged accountability by blocking an official state inquiry. They also accuse him of delaying a hostage deal and of failing to secure a decisive victory on any front.

Who serves in the army?

The issue that has stirred the most anger is conscription. Military service is compulsory for most Jewish Israelis, but Netanyahu’s coalitions have long depended on ultra-Orthodox parties that insist yeshiva students be exempt.

Resentment has grown as reservists have been called up repeatedly and the army struggles with a manpower shortage. Around 13,000 ultra-Orthodox men turn 18 each year, but fewer than one in ten enlist.

About a quarter of Jewish voters told the IDI the issue would weigh on their choice. IDI president Yohanan Plesner said it was “probably the number one issue” for the anti-Netanyahu camp.

The IDI’s Tamar Hermann said many Israelis see military service as a “kind of permit to citizenship”.

Netanyahu’s main challenger, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to end the de facto exemptions. Eisenkot, a centrist, lost his son and two nephews in the fighting in Gaza.

Judicial overhaul fades as an issue

The judicial overhaul brought hundreds of thousands onto the streets in 2023 and left Israel deeply divided when Hamas attacked. Netanyahu cast it as a check on unelected judges. Opponents saw a power grab by a leader under indictment on corruption charges, which he denies.

After 7 October, much of that protest movement turned its energy towards demanding the hostages’ release. Today, only 18% of Jewish Israelis say the overhaul will shape their vote, a sign of what Hermann described as “public fatigue”. It matters more on the left, where 22.5% cite it.

A law passed last year giving the government more say in judicial appointments will only take effect once the next Knesset is sworn in. The opposition bloc has promised to scrap it.

Coalition arithmetic

Israelis vote for party lists rather than individual candidates, and no party is expected to come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. The next prime minister will be whoever can assemble a governing coalition. If no one can, Netanyahu will stay on as caretaker until yet another election.

Netanyahu's party, Likud currently holds 32 seats in the Knesset. 13 October, 2025. AP Photo

More than a quarter of Jewish voters say the party leader is a decisive factor. Netanyahu’s backers see a seasoned statesman who has stood up to US presidents and refused concessions they believe would endanger Israel. His detractors see him as corrupt.

Eisenkot’s supporters cite his decades in uniform and his personal losses. The son of Moroccan Jewish immigrants, he would become Israel’s first prime minister of non-European heritage, though he has not campaigned on it.

The missing economic debate

Living costs are a major concern but have barely featured. Research by Sarit Menahem-Carmi of Reichman University’s Aaron Institute for Economic Policy found that Israel is now more expensive than wealthy European countries such as Austria, Denmark and Sweden.

The IDI found 38% of Jewish Israelis rank the economy as their first or second priority, rising to 46% among Arab citizens. Netanyahu credits his policies with fuelling growth and a thriving tech sector, while opponents say many have been left behind.

None of the leading candidates has put the cost of the wars at the centre of their campaign. Joseph Zeira, an economics professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, warned that heavy military spending cannot be ignored. “The cost of the conflict is tremendous,” he said.

World.title: Be nice, not nasty: Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton on why AI needs humans at its heart
World.content:
The 2023 Nobel Physics laureate Geoffrey Hinton is renowned for his words of wisdom regarding computer science having led groundbreaking research on artificial intelligence.

 

He's widely regarded as one of the godfathers of AI for his pioneering work on developing artificial neural networks which laid the foundations for many AI systems now used everyday by millions of people.

But in more recent years, Hinton's added his voice to others who've spoken out against the potential catastrophic consquences of leaving AI technology unchecked.

Euronews Culture spoke to the award-winning computer scientist at the Starmus Festival celebrating science and the arts about his predictions and why James Cameron's 'The Terminator' is one of his favourite films.

World.title: November 2026 travel guide: Where to go, what to see and the new hotels to book in Europe
World.content:
November can sometimes be an awkward month for travel. The days are shorter, the weather is less predictable, and much of Europe is firmly between autumn and winter.

 

However, that all tends to equal fewer crowds, plenty of cultural events and, by the end of the month, the first signs of Christmas appearing across European cities.

From early festive markets in Vienna to food and wine in Portugal, a major marathon in Athens and winter sun in Fuerteventura, there are still plenty of reasons to get away.

Here’s Euronews Travel’s guide for where to go, what to see and where to stay this November.

Destinations

Vienna, Austria

If you want to get into the Christmas spirit without waiting until December, Vienna is one of the best places to start.

The Austrian capital's Christmas markets begin opening early in the month, with both the Schönbrunn Palace and Stephansplatz markets opening on 6 November. The most famous market, Rathausplatz, follows on 13 November.

When you’ve had your fill of mulled wine and Christmas lights, November is a great time to explore Vienna's museums, grand coffee houses and palaces without the summer crowds.

Make sure to check out both the Belvedere and Hofburg palaces and head to the Kunsthistorisches Museum, which is filled with European old masters and Habsburg art treasures.

Fuerteventura, Canary Islands, Spain

For those who would rather avoid the cold altogether, the Canary Islands remain one of Europe's safest bets for some late-autumn sunshine.

Fuerteventura is particularly appealing in November, when its beaches, volcanic landscapes and enormous dunes can be explored without the intensity of the summer heat – and it’s one of the most affordable islands in the Canaries, too.

For those who suffer from seasonal depression, the sun sets in the Canary Islands later than in most places in mainland Europe, so it’s ideal for staying cheerful as the winter sets in.

There's also a new reason to stay here. The Elba Corralejo Resort & Spa is opening on 1 November, bringing with it 478 rooms, a staggering 20 swimming pools, restaurants and extensive wellness and family facilities.

With temperatures often in the mid-20s, Fuerteventura is a great destination for late autumn sun Michael Baccin/Unsplash

Hotel openings

Casa Verbena Madrid, Spain

Hilton's new Outset Collection is making its European debut in Madrid with Casa Verbena Madrid.

The 45-room hotel is set on Calle de Preciados, a pedestrianised shopping street in the heart of the Spanish capital, within walking distance of Puerta del Sol, Plaza Mayor and the Royal Palace.

It is designed by Spanish interior designer Lorenzo Castillo, with boutique rooms drawing on Spanish architecture and culture.

Hotel Maastricht-Maas, Netherlands

Maastricht is getting a new four-star-plus hotel this November, with the Van der Valk Exclusief Hotel Maastricht-Maas celebrating its grand opening on the banks of the River Maas.

The 113-room property has a contemporary design with South American influences, alongside a restaurant, bar, meeting spaces and a fifth-floor panoramic wellness area.

It is also within easy reach of Maastricht's historic centre, making it a useful base for exploring the buzzy Dutch city.

Events and attractions

Berlin Science Week, Berlin, Germany

Germany’s capital gets particularly cerebral in early November, when Berlin Science Week takes place from 1-10 November.

This year's theme is “In Touch”, exploring how science affects everyday life through exhibitions, workshops, talks, performances and events across the city.

A public weekend from 6-8 November is one of the highlights, making this a good option for anyone who wants something a little different from the usual museum-and-gallery city break.

Athens Marathon The Authentic, Athens, Greece

November is a particularly good month to visit Athens if you like your city breaks with a bit of sporting drama.

The 43rd Athens Marathon, the Authentic, takes place on 7 and 8 November, following the historic route from Marathon to the Panathenaic Stadium.

Even if you're not running, it's a chance to see one of the world's most famous marathon routes and enjoy Athens at a time when summer's heat has disappeared.

International Hot Air Balloon Festival, Alentejo, Portugal

The Alentejo region of Portugal is set to gain tonnes of popularity next year, thanks to its appearance in countless travel experts’ trend predictions.

To experience it for yourself before it blows up as a destination, why not visit the International Hot Air Balloon Festival taking place there from 7-12 November.

The festival, which has been running since 1997, will feature balloon flights, public displays and opportunities to see the colourful aircraft filling the skies over the Alentejo landscape.

While you’re there, you could head to Borba, which will host its annual Vine and Wine Festival from 11-15 November, bringing together wine tastings, regional food, entertainment, crafts and local producers.

November sees countless hot air balloons take to the skies of Portugal’s Alentejo region Ricardo Rocha/Unsplash

Planning ahead: Christmas markets, skiing and winter sun

November is also the month when Christmas travel starts becoming a much more immediate prospect.

If you want to visit some of Europe's biggest markets without the crowds of December, the final week of November is worth considering. Vienna starts early, while cities including Strasbourg, Nuremberg and Prague move into full festive mode later in the month.

It's also worth booking winter-sun trips now, with the Canary Islands and Madeira remaining as popular choices as temperatures fall across northern Europe.

Travelling over Christmas and New Year is notoriously tricky and sometimes pricey, so it’s best to book ahead to secure the best possible deals.

Finally, if you're thinking about skiing, November is the time to start looking ahead. A number of new Alpine hotels and lodges are opening for the 2026-2027 season, including The First Cortina in Italy, The Ski Lodge in Verbier and new properties in Morzine and Les Menuires.

World.title: Revolut to launch platform for investing in private tech companies
World.content:
Private technology companies are taking longer to go public, with the median age at listing rising from 6.9 years in 2014 to 11 years in 2025, according to figures cited by Revolut in an announcement released on Monday.

 

This means more of their growth takes place before shares become available on public markets and can be accessed by retail investors.

"With Revolut Ventures, we're aiming to dismantle one of the final barriers in wealth management: retail investor exclusion from non-listed companies," Rolandas Juteika, Head of Revolut Wealth and Trading (EEA) at Revolut stated.

"Value creation happens long before an IPO, and by managing our own platform, we're giving everyday investors the opportunity to access tomorrow's market leaders right from the Revolut app," Juteika added.

The new platform is expected to become available in 2027 and will be integrated into the Revolut app alongside existing investment options, including stocks, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), bonds and money market funds.

The announcement follows the introduction of private market investment products in selected European Economic Area (EEA) countries in July 2026.

However, investments in private companies carry significant risks.

Unlike publicly traded shares, they are more difficult to sell and investors could lose a substantial portion or all of their invested capital.

The launch comes as Revolut continues to expand its operations, having secured full banking licences in the UK and France earlier this year.

The UK fintech, which is seeking to diversify its revenue streams, is also considering a dual stock market listing in London and New York, although no date has been confirmed.

World.title: 'Pure garbage': Elon Musk’s AI-generated 'The Odyssey' clip ridiculed online
World.content:
This summer, Elon Musk promised that his AI tool Grok Imagine would create a feature-length version of Homer’s ancient Greek poem "The Odyssey", after spending months railing against Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey with racist and transphobic outbursts and "go woke, go broke" rants.

 

“Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer,” he posted.

Now, the trolling tech mogul has followed through. Partially.

Grok has shared a seven-minute, AI-generated episode of "The Odyssey” series on X, stated to be a “creative collaboration” with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker, both of whom specialise in AI filmmaking. And it's exactly what you'd expect.

Strange movements. Narratively all over the place. Airbrushed. White. Utterly soulless.

The AI slop clip has been blasted online, with some describing it as "pure garbage" and others commenting that the clip "shows you how little AI understands art or humans".

"Musk criticized Nolan, one of the best directors of our generation, for not being historically accurate in his ‘Odyssey’, and promises a better one created entirely by AI. He then proceeds to produce a 7 min trailer with dozens of historical inaccuracies," wrote one user. Another wrote: "If this is how you think the Odyssey should be. It's no wonder you keep thinking Russia started the Ukraine war. You should send the Russians this 'movie' it would probably finish them off. Utter waste of time and money like most of Musk Inc."

"As an artistic product it sucks as much as you would expect, too many details going wrong, dreadful pacing and dialogue - it's basically a 7 minute C level trailer," wrote another, while one user made a suggestion: ""Elon Musk knows shit about movies and I’d suggest that he should just stick to what he’s good at, but that seems to be white nationalism."

There are also several glaring elements in Grok's AI Odyssey which are at odds with Musk's claims that its version would be "historically accurate" - chiefly that it's not in the Greek language and shows the Greeks landing at Troy - something which happens before Homer's Odyssey begins.

Meanwhile, Nolan's The Odyssey, which opened in cinemas worldwide on 17 July, has made nearly $1.8bn at the box office and has received overwhelmingly positive reviews.

Euronews Culture included the film in our Best Movies of 2026... So Far rundown, writing: "While Nolan’s take on Homer's foundational epic is without a doubt his most ambitious undertaking, and there's so much to admire about this monumental technical achievement, it’s an uneven effort. The filmmaker's proclivity for non-linear plot structures proves to be a thorn in his side, as The Odyssey is often crippled by clumsy editing choices and pacing issues in its first half. Additionally, more time could have been spent on Odysseus’ dangerous adventures to make thrills truly register."

We added: "Once the film does coalesce into something more focused in the final act, you'll have felt awe but not much in the way of character-driven emotion. Or fun, which Homer’s epic had plenty of. Even if The Odyssey isn't the flat-out masterpiece many caught up in the hype are hailing, there's no denying that only Nolan could have accomplished such bold cinematic event."

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.

World.title: Jordan: 3 arrested over deadly church attack
World.content:
Three men have been arrested in Jordan in connection with an attack on a Greek Orthodox church last week. The arrests took place following a dawn shootout with security forces during which the suspects were wounded.

State security forces in Jordan arrested three men on Monday morning in connection with a deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday, in which nine people were killed and around 40 more injured.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.

All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties as they recovered firearms and ammunition.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.

"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."

Middle East conflicts take toll on Jordan's tourism sector To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jordan: King Abdullah calls for 'iron first' response

King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.



King Abdullah II (center) visited victims in hospital and called for Jordanian security forces to respond with an "iron fist." Image: Royal Court of Jordan/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable middle-eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Germany news: Union slams Audi CEO for joining Trump at campaign rally, while Chancellor Merz and President Steinmeier embark on separate Asia tours
World.content:
10/26/2026 October 26, 2026 German cruise ship cancels voyage after port collision

The ship collided with two container vessels in the port on Sunday, forcing the cancellation of a 20-day cruise to the Canary Islands Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

German cruise operator Tui Cruises has canceled a 20-day voyage to the Canary Islands after its cruise ship "Mein Schiff 3" collided with two container vessels in the northern port of Bremerhaven.

Tugboats were helping the nearly fully booked cruise ship, carrying 2,428 passengers and 922 crew members, leave port on Sunday evening when a gust of wind pushed it toward two moored container ships, police said.

All three vessels sustained damage. One container ship suffered extensive damage to its port side, with several meters of its hull torn open above the waterline. The cruise ship also suffered significant damage, including to its lifeboats and bridge.

There were no injuries or water ingress on any of the vessels. All three ships have been temporarily prohibited from leaving port while investigations continue.

Tui Cruises said technical experts had inspected the vessel and determined that repairs at a shipyard were necessary, forcing the cancellation of the planned voyage.

The company described the cancellation as "the only responsible decision," stressing that passenger and crew safety remained its highest priority.

World.title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado returns from exile, received by thousands of supporters in Caracas
World.content:
Nobel Peace Prize winner and popular Venezuelan political opposition figure Maria Corina Machado has returned from nearly a year in exile. She was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas.

Venezuela's opposition leader Maria Corina Machado was greeted by thousands of cheering supporters in Caracas on Sunday after returning from nearly a year in exile.

Her supporters stood along highways, toll plazas and city streets waving Venezuelan flags and chanting slogans like "freedom" as Machado made her way in a convoy of cars and motorcycles to the capital, Caracas.

Wearing her trademark white T-shirt and blue jeans, she leaned out of the sunroof and shouted "this country is giving lessons to everyone" as her convoy entered the capital.

Maria Corina Machado was see singing the national anthem at a church after returning to the country Image: Vente Venezuela Press/REUTERS

In Guacara earlier, the AFP news agency reported seeing Machado singing the national anthem in a plaza packed with supporters, waving flags and cheering her return.

Why was Machado in exile?

Machado left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in promoting democracy in autocratic Venezuela.

Facing arrest by the regime of former President Nicolas Maduro, she sought refuge in the Argentine embassy in Caracas and was smuggled out of the country with assistance from the United States.

At first she was unable to return for fear of detention by authorities.

After the US-led ouster and arrest of Maduro, she gave her Nobel medal to US President Donald Trump.

However, her inability to return to Venezuela for so long was partly due to the Trump administration.

Instead of backing Machado, Washington decided to support interim President Delcy Rodriguez.

Machado has said she faced travel restrictions and flight cancellations, partly due to Trump's worries that her presence in Venezuela could inflame tensions during a period of transition, and partly due to Rodriguez' interference.

World.title: From rotten food to political opponents: Researchers explore how disgust relates to our beliefs, and why the connection is complicated
World.content:
Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

Some studies have linked disgust sensitivity to socially conservative attitudes. But ahead of the US midterm elections, does disgust shape our politics, or do our beliefs shape what we find disgusting?

The smell of rotten food can make us recoil. Certain sexual practices can provoke a similar reaction. And in today's polarized political climate, even political opponents can become objects of disgust.

Psychologists have long investigated whether sensitivity to disgust helps explain political beliefs. A review of 24 studies found that people who reported being more easily disgusted tended to hold more socially conservative views.

One explanation begins with evolution.

"We think that it evolved in part to reduce exposure to things that could make you sick," psychologist Yoel Inbar, of the University of British Columbia in Canada, told DW.

What are the three types of disgust?

But disgust is not a single emotion. The Three-Domain Disgust Scale , developed in 2009, distinguishes three types:

Pathogen disgust: Reactions to potential sources of infection, such as rotten food, vomit or bodily waste.

Sexual disgust: Reactions to particular sexual behaviors or situations.

Moral disgust: Reactions to wrongdoing, such as betrayal or cruelty. Researchers debate whether this reflects physical revulsion or moral disapproval.

One theory is that people who are especially wary of germs and disease may also prefer traditional social rules.

Donald Trump used language evoking contagion when describing immigrants early in his 2024 presidential campaign Image: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP/Getty Images

Inbar explains that avoiding potential sources of infection can also mean missing out on new experiences.

"Some people are more on the cautious conservative side, and some people are more on the exploring risk-taking side when it comes to pathogen exposure," he said.

Indeed, the language of contamination also appears in political rhetoric. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Donald Trump repeatedly described immigrants as "poisoning the blood of our country." Trump has also described himself as a "germaphobe."

Inbar acknowledges that the evidence linking sensitivity to disgust with conservative political beliefs remains uncertain.

"We have hypotheses. I don't know that we have as strong of evidence as I would like," Inbar said.

Do liberals and conservatives feel disgust differently?

Disgust is not exclusively conservative. And what people find revolting can depend on their values.

A 2020 study titled "Is Disgust a "Conservative" Emotion?" found that liberals and conservatives were disgusted by different things.

Conservatives, generally aligned with the Republicans in US politics, reported greater disgust at examples involving sexual behaviors and drug use, while liberals, generally aligned with the Democrats, reported greater disgust at animal abuse and environmental pollution.

However, when asked how easily disgusted they were in general, there was no clear difference across the political spectrum.

Can our bodies reveal our politics?

Some early studies suggested conservatives showed stronger physical reactions to frightening or disgusting images, measured partly through changes in sweating.

Many US voters are undecided, disillusioned or disengaged To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But subsequent research, including a 2020 study by political psychologist Bert Bakker at the University of Amsterdam, struggled to reproduce those findings.

Studies based on questionnaires, however, have generally found that people with more conservative attitudes report being more easily disgusted.

"If bodily reactions don't differ across political groups, why do feelings?" Manos Tsakiris, of Royal Holloway and the Centre for the Politics of Feelings at the University of London, told DW.

How do gut feelings influence political beliefs?

Tsakiris and colleague Mariana von Mohr wondered whether the answer might lie in how people perceive and interpret signals from their bodies.

Scientists call the perception of internal sensations, such as hunger, breathing or a racing heart, "interoception." It's sometimes called our eighth sense, alongside the familiar five, plus our senses of balance and body position.

"A bodily signal doesn't arrive with a label attached," Tsakiris told DW. "We have to notice it and make sense of it."

The researchers surveyed 632 US adults , asking how much they noticed and trusted signals from their bodies — a measure known as "interoceptive sensibility."

They found that people who were more easily disgusted by sexual behavior tended to be more conservative, regardless of how aware they felt of their bodies.

But for moral disgust, the link to conservatism was found only among people who reported lower bodily awareness.

What particularly surprised Tsakiris was that perceived bodily awareness alone had no link to political views.

Pathogen disgust is one type of disgust thought to have evolved to protect us from infection Image: Elena Shishkina/Zoonar/picture alliance

"People who are highly attuned to their bodies were neither more liberal nor more conservative," he said.

Can disgust actually be measured?

Inbar questions whether all forms of disgust are equally useful for studying political attitudes.

He and Joshua Tybur, one of the creators of the Three-Domain Disgust Scale, generally prefer measuring pathogen disgust — reactions to potential sources of disease — rather than sexual disgust.

Questions about sexual disgust may already reflect conservative beliefs about sex.

"It's almost asking people the same thing twice," Inbar said.

The new study found no significant link between pathogen disgust and conservative views.

Inbar wants the findings on bodily awareness and disgust tested again, with predictions set out in advance. For now, he considers them "suggestive at best."

How might politicians exploit feelings of disgust?

Tsakiris suggests that people who struggle to understand their bodily feelings may be more vulnerable to political messages telling them what those feelings mean.

"I know what you're feeling. You're feeling angry or you're feeling disgusted about this thing," he said, illustrating how someone might put an emotional label on another person's unease.

Such labels could influence political behavior, he argues, although the study did not directly test this.

What's behind the rising polarization in German politics? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"This is how disgust can do political work: it can turn moral judgments about individuals into judgments about whole groups," he said.

Does disgust influence how people vote?

The research cannot establish whether disgust shapes political beliefs or existing beliefs shape what people find disgusting. Bakker notes that political beliefs can influence how people describe their own personalities, suggesting the relationship could work both ways.

"Voting behavior is very complex and citizens make up their mind about politics in a complex way," he told DW.

Inbar also cautions against exaggerating disgust's importance. "The thing to emphasize in your story is that the relationship, while it's consistent, is quite small," he said.

"It's one of the many influences on people's politics."

Tsakiris advocates what he calls "critical feeling": questioning our emotional responses to provocative material, including social media posts, just as we question the information itself.

He also emphasizes discussing our feelings with others and listening to different perspectives, even when we disagree.

"Life and politics and democracy is a contact sport," he said.



Edited by: Rosalie Delaney

World.title: India news: Remark on Modi's father stirs political row
World.content:
Skip next section India-China face-off: Beijing says it carried out normal activities in border areas

10/26/2026 October 26, 2026 India-China face-off: Beijing says it carried out normal activities in border areas

China's Foreign Ministry on Monday said it carried out normal patrol and control activities along its border with India, in response to New Delhi's claim that it deviated from established patrolling patterns leading to a tense military standoff in Arunachal Pradesh.

India's Foreign Ministry, on Friday, had said that the situation along the India-China border was periodically disrupted, blaming Chinese forces for "miscalculations" along the Line of Actual Control.

In response, Chinese diplomats said the country has consistently and strictly abode by the relevant agreements between the countries and conducted routine patrols and management activities in the region, as reported by Chinese Communist Party's Global Times newspaper

The nuclear-armed neighbors remain in communication through diplomatic and military channels, a ministry spokesperson said as per the report.

Last week, India's China border police chief, Shatrujeet Singh Kapur, said that face-offs between Indian and Chinese troops are continuing at multiple locations along the border in the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh, despite ongoing talks between the two countries.

The face-offs in Arunachal Pradesh underscore the challenges of maintaining peace along the border even as the two countries have held several rounds of military and diplomatic talks this year.

India has over the years reiterated that the northeastern state of Arunachal Pradesh is an integral part of the country, while China considers it to be a part of Tibet.

World.title: Brazilian leftist President Lula wins reelection against conservative challenger Flavio Bolsonaro
World.content:
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.

"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

He said Russia hoped for more of the same.

Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.

However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.

Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.

It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

World.title: Serbia election: Vucic concedes defeat to student-led movement
World.content:
In a seismic political shift, Serbia's longtime strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic has conceded defeat to a student-led opposition movement in the country's parliamentary elections.

Serbia's longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led movement in the country's parliamentary elections on Sunday in what represents a seismic political shift.

High turnout and growing tension marked a hotly contested parliamentary election that tuned into a showdown between the Balkan country's longtime leader and a diverse movement of university students who have led protests against him for almost two years.

The result brings an end to more than a decade of rule by Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

Pre-election polls had suggested a tight race between the SNS and the newly formed, youth-backed party Students' List, which emerged from a mass student protest movement.

lija Srdanovic, a physician who leads the student movement's list of 250 candidates, said after the results came in that "We are moving toward a more-civilized and better Serbia."

Vucic: 'It is clear that we lost these elections'

"Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we lost these elections," Vucic said as he addressed supporters at SNS headquarters in Belgrade.

In his concession speech, Vucic said projections had the youth-backed Students' List taking between 135 and 140 seats, whereas the SNS was projected to win around 105.

Vucic blamed Serbia's independent media for the loss, while also alleging interference from unnamed European countries and the "US deep state," which he claimed, without elaborating, is also "against President [Donald] Trump." Vucic also has maintained close ties with Russia and President Vladimir Putin throughout his tenure.

Celebrations erupted on the streets of the capital as soon as Vucic conceded defeat. Passing cars honked and crowds began to party near the election commission's headquarters.

At Students' List headquarters, supporters cried tears of joy, cheering, hugging and chanting — "Victory! Victory!"

What is Serbia's student protest movement

Sunday's result is the culmination of nearly two years of protests after the deadly collapse of a train station canopy in the city of Novi ‌Sad in 2024.

The disaster killed 16 people and stirred widespread anger over alleged corruption, poor construction standards and a lack of accountability for public infrastructure projects.

Protesters accused the government of allowing corruption and political patronage to undermine public safety, allegations authorities have rejected.

Demonstrations demanding accountability have ultimately snowballed into a movement larger than anything Serbia has experienced since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.

The scandals that rocked Serbia and are shaping the election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What began with university students staging blockades and marches soon drew support from teachers, farmers and other segments of Serbian society, turning demands for justice over the disaster into a broader challenge to Vucic's grip on power.

Vucic's tough election challenge

SNS won parliamentary elections in 2012 and has dominated Serbian politics ever since. Vucic himself first came to power as prime minister in 2014 before becoming president in 2017.

After calling snap elections last month, he stepped down as president to run for prime minister.

Vucic and the SNS have run Serbia for more than a decade Image: Zorana Jevtic/REUTERS

His second presidential term was due to expire in May 2027, and Serbia's constitution prevents him from serving a third term.

Critics have accused him of concentrating power, undermining independent media and weakening democratic institutions. He and his party deny the allegations.

The student movement has managed to channel the energy of the street protests into an electoral challenge the likes of which neither Vucic and his ruling party nor Serbia's established opposition has ever seen.

​Serbia's election commission put turnout at nearly 70%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.

Serbia vote draws EU attention

The election was closely watched in Europe, where Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership.

EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated the Students' List on their victory. "We stand ready to support reforms on the rule of law, media freedom, the fight against corruption and strong democratic institutions, and to work together to advance Serbia's future in the European Union," von der Leyen said on X.

Vucic has also refused to join Western sanctions against Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.

The vote comes six months after Peter Magyar's victory in Hungary , when he defeated Vucic's ally, Viktor Orban. Magyar congratulated Serbia’s student-led Students’ List on its victory in a post on X.

Serbia's bid to join the European Union has been hampered by concerns over democratic standards and the rule of law. But the election result has prompted a positive response from another European, non-EU institution — the Council of Europe.

"The Council of Europe stands ready to work with Serbia’s democratically elected leadership to strengthen human rights, democracy and the rule of law," the organization’s Secretary-General Alain Berset said on X.
