World.title: Grand Jour de Champagne Returns to Prague With 30 French Producers
World.content:
Prague will host the 19th edition of Grand Jour de Champagne from November 5, bringing together French champagne producers, exclusive tastings and a gala dinner prepared by a two-Michelin-starred chef.

The festival’s main event, the Champagne Exhibition, will take place at Kaiserštejn Palace in Malá Strana, featuring around 50 cuvées from more than 18 champagne houses.

Visitors can sample different styles, meet producers and discover brands including Louis Roederer, Piper-Heidsieck, Philipponnat, Telmont and G. H. Mumm. Selected bottles will also be available to purchase at special festival prices.



The exhibition will run in two sessions, from 14:00 to 17:00 and 17:00 to 20:00. Tickets cost CZK 2,180.

Two-Michelin-Star Chef to Prepare Gala Dinner

Another highlight will be the Champagne Gala Banquet at Prague’s Municipal House, where French chef Valentin Loison will prepare a five-course tasting menu paired with champagnes from selected producers.

Loison, 32, earned two Michelin stars at his restaurant Bulle d’Osier in Langres, France, within approximately 18 months. The evening will also feature a musical performance by Czech violist Jitka Hosprová.

The gala begins at 20:00, with individual tickets priced at CZK 9,400.

Exclusive Tastings and Masterclasses

The festival programme also includes specialist tastings and masterclasses for champagne enthusiasts.

One session will focus on Louis Roederer’s Cristal, featuring vintages including 2006 and 2016, at the Zlatá Praha restaurant. Other events will explore the Meunier grape variety and pair foie gras with a rare 1996 de Venoge Blanc de Blancs Magnum.

Some masterclasses are limited to just 12 participants.

Tickets

Tickets and the full programme are available here. For additional information, contact [email protected].

Readers registering through Prague Morning can enter the code PM2026 in the designated field after their surname to help organisers identify their registration. Priority consideration is subject to ticket availability.

World.title: Beyond Tacos: Meet the Founders of La Casa Azteca in Prague
World.content:
La Casa Azteca brings traditional Mexican food and cultural celebrations to Prague.

Run by Miguel, originally from Mexico, and Modar, who comes from Syria, the restaurant draws on their experience in the city’s Mexican food scene while introducing customers to dishes and traditions from beyond the familiar.

Two routes to Prague

Modar arrived for work as a structural engineer. While learning Czech, he found himself working in a Mexican restaurant, where he became interested in the food and the business.

“I fell in love with the Mexican concept and the Mexican food, so I had to stay,” he says.



Miguel, meanwhile, had already spent years living abroad, including five years in Montreal and time in the United States. He had always wanted to experience different countries, and Prague was another step in that direction.

Still, the city felt unlike anywhere he had been before. He remembers seeing a tram when he first arrived and feeling as though he had landed in a fairy-tale country.

The two eventually met through Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, around nine years ago. What started as a shared connection to Mexican food eventually grew into a business partnership.

Keeping Mexican food authentic — and introducing it to Prague

At La Casa Azteca, Miguel and Modar want to keep the food close to what customers would find in Mexico, combining street food with dishes more commonly associated with traditional restaurants. The menu includes mole, chiles, flautas and tacos, with each dish bringing its own flavours and character.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Azteca Cocina & Bar (@azteca_prague)

Keeping those flavours in Prague, however, sometimes means working with ingredients that are harder to find locally. Herbs commonly used in Mexico can be difficult to source, while ingredients such as tortillas and chillies can also be more expensive. Some elements therefore have to be substituted without losing the character of the dish.

They have also had to navigate some of the expectations Czech customers bring with them. Part of that process has been showing customers that Mexican cuisine goes well beyond the familiar image of tacos, enchiladas and very spicy dishes.

“People think that in Mexico we are always eating spicy food,” Miguel says. “It’s true, but not all our food is tacos and enchiladas. We eat normal food too — pasta, a piece of meat with rice.”

The same approach extends to drinks. Mezcal is still relatively unfamiliar to many Czech customers, so the team uses the restaurant as a place to explain where it comes from, how it is produced and how different varieties can taste.

“It’s something that people can explore,” Miguel says. “They appreciate the taste. They appreciate the liquor. It’s not just a party drink.”

Building a business abroad

Although Miguel and Modar have around nine years of experience in Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, La Casa Azteca is a newer chapter. The current project, which combines a restaurant with a neighbouring service window, has been running for around six months.

Starting their own business required learning how to navigate the Czech system from scratch. “We had to learn so much about running a business in the Czech Republic,” Modar says. “Everything is very well organized and very well thought out, so you really need to be prepared. You have to pay attention to every detail and every small thing.”

There was also the risk that came with building something abroad, without the same safety net they might have had at home. “I think it’s harder to take risks when you’re living abroad because, if you fall, there’s no one to pick you up. The stress is greater. But at the same time, you know there’s no way back, so you have to make it work,” Modar says.

Celebrating Mexican culture in Prague

Beyond the menu, Miguel and Modar celebrate Mexican traditions through events at the restaurant. After marking Mexican Independence Day in September, they are now preparing for the Day of the Dead, with Mexican dancers, live mariachi music, decorations and special dishes planned for the end of October.

World.title: Turn a Sleepover Into a Special Memory With atelier stories
World.content:
A sleepover with friends can be one of those childhood moments that children remember for years.

But for parents, organising one often means buying decorations, preparing bedding, rearranging furniture and dealing with the cleanup afterwards.

Prague-based atelier stories takes care of everything, bringing a fully styled teepee sleepover directly to the family home. Parents choose the theme, date and number of children, while the company handles the delivery, setup, styling and collection.

Founded by Jana Hrochová, who has a background in event production, organisation and guest services, atelier stories was created around a simple idea: making special moments for children without turning them into another project for parents.



The concept works for birthdays, but it doesn’t have to be a special occasion. A weekend with friends, a school holiday or simply an evening when children want to do something different can become a small adventure at home.

Families can choose from three themes: Mermaid World, Wizard Academy and SPA Night. Each setup features coordinated colours, soft textiles, fairy lights and themed accessories. The result is a playful sleeping space designed to appeal to children while remaining stylish enough to fit comfortably into the family home.

Every booking includes the equipment and styling, with teepees assembled and individual sleeping spaces prepared with mattresses, bedding, pillows, blankets, decorative cushions and other details suited to the chosen theme. Optional extras include creative kits, themed activities, photography and Instax memories.

The service is designed to make the experience as easy as possible for parents. There is no need to buy decorations, assemble teepees, wash bedding or find storage space for the equipment afterwards. Once the sleepover is over, atelier stories returns to dismantle the setup, pack everything away and collect it.

Quality, comfort and hygiene are central to the service. The equipment and textiles are cleaned and prepared between bookings, and each sleeping space is carefully arranged to ensure children have a comfortable place to settle in for the night.

Families can book a sleepover for one night or an entire weekend. Prices start at CZK 3,490 for two children for one night, or CZK 4,900 for two children for a full weekend, from Friday to Monday. Both options include the equipment, styling, setup and collection, with delivery within Prague included free of charge.

The service can also make a thoughtful gift from grandparents. Instead of another toy or physical present, a gift voucher gives grandchildren an experience to look forward to.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by atelier stories | tématické přespávačky pro děti (@atelierstories.cz)

Vouchers can cover a complete sleepover or contribute towards one, allowing the family to choose the theme and date later. They are valid for one year and delivered by email within 24 hours of payment.

While at-home sleepovers remain the main focus, atelier stories also creates children’s lounges and play areas for weddings and other events, giving younger guests a dedicated space to play and relax while adults enjoy the occasion.

World.title: Czechia Has the EU’s Lowest Poverty Risk Rate, Eurostat Finds
World.content:
Czechia has the lowest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the European Union, with 12% of its population affected, according to 2025 data from Eurostat.

The figure is well below the EU average of 21%, meaning that around one in five people across the bloc face the risk of poverty or social exclusion. Among children, the proportion rises to one in four.



The EU measure covers people whose incomes fall below the poverty-risk threshold, those experiencing severe material and social deprivation, and those living in households with very low work intensity.

Poland also records a relatively low rate, at 15%, followed by the Netherlands and Slovenia at 16%. Slovakia, Belgium, Finland and Cyprus each report 17%, while Austria stands at 19%.

At the other end of the scale, Bulgaria has the highest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, at 29%. Greece follows at 28%, and Romania at 27%. Lithuania and Spain each report 26%, while Latvia stands at 25%. Italy records 23%, Estonia 22%, and Germany, France and Croatia each match the EU average of 21%.

EU Moves to Strengthen Anti-Poverty Measures

The figures come as European institutions seek to strengthen measures to reduce poverty and social exclusion across the bloc.

Earlier this year, the European Parliament called for more decisive action, stressing that poverty undermines human dignity and that everyone should have access to basic necessities.

In May, the European Commission adopted the EU’s first-ever anti-poverty strategy, setting out measures intended to prevent and reduce poverty across member states.

The strategy addresses several areas, including access to affordable housing, employment opportunities and support for families raising children. It also seeks to remove barriers to employment and tackle in-work poverty, which affects people who have jobs but still struggle to make ends meet.

Housing exclusion and the availability of social and affordable housing are among its priorities. The strategy also focuses on child poverty, support for older people through adequate pensions and opportunities to remain in employment, and efforts to combat discrimination and stigma.

World.title: Internationally Acclaimed Chef Meir Adoni to Open New Restaurant in Prague
World.content:
An internationally acclaimed chef is preparing to open a new restaurant in Prague’s Old Town.

Samna, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant by Israeli chef Meir Adoni, will open at Ovocný trh on November 5, 2026.

The restaurant is being developed in partnership with the team behind SaSaZu and will combine Mediterranean cuisine with Middle Eastern and Moroccan influences.



Adoni has built an international reputation through restaurants in Tel Aviv, New York, Berlin, Singapore and Marbella. His cooking draws on Middle Eastern traditions, modern techniques and the flavors of his Moroccan heritage.

His previous projects include Catit and Mizlala in Tel Aviv, Nur in New York, Layla in Berlin and Aniba in Singapore. He has also appeared as a judge on television cooking competitions, including MasterChef and Game of Chefs, and mentored participants in the S.Pellegrino Young Chef competition.

Samna follows a concept already established by Adoni in Marbella, bringing together Mediterranean recipes, contemporary techniques and bold flavor combinations.

The chef’s approach draws on childhood memories and traditional home cooking, reinterpreted through a modern culinary perspective.

Further details about the menu and the restaurant’s opening arrangements have not been announced in the provided information.

World.title: Prague Airport Adds 20 Destinations to Winter Flight Schedule
World.content:
Prague Airport will offer direct flights to 145 destinations this winter, including 20 new destinations, as its winter flight schedule takes effect on Sunday, October 25.

The 2026/2027 winter schedule will run until March 27, 2027, with 69 airlines operating flights from Václav Havel Airport Prague.

Among the new destinations are Lille, Palermo, Turin, Venice and Bergen. Travellers will also have new options for reaching ski destinations, including Bolzano in Italy and Poprad in Slovakia.



The winter schedule also introduces new long-haul connections to Almaty in Kazakhstan and Hanoi in Vietnam, operated by Vietjet.

Charter flights will add further options, including Phuket in Thailand, La Romana in the Dominican Republic and Sihanoukville in Cambodia.

EasyJet will launch a new route to Marrakesh, Morocco, while Smartwings will introduce scheduled flights to Lisbon, Portugal.

Several routes previously operated mainly during the summer will continue into the winter season. These include easyJet flights to Newcastle in the UK and Wizz Air services to Vilnius in Lithuania.

More Flights to Popular Destinations

Several existing routes will see increased frequencies during the winter months.

Air Serbia will increase its Prague–Belgrade service from nine to 11 flights per week, while Pegasus Airlines will raise the number of weekly flights to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen Airport from 14 to 17.

TAP Air Portugal will increase flights to Lisbon from seven to eight per week. Korean Air will also add a weekly service to Seoul, bringing the total to four flights per week.

Jazeera Airways will operate flights to Kuwait during the winter season for the first time.

New airlines operating passenger services from Prague this winter include Vietjet, SkyAlps, Fly2Galicia, Jazeera Airways and STARLUX Airlines. TUI Airways and Enter Air will also operate charter flights.

More Routes Planned for Summer 2027

Prague Airport has also confirmed new routes for the 2027 summer season. Delta Air Lines will launch flights to New York in mid-April, while SkyUp Airlines will introduce a new connection to Chișinău, the capital of Moldova.

World.title: Prague Reopens Bobsleigh Track With a New Alpine Coaster
World.content:
Prague’s Prosek bobsleigh track has reopened after a CZK 100 million renovation, introducing a second alpine coaster and doubling the attraction’s capacity.

Located on Mahalka Hill in the Prosek district, the facility has operated for 22 years. It reopened on Wednesday, October 21, with two tracks supplied by German manufacturer Wiegand.



The original track, measuring 700 metres, features a stainless-steel trough in which wheeled carts travel along a concave surface. The new 650-metre track uses the Alpine Coaster 2.0 system, with carts running on a monorail.

Both tracks allow riders to reach speeds of up to 45 kilometres per hour. Passengers can regulate their speed using a manual handbrake.

The newer coaster also incorporates an automated safety system. Around 2,000 magnetic sensors positioned along the track monitor the location and speed of individual carts. If necessary, induction brakes are activated automatically to prevent collisions or carts leaving the track.

Unlike the original ride, the Alpine Coaster 2.0 requires passengers to wear seatbelts.

The renovation has also brought improvements to the surrounding facilities, including a new café and an observation deck. A children’s playground and a rooftop relaxation area are still under construction, with completion planned for spring 2027.

Prices and Opening Hours

The attraction is located at Prosecká 906/34b in Prague 9. Tickets can be used on either track, with visitors choosing which one to ride when they arrive.

Ticket prices

– One ride – CZK 99

– Five rides – CZK 400

– Ten rides – CZK 700

– Twenty rides – CZK 1,300

– Thirty rides – CZK 1,800

Tickets for one, five and ten rides are valid for three months from the date of purchase. Twenty- and thirty-ride passes are valid for one year.

Opening hours

– Monday to Thursday – 10 am to 10 pm

– Friday and Saturday – 10 am to 11 pm

– Sunday – 10 am to 8 pm

World.title: GALLERY: The Czech Republic’s Largest LEGO Store Opens in Prague
World.content:
The Czech Republic’s largest official LEGO Store opened on Thursday, October 22, on Na Příkopě.

The two-storey store covers 496 square metres and combines retail space with interactive attractions, creative activities and displays inspired by the Czech capital.

Among the features greeting visitors at the entrance are the words “Ahoj Praha” (Hello Prague), a model of a No. 23 tram, and figures depicting a lion, Emperor Charles IV and a traditional Prague lamplighter.



The ground floor houses shelves of LEGO sets alongside glass display cases showcasing models and figures. The displays were developed with the involvement of staff at the LEGO factory in Kladno, whose work is also reflected in the store’s custom-built models.

The first floor features a Christmas-themed play area where visitors can build their own decorations from LEGO bricks and hang them on a specially prepared Christmas tree. The activity is open to children and adults alike.

A separate wall made entirely of LEGO bricks gives visitors the freedom to create their own pictures without following instructions or predefined designs.

Visitors who take the stairs to the second floor will find another part of the store’s design. The staircase and surrounding walls feature murals inspired by Prague, including a city panorama and Prague Castle.

The second floor contains further interactive attractions and creative spaces. Its centrepiece is a three-metre-tall replica of Prague’s Astronomical Clock.

World.title: Could Viktor Orbán become UN Secretary-General? Trump administration reportedly wants him to
World.content:
The Wall Street Journal reports that Washington has encouraged former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán to enter the race for the United Nations’ top job, with Russia and China reportedly open to backing his candidacy. No final decision has been made, and Orbán has declined to comment.

The Trump administration is considering former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán for the post of United Nations Secretary-General, according to a Wall Street Journal (WSJ) opinion article published on Sunday, 25 October. The newspaper, citing sources from three countries, reports that Washington has raised the idea directly with Orbán and encouraged him to compete for the position.

According to the report, US officials believe Russia and China could also support the proposal, potentially making Orbán a joint candidate backed by three major powers. However, the plan has yet to receive final approval, and no formal nomination has been announced.

If you missed it: JD Vance refuses to endorse Benjamin Netanyahu, brings up Viktor Orbán’s election defeat as a reason

Why Washington is reportedly backing Orbán

A US State Department official quoted by the WSJ acknowledged that the idea might initially sound far-fetched. Nevertheless, the official suggested that Orbán could attract sufficient support in the UN Security Council.

The official estimated that eight of the council’s 15 members would support the former Hungarian prime minister, with backing from as many as 10 potentially within reach. Whether the United Kingdom and France would oppose his candidacy remains a key question, as both countries are permanent members with veto powers.

The newspaper reports that Orbán’s political outlook is a major attraction for the Trump administration. One US official described him as a “dream candidate for MAGA conservatives”, pointing to his positions on mass immigration and liberal non-governmental organisations, as well as his record of challenging the European Union.

The article also highlights Orbán’s close relations with Russia and his efforts to strengthen Hungary’s ties with China. While the WSJ notes that his perceived defence of leaders such as Vladimir Putin could count against him, the newspaper reports that US officials have continued to raise his name in discussions with Russian and Chinese counterparts.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Orbán is reportedly interested, but cautious

According to the WSJ, American officials initially approached Orbán to find out whether he would consider taking on an international role. The former prime minister reportedly appeared open to the idea but was reluctant to enter the race without a strong prospect of winning.

The report suggests that an announcement could come after the US midterm elections, with President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance expected to support Orbán’s candidacy if he decides to run. Orbán declined to comment on the newspaper’s claims.

The prospect of an international appointment is not entirely new. In May 2026, investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi reported that positions at the UN, including a deputy secretary-general role, had been discussed as possible options for Orbán. The latest report, however, concerns the organisation’s top leadership position.

Who will become the next UN Secretary-General?

The selection process for the next secretary-general is already under way. António Guterres’ term ends on 31 December 2026, and several potential candidates are being considered. Among them is Lana Nusseibeh, a diplomat from the United Arab Emirates, who announced her candidacy last week.

The appointment requires a recommendation from the UN Security Council, which has 15 members. A candidate needs at least nine votes and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members: the United States, Russia, China, the United Kingdom and France. The UN General Assembly then appoints the secretary-general following the council’s recommendation.

World.title: Hungary fines Aldi EUR 335,000 over advertising claims
World.content:
Hungary’s competition authority says Aldi misled consumers by claiming to offer the widest range of products and the best deals without sufficient objective evidence to back up the slogans.

Aldi has been fined HUF 123 million (approximately EUR 335,000) by Hungary’s Competition Authority (GVH) over an advertising campaign that claimed the supermarket chain offered the “Widest Range!” and the “Best Deals!”. The authority ruled that the statements were not adequately supported by objective evidence and were capable of misleading consumers.

The GVH launched competition proceedings against the retailer in the summer of 2025 after Aldi began using the slogans in its commercial communications in March that year. The company has since stopped the practice that prompted the investigation.

Why did Aldi receive the fine?

According to the GVH, Aldi based its claims on first-place awards it had won in the “Widest Range” and “Best Deals” categories at the 2024 Nők Lapja Food Awards.

However, the authority concluded that these awards were insufficient to substantiate claims of market leadership. The results were based on a subjective public vote, and relatively few businesses entered the relevant categories.

The GVH also argued that the categories’ very names could be misleading when used to support broad claims of superiority over competitors, given the limited number of participants.

What did the authority find misleading?

The GVH’s Competition Council determined that average consumers would interpret the advertising as meaning that Aldi objectively offered a wider product selection than its competitors and ran promotions providing greater discounts than those of other retailers. The campaign also suggested that these advantages had been independently recognised through an award.

According to the authority, Aldi did not have up-to-date, objective data at the time of publication to substantiate either claim. The HUF 123 million penalty was calculated with reference to the costs of the advertising campaign, the GVH said.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Lidl was fined over similar claims

The authority also used the case to remind businesses that claims of market leadership must be supported by objective evidence that clearly substantiates them when an  is published.

Aldi is not the first major supermarket chain in Hungary to face a penalty over advertising practices. In August 2026, rival retailer Lidl was fined HUF 48 million following a separate GVH proceeding, Telex reported.

World.title: Major roadworks to close lanes on 3 busy Hungarian motorways: Here’s what drivers need to know
World.content:
Drivers around Budapest should prepare for lane closures and temporary traffic restrictions as extensive resurfacing works begin on 26 October on the M1–M7 shared motorway section, the M7 motorway and the M0 expressway. The works will mainly affect the areas around Budaörs, Törökbálint and Diósd, and are expected to continue in several phases until the third week of November.

Hungarian road operator Magyar Közút Nonprofit Zrt. announced the works, which will cover almost 35,000 square metres across approximately nine kilometres. Around 8,400 tonnes of asphalt are expected to be used as part of the project.

The aim is to replace deteriorating road surfaces before winter, rather than simply repair individual potholes. According to Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy, both the binder and wearing courses need to be replaced on the affected sections.

26–27 October: Lane closures near Budaörs and the M0 exit

The first phase will begin on Monday, 26 October, and continue until Tuesday, 27 October.

M1–M7 shared section: The middle lane will be closed on the section leading out of Budapest, near Budaörs, where the two motorways split. Traffic heading towards the M7 will use the inside lane, while traffic towards the M1 will use the outside lane.

The middle lane will be closed on the section leading out of Budapest, near Budaörs, where the two motorways split. Traffic heading towards the M7 will use the inside lane, while traffic towards the M1 will use the outside lane. M7 towards Lake Balaton: The exit leading to the M0 expressway and Road 8103 will be closed. Drivers will need to use the Érd junction as a diversion.

On 26 October, workers will mill and prepare around 1,800 square metres of road surface at the affected locations. Asphalt laying is scheduled for the following day.

27–28 October: Restrictions at the Budaörs Sport Street junction

From Tuesday, 27 October, to Wednesday, 28 October, works will affect the M7 motorway’s carriageway towards Budapest, at the Sport Street junction in Budaörs. The outer of the two deceleration lanes will be closed. Drivers will still be able to exit the motorway, but should expect possible delays as traffic passes through the restricted area.

Around 2,300 square metres of road surface will be prepared and milled before the new asphalt layers are laid.

28–29 October: M0 junction and Budaörs access affected

Further restrictions are planned from Wednesday, 28 October, to Thursday, 29 October.

Near the M0 junction: The outside lane on the M7 towards Budapest will be closed for approximately 500 metres. Traffic will be able to continue in the inside lane.

The outside lane on the M7 towards Budapest will be closed for approximately 500 metres. Traffic will be able to continue in the inside lane. Budaörs junction: The outer part of the acceleration lane used to join the M7 towards Budapest will be closed. However, joining the motorway will remain possible via the inner part of the acceleration lane.

Around 1,400 square metres of road surface will be prepared and milled during this phase, with asphalt laying scheduled for 29 October.

Further motorway works planned for November

The resurfacing programme will continue at additional locations along the M7 motorway and M0 expressway in November. Magyar Közút will announce the exact dates and traffic restrictions for the later phases separately. The schedule may change depending on weather conditions and construction progress.

The road operator has warned that congestion and longer journey times are possible throughout the affected areas. Drivers are advised to check traffic conditions before setting off and allow extra time for their journeys.

World.title: Belgrade-Budapest trains to launch in December – Direct Vienna services also planned
World.content:
Passenger trains between Belgrade, Budapest and Vienna could return on 13 December, with direct services expected to connect the Serbian capital with both cities, according to the head of Serbia’s state railway company. The planned launch would restore passenger services between Belgrade and Budapest after a seven-year suspension caused by the modernisation of the railway line.

According to Szabad Magyar Szó, Ljubiša Pejičić, acting director-general of Srbija voz, announced the date ahead of the introduction of the new international railway timetable. While the Serbian railway operator says the necessary additional safety tests on the Hungarian section have been completed successfully, final Hungarian regulatory approval has not yet been officially confirmed.

Eight daily departures planned, including direct trains to Vienna

Under the proposed timetable, eight trains would depart from Belgrade each day. Six would travel to Budapest, while two would continue to Vienna via the Hungarian capital. The planned journey times and indicative ticket prices are:

Belgrade–Budapest: approximately three hours, with tickets expected to cost EUR 35.

approximately three hours, with tickets expected to cost EUR 35. Belgrade–Vienna: approximately six hours, with tickets expected to cost EUR 43.

The fares are provisional, as discussions between the Serbian, Hungarian and Austrian railway companies are still under way. A discounted ticket sales period is also planned after services begin.

Passengers travelling to Vienna would not need to change trains in Budapest. Hungarian railway rolling stock is expected to operate the direct Vienna services, while Chinese-built multiple-unit trains operated by the Serbian railway company would serve the route to Budapest.

Trains will be able to reach speeds of up to 200 km/h on the Serbian section and 160 km/h on the Hungarian section. Actual journey times may also depend on border checks.

Border checks could affect journey times

Border controls will be an important factor in determining how competitive the new services are. Serbia is not part of the Schengen Area, so passengers will still need to undergo document checks when travelling between Serbia and Hungary.

According to earlier reports, the two countries have sought to reduce the time needed for border procedures to around 21 minutes. Under the Serbian plans, passengers on the first and last trains of the day would undergo checks at Belgrade’s Prokop central railway station, while checks for other services would take place at Kelebia, near the Hungarian-Serbian border.

If the planned three-hour journey to Budapest can be achieved consistently, the railway could offer an alternative to road travel, particularly when border crossings are congested.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

The Budapest–Belgrade line has already reopened to freight traffic, which began operating on 27 February. Passenger services would mark another milestone for a project whose construction was partly financed through Chinese loans and carried out with Chinese involvement.

The investment has also attracted scrutiny over transparency. In summer 2026, Vitézy said the Hungarian government would seek to lift the confidentiality restrictions covering the project, including its Chinese loan agreement. The documents had been classified for ten years under the previous government, and lifting the restrictions requires Chinese approval.

World.title: Finding friendship: How women’s communities in Budapest bring strangers together
World.content:
From walking clubs and coffee mornings to feminist book discussions, women’s communities in Budapest are bringing people together beyond traditional social gatherings.

At the first two gatherings of The Girlie Walk Club Budapest, around 20 to 30 women turned up. By the third, more than 90 had joined, according to founder Laura Kelemen. What began as an idea inspired by walking clubs abroad quickly found an audience in the Hungarian capital, where making friends as an adult can sometimes feel like unfamiliar territory.

Elsewhere in Budapest, women meet over coffee, attend cinema screenings and yoga sessions, or explore vintage shops together. Others connect through literature, film and discussions about feminism. For Laura and Claudia Jolly, founder of Social Girls Budapest, the challenge goes beyond bringing strangers together. It is helping them feel comfortable enough to strike up a conversation.

When making friends means starting from scratch

For Claudia, the inspiration behind Social Girls Budapest came from a familiar predicament: having plenty of things she wanted to do but nobody available to join her. “I often had so many ideas for things I wanted to do, but no one to do them with, and I realised that other women might be experiencing the same thing,” she told Daily News Hungary.

Claudia felt many social gatherings were difficult for newcomers to enter or centred on drinking and noisy environments. She wanted something more personal, where women could arrive alone without feeling out of place. “I wanted to create a community where women could arrive without knowing anyone and feel welcome from the start,” she said.

Social Girls Budapest is free to join, with no membership requirements or expectations of regular attendance. Activities range from coffee mornings and cinema nights to yoga, comedy shows and vintage shopping. Most participants are international women aged 20 and above, although Hungarian women, including those returning after living abroad, are also welcome.

Breaking the ice, one step at a time

While Claudia brings women together through different activities, Laura has built her community around something simpler: walking. Inspired by walking clubs abroad and a video featuring writer Roxie Nafousi, she wanted to introduce a similar concept to Hungary.

“Walking side by side makes starting a conversation feel much more natural and less intimidating than approaching someone in a traditional social setting,” Laura explained. Unlike conventional networking events, the walks require no rehearsed introductions. Shyer participants can enjoy their surroundings until they feel ready to engage, while occasional activities help break the ice.

Most members are Hungarian, although international residents and visitors have also joined. Laura hopes to welcome more diverse participants while encouraging women to explore Budapest, spend time outdoors and look after their mental well-being.

The challenges of building a social circle in Budapest

For international women, settling into Budapest can mean rebuilding their social lives from scratch. Claudia identifies language barriers as one obstacle. She recalled attending dance classes advertised in English where instructors and participants communicated primarily in Hungarian. Such experiences, she believes, can make it difficult for newcomers to establish friendships.

Another challenge is the transient nature of the city’s international population, as students and professionals arrive and eventually leave. “Building meaningful relationships takes time and consistency, and it can be challenging to establish that when social circles are constantly changing,” Claudia said.

Yet finding friends can be difficult even for long-term residents. Some women join Social Girls Budapest after a breakup or a change in their social circumstances. Laura recognises similar challenges among adults who have lived in the city for years. “I think making friends as an adult can be surprisingly difficult, especially when you’re trying to find people who share your interests and values,” she said.



More than coffee dates and weekend walks

Other communities in Budapest bring women together through shared professional, cultural, and intellectual interests.

Feminista Meetup Budapest traces its beginnings to 2023, when Florence established a feminist book club at the French Institute. According to the collective’s Instagram account, the initiative later moved to Közkincs Könyvtár and switched to English. Its book and film clubs came together under Feminista Meetup in 2025, and the group has since announced plans for a Hungarian-language feminist book club.

Meanwhile, Women’s Coffee Network connects local and international female professionals through small, facilitated gatherings. Established organisations such as the North American Women’s Association of Budapest and the International Women’s Club of Budapest also organise social, cultural and charitable activities.

Facebook groups and friendship apps such as Bumble BFF provide additional ways to meet people, particularly for those looking to expand their social circles beyond organised gatherings.

Why women-focused spaces matter

Despite the enthusiasm surrounding her walking club, Laura said its women-only format initially attracted criticism. “In the beginning, I received quite a lot of negative comments questioning why men weren’t allowed to participate,” she recalled.

“Having a space where women feel comfortable opening up, sharing their experiences and supporting one another doesn’t mean excluding others out of negativity. It simply means creating an environment with a particular purpose.”

Claudia similarly believes smaller gatherings help women who find large social events intimidating. At Social Girls Budapest, participants can get to know one another gradually, without pressure to form immediate friendships. “There is no single way to socialise or form friendships,” she said.

Perhaps that is what makes these communities appealing. Some friendships begin over coffee, others through a shared book or a walk around the city. Sometimes, all it takes is showing up.

World.title: Different steps, different stories: Why young Hungarians are taking up international dance
World.content:
Discover why young Hungarians are taking up K-pop, salsa, and bachata in Budapest, from cultural curiosity and personal expression to meeting new people.

K-pop choreography, Cuban salsa, and Dominican bachata come from different cultural traditions, yet each has found a place in Budapest’s dance studios. For some young Hungarians, an interest in these styles begins with a favourite song or a video online. For others, an invitation from a friend or family member is enough to encourage them to try something new.

Learning the movements is only part of the experience. Dance classes can also introduce participants to unfamiliar cultures and new ways of expressing themselves. Three young Hungarians spoke to Daily News Hungary about what first drew them to these traditions and why they continued dancing.

A shared interest in Korean pop culture

For Júlia Donovitz, an interest in K-pop began in 2020 with BTS’s Dynamite. Already fond of dancing, she was intrigued by music that felt both familiar and different from what she had previously heard. She began attending K-pop dance classes before exploring hip-hop and commercial dance, eventually becoming an instructor herself.

Today, Donovitz teaches at Under Cover, a Budapest-based K-pop dance school. Her decision to teach grew out of her own experience as a student. “I wanted to teach people so they could have the same experience and happiness I found,” she told Daily News Hungary.



She has also watched friendships develop among students who share an interest in Korean music and choreography. “The friendship they create while coming to classes – they get to know other kids who like the same thing as them: dancing and K-pop,” she said.

K-pop’s presence in Hungary extends beyond individual dance studios. A study examining the development of the Korean Wave in Hungary explored how Korean entertainment encouraged participation in fan communities and cultural activities, including dance.

Photo: Júlia Donovitz

Meeting people through salsa and bachata

While Donovitz discovered dancing through popular music, Álmos Berzi’s introduction to salsa came through his older sister, who encouraged him to give it a try. He eventually attended a class with a friend and was pleasantly surprised by the atmosphere.

“Everyone smiled, and it was a really good mood there, so we stuck with it,” he recalled.

Berzi attended classes at Balázs Tánc, where he found that the social nature of salsa helped him overcome some of his shyness. Partner dancing gave him a natural way to interact with people he might otherwise have found difficult to approach.

“In today’s world I think it’s hard to approach women, but in a dance class you will dance with them anyway, and you can meet lots of new people there,” he explained.

He also found that attending classes could improve his mood after a difficult day. What began as a suggestion from his sister became an activity he looked forward to.

Krisztina Rikker, Berzi’s girlfriend, discovered bachata through videos online. Originating in the Dominican Republic, the dance attracted her attention through its music, rhythm, and interaction between partners.

Rikker initially found meeting new people challenging and saw dancing as a way to become more comfortable in social situations. She was particularly drawn to bachata’s emphasis on communication and interaction between partners.

For Rikker, one of bachata’s most appealing qualities is the ability to connect with another person without words. She believes this aspect of the dance can make meeting new people feel more natural, particularly for younger dancers.

Their experiences are consistent with a recent Hungarian study on international social dancing, which identified social connections, community involvement, and personal well-being among the benefits reported by participants.

Budapest has an established network of Latin dance schools and social events. Salsa Diabólica, which has operated since 2003, runs salsa and bachata classes and reports teaching hundreds of students each week. Other communities, including Bachata Club Hungary, organise regular classes and social dancing events for participants at different levels.

A wider dance scene for young Hungarians

The interest in international dance traditions extends to other communities across Budapest. Alongside K-pop, salsa and bachata, young people can explore hip-hop, house, breaking and Afro dance through classes, workshops and local events.

Studios such as Vibes and Stuff introduce participants to different street and club dance styles, while events such as We Got the Vibes, held at the House of Music Hungary in June 2026, bring dancers together for workshops and competitions. These activities are part of a larger dance scene in which international influences have become part of Budapest’s cultural life.

For Donovitz, Berzi and Rikker, the decision to take up dancing began with different interests and circumstances. Their experiences show how music, cultural curiosity and the desire for human connection can lead young Hungarians to traditions that originated far outside their own country.

The music may come from thousands of kilometres away, but the friendships, confidence, and sense of belonging that develop on Budapest’s dance floors are very much local.

World.title: Budapest Airport winter schedule brings 185 destinations, new routes and more flights
World.content:
The Budapest Airport winter schedule for 2026/27 offers travellers more than 185 destinations, increased flight frequencies to popular European and Asian cities, and a brand-new route to Egypt. Whether passengers are planning a festive city break, a Christmas market getaway or an escape to warmer climates, Hungary’s main international airport is expanding its options for the colder months.

The aviation industry’s winter season begins on 25 October, coinciding with the autumn clock change in Europe. For Budapest Airport, the new season brings a continued focus on expanding connectivity, increasing flight frequencies and offering passengers greater flexibility.

Compared with the previous winter, the airport’s airlines are offering 10% more bookable seats, largely thanks to additional services on established routes. The expanded network aims to accommodate both leisure travellers and passengers visiting friends and family during the festive period.

Budapest Airport winter schedule expands flights to Asia

Travellers hoping to exchange Europe’s short winter days for a longer holiday in Asia will benefit from more frequent connections during the 2026/27 winter season.

Daily direct flights will connect Budapest with Shanghai and Beijing, while Guangzhou will be served three times a week. These routes also provide connecting opportunities to destinations across Southeast Asia, making it easier for passengers to plan longer journeys.

However, travellers heading to tropical destinations should check local weather patterns before booking, particularly as monsoon seasons vary significantly across the region.

More flights to Scandinavia and European Christmas markets

The Budapest Airport winter schedule also strengthens European connections, particularly for passengers planning long weekends, festive breaks and Christmas market visits.

Seat capacity on Scandinavian routes will increase by 35% compared with last winter. Wizz Air will operate four weekly flights to Oslo, opening up opportunities to explore Norway’s winter landscapes, forests and mountains.

Meanwhile, SAS Scandinavian Airlines will offer two daily flights between Budapest and Copenhagen on several days in November and December. The Danish capital is particularly attractive during the festive season, with its Christmas decorations, cosy cafés and renowned hygge atmosphere.

Several other European regions will also see increased capacity:

Poland: 50% more available seats compared with the previous winter.

Baltic region: 7.4% more seats, providing additional opportunities to explore historic cities.

Spain: 12% more seats, offering greater flexibility for travellers seeking milder temperatures.

These developments will make it easier to plan short European escapes without committing to a lengthy holiday.

If you missed it: More Chinese flights from Budapest cancelled as airlines suspend routes – what could be behind the cuts?

easyJet launches four new routes between Budapest and the UK

The United Kingdom is another major focus of the winter schedule, with easyJet introducing four additional connections from Budapest.

The airline is launching services to Belfast, Bristol, Liverpool and London Southend, providing more travel opportunities in both directions.

The London Southend route will operate throughout the year, while the other three destinations will be served twice weekly from mid-November until the end of December.

The additional flights are expected to support inbound tourism to Budapest during the festive period while giving Hungarian travellers more options for exploring British cities and their Christmas attractions.

With these additions, easyJet’s Budapest network will have expanded from three to eleven routes over three years.

New Budapest–Marsa Alam flight offers a winter sun escape

For passengers who would rather swap winter coats for swimwear, one of the most appealing additions is Wizz Air’s new direct service to Marsa Alam, Egypt.

Situated on the western coast of the Red Sea, Marsa Alam is known for its beaches, coral reefs and marine wildlife. Visitors can enjoy snorkelling and diving, look for sea turtles in their natural habitat or take part in desert excursions.

The destination offers an alternative to Europe’s colder weather, particularly for travellers who missed their summer holiday or want to enjoy a sunny break towards the end of the year.

What the winter schedule means for travellers

Budapest Airport, officially known as Ferenc Liszt International Airport, is Hungary’s principal international aviation hub and an important gateway to Central Europe.

With more than 185 destinations, increased capacity across several regions and new routes serving both European cities and winter sun resorts, the 2026/27 winter schedule offers considerably more choice than the previous season.

Passengers planning trips around Christmas or New Year should nevertheless check operating dates and frequencies carefully, as some newly introduced services are seasonal.

For travellers departing from Hungary, the expanded schedule means that a festive weekend in Copenhagen, a longer Asian adventure or a sunny escape to Egypt could all begin at Budapest Airport this winter.

World.title: From the Ganges to the Danube: Why Mukesh Srivastava fell in love with Hungary – Exclusive interview
World.content:
From the Ganges to the Danube, Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s journey in Hungary became far more than a diplomatic posting. Having completed her tenure as director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest, he returned to India from Hungary – the country where his child was born – with unforgettable memories, lasting friendships and a deep personal connection. In an exclusive interview with Daily News Hungary, Dr Srivastava reflects on his love for Hungary, his experiences learning the Hungarian language, the growing cultural ties between India and Hungary, and why Budapest will always feel like a second home.

Daily News Hungary (DNH): As you have concluded your tenure as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and returned to India, how do you look back on your time in Hungary?

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava: I look back on my time in Hungary with immense gratitude, a deep sense of fulfilment and countless cherished memories. Serving as Director of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre was both an honour and a privilege. For me, it was much more than a professional assignment; it was a beautiful journey of cultural exchange, lasting friendships, learning and personal growth.

What I will treasure most are the people I have met along the way. I have had the privilege of interacting with remarkable Hungarian artists, scholars, Indologists, students, cultural practitioners, Yoga enthusiasts, Ayurveda experts, journalists, and other countless friends of India, as well as the vibrant Indian community in Hungary. Their warmth, enthusiasm and genuine affection made my journey truly special. Through these interactions, I witnessed how culture has the extraordinary power to bring people together, transcending differences of language, geography and traditions.

Hungary also holds a deeply personal place in my heart, as my child was born in Budapest. The city will therefore always be part of our family’s story and most precious memories.

Now that I have returned to India, I look back with a sense of professional satisfaction, but also with the emotions that come from leaving behind a place that became so close to my heart. I have brought home enduring friendships, wonderful memories and a firm belief that the cultural relations between India and Hungary will continue to grow stronger in the years ahead.

DNH: What were your first impressions of Budapest, Hungary when you arrived?

Srivastava: My first impression of Budapest was of a remarkably beautiful and historic city. The majestic Danube, magnificent architecture, iconic Parliament Building, elegant bridges and rich cultural heritage captivated me from the very beginning.

What particularly struck me was the wonderful balance between old-world charm and modernity. Budapest is a cosmopolitan city with a vibrant cultural and social life, yet it retains a very strong sense of its history and traditions. I admired the respect Hungarians have for their heritage, culture and language, as well as their deep appreciation for arts.

Over time, however, Budapest became much more than a beautiful city. I began to discover its people, artistic traditions, intellectual life and sense of history. I also came to appreciate the warmth, resilience and creativity of Hungarians. Initially, I saw Hungary largely through the eyes of a visitor; gradually, I began to experience it as a home.

DNH: What was the first year like for you, both professionally and personally?

Srivastava: The first year was a period of adjustment, discovery, and learning, both professionally and personally.

Professionally, there was much to explore and understand—the Hungarian cultural landscape, the interests and perspectives of the local community, the institutional environment, and how best to present Indian culture in ways that would resonate with the Hungarian people.

Personally, adapting to a new country and a different rhythm of life brought learning experiences and rewarding discoveries. The warmth and hospitality of the Hungarian people made the transition much easier.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Looking back at your time in Hungary, how have you seen the cultural relationship between India and Hungary evolve?

Srivastava: During my tenure, I have witnessed a meaningful and encouraging evolution in the cultural relationship between India and Hungary. What has impressed me most is the growing sense of mutual understanding, appreciation and curiosity among people from both nations.

There has been increasing interest in Indian art, literature, classical music, dance and cinema. However, what stands out most is the remarkable popularity of Yoga and Ayurveda, particularly for their holistic health and well-being benefits. This growing interest is also reflected in the increasing presence of Yoga and Ayurveda institutions across Hungary.

I have also observed that cultural exchange is becoming more reciprocal and collaborative. Beyond showcasing Indian culture and traditions in Hungary, artists, institutions and communities from both countries are increasingly coming together to share ideas, celebrate their heritage and build lasting connections.

The cultural and community activities during my time in Hungary have reinforced that the strongest bonds between nations are often built through people-to-people connections; it is also about the friendships, shared experiences and mutual understanding that remain long after an event has concluded.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre in Budapest and the Liszt Cultural Institute in New Delhi have played significant roles in strengthening cultural relations between the two countries, providing continuity to cultural engagement and transforming programmes into enduring relationships.

DNH: Which event, programme or initiative organised during your tenure are you most proud of, and why?

Srivastava: It is difficult to single out just one programme, as every successful initiative was the result of collective effort, dedication and teamwork. What made these experiences truly special was the opportunity to bring people together, encourage cultural dialogue and strengthen the bonds of friendship between India and Hungary.

Several initiatives remain particularly close to my heart: India Knowledge Series, which introduced Hungarian audiences to India’s rich cultural heritage, philosophy and traditions through lectures and discussions in the Hungarian language; Yoga at Liberty bridge, unique experience of Yoga on a moving cruise along the Danube, Indian Film Festival at Budapest’s historic Puskin Cinema, 100+ Yoga events organised across Hungary as part of the International Day of Yoga (IDY) 2026; and the School and college Connect Programme, which brought Indian culture closer to young Hungarian students.

However, one initiative of which I am particularly proud is the proposed establishment of a statue of Swami Vivekananda at Széchenyi István University in Győr. I am deeply grateful that the University leadership graciously accepted the proposal of the Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre, Embassy of India and extended its support for installing the statue at a prominent location on the University campus, continuing its longstanding support for our cultural initiatives.

I sincerely believe that, once realised, this initiative will not only honour the legacy of Swami Vivekananda but also serve as an enduring symbol of India–Hungary friendship, inspiring future generations and further strengthening the cultural and intellectual ties between our two nations.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Were there any moments when you felt that Hungarian audiences connected with Indian culture in a particularly meaningful way?

Srivastava: Absolutely. There were many unforgettable moments when I witnessed the genuine warmth and appreciation of Hungarian audiences for Indian culture.

One particularly touching experience was this year’s Indian Film Festival at Puskin Cinema in Budapest. After the final screening, the audience responded with such tremendous enthusiasm that the applause seemed endless. What moved me even more was that several people personally approached me to thank for the festival and share how much they had enjoyed the films. At that moment, I felt how beautifully Indian cinema could touch hearts and bring people together beyond language and borders.

Another memorable moment was the Yoga event at Budapest’s Liberty Bridge in 2024. Seeing the bridge filled with people practising Yoga together was extraordinary. I felt the same spirit during the IDY celebrations at Dr. Koltai Jenő Sportközpont at the Hungarian University of Sports Science, where people of different ages and backgrounds came together in a shared spirit of harmony and well-being. It was a powerful reminder of how an ancient Indian tradition has become an integral part of everyday life in Hungary.

What was most striking is the genuine love and respect that so many Hungarians have for Indian culture, Hindu philosophy and spiritual traditions. Their enthusiasm for Yoga, Ayurveda, Indian festivals, ancient wisdom and spiritual heritage is truly remarkable. Krishna Valley in Somogyvámos is a wonderful example of how Indian spiritual traditions and philosophy have taken deep root in Hungary, reflecting this profound cultural connection.

During my tenure, I met many Hungarians whose knowledge and understanding of Indian philosophy and traditions are extraordinary. One of my most meaningful experiences was the personal conversations after cultural events, when Hungarian audience shared their appreciation for Indian culture and often discovered similarities with their own values and culture.

DNH: How could cultural, educational and people-to-people ties between Hungary and India be strengthened further?

Srivastava: We should invest even more in sustained exchanges rather than one-time events. Artist residencies, University partnerships, student exchanges, joint research, translation projects, collaborations between museums and cultural institutions, and opportunities for young artists would all be valuable.

Hungarian Indologists, artists, and practitioners who have dedicated themselves to the study, preservation, and promotion of Indian culture, traditions, and heritage should also receive greater encouragement and support. Their invaluable contributions reflect the depth and vitality of the people-to-people ties that have long enriched relations between India and Hungary.

There is also considerable scope for greater engagement beyond Budapest and beyond the major institutions. Digital platforms can help connect audiences, but physical interaction remains extremely important. When students, artists, academics and people from all walks of life spend time in each other’s countries, they develop a deeper mutual understanding that cannot be achieved through formal diplomacy alone.

DNH: What was everyday life like in Budapest for you and your family?

Srivastava: Everyday life gradually developed its own rhythm. Budapest is a city where history and modern life coexist beautifully. We enjoyed walking along the Danube, discovering different parts of the city, visiting cultural institutions and simply observing everyday Hungarian life.

One of the things I particularly enjoyed was the Danube. Coming from Varanasi, where the Ganges River is such an important part of life and identity, looking at the Danube often reminded me of the Ganges in Varanasi. Of course, the two rivers are very different in their character and history, but both have a powerful presence in the life and imagination of the people living along their banks. That created a very personal connection for me.

Living abroad also teaches you to appreciate small things—local neighbourhoods, familiar cafés like Vaj at Hello Buda and Mandragora near Batthyány tér, public transport, seasonal changes, food and conversations with friends you meet regularly. Over time, these experiences become some of your strongest memories of a place.

During my tenure, I was fortunate to make wonderful friends who stood behind me like pillars of support. Their friendship and kindness made my life easier, happier and much more enjoyable.

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: During your time in Hungary, you often expressed your deep affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their culture, frequently greeting audiences in Hungarian during your speeches and even delivering messages in the language at national celebrations, International Day of Yoga events and other cultural occasions. Given that Hungarian is widely regarded as a particularly challenging language for foreigners, how did you approach learning it, and what did the experience mean to you personally?

Srivastava: Learning Hungarian was certainly challenging, but equally rewarding. I have always believed that making an effort to speak the language of a country is not only a gesture of respect but also a genuine way to connect with people and understand their culture.

I approached it with patience, curiosity and determination, beginning with simple phrases and gradually gaining confidence. Over time, I realised that even a few words spoken sincerely in someone’s native language could create a special connection.

Speaking Hungarian on occasions such as Hungary’s State Foundation Day, International Day of Yoga celebrations, the Indian Film Festival and, finally, in my farewell video was my way of expressing my affection and respect for the Hungarian people and their language.

Although I am far from fluent, the response I received was overwhelmingly encouraging. For me, the Hungarian language became another beautiful bridge connecting me with the people and culture I deeply admire.

Simply put, I love Hungary and its language.

If you missed it: Youngest Indian diplomat Dr. Mukesh Kumar Srivastava’s Hungarian farewell message draws widespread public appreciation

Dr Mukesh Kumar Srivastava

DNH: Apart from your cherished memories and friendships, what is one thing you have brought back with you from Hungary to India?

Srivastava: Beyond the wonderful memories and enduring friendships, one of the most valuable things I have brought back from Hungary is a deep appreciation for the way Hungarians cherish their cultural heritage and the dedication with which they preserve and pass it on to future generations.

I have also been deeply inspired by the spirit of collaboration among Hungarian artists, scholars and cultural practitioners. My experiences in Hungary reinforced my belief that tradition and innovation are not opposing forces; rather, they can complement and enrich each other, keeping cultural heritage alive while embracing new ideas and perspectives.

DNH: How would you describe the Indian community in Hungary today and its role in preserving and promoting India’s rich cultural heritage?

Srivastava: The Indian community in Hungary is vibrant, diverse and deeply connected to its cultural roots. During my tenure, I witnessed a strong sense of preservation of Indian traditions while embracing Hungarian society and culture.

Festivals such as Holi, Diwali, Navratri and various regional celebrations bring families and younger generations together, keeping our rich cultural heritage alive. The community also enthusiastically shares these traditions with Hungarian friends.

Amrita Sher-Gil Cultural Centre provided an important platform for such cultural exchanges, while community-led initiatives further strengthened the cultural bonds between India and Hungary.

DNH: Now that you have concluded your tenure in Budapest and returned to India, what message would you like to share with the people of Hungary?

Srivastava: My message is simple, but it comes from the bottom of my heart: Thank you for everything.

I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the Government and people of Hungary, my Hungarian friends and everyone who contributed to strengthening the cultural bonds between India and Hungary. Your warmth, generosity, support and friendship made my journey truly unforgettable.

Hungary was my first overseas posting, and it will always hold a special place in my heart. I arrived to share India’s rich cultural heritage and returned with something precious: lasting friendships, beautiful memories and a deep affection for Hungary and its people.

Although I have returned to India, the friendships and connections I built remain as meaningful as ever. I sincerely hope to return one day, not merely as a former Director, but as a friend.

I firmly believe that the cultural bonds between India and Hungary will continue to flourish, bringing our people even closer together.

In hindsight, my tenure in Hungary may have come to an end, but the bond I have built with this country and its people will last a lifetime.

Until we meet again – Viszontlátásra !!
