Ten was also known beyond the rink for his artistic interests, language skills and commitment to learning. His career demonstrated how an athlete from Kazakhstan could reach the highest levels of international sport while building a broader cultural and intellectual life.

His death in 2018 was a profound loss for Kazakhstan and the international figure skating community. The memorial foundation was established that year to ensure his projects and ambitions would continue beyond his lifetime.

The tournament that followed became one way to put that commitment into practice. Rather than limiting the memorial to an annual tribute, the foundation created an event where young skaters could compete against international opponents, gain experience and develop their skills without having to travel abroad for every major opportunity.

Why the tournament matters for Kazakhstan

International competitions play an important role in developing athletes. They allow skaters to test their preparation against competitors from other countries, perform before international judges and audiences, and build the experience needed to progress through the sport’s competitive levels.

The Denis Ten Memorial Challenge is part of the ISU Challenger Series, an international circuit for senior skaters that offers competition between national events and the Grand Prix series. Results from eligible competitions contribute to the ISU World Standings, helping athletes build their international rankings.

The series also gives Kazakhstan an opportunity to host high-level skating and bring the international figure skating community to the country. Challenger events must meet ISU requirements for participating countries and disciplines, placing them within a broader international competition structure.

According to the organizers, the growth of the memorial tournament has coincided with the development of new figure skating schools and the establishment of a figure skating academy in Kazakhstan. Domestic competitions with international participation have also given Kazakhstani athletes more opportunities to earn ISU ranking points on home ice.

The significance of that development became especially visible with Kazakhstan’s success at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where Mikhail Shaidorov won gold in men’s singles. His achievement marked a major milestone for the country’s figure skating community and brought renewed attention to the importance of sustained athlete development.

Oksana Ten reflected on that progress, noting the growth of the sport in Kazakhstan and the country’s Olympic success.

“I realized how necessary this tournament is for Kazakhstan. You can see how much the number of figure skaters in our country has grown, both in quality and quantity. We finally have Olympic gold. This is a huge achievement not only for our country; the whole world admires it. That is why I think holding this tournament is worthwhile,” she said during a press conference ahead of the tournament’s 2026 edition.

The memorial has also welcomed skaters who later achieved international recognition. Over the years, its winners have included Shaidorov, Russian skater Petr Gumennik, Belarusian skater Viktoria Safonova and Japanese figure skating legend Daisuke Takahashi. Their participation has helped connect younger competitors with athletes at different stages of their careers.

Held in Almaty and Astana over the years, the tournament has featured singles skating and ice dance, as well as pair skating in some editions. Its broader purpose remains consistent: to create opportunities for athletes to compete internationally while strengthening Kazakhstan’s figure skating community.

The 2026 edition brings together more than 20 countries

The eighth Denis Ten Memorial Challenge took place at Halyk Arena in Almaty from Oct. 7 to 10, bringing together around 150 athletes from more than 20 countries. Senior and junior athletes competed in six categories: Junior Men, Junior Women, Women, Men, Junior Ice Dance and Ice Dance.

In women’s singles, Alexandra Ignatova won gold with 226.01 points. South Korea’s Kim Yu-jae took silver with 209.20 points, while Kazakhstan’s Sofia Samodelkina claimed bronze with 204.36 points. Vladislav Dikidzhi won the men’s competition with 312.79 points, followed by Gleb Lutfullin with 277.23 points and Petr Gumennik with 261.76 points.

In ice dance, Finland’s Juulia Turkkila and Matthias Versluis took gold with 191.32 points. Vasilisa Kaganovskaya and Maxim Nekrasov finished second with 187.20 points, while the United States’ Caroline Green and Michael Parsons won bronze with 180.37 points.

For Samodelkina, the atmosphere in Almaty was an important part of the experience. The participant in the 2026 Winter Olympics and silver medalist at the ISU Grand Prix event in Osaka said the crowd’s support gave skaters an additional source of energy.

“The audience applauds so loudly that you feel as if you’re on a whole different level. They give you incredible energy and strength, and that helps you skate,” she said.

Remembering Denis Ten through sport and art

The memorial’s purpose extends beyond competition. Each edition also creates space to remember Ten’s personality, artistic interests and influence on those who knew him. The highlight of the 2026 event was the gala show, “The Ice That Remembers,” which brought together competition medalists, invited skaters and athletes from the Denis Ten Academy. The program combined figure skating with music and aerial acrobatics.

Marie-Pierre Leray, a French figure skater and longtime friend of Ten, took part in the show. She had also performed in the “Denis and Friends” program in 2013. Vocalists Daniil Yun and Sanat Asuat presented songs dedicated to Ten’s memory. The evening also featured a specially composed tournament anthem, an AI avatar of the skater and excerpts from his poetry.

The Denis Ten Memorial Challenge continues to serve two connected purposes: honoring an athlete whose achievements changed the history of figure skating in Kazakhstan and creating opportunities for the next generation to pursue their own ambitions.

The event is organized by the Denis Ten Foundation, with the assistance from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Tourism and Sports, the Almaty city administration and Samruk Kazyna.

World.title: Republic Day Is Reminder That Kazakhstan Belongs to Its People
World.content:
Every year, as Kazakhstan marks Republic Day on Oct. 25, we return to a moment in our history that is easy to describe in legal terms but harder to appreciate in its broader meaning. On Oct. 25, 1990, the Declaration of State Sovereignty of the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic laid the foundations for the country’s future statehood, establishing principles of territorial integrity, political self-determination and national identity that would become central to independent Kazakhstan.

Yet this date’s significance extends beyond the document itself. It invites us to consider what it means to be a republic, not simply as a form of government, but as a country whose future cannot be separated from the people who inhabit it.

In June 2022, at the first meeting of the National Kurultai in Ulytau, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev proposed restoring its status as a national holiday. Parliament passed the relevant amendments on Sept. 29, 2022, and the country celebrated Republic Day again that October.

For much of Kazakhstan’s post-independence history, the story of the state was closely tied to the figure of its first president. This made sense in a country undergoing profound political and economic transformation, where building new institutions and seeking stability became defining priorities. But a state is larger than any individual’s political career, however consequential that career may be. Leaders come and go, political narratives change, and the durability of a country ultimately depends on its institutions, shared values and the strength of its civic life.

Seen in this light, the return of Republic Day means more than restoring a holiday. It brings the idea of the republic itself back into focus: the country as a shared political space, rather than an extension of any one person’s legacy. Perhaps Tokayev was guided by precisely this understanding when he proposed restoring the holiday, recognizing that the idea of statehood must ultimately rest on something greater than the legacy of an individual leader. A republic derives its strength not from any one political figure’s permanence, but from the people who sustain it, the institutions they build and their commitment to a common future.

This also carries deeper historical resonance. The steppe that shaped Kazakh society was vast, and survival across it required more than individual strength. Communities depended on agreements, customary law, mutual obligations and an understanding that disputes had to be resolved within a shared social order. These traditions should not be romanticized as a history without conflict or inequality, but they do remind us that collective life has always required rules, negotiation and an ability to find common ground.

Modern Kazakhstan is, of course, a very different society. Its citizens live in cities and villages, work in a highly connected economy, participate in institutions and increasingly engage with the world beyond their borders. Yet the underlying question remains familiar: what holds a community together, and what makes its members feel that the place they inhabit is genuinely theirs?

Patriotism is often expressed through symbols, ceremonies and declarations of loyalty, but its more meaningful test lies in everyday choices. It is reflected in whether we respect the law when doing otherwise would be easier, whether we demand accountability from public institutions, whether we treat public property as something we share rather than something that belongs to nobody, and whether we contribute to the communities in which we live. It also requires us to recognize that we cannot delegate the country’s future entirely to the government, just as we cannot simply blame those in power for every problem.

This does not diminish the role of the state. On the contrary, public institutions must create the conditions for citizens to participate meaningfully, exercise their rights and see that their voices matter. The relationship between the state and society cannot be one-sided: a government may set priorities and introduce reforms, but their success depends in large part on whether people trust institutions, take part in public life and believe that their actions can make a difference.

Republic Day also reminds us that sovereignty has a geographical dimension. Kazakhstan’s territory, stretching across the steppe and connecting different parts of Eurasia, is not merely a feature on a map or an economic asset. It is the space within which a political community can determine its own future. Preserving that sovereignty requires capable institutions and sound strategic decisions, as well as a shared sense of belonging and an understanding of what is at stake when the country’s long-term interests are discussed.

National identity, meanwhile, should not be understood as something fixed or inherited without question. It is shaped by the way we understand our history, preserve our cultural heritage, relate to one another and imagine the country we want to leave to the next generation. It can accommodate different backgrounds, languages and experiences without losing its central commitment to a common future.

Perhaps this is the most important meaning of Republic Day today. The 1990 declaration marked a decisive step toward sovereignty, but the work of building a country did not end with independence, nor can any single generation or political leader complete it. Statehood endures through functioning institutions, communities that support one another, and citizens who understand that the country’s future is not something that happens to them, but something they help shape. On Oct. 25, we celebrate not only a defining moment in Kazakhstan’s journey toward independence, but also the idea that this country belongs to all of us.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Recycling Problem Is Not Lack of Willingness
World.content:
Editor’s note: The Astana Times continues a section featuring articles by our readers. As a platform that values diverse perspectives and meaningful conversations, we believe that this section provides space for readers to share their thoughts and insights on various topics that matter to them and the AT audience.

Kazakhstan has entered 2026 with an ambitious new plan for dealing with its waste. The government’s Waste Management Concept for 2026–2030 calls for less landfill disposal, more recycling and better monitoring of where waste ultimately goes. The timing could hardly be better. In 2025, Kazakhstan collected 4.1 million tonnes of municipal waste — 7.7% more than the year before. The country is producing more waste, and the question is no longer whether recycling matters. It is whether the system makes recycling easy enough for ordinary people to participate.

The central problem is surprisingly simple: Kazakhstan’s waste system still places too much responsibility on individual citizens and too little on the infrastructure surrounding them.

I see this problem in Astana. At home, I separate plastic, paper and cans instead of throwing everything into one bin. But doing so is only the first step. I often have to take recyclable materials myself to private collection points. For someone already motivated to recycle, this is possible. For a family rushing to work, taking children to school and dealing with daily responsibilities, it becomes a lower priority. This is why telling people to “be more environmentally responsible” will never be enough.

Kazakhstan is not starting from zero. Astana already operates a two-fraction collection system separating “dry” materials such as paper, plastic, glass and metal from “wet” waste such as food. The city has thousands of waste containers and collection sites. Nationally, progress is also visible: 1.5 million tonnes of municipal waste were sorted in 2025, 16.3% more than in 2024. Astana alone accounted for 377,000 tonnes of sorted waste.

Yet sorting statistics tell only part of the story. Waste must be separated correctly, collected separately, transported without being mixed again and eventually reach a recycler that can use it. If any step in that chain fails, a carefully separated plastic bottle may ultimately have the same destination as ordinary household rubbish.

A more effective waste system therefore has to make separation convenient, rewarding and accountable. Convenience comes first. Residents should encounter the same simple system wherever they live: clearly marked containers, consistent colours and straightforward instructions showing what belongs where. Collection schedules should ensure that separated waste remains separated throughout transportation. Organic waste deserves particular attention because food mixed with paper and other recyclables can contaminate material that might otherwise be reused. Kazakhstan’s Environmental Code already assigns local authorities responsibility for organizing environmentally safe municipal-waste systems, including separate collection. The challenge is turning that principle into an everyday routine people can trust.

Incentives can reinforce that routine. Deposit-return systems for bottles and cans, discounts or rewards for recycling, and convenient collection points can give recyclable materials visible value. The objective is not to pay people simply for behaving responsibly. It is to design a system in which throwing valuable materials into a landfill becomes the least attractive option.

Finally, accountability matters. Residents are less likely to spend time separating waste if they suspect everything is mixed together later. Municipalities and waste operators could publish simple data showing how much waste was collected separately, how much was actually recycled and how much went to landfill. Digital tracking, one of the priorities in Kazakhstan’s new waste strategy, could help make those flows more transparent.

Kazakhstan’s new waste policy sets a target of reducing the amount of municipal waste sent to landfills by 10% from the 2025 level by 2030. Meeting targets like this will depend not only on new recycling plants or government strategies, but on millions of small decisions made every day in kitchens, apartment courtyards and workplaces.

The important lesson extends far beyond Kazakhstan. Governments often treat recycling as a question of environmental awareness: educate people, run campaigns and hope for behaviour changes. But awareness works best when infrastructure makes the responsible choice the easy choice.

People should not have to be environmental enthusiasts to recycle. A successful waste system is one in which an ordinary resident can separate a bottle, a cardboard box or food waste without giving the process much thought. That is when recycling stops being an individual effort and starts becoming normal urban infrastructure.

The author is Samat Tulepbayev, a graduate student at the Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Public Policy.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Serbia protests timeline: how students brought Vucic’s 12-year rule to end
World.content:
The end of Vučić’s rule

Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s former president and the ruling party’s candidate for prime minister, conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary election held on 25 October. He said the “Student List” had won.

“Judging by the preliminary results, it is clear that we have lost this election. The Student List has won — they will get between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105,” Vučić said.

The snap election, which Vučić called before stepping down as president, followed a wave of student-led protests that had lasted for almost two years.

The demonstrations began after a disaster at the railway station in Novi Sad in 2024 that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and negligence for the tragedy and demanded that those responsible face justice.

Vučić’s party had been in power in Serbia for 12 years.

Here is a chronological account of how the protests began, grew into a student movement, challenged Aleksandar Vučić’s government and brought Serbia to the 25 October 2026 election, in which Vučić conceded defeat.

From a spark to a change of government

Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have dominated Serbian politics since 2012. Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president in 2017.

Government supporters portrayed him as a guarantor of stability, economic development and a foreign policy that balanced relations with the West and Russia. Critics, however, pointed to the concentration of power, the ruling party’s influence over the media, corruption and concerns about the independence of state institutions.

Public discontent periodically spilled onto the streets. Protests included demonstrations over electoral fairness and rallies against a proposed lithium mining project. Until 2024, however, the government had largely managed to prevent the emergence of large-scale, sustained protest movements.

1 November 2024: the tragedy that changed everything

On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad, a city in northern Serbia, killing 16 people.

The station had undergone renovation shortly before the disaster, prompting immediate questions. How could recently refurbished infrastructure collapse? Who was responsible for the quality of the work? How transparent were the public procurement procedures and the renovation project itself?

Authorities opened an investigation, but for many people, the fact that an investigation had begun was not enough. Suspicions grew that the collapse might not have been merely a technical failure, but could also involve corruption and attempts to evade accountability. Further concerns over access to project documents only deepened those suspicions. Protesters demanded that those responsible be identified.

The tragedy, which claimed 16 lives, became more than a moment of mourning. It turned into a test of accountability for state institutions. People wanted to know not only what caused the canopy to collapse, but also who had allowed potential wrongdoing to take place and why the oversight system had failed.

November 2024: students take to the streets

On 22 November, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade were attacked during a silent protest in memory of those killed in the disaster. The incident gave the protests a new focus: students demanded that authorities identify the attackers and hold them accountable.

University students soon began disrupting classes. The movement spread from Novi Sad and Belgrade to other cities across the country.

The way the protests were organised was also significant. Students made decisions at general assemblies known as “plenums”. From the outset, the movement had no single central leader whose removal would have allowed the authorities to bring the entire campaign to a halt.

What were the students demanding?

Make all documents related to the station’s reconstruction publicly available;

Identify those responsible for the disaster and hold them accountable under the law;

Punish those involved in the attacks on students and drop charges against detained protesters;

Increase funding for higher education by 20%.

In other words, the movement was never solely about calling for the government to resign. Its main goals were transparency, justice and accountability from state institutions.

By December, the protests had evolved beyond a reaction to the Novi Sad tragedy. University blockades, daily demonstrations and public support for the students had turned the movement into a nationwide campaign.

One of its most powerful symbols was the minute of silence. Every day at 11:52 — the exact time the canopy collapsed — protesters stopped to honour the victims. They also held 16-minute silences in memory of the 16 people who died.

The movement drew its strength from the fact that it differed from a typical political opposition campaign. Students stressed that political parties should not dictate their demands. This helped bring a wide range of social groups into the protests.

January 2025: the first major political outcome

On 28 January 2025, Prime Minister Miloš Vučević announced his resignation. Around the same time, the mayor of Novi Sad also stepped down.

This marked a significant political concession. The authorities could no longer maintain that street protests were failing to achieve any tangible results.

However, the students continued their protests. In their view, the resignation of individual officials did not answer the key questions: who was responsible for the disaster, how independent was the judicial system, and how should the system of government be reformed?

This marked an important turning point. The protests showed that a sustained, organised mass movement could impose significant political costs on the authorities.

The students adopted a new strategy. Rather than limiting their demonstrations to the capital, they began organising marches, cycle rides and meetings with local residents across the country.

This strategy was important for several reasons:

The protests spread beyond the capital. The movement built ties with residents of smaller towns and regional communities;

Students positioned themselves as representatives of society as a whole. They won support from university staff, teachers, ordinary citizens and people from a wide range of professions;

The movement built its own communications network. Citizens critical of the government ensured that the flow of information no longer depended solely on traditional media.

By this stage, the student protests had become one of the largest popular movements in Serbia’s recent history.

Miloš Vučević

15 March 2025: the historic rally in Belgrade

The rally on 15 March 2025 marked a pivotal moment for the movement. Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Belgrade.

The independent organisation Archive of Public Gatherings estimated that between 275,000 and 325,000 people took part. Serbia’s Interior Ministry gave a significantly lower figure. The discrepancy itself became a subject of debate.

Why was this event important?

First, it showed that the students enjoyed support well beyond university campuses;

Second, the government faced a challenge not only from the traditional opposition, but also from a broad coalition of citizens united by a common demand for justice and state accountability;

Third, the movement had grown so powerful that the question of Serbia’s political future could no longer be ignored.

Once again, the protest showed that calls for a change of government were coming from beyond political parties. A sense emerged across society that the existing system could be changed.

Spring and summer 2025: when the demands turned into a political struggle

On 5 May 2025, the student movement called for snap parliamentary elections. This broadened the scope of the protests. Vučić’s government, meanwhile, said the demonstrations aimed to destabilise the state and alleged that foreign powers were involved. The student movement rejected these accusations, identifying its main goals as fighting corruption, establishing independent institutions and holding fair elections.

Tensions continued to rise throughout this period. Reports emerged of arrests, clashes and acts of violence against protesters. Government opponents accused the authorities of controlling the media and weakening democratic institutions — allegations the government denied.

One of the movement’s most significant decisions was to create a political alternative from within the protest movement.

Students began selecting candidates to represent them in the parliamentary election. They formed an electoral list called “Student List — Students Win”. The aim was to broaden the movement’s representation by including people from different professions and social groups.

On 9 September 2026, Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for 25 October. He made the announcement amid a prolonged political standoff, as the student movement was already preparing to contest the election.

22 октября 2026 года: сотни тысяч сторонников движутся к предвыборной финишной прямой

За несколько дней до выборов, назначенных на 25 октября, студенческое движение провело в Белграде масштабный заключительный митинг. Сторонники из разных городов страны направились в столицу.

Согласно данным, опубликованным накануне выборов, между студенческим списком и правящей партией развернулась упорная борьба. Вучич предрекал победу, хотя и признавал, что она достанется нелегко.

Это стало кульминацией движения, которое продолжалось почти два года: протест, начавшийся с требований справедливости после гибели 16 человек, теперь стремился обеспечить себе большинство в парламенте.

25 October 2026: Vučić concedes defeat

On election night, something that many in Serbian political circles had long considered unthinkable happened.

Vučić announced that his political camp had lost the election and that the Student List had won. He estimated that the Student List would secure between 135 and 140 seats in parliament, while his own camp would get around 105.

According to Reuters, preliminary projections gave the Student List 138 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 104 for Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. The Student List had therefore secured a parliamentary majority. Voter turnout stood at around 70%, one of the highest levels since 1992.

According to Serbian political sociologist Gazela Pudar Draško, writing in The Washington Post, the student movement had taken the protests to a new level: citizens had moved beyond simply expressing discontent and begun taking direct part in political change. Students across the country had created an alternative model of political mobilisation by building relationships with local communities and making decisions collectively.

Radomir Šajčić, a professor at the University of Belgrade, commented on the victory at the students’ campaign headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate our victory, and tomorrow we will start building the future!” he said, Reuters reported.

The end of Vučić’s rule

World.title: Two teenagers arrested in Tbilisi over alleged plot to attack school: what we know
World.content:
School attack plot in Georgia

Two 14-year-olds have been arrested in Tbilisi on suspicion of planning an attack on a school and acts of violence against pupils. They attend different schools and communicated with each other through social media.

According to the prosecutor’s office, the teenagers had already chosen a specific school and planned their actions.

One of the teenagers has already been remanded in custody. The court is due to hold a hearing on the second suspect today.

What we know about the case

The Georgian outlet Sando Tskaro was the first to report the teenagers’ arrests. According to its report, police detained 14-year-old S.T. on the afternoon of Thursday, 22 October.

The following day, 23 October, police arrested the second teenager at his home. The first suspect exercised his right to remain silent, while the second denies the charges against him.

Police searched both teenagers’ homes. They seized a number of items, including a starter pistol, ammunition, pepper spray, gloves, a helmet and a knife.

The father of the first suspect, S.T., told Sando Tskaro that he did not know who the teenager was with whom his son had allegedly planned to commit the crime.

According to the father, the teenagers communicated through video calls on Telegram and TikTok.

He said they had discussed the 2011 terrorist attacks in Oslo. They had also talked about films based on real events that depicted acts of violence.

The prosecutor’s office has largely confirmed this account. It issued an official statement only after the information had already appeared in the media.

According to the statement, the teenagers met in April and May 2026. They chose a specific school in Tbilisi, studied its layout and began preparing an attack.

The prosecutor’s office says the teenagers planned to place a dummy explosive device outside the school. This would have allowed them to enter the building undetected, cause a disturbance and use weapons to injure people inside.

“They acquired various items and created all the necessary conditions to commit the crime. However, they failed to carry out their plan because law enforcement officers uncovered their activities,” the prosecutor’s office said.

Defence lawyer’s position

Gia Darchia, the lawyer representing one of the teenagers, told Radio Liberty that the prosecution had no evidence in the case.

According to Darchia, the case file contains only two days’ worth of messages from October, none of which mentions organising anything.

According to the defence, the items seized from the suspects’ homes as evidence were intended for personal use. They included souvenirs given to them by their parents and ordinary household objects. The lawyers argue that any claims that the teenagers were “preparing to commit a crime” are therefore entirely “unserious”.

“These people did not know each other. They had never even seen each other and had made no attempt to meet. What is more, they had never been to the school they allegedly planned to attack.”

The lawyer says his client would not even recognise the second suspect if someone showed him to him. He notes that his client had never seen a photograph of the other teenager, who used an avatar on social media. He also stresses that the teenagers never communicated via video calls.

The defence lawyer says the investigation began after the second suspect published a social media post calling for violence. However, the case file contains neither a screenshot nor any other visual evidence that the post existed. The lawyer argues that neither the investigative materials nor interviews with the suspects indicate any links between the teenagers and radical groups. Nor had anyone observed any suspicious behaviour on their part.

“They had no intention of blowing anything up or harming anyone. There is no basis for talking about any kind of organised activity,” he says.

The lawyer representing the second suspect has declined to comment to the media at this stage.

Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 225, parts 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code. The article covers organising group actions involving violence, looting, damage to or destruction of other people’s property, and the use of weapons. It also covers preparing to take part in such actions.

The article provides for a prison sentence of six to nine years.

School attack plot in Georgia

World.title: ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’: Opposition launches new wave of protests – photos and video
World.content:
New wave of protests in Georgia

On 25 October, thousands of people gathered in Tbilisi for a major opposition-organised protest under the slogan ‘Georgia without Ivanishvili’.

Waving flags and blowing horns, protesters gathered outside Tbilisi State University before setting off on a mass march towards Rustaveli metro station.

With this rally, the opposition announced the start of a new wave of protests in Georgia. The next rally is scheduled for 28 November.

The date is symbolic: exactly two years earlier, the ruling Georgian Dream party publicly announced that it was suspending EU accession talks.

The announcement sparked ongoing pro-European protests, with demonstrators demanding fresh, free and fair parliamentary elections.

Key messages from opposition leaders

The rally’s organisers, leaders of the pro-Western opposition, addressed the demonstrators.

“This day, 28 November, represents a defeat for all of us as long as Bidzina Ivanishvili remains in power. The postponement of our integration into the European Union is a defeat for all of us. The indefinite delay of a brighter future for our children is a defeat for all of us,” said Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Coalition for Change.

“Ivanishvili’s group is trying to formally strip us of one of the most important achievements secured by the United National Movement – multiparty elections in Georgia. They now seek to legally establish a one-party dictatorship,” said Levan Tsutskiridze, leader of the Freedom Square party.

“It may seem that Bidzina Ivanishvili is making such a brazen decision that we should all despair. In fact, the opposite is true. By banning any alternative, Ivanishvili is acknowledging a crisis of his own legitimacy. He is admitting that he no longer trusts the Georgian people – that he fears the free choice of Georgian citizens, and quite rightly so,” said Tamar Chergoleishvili, leader of the Federalists movement.

Young people and other protesters were also among the speakers.

“Look at one another – you are surrounded by people who refuse to give up, who continue to fight for a better future for our country,” student Luka Mishveladze told the crowd.

Background

The 25 October rally was part of Georgia’s pro-European protest movement, which has been ongoing for nearly two years. The demonstration was announced and organised by the opposition.

The date was no coincidence: on 24 October 2024, Georgia held crucial parliamentary elections, with the country’s European future at stake.

The election results remain disputed both domestically and internationally. The vote marked the beginning of a major political crisis in Georgia, leading to strained relations with Western partners, sanctions and the suspension of multimillion-dollar aid packages.

The protests were met with violent police crackdowns, including beatings, torture and arrests of activists. Several packages of repressive laws were adopted, while pressure on the media and civil society intensified, including measures that effectively blocked access to funding.

Western institutions adopted numerous resolutions criticising these developments.

The political crisis entered a new phase when the ruling Georgian Dream party moved to ban pro-Western opposition groups it deemed unacceptable.

Almost all the parties that organised the 25 October rally and announced a new wave of protests were among those facing a proposed ban.

World.title: Why are Abkhazia residents with dual citizenship asked to show Russian passports at Moscow airports?
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s Foreign Ministry has said that some residents of the breakaway republic who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship are experiencing difficulties crossing the Russian border at Moscow airports.

Russian border guards have reportedly been refusing to allow dual nationals to enter or leave the country using their Abkhaz passports, instead demanding Russian documents.

As Abkhazia is a largely unrecognised republic, its passports are also not widely recognised internationally. Travelling on an Abkhaz passport is virtually impossible, except to a handful of countries, including Russia. For Abkhazians, obtaining a Russian passport is therefore practically the only way to travel internationally. However, this generally means a Russian international passport rather than a domestic identity document. Most do not hold Russian internal passports because they permanently reside in Abkhazia, where Russian passport holders account for around 70% of the population.

The ministry added that people holding only Abkhaz citizenship do not encounter such problems at airports. Similar incidents have not been reported at other border crossing points either.

Russia explains its position by saying that, for dual nationals, a Russian passport is not merely the primary document required to cross the border, but the only acceptable one. However, the explanation has been met with scepticism in Abkhazia, where some suspect the border guards may have other motives.

The issue was discussed by Abkhaz and Russian foreign ministers Oleg Bartsits and Sergei Lavrov during a recent meeting in Moscow. However, no solution has yet been found. According to Abkhazia’s Foreign Ministry, the matter remains subject to “consultations with the competent authorities of the Russian Federation, taking into account the provisions of existing bilateral agreements”.

In the meantime, the ministry has advised Abkhaz citizens experiencing difficulties at border crossings to formally report the incidents to the ministry, providing detailed accounts of what happened.

From the perspective of international practice, border guards at Moscow airports are not doing anything unlawful.

As a general rule, people holding two or more citizenships are required to present the passport of the country whose border they are crossing, if they are citizens of that country. This requirement is enshrined in national legislation and strictly enforced in countries including Georgia, the United States and many others.

This raises the question: what exactly is the problem, why are Abkhaz citizens unhappy, and why are they reluctant to present their Russian passports at the border if they have them?

For some Abkhazians with dual citizenship, the right to use an Abkhaz passport is a matter of principle and national pride. While this argument carries little legal weight, it is highly significant in Abkhazia.

Others simply want the option of crossing the border using their Abkhaz documents in certain circumstances, such as when their Russian passport has expired and they have not yet received a replacement.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Making a living in dangerous waters: Challenges facing Azerbaijani sailors in Black Sea
World.content:
Azerbaijani sailors in Black Sea

Rufan Ahmadov was among the Azerbaijani sailors rescued from a vessel attacked off the coast of Romania on 23 October. According to Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry, he sustained minor injuries and was accommodated in a hotel after undergoing a medical examination.

Russia was behind the drone attack on the Khoryv vessel. Two other Azerbaijani nationals on board were also rescued. This time, the sailors’ families received news that their loved ones had survived.

However, in recent months, families of other Azerbaijani sailors working in the Black Sea have received news of their loved ones being killed or going missing.

According to Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry statements on individual incidents, at least 48 Azerbaijani nationals were on board vessels targeted in attacks between June and October. Six Azerbaijanis were confirmed killed. Two others, initially reported missing, were subsequently declared dead. One person remains missing. At least 39 survived, ten of whom were injured or hospitalised.

Both Russia and Ukraine regularly launch strikes against merchant vessels in the Black Sea. Azerbaijani nationals work on these ships as captains, engine operators and in other roles. They transport civilian cargo, but their routes take them through areas affected by hostilities.

When a vessel comes under attack, the entire crew is put at risk. If a voyage is interrupted, the threat to their safety is compounded by other concerns: will the sailors receive their wages, will they be able to return home, and who will cover the cost of their repatriation?

Azerbaijani sailors killed or missing following attacks

Rustam Hasanov was killed on 5 October in an attack on the Royad Mammadov vessel. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the vessel had been struck by two Russian drones.

The victim’s father, Ismail Hasanov, last spoke to his son on 4 October, a day before the attack. In an interview with Khazar Khabar TV, he said Rustam had been working as the vessel’s captain since August.

Joshgun Mammadaliyev, a native of Digah village in Azerbaijan’s Masalli district, who worked as an engine operator on the same vessel, was injured and hospitalised in Romania. According to the broadcaster, he had worked in this role for three years.

In a statement issued on 6 October, Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry listed another Azerbaijani sailor, Muhammad Suleymanzade, born in 2002, as missing. At the time, three rescued Azerbaijani nationals were reported to be in hospital. There has been no further information about Suleymanzade’s fate.

Attacks continue

On 14 July, the Atlas Bey vessel, carrying 11 Azerbaijani nationals, came under attack off the coast of Odesa. Ukrainian officials described the incident as part of a series of Russian attacks on civilian vessels.

Ten sailors were brought ashore. The body of the vessel’s captain, Samad Nasrullayev, was recovered during a search operation and repatriated to Azerbaijan on 17 July.

Azerbaijani sailors were also affected by attacks on the Natra and Zirkon vessels in the Sea of Azov on 5 June. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said the vessels had been struck by Ukrainian drones.

These incidents suggest that the threat is not confined to a single vessel or voyage. Over several months, Azerbaijani sailors have repeatedly faced attacks in the same region.

Crew awaiting wages and hoping to return home

The difficulties facing sailors extend beyond the threat of attacks. On 7 October, Sabukhi Salahov, captain of the Consul vessel, told Konkret that his crew had been stranded in Rostov-on-Don for several months without receiving their wages. According to the sailors, ongoing drone attacks near the vessel’s mooring location have prevented them from leaving the ship and returning to Azerbaijan.

“We want to get the money they owe us and return to Azerbaijan. But there’s nothing we can do,” the captain said.

According to Salahov, the crew have been waiting for their wages for several months and remain unable to return home. There has been no information about whether the sailors have since received their outstanding pay or been reunited with their families following their complaint.

“We were transporting dry cargo from Russia. Our last delivery was coal to Moldova. We then set off to collect a similar cargo, but the routes were blocked. Around 200 vessels have come under drone attack in the Azov-Black Sea region. Since then, we’ve been in the Russian city of Rostov-on-Don. We’ve been here for almost three or four months,” Salahov said.

The complaint also raises questions about how to ensure the safe return of Azerbaijani nationals from the dangerous region. If, as the captain claims, the crew are not receiving their wages and cannot return home, the sailors need consular assistance. However, there is no information about what steps Azerbaijani authorities are taking to repatriate the sailors or resolve the issue of unpaid wages.

Do all sailors have the right to refuse dangerous voyages?

The International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) has established rules for seafarers covered by certain collective bargaining agreements. Depending on the level of risk in the area of operation, these rules provide for additional payments, the right to refuse dangerous voyages and repatriation at the employer’s expense.

However, these protections do not automatically apply to all Azerbaijani sailors. To establish whether an individual seafarer is entitled to such protection, it is necessary to examine the terms of their employment contract, determine which collective bargaining agreement applies to the vessel and establish the risk classification of the area of operation.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry warns citizens about the risks of working in regions affected by war and instability. However, for those already working on vessels in such areas, it is important not only to be aware of the dangers but also to have a genuine opportunity to refuse to continue a dangerous voyage.

The ministry has also reported providing medical and consular assistance to sailors following attacks. However, measures to ensure their safety should not be limited to rescue operations and the repatriation of those affected.

It is also important to establish what support is available to Azerbaijani nationals who wish to leave dangerous areas, recover unpaid wages and provide for their families. For these sailors, warnings about the risks are not enough. They also need practical assistance that would enable them to refuse dangerous work.

World.title: Saturday march in Tbilisi “against oligarch Ivanishvili’s rule”. ‘Protests in Georgia’ video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for more than 700 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: “Don’t like it? Too bad”: third day of Constitutional Court hearings on opposition ban in Georgia
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban case

On 23 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court held the third day of hearings on a lawsuit filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party seeking to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream argues that the parties have violated Article 23 of the constitution, which prohibits political parties whose objectives include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited in the lawsuit is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The party is held responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the allegations.

Hearings will resume on 26 October and continue throughout the week. The court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Key events and statements from third day of Constitutional Court hearings

The day focused on motions submitted by Gakharia for Georgia, all of which were rejected by the court.

No opposition motion has been granted during the three days of Constitutional Court proceedings in the case.

Court rejects request to postpone hearings by a month

Berdia Sichinava, representing Gakharia for Georgia, asked the court to postpone the hearing by one month. He argued that procedural rules allow that much time to prepare a response, but his party had only seven days from the announcement that hearings would begin. The United National Movement, Lelo and Coalition for Change joined the motion.

Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee and one of the MPs who filed the lawsuit, argued that neither the procedural rules, the organic law nor the constitution stipulates that failure to submit a response prevents the court from hearing the case.

The judges deliberated and unanimously rejected the motion. Court president Revaz Nadaraia said the request should have been submitted earlier, as proceedings had already been under way for three days. He added: “If you don’t like it, you don’t like it. What can I do about that?”

Judge Eva Gotsiridze noted that the proceedings would take a long time, adding: “You will have the month provided for in the procedural rules.”

Request to recuse judge Sergo Metopishvili rejected

Gakharia for Georgia’s legal team filed a motion seeking the recusal of judge Sergo Metopishvili. The full bench rejected this request too.

Court rejects request to summon Bidzina Ivanishvili and Irakli Kobakhidze as witnesses

Berdia Sichinava asked the court to summon senior Georgian Dream figures as witnesses, including the party’s founder and honorary chair, billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili; Tbilisi mayor Kakha Kaladze; prime minister Irakli Kobakhidze; and current and former senior officials Archil Talakvadze, Mamuka Bakhtadze, Vakhtang Gomelauri and Grigol Liluashvili.

He said their testimony was relevant to the criminal case against party leader Giorgi Gakharia.

Criminal proceedings against Giorgi Gakharia, Georgia’s former prime minister and current leader of the For Georgia party, began on 12 November 2025 and relate to two separate incidents. Gakharia has left the country and is currently abroad. One case concerns events in 2019, when Gakharia was interior minister. He is accused of unilaterally deciding to set up a police post near the village of Chorchana, in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone, triggering a sharp escalation of tensions. Prosecutors say Tbilisi subsequently lost control of another section of its territory. The second case relates to the dispersal of a mass protest in Tbilisi on 20 June 2019. Police used force, including rubber bullets, without prior warning. Two people lost an eye and five others sustained serious injuries. Gakharia is accused of ordering the police operation in his capacity as interior minister.

Berdia Sichinava said that under direct questioning, Ivanishvili, Kaladze and others would not be able to evade responsibility for the 2019 decision to establish a police checkpoint in the village of Chorchana.

He also argued that the events of 20 June 2019 in Tbilisi could not be used as grounds for banning the party. “This is an issue on which society cannot reach a consensus,” Sichinava said, adding that “the protest was genuine, but the attempt to storm parliament was unacceptable”.

In response, claimant Archil Gorduladze reminded the court that Giorgi Gakharia was currently wanted and argued that the evidence in the two criminal cases against him should not be considered by the Constitutional Court.

The court rejected this motion too.

Georgian Dream’s position

Before the hearing, claimant Archil Gorduladze, chair of parliament’s legal affairs committee, told journalists that the opposition’s statements “only strengthen the case filed with the Constitutional Court”.

Asked about the opposition’s request to invite experts from the Venice Commission to take part in the proceedings, Gorduladze replied: “The opposition apparently believes that a foreigner knows Georgia’s constitution better than the Constitutional Court judges.”

Responding to criticism that a single lawsuit had been filed against all five parties, Gorduladze said: “They are all just the same National Movement.”

Tengiz Sharmanashvili, another Georgian Dream MP who filed the lawsuit, also told journalists that “the opponents want to drag things out”. He said he was concerned that the opposition was deliberately submitting motions in a form that made it impossible for the court to grant them.

“The opposition is collecting rejected motions for the Strasbourg court, and none of the five parties intends to engage seriously with the proceedings at the Constitutional Court,” Sharmanashvili said.

Outside the court

Opera singer Paata Burchuladze, who was convicted over an attempt to seize the presidential administration on 4 October 2025, has sent a letter to the Constitutional Court offering to testify if the events of 4 October are discussed during the proceedings.

Burchuladze argues that opposition parties are being unfairly accused of organising the events. “I was the organiser of those events, and I alone,” he said, urging the opposition to file a motion to have him summoned for questioning.

Sopio Khorguani, an MP from the opposition party Gakharia for Georgia, told journalists that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s statement that “the days of this opposition are numbered” was unacceptable. Khorguani described the remark as a direct instruction to the Constitutional Court on the verdict the government expects it to deliver.

Another representative of the party, Giorgi Sharashidze, said that “the whole process resembles a theatre of the absurd”. He said Gakharia for Georgia had been added to the lawsuit at the last minute, calling its inclusion “entirely artificial”. The claimant, he added, had still been unable to specify which article of the constitution the party had violated.

News in Georgia

World.title: ‘Buying Czech aircraft is part of Armenia’s air force modernisation’ — military expert
World.content:
Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase

Armenian Defence Minister Suren Papikyan is on an official visit to the Czech Republic. He began his visit with a trip to Aero Vodochody, a Czech defence industry company. According to reports, he discussed the possibility of further cooperation with the company’s management. He also examined Aero Vodochody’s products in detail.

“These marvels will soon take to the skies over Armenia,” the defence minister wrote in a caption accompanying a video he posted shortly after visiting the company.

Papikyan also shared photographs, captioning them: “One of the landmark days in the history of the Armenian Armed Forces’ aviation.”

Experts have speculated, based on the video and photographs he posted online, that Armenia is preparing to receive Czech-made L-39 Skyfox aircraft. These are a new generation of jet trainers.

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan believes that Armenia, which has a limited fleet of aircraft, could use the L-39 Skyfox not only for training but also for certain operational tasks:

“As a result, the purchase could become a practical step towards modernising the air force. However, its scale does not yet justify claims that it would significantly change the combat capabilities of Armenian aviation. For training purposes, four aircraft could serve as the first batch in a transition to a new training system and curriculum. If the Skyfox purchase forms part of a broader restructuring of the air force, expanding the fleet further would be the logical next step.”

The L-39 Skyfox is a new-generation jet trainer designed for advanced pilot training. It features modern digital avionics, multifunction displays and an integrated virtual training system. These capabilities allow pilots to simulate various tactical scenarios during training flights. According to Defense Mirror, one Skyfox costs less than $10 million. The final price depends on the aircraft’s configuration and delivery terms. Depending on its configuration, the aircraft can carry air-launched weapons, reconnaissance equipment and additional external systems. This allows it to perform limited military and reconnaissance missions.

What we know about the defence minister’s visit

The defence minister arrived in the Czech Republic on 20 October. During his visit, Suren Papikyan attended the opening ceremony of the Future Forces Exhibition & Forum. He toured the exhibition halls and viewed the latest technologies and advanced military equipment on display.

The Armenian minister also held talks with Czech Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna.

Armenia’s Defence Ministry said the two ministers discussed:

Armenian-Czech defence cooperation, including military-technical cooperation;

reforms in the Armenian Armed Forces and cooperation in military education.

“Both sides stressed the importance of cooperation in multilateral formats, including within the EU and NATO,” the statement said.

Papikyan also discussed bilateral military-technical cooperation with Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlíček.

Commentary

Military expert Eduard Arakelyan noted that a Czech defence industry source had reported a month earlier that AERO Vodochody Aerospace was producing four L-39 Skyfox aircraft for Armenia. Specialist publications had also circulated the information, but none identified the customer or disclosed the terms of the deal.

Meanwhile, Arakelyan said, the Armenian Air Force already operates Czech-made L-39 Albatros trainers. Armenia acquired these second-hand aircraft in 2004 and 2010–11. It purchased some of them from Ukraine.

“However, the exact number of aircraft that remain in service with the Armenian Air Force and can still fly regularly is unknown,” the expert said.

In Arakelyan’s view, the Skyfox purchase fits Armenia’s strategy of diversifying its arms suppliers and expanding cooperation with European defence manufacturers:

“An Armenian-Czech agreement on military-technical cooperation, which has been in force since 2023, provides an additional basis for collaboration.”

Arakelyan believes the Armenian defence minister’s statement signals that the Skyfox acquisition has reached a practical stage.

“Nevertheless, until the parties officially disclose the terms of the deal, questions remain about the actual cost, delivery schedule, configuration and maintenance. These include technical support from the manufacturer and specialist training.

“The delivery of four Skyfox aircraft would represent a generational shift in Armenia’s training platform rather than a numerical expansion of its air force. The deal’s significance will depend on whether it remains a standalone purchase or marks the first stage of a broader overhaul of pilot training and air force capabilities. In the latter case, the Skyfox could bridge the gap between existing training aircraft and future combat platforms, with the four aircraft serving as the first batch in an air force modernisation programme.”

Expert opinion on Armenia’s Czech aircraft purchase

World.title: Azerbaijan prepares master plans for 68 of 79 cities - state committee
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Master plans for 68 out of 79 cities have been prepared or updated in Azerbaijan, and a development framework covering the next 20 years has been established for these cities, head of the department for project management in the liberated territories at the State Committee on Urban Planning and Architecture, Ramil Jahangirov, said during a press conference regarding the AIREX 2026 international real estate and investment exhibition in Baku on Monday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that the key priorities in the field of urban planning include strategic planning, the creation of modern infrastructure, ensuring sustainable development, and fostering a favorable environment for investment.

"Investors are not merely investing in individual buildings; they are investing in the future of cities and their development potential. Therefore, a clear planning framework and modern infrastructure play a crucial role in the development of the real estate market," Jahangirov remarked.

According to him, the preparation of master plans for the remaining cities is also underway. The application of international best practices and modern urban planning trends is of particular importance in this process.

Jahangirov pointed out that the master plan for the development of Baku city up to 2040 was approved a few days ago. The document aims for a polycentric, interconnected, and balanced development of the capital.

He mentioned that the master plan envisions the creation of new urban centers, the improvement of transport and utility infrastructure, and the transformation of former industrial areas.

The department head emphasized that the restoration and reconstruction of the Karabakh and East Zangezur regions also constitute a key focus of urban planning policy.

"Our goal here is not merely to restore settlements, but to establish new cities and economic hubs based on modern infrastructure and principles of sustainable development," he said.

According to Jahangirov, work is currently underway to develop master plans for 12 cities in the liberated territories. Meanwhile, spatial planning for over 100 villages and settlements has already been completed.

He added that the declaration of 2026 as the Year of Urban Planning and Architecture in Azerbaijan, as well as the hosting of the UN World Urban Forum in Baku in May, serve as an indication of the importance placed on this field in the country.

World.title: Hikmet Hajiyev says Azerbaijan-Armenia peace deal must improve people's lives
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. A peace agreement should contribute to the lives of the countries, Hikmet Hajiyev, Assistant to the President of Azerbaijan and Head of the Foreign Policy Affairs Department of the Presidential Administration, said during a special session of the Baku Platform for Cultural and Media Dialogue, themed "The language of peace and combating disinformation" on Monday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

“A peace agreement could be signed, or it could simply remain on paper. This agreement must also make a tangible contribution to the lives of the countries involved,” Hajiyev explained.

He noted that reaching an agreement on a peace treaty in 2023 was not an easy decision for Azerbaijan.

"Achieving peace after a war that lasted for many years wasn't simple. President Ilham Aliyev demonstrated his good will. The peace agreement was presented to Armenia by Azerbaijan, and its foundational principles were drafted by Azerbaijan. The peace agreement was initialed at the Washington Summit. Subsequently, Azerbaijan took significant steps toward peace," the Presidential Assistant added.

World.title: Eni completes sale of Nigerian subsidiary AENR to Apex Global Energy
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Eni, an Italian energy company, has completed the sale of its subsidiary Agip Energy and Natural Resources (Nigeria) Limited (AENR), the company said on October 26.

AENR has been acquired by Apex Global Energy Limited (APEX), a company wholly owned by Sterling Oil Exploration and Energy Production Company Ltd, one of Nigeria’s leading operators in the onshore sector.

AENR, a wholly owned subsidiary of Eni, conducts onshore and shallow-water hydrocarbon exploration and production in Nigeria. It holds a 5% stake in the Renaissance joint venture (JV), operated by Renaissance with a 30% interest. Other partners are TotalEnergies, with 10%, and Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC), with 55%.

“The transaction, which has received approval from all relevant authorities, is in line with Eni’s strategy to optimize its upstream activities by rebalancing the portfolio and divesting non-strategic assets. Eni will continue to maintain a presence in the country through exploration and development of deep offshore assets as well as through its participation in Nigeria LNG,” said Eni.

Eni is an integrated energy company, founded in 1953, with 31.376 employees in 69 countries around the world, including Algeria, Angola, Mozambique, Mexico, Indonesia and Italy. In 2021, the company launched a new strategy that will enable it to provide a variety of fully decarbonized products, combining environmental and financial sustainability. The recent merger of the renewable and retail businesses in Plenitude (formerly Eni gas e luce), the development of bio-refineries and biomethane production, and the sale of low-carbon energy carriers and mobility services at service stations are among the main levers for taking the path towards decarbonization.

The company adopts an integrated model based on satellite companies, strategic companies for the transition and innovation, and subsidiaries.

World.title: Armenia should take concrete steps toward peace – Azerbaijani analyst
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Armenia should take concrete steps instead of delaying the peace process, Azerbaijani political analyst Azer Garayev told Trend.

According to him, after many years of conflict in the South Caucasus, a real opportunity has emerged to achieve peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia. The signing of the peace agreement can create conditions for the beginning of a new stage in the region, the expansion of economic relations, and the prevention of future conflicts. However, political statements aren’t enough for this, and the parties should take concrete steps and fulfill their obligations.

“Azerbaijan has repeatedly declared its readiness to sign a peace treaty with Armenia. The position of official Baku is clear: the chapter of the past conflict must be closed, mutual territorial integrity must be respected, and relations must be established based on the principles of international law. Such an approach also offers Armenia the opportunity to emerge from a long-standing confrontation, participate in regional cooperation, and expand its economic prospects.

However, it remains an open question as to how soon this opportunity will be realized. Although significant progress has been made in the negotiations, a peace treaty has not yet been fully signed. The approach taken by the Armenian authorities toward certain issues, as well as their suggestion of distant dates for the signing of the treaty, raises questions as to why the process is being prolonged. If a genuine opportunity for peace exists, why should the conclusion of this process be delayed for years?

"Armenia might think that by dragging out the process, it is gaining time. However, such a delay actually harms its own interests. Normalizing relations with Azerbaijan is crucial for Armenia to emerge from regional isolation and to benefit from transport links and opportunities for economic cooperation. Yet, these opportunities can only be realized through political decisions and concrete steps. In other words, delaying peace doesn't merely slow down the political process, but also postpones the opportunities that have arisen for Armenia," he remarked.

Garayev pointed out that Azerbaijan has repeatedly articulated its position on this matter. On March 13, 2025, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan announced the conclusion of negotiations regarding the text of a peace treaty between the two countries. Nevertheless, official Baku has stipulated that the removal of provisions from the Armenian Constitution, which it links to claims against Azerbaijan’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, is a necessary condition for the signing of the agreement.

"The next significant milestone took place on August 8, 2025, in Washington. The leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia initialed the text of an agreement on the establishment of peace and adopted a joint declaration. This represented substantial progress in the negotiation process. However, the initialing of the document does not equate to a fully signed peace treaty that has entered into force. Achieving the final outcome still requires political will and concrete decisions from the parties.

At the heart of the issue lies the Constitution of Armenia. The reference to Armenia’s Declaration of Independence is linked to past claims regarding Karabakh and carries the risk that territorial claims could be revived in the future. Official Baku has stated that the long-term viability of any agreement signed without resolving this contradiction could be called into question," he noted.

The analyst emphasized that one of the points raising the most questions concerns the statements made by Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan regarding the timing of the agreement's signing. Uncertainty has increased following Pashinyan’s statement on October 15, 2026, that the agreement should be signed and ratified by 2031, contrasted with his remark just a week later, on October 22, that the agreement could potentially be signed between 2027 and 2028.

"If the text of the peace treaty has already been agreed upon and the parties have made significant progress, why is there a need to prolong the process further? Certainly, a lasting peace requires the resolution of legal and political issues. However, discussing distant timeframes instead of taking concrete steps does not strengthen mutual trust; rather, it prolongs uncertainty.

The Azerbaijani side has stated that the treaty could be signed the very next day, provided that the necessary amendments are made to the Constitution of Armenia. This position clearly reflects Baku’s expectations: the resolution of issues deemed contentious and the strengthening of the legal foundations for peace. It means that the issue is not merely the date on which the treaty is signed, but rather the extent to which it will remain robust and reliable in the future.

The Armenian authorities must understand that they cannot gain any additional advantage by dragging out the peace process. On the contrary, such delays could limit opportunities for regional cooperation, hinder the establishment of economic ties, and impede the development of mutual trust. Peace with Azerbaijan represents a genuine opportunity for Armenia to secure a more stable and secure future," he explained.

Garayev noted that Armenia faces a choice: either seize the current opportunity to contribute to the realization of peace, or prolong the process and leave both its own future and that of the region in a state of uncertainty.

"Azerbaijan’s position and expectations are clear. The key question now is how effectively Armenia will utilize this opportunity. Peace is not merely the absence of war; it entails respect for mutual territorial integrity, legal guarantees, and clear commitments. Building relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia on these principles could pave the way for a new phase in the South Caucasus. Instead of dragging out the process, Armenia should take concrete steps, because delaying peace also means forfeiting future opportunities," the analyst added.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. An international scientific conference on the topic “Uzbekistan and Azerbaijan : Common Historical Heritage, Islamic Civilization, and Contemporary Scientific Cooperation” is taking place in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

The event is attended by government and diplomatic representatives from Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan, religious leaders, scholars, researchers, and cultural experts.

The conference features presentations on the activities of the Center for Islamic Civilization, the main areas of its research, and opportunities for international cooperation.
