World.title: Azerbaijan's minister calls for immediate investment in gas supply (PHOTO)
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Energy of the Republic of Azerbaijan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 26. Investment decisions must be made today in light of growing demand for natural gas, Azerbaijani Minister of Energy, Parviz Shahbazov said at the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF), currently taking place in the Russian Federation.

This was announced in a statement published by the country's Ministry of Energy.

In his speech, the minister addressed challenges in the global gas market, the growing role of natural gas in energy security, investment needs, and Azerbaijan’s gas policy.

In addition, it was noted that geopolitical tensions, security risks along supply routes, and shifting priorities in energy policy are increasing uncertainty in the gas market. At the same time, the electrification of the economy, the development of artificial intelligence and data centers, as well as the need to balance renewable energy, are strengthening the strategic importance of natural gas.

Furthermore, it was emphasized that limiting investment in the gas sector amid growing demand poses risks to future supply security. “Investment decisions for reliable gas supplies tomorrow must be made today,” the minister stated.

Speaking about Azerbaijan’s gas strategy, which is based on energy security and long-term partnerships, the minister noted that the Southern Gas Corridor is a successful model of cooperation.

It was noted that Azerbaijan has expanded its gas production and export capacity and increased its participation in international gas projects to meet growing demand. It was noted that policies on renewable energy and energy efficiency support the country’s gas export policy.

The minister emphasized the importance of cooperation within the framework of the Global Gas Corridor to maintain stability in the global gas market, attract investment, and strengthen dialogue between producers and consumers.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan has been represented at the Forum as an observer since 2015.

World.title: Liberal candidate's husband allegedly assaulted over campaign sign
World.content:
The husband of a Victorian Liberal Party candidate has allegedly been assaulted during a confrontation over election signs.

The party said the husband of Amanda Dow — the candidate for the seat of Yan Yean in Melbourne's outer north — was involved in an incident in Mernda on Sunday afternoon.

"We understand Ms Dow's husband approached a member of the public who was removing Liberal Party campaign signage and was allegedly assaulted," it said in a statement.

"He suffered facial injuries and was taken to hospital and was discharged today."

Amanda Dow campaigning in Mernda the day before the incident. (Supplied)

Police said a 59-year-old Mernda man was charged with recklessly causing injury, criminal damage and unlawful assault over an incident near Abundant Avenue and Bridge Inn Road at about 2pm.

"Police have been told the victim attended an address to retrieve political campaign signage when he was assaulted," a spokesperson said.

The accused has been released on bail to appear before Heidelberg Magistrates' Court on February 1.

The Liberal Party said it could not make any further comment on the matter.

"We ask that the privacy of Ms Dow and her husband be respected while he recovers," it said.

Yan Yean is held by Labor with a margin of 4.3 per cent.

World.title: Rescuers praised after hauling young dugong to safety
World.content:
Wildlife officials have hailed the "all hands" rescue of a young dugong tangled in a car fanbelt along Western Australia's north-west coast.

The globally vulnerable marine mammal was spotted struggling on Wednesday at Wapet Creek, a tidal estuary popular with flat fishers near Exmouth, 1,230 kilometres north of Perth.

Roughly two metres long, it took 15 responders less than 24 hours to return the dugong to deeper water.

"This was a smaller animal," said Sam Miles, acting marine program coordinator at WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA).

" But even a two-metre dugong can weigh a couple of hundred kilograms. "

The animal was wrapped in a cargo net before being hoisted over sand flats. (Supplied: DBCA)

The crew dubbed the dugong "Wapi" for the creek where it was found.

After assessing its health and contacting experts at Perth Zoo and the Sea World Foundation for advice, the group restrained the dugong before cutting it free.

They wrapped Wapi in a cargo net, hoisted it up from the shallows and over a sandbar back to sea.

Rescuers moved at a steady clip to get the marine mammal back in the water. (Supplied: DBCA)

Mr Miles said the team effort was "heartening".

"It took all hands on deck to lift the animal over the sand flats and back into the gulf," he said.

"Dugongs are endangered and we know that every dugong we save will help the overall population in the Exmouth Gulf."

Species under pressure

The dugong was caught in the rubber fanbelt of a car, bewildering its rescuers.

"We haven't seen entanglements in this kind of thing before, so we're not sure where it picked the entanglement up," Mr Miles said.

"It wasn't showing any signs of major distress, which was really important."

Sam Miles says a quick report from the public helped save the dugong. (Supplied: DBCA)

Exmouth Gulf is home to WA's second highest concentration of dugongs, behind Shark Bay.

But the gentle species is increasingly under threat around the country.

In the gulf, a record-breaking marine heatwave during the summer of 2025 devastated some seagrass stocks, scorching two varieties of the dugong's preferred food source.

Last month, aerial surveys of Queensland's Gulf of Carpentaria revealed its dugong population had suffered a 50 per cent drop in the past 20 years.

Huge dugong population decline The number of dugongs in the Gulf of Carpentaria has halved in the past two decades.

Helene Marsh, professor emeritus in conservation science at James Cook University, said she was "delighted" to see the animal move so strongly following its release.

"Australia's unquestionably the dugong capital of the world," she said, adding that they should be protected for animal welfare, scientific and cultural reasons.

"I think we're starting to understand we don't only need to protect animals because of their conservation significance, but we also need to think about their cultural significance."

Mr Miles said the rescue was a much-needed morale booster after a challenging year of entanglements off the remote Ningaloo coast.

"Sometimes we don't have the same positive outcomes," he said.

In a video captured by one of the DBCA staff, they can be heard calling out "yadiyarra”, or dugong in the language of the gulf's Baiyungu traditional owners, as it swims off.

"And stay out," one of the helpers said.

World.title: Dr Redmayne aims to lift Brisbane Heat's WBBL fortunes
World.content:
New Brisbane Heat captain Georgie Redmayne returned to work as a doctor this year and will now help improve the side's form after last season.

The wicketkeeper-batter takes over from all-rounder Jess Jonassen, who led the side for the past six WBBL seasons.

In 2025, the Heat finished last and did not win a match. The Queensland Fire, with many Heat players, then won the 2025-26 WNCL final with Redmayne captaining the 50-over side and scoring a century in the decider.

Strikers pip winless Heat The Adelaide Strikers pull off a tense WBBL victory over the struggling Brisbane Heat.

She said the form in the 20-over format was achievable for the Heat.

"If we win one game we are on the up," Redmayne said, grinning.

"To be more serious, pre-season has been really good and winning the WNCL was massive for us with a lot of the same core group, so we know we are still a winning team.

"We just have to tweak a few things to be successful in that T20 format. We have got our first game at home (on Friday night) against the Sixers, which is always a good rivalry.

"Last year we didn't really turn up in the high-pressure moments … but hopefully we go back to the winning ways which we were known for in the past"

Redmayne said she got a lot out of returning to work as a doctor after a few years where cricket took centre stage.

"I actually came back to it this year. It was really nice," she said.

"I did a bit of a stint in April and another stint in August/September this year at Greenslopes Private Hospital in Brisbane.

"It helps provide a great bit of grounding for me, especially when you go away playing cricket.

"You can think it is the be-all and end-all playing professional sport, but it is literally grounding seeing some real world problems."

Redmayne has been a great success at the top of the order for the Brisbane Heat and was the leading run scorer in three consecutive seasons from 2020-2022.

Grace Harris, her opening partner much of the time, topped the aggregates in 2023 and 2024. The Heat made the finals in all five of those years and were runners-up twice.

The Heat moved Redmayne down the order last season, but it did not work, so a return to opening with Harris would be a good place to start for the side to turn their form around.

"(Opening) is somewhere I really enjoy batting and where I would like to bat," Redmayne said.

"My favourite time playing cricket was always opening the batting with Grace. We had a couple of very successful seasons.

"Last year our order was very changeable. I started at number eight and ended up at number four.

"I don't mind where I bat, so long as we are winning games."

AAP

World.title: Parliament grieves as cardboard cockatoo serves as Helen Haines tribute
World.content:
Far from the gum trees of north-east Victoria where cockatoos gather in noisy flocks, an orange cardboard bird perched in the parliament on Monday, saving a seat for Helen Haines.

"How lonely it looks," Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said.

But cockatoos are not normally lonely birds, and Ms Haines has built her life in much the same way.

The Independent Member for Indi could be loud for those she cared about. She made sure her people were impossible to ignore, and was surrounded by her community, building her political career from a grassroots campaign run by locals.

And unlike the rest of parliament, loud and raucous, Ms Haines was calm.

A week ago, she was standing by the boot of her car outside her Wangaratta office when a man hit her with his own car in what police say was a targeted attack.

The injuries were so severe both of her legs were later amputated.

"This should not just shock us," Wentworth MP Allegra Spender said.

" It should change us. "

As the parliament suspended normal business to make time for messages of support for Ms Haines and her family, it was hard to escape the feeling that something had shifted.

One after another, for hours, MPs stood up to speak in the House about Ms Haines's uncommon kindness, wisdom and respect for civility as a politician.

Nicolette Boele, independent MP for Bradfield, wipes her eyes in Parliament. ( )

Sophie Scamps wipes her eyes as parliamentarians give speeches honouring Helen Haines. ( )

Monique Ryan tears up and is comforted by crossbenchers in Parliament. ( )

Michelle Landry, member for Capricornia, wipes away tears. ( )

"These are the type of politicians we wish we had more of," friend and crossbench colleague Kate Chaney said.

Like a "trick the heart plays on the mind", Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described finding himself looking across to where Ms Haines would normally sit, expecting to see her there.

"It is hard to think of anyone in this place with a more irrepressible twinkle in the eye," he said.

But the tributes were also threaded with another message: that the tenor of Australian politics must change, and that the country needed to find a better way to argue.

"And this is a moment for all of us to rise to the challenge," Speaker of the House Milton Dick said.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks of Helen Haines's empathy, kindness and compassion. ( )

What Would Helen Do?

Members of the crossbench cried as they listened to messages of support for the woman they regard as the "matriarch" of Australia's independent movement.

Ms Haines was among the first wave of community-backed independents to reshape Australian politics, winning Indi after the retirement of fellow independent Cathy McGowan.

Zali Steggall looks across at the empty seat next to her in Parliament. ( )

Community Strong MP Zali Steggall spoke of the role Ms Haines had played in helping shape the modern crossbench, guiding newly elected independents through the workings of parliament and teaching them how to advocate for their communities without the backing of a major party.

"There will be much discussion ahead about the need for better health and mental health services in the regions, our increasingly polarised political environment, harmful online debate and the need for greater civility in disagreement in parliament, in our media, online and in our communities," she said.

" So, Helen, I look forward to seeing you back here and getting on with the job. Let light win over darkness. "

Independent MP Allegra Spender shared the first words Ms Haines spoke after the attack, as relayed by her husband, Phil Haines, who had met with parliamentarians earlier on Monday.

"Your first concerns were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders," she said.

"And that exactly speaks to the character of who you are."

But for all her decency, Ms Spender said, Ms Haines was not a "benign force wandering through the parliament".

"People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition," she said.

"What I will say is that you are also a force for change."

After winning Indi, voters have rewarded Ms Haines with two further terms, entrusting her with an electorate of mountains, rivers and fertile farmland, which was also acutely exposed to the effects of a warming climate.

Crossbenchers sit in parliament as tributes are made to Helen Haines on October 26, 2026. ( )

Parliamentarians wore baby's breath to signify Helen Haines's resilience. ( )

Parliamentarians wore a small sprig of baby's breath to honour Helen Haines. ( )

After years of advocacy by Ms Haines, the federal government adopted temporary disaster roaming, an emergency system that allows mobile phones to switch to another carrier's network when their own service fails during a major disaster.

But few issues, her friends and colleagues said, animated her more than integrity in government.

Independent MP Andrew Gee was emotional speaking about the National Anti-Corruption Commission (NACC), which she is credited for establishing.

Several politicians chose to commit to a Civility Pledge, inspired by the family of British MP Jo Cox, who was murdered in 2016. Ms Haines was the first MP to sign the pledge earlier this year.

MP Kate Chaney spoke about t-shirts printed for a Christmas party in her first year in parliament with the slogan: What Would Helen Do?

"I ask myself that question all the time," she said.

"Helen, please come back to us. We need you here more than ever".

The rage is getting worse, but we can get better

Mr Albanese said Australia had a proud tradition of disagreement but warned against confusing the vigour of democracy with "this rising tide of rage".

"We cannot allow disagreement to become a full stop. We keep talking. We keep working towards something better," he said.

Many parliamentarians wore white or orange to honour Helen Haines. ( )

There was a shared disbelief in the chamber that someone like Helen Haines, among parliament's most respected and unassuming figures, had become a target.

She had been "so, so far down" his list of potential security concerns, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said.

Mr Burke said Phil Haines had earlier urged the parliament to think not only about the words they choose, but about who might hear them.

"It goes to not simply would I be capable of doing something horrific, but would my words, if heard by someone on the edge, potentially have an impact that I wouldn't want them to have," Mr Burke said.

A number of people also called for an honest conversation about mental health, including Liberal MP Dan Tehan.

Ms Haines is a former nurse and maternal health expert, and has long campaigned for additional support for regional services.

"We have to look at mental health services in and around regional and rural Victoria and across this nation," Mr Tehan said.

"We have to see whether we can do better."

As one man hurt Haines, others ran to help

Many MPs said they had spent the week hearing from Australians worried about a country growing more angry and more divided.

But in the same breath, they pointed to people like Ricky Jefferies, the local barber who ran towards danger when Haines needed help.

"One man drove at Helen, but others ran to her instinctively and courageously, and they saved her life," Independent MP Monique Ryan said.

" Our basic decency and our selflessness are there still, and we have to use those muscles, not the others. "

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie said Mr Jefferies knew most of the first responders because he cut their hair, "not because of social media networks".

Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie speaks about Helen Haines. ( )

"And there's something in that," he said.

"We thrive as a nation when we are in a community with our neighbours, when we are known by them and they are known by us."

He encouraged all politicians to behave better in parliament and online.

"We can all go better and we should strive to do better," he said.

" Lets play the ball, not the person and leave nasty personal politics of MAGA in the US. "

Labor MP Ged Kearney broke down as she spoke about Ms Haines but said she had tried to honour her example by making herself as "visible as possible" over the weekend.

"I walked the streets amongst kids in Halloween costumes. I went to listen to music. I had lunch in a cafe, and visited a scouts party," she said.

"We all have fears and we do things differently now to assess risks … but at the end of the day, if I can't walk down High Street or Edward Street or Station Street and be with the people I represent, then well, what is this for?"

Parliament looks to the day it is made whole again

At a vigil held in Wangaratta to honour Ms Haines in the days after her attack, cockatoos wheeled overhead.

"They make a lot of noise, but they're very supportive of each other as a flock," former politician and friend Cathy McGowan told the ABC.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says robust debate should never cross the line into violence. ( )

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said when Ms Haines resumed her seat, it would be a "resounding moment for democracy".

"In those horrific moments last Monday, and in the critical hours and days afterwards, one man's cruelty stood in stark contrast to the courage and decency of so many Australians," he said.

In her maiden speech, Ms Haines had reflected on the erosion of trust affecting democracies around the world.

Indi, she argued, offered a different lesson.

"Division and polarisation are not the inevitable outcome," she said then.

World.title: NSW premier says barracks sale a 'big missed opportunity'
World.content:
Defence personnel based at Victoria Barracks in Sydney have begun "packing boxes" for a Christmas eviction, despite the NSW premier calling on the federal government to reverse its move to sell the historic site.

The 176-year-old Australian Army base, located in Paddington, is one of 67 underused or vacant Defence properties that have been earmarked for sale by the federal government.

The nationwide initiative, which would also see HMAS Penguin on Sydney's Middle Head sent to market, was prompted by a recent independent audit and is expected to generate up to $3 billion in revenue.

Figures from across the political spectrum, including former prime minister John Howard, state Labor MPs, One Nation supporters and members of the Greens, joined thousands of protesters at a rally in Sydney over the weekend calling for the sale of the barracks to be scrapped.

Despite the outcry, Defence sources told the ABC on Monday there were currently "people packing boxes", with the goal of having everyone moved out by Christmas.

Defence personnel expect to be out by Christmas. (ABC News: Paul Pandoulis)

NSW Premier Chris Minns on Monday again criticised the proposal and said it would be a "big missed opportunity" for his federal Labor counterparts to go against what the community wanted.

"There's a good chance here to say, we've listened to the public, clearly Victoria Barracks should stay both in government hands and be used by the Australian Defence Force," Mr Minns said.

"I just think they need to rethink it. [It would] be an easy one to make and I'd love to see it reversed."

Minister vows to protect buildings

About 500 people currently occupy the 13-hectare site, including members of numerous army commands and other support units.

Under the current relocation plan, the majority of those personnel will be shifted to the Randwick Barracks, while others will be temporarily moved to Defence Plaza Sydney, a commercial office tower located 2 kilometres from the barracks in the CBD.

Richard Marles has defended the move to sell the Victoria Barracks site. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

During question time, Defence Minister Richard Marles defended the move and assured the public that every building on the site would be protected even if the site were to be sold.

"Victoria Barracks Sydney is not fundamental to the defence of the country and what we face in respect to Victoria Barracks Sydney specifically is a bill of $200 million over the next decade to secure it as a defence site," Mr Marles said.

"The fundamental function of what happens at Victoria Barracks Sydney is office work.

"Given the strategic landscape that we face, we simply cannot afford to be wasting money, and that's what we're doing, in this way."

What will become of the Victoria Barracks? Veteran, housing, heritage and community organisations are urging the government to put public needs first as dozens of defence sites get prepped for sale.

Victoria Barracks, which also contains the Army Museum of NSW, was built by convicts in the 1840s and originally occupied by the British Army.

Mr Marles said Defence Plaza Sydney, which was established by the former Coalition government, currently sat 60 per cent empty.

In a statement, the Defence Department said Victoria Barracks' personnel were given an update about their future workplace locations last week.

"To minimise the length of disruptions, keep units together, and provide certainty for future postings, Defence is working to relocate units from Victoria Barrack Sydney as quickly as possible, and it is expected that the majority of personnel will move off site before the end of 2026," a Defence spokesperson said.

World.title: Fatigue concerns after Virgin jet cut in front of Qantas plane
World.content:
An air traffic controller with a high risk of fatigue was on duty when a Virgin Australia jet cut in front of a Qantas plane at Sydney Airport in August, safety investigators have revealed.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) has released two preliminary reports into close-call incidents at the airport in August.

The reports did not make findings or recommendations, but outlined the sequence of events, and the conditions at the time.

The two reports are among six investigations underway into close call incidents at the airport.

The first incident happened on August 17, when Virgin flight VA1589 was taxiing to the domestic terminal after diverting from Newcastle because of bad weather.

About 9:40am, the air traffic controller told the Virgin crew to "follow the Qantas to vacate ahead, hold short runway 25".

The first incident involving Virgin flight VA1589 took place on August 17. (Supplied: ATSB)

According to the report, the Virgin captain read back only the hold-short instruction, and the controller did not recognise the incomplete read back and moved on to other tasks.

Shortly afterwards, the crew of Qantas flight QF420 saw the Virgin jet approaching a taxiway intersection at a speed that suggested it would not give way.

They were forced to stop the aircraft using normal braking.

The Virgin jet passed in front of the Qantas aircraft, and its crew did not realise there was a conflict until the Qantas crew queried it with the controller.

The controller was removed from duty for the rest of the day, and later told investigators their view of the taxiway intersection from the tower was limited by equipment in the tower cab.

The taxiing incident involving Qantas flight QF420 and Virgin flight VA1589. (Supplied: ATSB)

Fatigue concerns

The air traffic controller, according to the report, was rostered to finish at 8:50pm the night before the August 17 incident, and start again at 5:30am the next day.

Sydney runway conflict 'severe' The Australian Transport Safety Bureau delivers findings on four of six ongoing investigations at Sydney Airport.

They were the only controller in the tower, with a high predicted fatigue level.

The report said predicted fatigue did not mean a controller was necessarily fatigued, only that they were at risk based on their roster.

The controller described their mental fatigue level at the time as "fine and alert", and that they were "fit for duty".

The report also noted that Airservices Australia, which provides air traffic control at Sydney, does not have a fatigue management system approved by the Civil Aviation Safety Authority.

In a statement, Airservices Australia said it acknowledged the interim reports and would "review the findings once these investigations are complete".

Pushback conflict

The second incident happened on August 25, when a controller cleared a Jetstar A320 operating as JST745, to push back from bay 59 onto a taxiway.

About 30 seconds later, the same controller cleared a QantasLink Dash 8, with the call sign QLK427D, to taxi along the same taxiway, past the A320's bay.

The Dash 8 crew saw the A320's tail moving backwards and stopped about 100 metres from the bay.

The A320's pushback driver and dispatcher also stopped the pushback and warned the flight crew.

Flights QLK427D and JST745 at their closest point. (Supplied: ATSB)

The Jetstar jet was then towed back onto its bay so the Dash 8 could pass behind it.

Three air traffic controllers told the ATSB that push backs from some gates were prone to conflicts, because aircraft push straight onto an active taxiway rather than an "apron".

The tower shift manager and a supervising instructor also said the area could be a "black spot" where aircraft were not always detected.

The shift manager was returning to Sydney after time at another airport, and was working under supervision while their endorsements were reinstated.

Three trainees were also on shift.

The controller on duty said they "felt fine", but had "not had many days off in the past month".

Aircraft taxiing routes. (Supplied: ATSB)

ATSB says crews acted in incidents

ATSB chief commissioner Angus Mitchell said both incidents were mitigated because flight crews and ground staff identified the conflicts and acted accordingly.

"As such, an important safety defence acted appropriately, but our role is to establish why crew actions were necessary to prevent a more serious outcome," he said.

Mr Mitchell said investigators were yet to determine whether staffing contributed to any of the six incidents they are examining or whether it was an underlying condition being effectively managed by Airservices.

World.title: 'Tyranny of distance' weighs against big cycling call
World.content:
Cadel Evans is intrigued by the revolutionary idea of Australia hosting a Tour de France stage, especially given he's long retired as a pro cyclist.

The 2011 Tour champion, the only Australian to win cycling's most famous event, remains heavily involved in his sport as a race promoter and commentator.

Cycling's three-week Grand Tours, the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España, regularly start with stages outside their own borders.

Next year, the Tour's "Grand Depart" will be three stages through Scotland, England and Wales.

But it would be something else entirely to bring a Grand Tour start to the other side of the world.

Melbourne's NFL game is a battle of opposing jet lag strategies The San Francisco 49ers arrived a week in advance of their Melbourne NFL game, while the Rams will arrive the day before. A sleep expert says both strategies have merit, but one may have a slight edge.

The San Francisco 49ers and LA Rams faced massive logistical challenges last month to stage their NFL game at the MCG and they didn't have to play again until several days later.

"It would be possible — I wouldn't want to be the one telling the riders," Evans said on Monday.

"But it's never out of the question. There's been talk before … some Grand Tours are maybe considering stages in America.

"I'd be totally open to it, but I wouldn't want to ride it myself. Australia — as we all know, the tyranny of distance — it's pretty far."

Cadel Evans (centre) remains the only Australian to win the Tour de France. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

There was speculation last summer that the WA government was sounding out Giro organisers.

While a Grand Tour start remains at long odds, the likelihood of cycling superstar Tadej Pogačar returning to race in Australia may well be firming.

Pogacar crashed out of the Vuelta in late August, ending his season early.

Tour Down Under race director Stuart O'Grady has been trying to lure Pogačar to Adelaide for several years. The project took a step forward this year when Pogačar's manager visited and spoke highly of the race.

If Pogačar returned to Adelaide, he would most likely also race at the Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race in Geelong the following weekend.

Pogacar competed at the two events in 2019 and last raced in Australia at the 2022 Wollongong world road championships.

Tadej Pogačar crashes out of La Vuelta a España Tadej Pogačar abandons the Vuelta a España after crashing during the eighth stage of the race.

"He wants to start his season early, apparently. If he would like to come back to our race, that would be amazing," Evans said.

"When you have the opportunity to see the greatest of all time in any sport, it's pretty unique for any sporting fan."

The Slovenian's stunning run of sustained success has invited comparisons with Belgian Eddy Merckx — until now, cycling's all-time greatest rider.

Evans gives the nod to Pogačar.

"It's unfair to compare periods, but it's a far more competitive environment that we race in now," he said.

"There are so many more specialists in our sport now and he's been an all-rounder, winning everywhere, It's just remarkable, and at such a young age as well [28].

"One thing that's so great about Pogačar, other than that he's just an amazing rider, is he wants to win everything."

Evans, at 174 centimetres, was standing alongside Max Gawn, at 209cm, to announce the Melbourne captain as an ambassador for the People's Ride, held on January 30 before the women's road race at Geelong.

"Particularly someone like Pogačar, he goes beyond our sport — and of course, that's having Max part of it [as well]," Evans said.

AAP

World.title: Boy, 13, stays locked up after Perth drive-by shooting charges
World.content:
A 13-year-old boy accused of a drive-by shooting in Perth will spend the next six weeks locked up, as his mother tries to find them accommodation.

The pair recently moved to WA.

In the meantime, the boy will stay in custody at the Banksia Hill Detention Centre after choosing not to apply for bail.

Police allege he used a semi-automatic rifle to fire more than 20 shots into a house on Bert Street in Gosnells earlier this month.

The home was shot at more than two dozen times, with seven people home at the time of the incident. (ABC News)

Seven people, including children, were inside the home in the early hours of October 17, but no one was seriously injured.

CCTV footage captured audio of the alleged drive-by shooting, with the sound of 27 gun shots heard on the recording.

Loading...

The 13-year-old was arrested in a Belmont car park the following day and charged with eight offences including unlawful use of a firearm, endangering life, possession of stolen property and no authority to drive.

The boy made a brief appearance by videolink in Perth Children's Court on Monday.

The court heard the family was "new to Perth" and his mother needed to find "stable" and "suitable" accommodation before bail could be considered.

The court also heard the child's capacity to understand the seriousness of his actions would be an issue in the case, as he is under the age of 14.

The boy faced Perth Children's Court on Monday. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

In Western Australia, the principle of "doli incapax" applies, which means the state must be able to prove a child under the age of 14 understood their alleged crimes were seriously wrong.

The prosecution was ordered to provide a brief of evidence to the defence team, including matters from Victoria.

'Shocking' incident

At the time, senior police described the incident as "shocking and deeply concerning", including that a young teenager is alleged to have had access to a firearm.

Underworld link to drive-by shooting probed WA police probe whether a 13-year-old boy allegedly involved in a drive-by shooting in suburban Perth on the weekend was recruited by an underworld organisation.

"The consequences could have been far worse," Senior Sergeant Heath Atkinson told reporters.

Police have not located the semi-automatic carbine firearm they allege the 13-year-old boy used and the ABC understands officers are investigating possible links to organised crime.

The alleged weapon is a Category D firearm, a type that has been illegal in Australia for civilian use for 30 years.

The boy will reappear in Perth Children's Court in December.

World.title: AI supercharges cyberattacks on Australia, with superannuation savings in the firing line
World.content:
PoliticsFederalCyber threat AI supercharges cyberattacks on Australia, with superannuation savings in the firing line Shane Wright October 26, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Breakthroughs in AI have helped fuel an 80 per cent surge in attacks on the nation’s businesses and government agencies by criminals and countries such as China and Russia, with warnings the new technology could be used to wipe out the superannuation savings of ordinary Australians. In its annual assessment of cyber threats, to be released on Tuesday, the Australian Signals Directorate said the nature and speed of attacks had changed sharply since the emergence of so-called “frontier” AI this year, jeopardising businesses and the overall economy. New forms of AI are contributing to a surge in more, and possibly dangerous, cyber attacks. iStock Frontier AI models, such as the latest and most advanced versions of artificial intelligence such as Anthropic’s Mythos, deliver complex problem-solving and advanced scientific modelling but has also been used to identify vulnerabilities in computer software. The technology uncovered vulnerabilities in the computer programming language PHP that forced numerous websites offline last week for patching, including the Australian Bureau of Statistics.



Related Article Exclusive

NSW State Parliament Electoral Commission warns of ‘intolerable risk’ of interference, cyberattack at NSW election But ASD director-general Abigail Bradshaw said while AI enabled agencies such as hers to identify and take swift action against cyberattacks, it was also used by criminals and bad actors to mount more dangerous digital assaults. “They [frontier AI] are creating enormous opportunities, but they are also enabling malicious cyber actors to identify vulnerabilities and conduct attacks faster, at a greater scale and with the greater precision than ever before. This shift will only accelerate,” she said. “As the global security environment remains challenging, state-sponsored cyber actors will increasingly leverage AI to enhance the scale, speed and effectiveness of their operations.” David Bradbury, deputy chairman of the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority, told The Australian Financial Review’s Super and Wealth Summit on Monday that the risk posed by cyberattacks kept him awake at night.



“It’s important and central that we’re ensuring that members’ best interests are being observed, but when you’re talking about things like a cyberattack that might be amplified by AI, driven by foreign actors; something like this could actually start to clean out people’s accounts,” he said. Australian superannuation funds hold more than $4.5 trillion in assets spread across at least 25 million accounts. In the 2025-26 financial year, the ASD notified companies and agencies more than 4400 times of potentially malicious cyber activity in a bid to prevent an attack – an 80 per cent jump on the previous year. The agency responded to more than 1500 incidents in 2025-26 – up from the 1200 in 2024-25. The Sydney Roosters and Canberra have sensationally spiked their lucrative offers to representative stars Sam Walker and Hudson Young – just six days before they will now become free agents. Walker debuted for Australia against Fiji on Sunday night, then met with his management team first thing on Monday in the hope of thrashing out a three-year extension with the Roosters. Loading The playmaker parked all contract talks late in the regular season when the Roosters’ initial offer fell almost $1 million below his hopes. The Roosters had given Walker’s management until Monday to accept their revised offer, which was understood to be worth about $1.4m a season, including ratchet clauses, which would keep him at Bondi until the end of 2030.



Walker, who made his Queensland Origin debut this year and won his first premiership with the Tricolours, said after the Kangaroos’ 36-22 win that included him scoring a try he was eager to lock down his future. “I’ve spent this week not worrying about [the contract] and letting my manager do his job in the background,” Walker said. “My job was to go out and play football. I’m sure on Monday I’ll have a conversation with him, and we’ll sit down and hopefully get something sorted. “I’m sure I’ll have time over the next couple of days to [go through it]. “It’s nice to be wanted. I’m going to make a decision soon on my future. But right now, my focus was completely on making sure I got the win for Australia.”



The Roosters, however, confirmed late on Monday that they had withdrawn their offer. “The Sydney Roosters have this evening advised the management of Sam Walker that the club’s offer for a contract extension beyond the 2027 season has been withdrawn after the parties were unable to reach an agreement on terms,” the club said. Sam Walker made his Test debut on Sunday night. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images “The club remains focused on maintaining a premiership-winning roster, with all recruitment and retention decisions made to support the strength, balance and long-term success of the playing squad.” The Roosters will now turn their own focus to securing a topline playmaker. Nathan Cleary was linked to the club earlier this year, but the game’s best player has already commenced discussions about an extension at the Panthers.



Walker will head to the open market where he will attract plenty of interest, including the PNG Chiefs who are desperate to land a marquee playmaker. Young will also pop up on the Chiefs’ radar after his own negotiations with Canberra broke down. The Raiders wanted to make Young a one-club player, and tabled a four-year, $4.4m contract which would have been the richest deal in the club’s history. But sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly confirmed that as late as last week, Young’s management wanted Canberra to include ratchet clauses in the contract. With the salary cap expected to rise between 15 and 20 per cent under the new collective bargaining agreement, Young’s wage would have pushed towards $1.3 million – money normally reserved for playmakers.



“The club’s offer to Hudson and his management was intended to keep him at the Raiders for the rest of his career, as an integral part of the club and a potential future leader,” the club said in a statement. Young was a key part of NSW’s Origin winning side this year. Getty Images “The offer that was made was the largest in club history. The PNG side baulked at Young’s $1.1m asking price, but are now expected to fly the representative forward north for talks. The Mad Monday involving Walker and Young will cause an enormous ripple effect through the player market as clubs begin sharpening their pencils. World.title: The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide: Full list of hats
World.content:
Heard the expression, “It’s a hatted restaurant”? The chefs’ hat rating system was created by the Good Food Guide more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service and experience. It has been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system ever since.

Each restaurant reviewed in the Guide is scored out of 20: 10 points for food, five for hospitality, three for setting and experience, and two for value. Restaurants scoring 15 or above are awarded one hat, those scoring 16 or 17 receive two hats, and those between 18 and 20 receive three hats.

The main goal of our reviewers isn’t to tell you whether we like a restaurant. It’s to paint a picture of the experience so you can decide whether you might like it, and to explain how it sits within Australia’s dining landscape.

World.title: Market board members quit after former Demons boss Paul Guerra takes top job
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCBD Market board members quit after former Demons boss Paul Guerra takes top job Fiona Byrne October 26, 2026 — 8:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Well, this is awkward. Just days after former Victorian Chamber of Commerce and Industry boss Paul Guerra was announced as the new chair of the Melbourne Market Authority, his appointment may have been the catalyst for an almighty upheaval of the board. Acting chair Angie Bradbury confirmed on Monday she had quit the board after being overlooked for the role. She had been acting chair since May this year. Newly appointed chair of the Melbourne Market Authority Paul Guerra. In what looks very much like a revolt, her fellow board members Margaret Burdeu and Emma Germano, the former president of the Victorian Farmers Federation, have also quit. Bradbury, Burdeu and Germano’s resignations take effect on Thursday (October 29). Are you keeping up?



The Market Authority’s acting chief executive Keith Louie is, according to the ABC, also departing. The Age attempted to contact Burdeu, Germano and Louie without success. Guerra will begin as chair on Friday. Bradbury says, having thrown her hat into the ring for the chair role, she was disappointed at missing out. Angie Bradbury (left). Instagram “I thought I had done a really good job in the (acting) role in some very challenging times and stabilised the organisation [and] recruited the new CEO and I didn’t get the role and I wasn’t really afforded with any compelling reasons as to why not from the government,” Bradbury said. “I wanted to do the job and I didn’t want to just step to the side and continue to serve on the board under somebody else’s leadership.



“I make no bones about it; I wanted the job. I worked hard in the job to establish the relationships and build trust with the board amongst the market community and I’m really disappointed that I didn’t get it, so, I chose to step down.” Editor's pick Exclusive

Victorian election Coalition says it will sell key Melbourne market if it wins election Bradbury said her fellow board members had acted under their own steam when deciding to resign. “I did not ask for anybody to follow, it was not meant to be a coup, but there we are, that is what the other directors have decided to do,” she told CBD. Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle said Guerra brought experienced leadership to the “vital work” of getting Victorians their vegies.



“Paul knows what it takes to lead a major market from his time chairing Queen Victoria Market, and I look forward to seeing him lead Melbourne Market into its next chapter,” she said. Bradbury, a former chair of Wine Victoria, said her decision had nothing to do with Guerra personally, as the Victorian government made the appointment. “I know Paul well. He was the CEO of the Royal Agricultural Society. I was the chair of the wine show committee at the time. I was chairing Wine Victoria when he was serving as the CEO of VCCI,” she said. “This is not about Paul. It’s about the fact that I wanted the job and that’s not the way that it played out, so I decided to step down.” Guerra was announced as the Market Authority chair following a competitive recruitment process.



Guerra has found himself on a wild rollercoaster ride this year, having been sacked as chief executive of the Melbourne Football Club in April after seven months in the gig. In August, he launched an unfair dismissal claim in the Federal Court against the Demons. The brouhaha pushes the market further into the spotlight heading into the state election with the opposition pledging to privatise it if it wins the November poll. Opposition spokesman James Newbury described the saga as emblematic of an “end-of-days” government. “When experienced board members would rather resign than endorse Labor’s decision, it shows just how badly this government has undermined confidence in merit-based appointments,” he said.



The government was contacted for comment.

World.title: The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide: Full list of hats
World.content:
Heard the expression, “It’s a hatted restaurant”? The chefs’ hat rating system was created by the Good Food Guide more than 40 years ago to give readers a sense of what to expect in terms of food, service and experience. It has been the cornerstone of Good Food’s rating system ever since.

Each restaurant reviewed in the Guide is scored out of 20: 10 points for food, five for hospitality, three for setting and experience, and two for value. Restaurants scoring 15 or above are awarded one hat, those scoring 16 or 17 receive two hats, and those between 18 and 20 receive three hats.

The main goal of our reviewers isn’t to tell you whether we like a restaurant. It’s to paint a picture of the experience so you can decide whether you might like it, and to explain how it sits within Australia’s dining landscape.

World.title: Evacuations in Otago township, firefighters battle several blazes
World.content:
A scrub fire that forced evacuations in the central Otago town of Roxburgh is still uncontained, with crews battling the blaze into the night.

Evacuations began Monday evening. Hundreds of homes are without power in the area, with at least seven fire crews at work fighting the blaze.

It was thought the fire started in trees about 2.45pm Monday, with strong winds adding to the problem.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said crews were working to protect residential buildings and to contain the fire.

Strong winds initially grounded efforts to fight the fire from the air, but conditions eased by about 6.30pm, allowing a helicopter to assist efforts until dark, FENZ said.

Homes were evacuated on Ladysmith Road, east of Roxburgh township, by police and FENZ working together, and residents from six houses remained evacuated by 9pm Monday.

Power had been disconnected earlier for more than 220 Roxburgh homes as a safety precaution, the Aurora Energy website said. But the number in the dark was listed as more than 30 homes by Monday night.

Firefighters were also battling large blazes in Southland and near the Desert Road on Monday night, with much of the South Island and some of the lower North Island affected by rough weather which was moving up the country, prompting a raft of warnings or watches from MetService.

Central Otago's orange level wind warning was lifted about 9pm Monday.

Homes were evacuated on Ladysmith Road, east of Roxburgh township. Screenshot / Google Maps

Winds fanning Otago fires, FENZ says

Otago firefighters had been battling several vegetation fires on Monday, with the wind making the situation worse.

All of the fires had escalated quickly, FENZ District Commander Blair Kiely.

"Strong winds and warm temperatures mean that fires spread quickly and are much more difficult for our firefighters to contain and bring under control.

"The winds were so strong today that in most places we were not able to use aircraft."

He thanked everyone who had pitched in to help on the holiday: "I would like to thank every firefighter who has responded to the fires across Otago today, and all those who have been in support roles.

"Giving up their Labour Day holiday to fight fires was a selfless act to support our communities."

Crucial to prepare for El Niño, FENZ says

Most wildfires in New Zealand are caused by people, Kiely said. And with a dry El Niño season expected to peak during the New Zealand summer, these fires are a reminder of just how necessary preparation and care are.

"Fire and Emergency New Zealand is asking everyone to take extra care with fire outdoors as the region heads into what is expected to be a challenging wildfire season," he said.

"Everyone can help by taking extra care with fire and getting prepared now, before conditions get any drier."

World.title: Seriously injured person found in Christchurch, police say
World.content:
Cordons are in place at a property in the Christchurch suburb of Phillipstown following a reported assault, police say.

Emergency services were called to Olliviers Road about 5.40pm on Monday, where a person was found with serious injuries.

Some local residents said on social media that police responding were armed.

The injured person was taken to Christchurch Hospital.

In a statement on Monday, Senior Sergeant Kerry Joyce said the exact circumstances of what happened were still being investigated.

"Police have a visible presence in Phillipstown, Christchurch, following a reported assault this afternoon," Joyce said.

"Cordons are in place and members of the public are asked to avoid the area."

World.title: Dogs learning to sniff out diseases from urine samples
World.content:
Audio player for " Dogs learning to sniff out diseases from urine samples " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2171686%2Fdogs-learning-to-sniff-out-diseases-from-urine-samples

Dogs learning to sniff out diseases from urine samples Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Researchers are teaching a select few Waikato dogs to sniff out a tropical disease known as snail fever.

Schistosomiasis, known as snail fever, is caused by a parasitic worm and can cause serious complications.

Waikato University's Scent Detection Research group is training dogs to identify infected urine samples.

Director of the unit, Associate Professor Tim Edward told Checkpoint the goal was to find out whether dogs could tell the difference between people who had snail fever and those who did not.

There had not been any research on whether it was possible to identify people who had the disease by using scent, he said.

"This is really a pilot project to see if they can do it, if they can, it suggests this might be a way of screening people to see if they might have the disease in places where it's likely to affect people, typically in developing countries."

Edward said initially they had to train the dogs using an automated apparatus.

"[It] allows them to indicate a sample is positive by holding their nose in the port where they could access the sample, or sniffing a sample and pressing a lever on the side of the apparatus.

After that the dogs were introduced to the odour that researchers wanted them to learn which in this case was urine samples from people infected by the disease, he said.

Mac is already showing an ability to discriminate between positive and negative samples. University of Waikato

The dogs were also introduced to urine samples of people who were not infected, he said.

"So they can start to learn to reject those negative ones and indicate on those positive ones."

He described the apparatus as a rotating carousel and the dogs could access one sample at a time from the panel on the front of it.

"If they're correct and they've indicated on a positive sample then it automatically gives them a food reward."

Asked whether they used particular breeds of dogs in the research, he said all dogs had incredibly sensitive olfaction or sense of smell, he said.

"They're pet dogs from the community but we screen them to see which dogs really perform well in the laboratory environment and seem to enjoy being here," he said.

"Our top performer at the moment is chocolate labrador named Mac and it's actually quite exciting because even though we're only about six to eight weeks into the project, he's already showing an ability to discriminate between positive and negative samples."

That was with samples that Mac had never sniffed before, so the first time he came across a sample for the first time he was starting to "quite accurately tell us whether they're positive or negative".

Edward said snail fever was a nasty disease which sounded a bit like something out of a horror or science fiction film plot.

"This flat worm spends part of its life cycle in a freshwater snail and then it leaves the snail and lives in a microscopic form in fresh water and if people are in the water, come into contact with the water it can actually penetrate their skin and then it lives inside their circulatory system and breathes and lays eggs and then those eggs get lodged in their tissues, that can be their bladder or their liver other parts their intestines.

World.title: Firefighters battle blaze in Central Plateau military zone
World.content:
A large scrub fire near the Desert Road continues to grow, with helicopter crews and firefighters working to bring it under control in the Waiouru military zone.

Fire crews responded to the blaze on the Central Plateau about 10.15am Monday, Fire and Emergency (FENZ) shift manager Becca Jennings said, and it appeared to be a continuation of a fire from the previous day, which had escalated.

Mid-afternoon Monday, the flames covered an area about 400x400 metres, but it had spread to about 1.5k sq m (238 hectares) of vegetation by evening.

Five helicopter crews and nine firefighting crews were working on the blaze.

New Zealand Defence Force said the fire in their military training area was sparked by gunfire.

"The fire initially started on Sunday, during live fire training, and was thought to be controlled and extinguished, before it re-ignited on Monday morning," they said. "The blaze may take a further 24 hours to extinguish."

Thirteen defence force staff are battling the blaze alongside FENZ efforts.

Supplied/ Sarah Moodie

The fire was in a fairly isolated area. There had been no reports of injuries and it did not pose a threat to the Desert Road or to buildings in the area, Jennings said.

Motorists travelling on the Desert Road - State Highway 1 captured footage of large plumes of smoke just south and north of the Waiouru township.

World.title: Flights disrupted in Wellington, wet and windy end to long weekend for South Island
World.content:
Orange weather warnings cover much of the South Island and some of the lower North Island, as gusty winds cause disruptions to flights and hamper firefighting in several other parts of the country.

The strong winds have moved up the country through Monday.

Evacuations were underway Monday evening in the central Otago town of Roxburgh, where a scrub fire that appeared to have started in trees was threatening homes. Firefighters were battling strong winds in the area, and power had been turned off to a surrounding area as a precaution.

Firefighters were also working in the wind at large scrub fires in Southland, and near Waiouru and the Desert Road in the Central Plateau.

By 7pm Monday, at least 20 flights had been cancelled or diverted, a Wellington Airport spokesperson said. They warned that number could rise, and said passengers travelling to or from the city should check directly with their airline for information about flights.

An RNZ reporter said his plane from Auckland tried to land in Wellington twice, before returning to Auckland.

Earlier, police said they were closing a central road in Wellington due to high wind gusts: A stretch of Oriental Parade and Evans Bay Parade was shut after reports of multiple people falling off bicycles and wing mirrors being blown off cars.

The road around that section of Wellington waterfront was closed from Carlton Gore Road in Oriental Bay to Maida Vale Road, at the intersection with Evans Bay Parade. But it was reopened by late Monday evening.

Fire and Emergency said crews had been called to five wind-related incidents in Wellington by late Monday afternoon, including material falling from buildings and downed power lines.

FENZ shift manager Becca Jennings said a piece of panelling had fallen off the ceiling of Jetts Fitness in Miramar, and glass had fallen onto the footpath and street from a balcony in Mount Victoria.

Crews in both areas were trying to keep the area safe, Becca said.

Embedded content removed for printing https://twitter.com/MetService/status/2114521119520940416

In the lower North Island, weather warnings and watches for strong winds were expected to be in place into Tuesday for Wellington, Wairarapa, Horowhenua and Kāpiti, and heavy rain was expected for the Tararua Ranges.

Weather warnings for South Islanders

Many parts of the South Island were being lashed by heavy rain and severe gales on Monday, as the active front moved up the country.

MetService meteorologist Samkelo Magwala said a wind gust of about 200km/h was recorded at Mount Hutt, Canterbury, about 8am on Monday.

He advised people in affected areas to keep an eye on the weather and road conditions.

"Those people who are planning to travel after the long weekend ... should be vigilant when driving, especially in those areas where the weather won't be so pleasant," he said.

Up to 250mm, and 210mm of rain could fall in parts of Westland and Fiordland (respectively), and warnings up to 300mm could fall near some Westland peaks by early Tuesday morning, MetService said. Intense downfalls were possible in those areas, which could dump up to 35mm an hour.

Southland, Stewart Island, and Queenstown Lakes and could also see heavy rain.

The Grey and Buller districts could be in for up to 110mm of rain into Tuesday morning, which could peak at 25mm an hour, and in Canterbury Arthur's Pass and other inland areas could be in for 160mm of rain, peaking up to 35mm an hour.

Severe gales were expected to last into Monday night in Otago; and into Tuesday morning for Canterbury and Marlborough. And MetService said damage to trees, powerlines and unsecured structures was possible, and advised caution when driving.

The Transport Agency Waka Kotahi said heavy rain would make roads slippery, meaning drivers should think about adjusting their speed and travelling distances, avoiding sudden braking and staying visible.

"People are also urged to avoid driving through any floodwaters, especially where the depth is unclear and there may be hidden obstructions," they said.

World.title: Employment lawyer to lead review of Hepworth's City Mission stay
World.content:
Further details of a forthcoming independent review into the care Braydon Hepworth received at the Christchurch City Mission have been revealed.

The 21-year-old father was told to leave the mission's transitional housing less than two months before he disappeared.

His body was found buried in a shed in Linwood earlier this month.

Two Christchurch men have been charged in connection to the disappearance and death of Hepworth.

A 60-year-old man was charged with concealing his body and making a false statement to police.

A 34-year-old man also appeared in court on Friday on charges relating to the concealment of Hepworth's body.

The mission's board confirmed a fortnight ago that an independent review into Hepworth's time with the mission and the decision-making involved in his care would take place.

On Monday, the board said the review would be led by Wellington barrister Andrew Scott-Howman.

Scott-Howman is an experienced employment lawyer and workplace investigator.

In a statement, board chair Jane Evans said Hepworth's death had left the City Mission community deeply saddened.

"Our thoughts continue to be with his family and friends, and the staff who knew him. We've asked for a thorough and candid examination of Braydon's time with the Mission and whether anything could have been done differently," Evans said.

"The review will look at the Mission's responsibilities in relation to Braydon. It will not consider the cause of death or any criminal matter, which are for the police and the courts."

Scott-Howman was due to report to the board at the end of November with a summary of findings and response to be released soon after, "subject to privacy and legal limitations".

Christchurch City Mission chief executive Corinne Haines earlier confirmed Hepworth was asked to leave the transitional housing complex Whakaora Kāinga in mid-July.

"Our services support many people with complex needs and there are occasions when we must ask someone to leave accommodation because important behavioural expectations have repeatedly not been met," she said in a statement.

However, the circumstances surrounding Hepworth's departure from the Whakaora Kāinga complex have raised concerns and questions from staff.

Former staff member Alex - who did not wish to use her surname - told RNZ that Hepworth's death was the catalyst for her resignation because of serious concerns about the mission's direction.

"I believe the shift towards a more rigid, business-oriented approach contributed to the loss of experienced staff and undermined the quality of support [Whakaora Kāinga] was established to provide," she said.

In her resignation letter, seen by RNZ, Alex said Hepworth was given 15 minutes to pack his belongings and leave.

"A year of familiarity, relationships and a place to turn when life became overwhelming, reduced to 15 minutes to gather his possessions and walk away," her letter said.

"I find it difficult to comprehend how this could be considered an appropriate way to exit someone whose circumstances called for compassion, careful consideration and trauma-informed practice.

"Braydon deserved better. His daughter deserved better. And every person who comes to Whakaora Kāinga seeking safety, stability, and support deserves better."

World.title: Homes selling for less than asking price - but only just, Realestate.co.nz says
World.content:
Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2171018%2Fhomes-selling-for-less-than-asking-price-but-only-just-realestate-co-nz-says

Houses are selling near the price vendors are asking, Realestate.co.nz says, but in some parts of the country, the method of sale may be affecting the calculation.

Realestate.co.nz has compared the average selling prices over the year, using Real Estate Institute data with the site's average asking prices.

Audio player for " Should you buy a house from your mother-in-law? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2171018%2Fhomes-selling-for-less-than-asking-price-but-only-just-realestate-co-nz-says

Over the year, the average asking price of $830,022 was 0.6 percent above the average selling price of $824,698.

Coromandel had the biggest gap, with properties selling for 4.5 percent below asking price.

"Even in the region with the biggest gap, there was less than a 5 percent difference between average asking prices and average selling prices," said spokesperson Vanessa Williams. "That's a surprisingly small difference and a useful reminder that asking prices remain a credible starting point for negotiations."

Wairarapa was 3.4 percent below asking price, Auckland and Bay of Plenty 2.1 percent, and Northland 2 percent.

Canterbury was 1.8 percent above, Southland 1.6 percent above and Central Otago/Lakes had homes going for 2.1 percent more.

Wellington properties sold for 0.9 percent more than asking price, but Williams said many were being sold by tender.

"There are quite a lot of tenders and auctions in that market, so I wonder if, as an example, people are going, 'It's quite a suppressed market. Your house could go for $750,000 to $800,000... let's put it into realestate.co.nz at $750,000, because we want to make sure we're collecting all that demand'.

"Then people put a tender in at $775,000."

She had expected the gap could be larger nationally, but buyers may initially make lower offers and negotiating closer to what vendors wanted by the time the deal was done.

"I think there's still people who are trying to get a bargain, but the reality of it is they still want to do a deal, so they're stoked if they can be cheeky. The reality of it is they're actually coming up to meet the market.

"If they're coming in at $600,000, the market's at $800,000, they're getting to $750,000 anyway."

She said the gap was probably a lot smaller than it had been, "because of how stable the market is, because it's just been here for so long".

"I would anticipate we are not going to see the gap widen, until we see some real stimulation in the market. We've still got over 37,000 homes for sale at the moment... sellers are quite motivated.

"Buyers are holding off, i would say, because of the election, so the sell-through rate has dropped off quite considerably."

World.title: Southland scrub fire still burning as wind hampers firefighting efforts
World.content:
High winds have prevented firefighters from working on a scrub fire burning in about 80 hectares of Southland land.

Six helicopters worked with monsoon buckets to protect two communications towers in the Centre Hill area, after emergency services were alerted to the blaze at about 4pm Sunday.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) said high winds on Monday prevented helicopters from accessing the fire, while difficult terrain meant ground crews could not go on foot.

MetService issued a orange strong-wind warning for Southland on Monday, with gales forecast to reach up to 130 km/h in exposed places.

Fire and Emergency incident controller Hamish Angus said an assessment of the vegetation fire would be made as soon as conditions allowed.

While rain on Monday afternoon would help suppress any remaining fire in the open country, deep-seated areas of burning in mature beech forest would need checking, and any pockets of fire dug out and extinguished, he said.

The fire affected an area of about 80 hectares, mostly high country grazing and an area of native bush on adjoining public conservation land.

There were no reports of livestock being affected.

Fire crews from Southland volunteer brigades and the Department of Conservation were being arranged for Tuesday morning. FENZ said the crews were all experienced in arduous conditions.

World.title: Three-game Bledisloe Cup series looms as new deal struck
World.content:
The Wallabies are set to play two Bledisloe Cup Tests at the MCG in a matter of years, fuelling hopes that one of rugby union's biggest rivalries could be permanently returning to a three-game series.

Rugby Australia struck a multi-year deal with the Victorian government which secures Melbourne to host the Wallabies and New Zealand in the Rugby Championship in 2027 and an additional Bledisloe Cup Test in 2029.

It comes as Lang Park in Brisbane is set to stage the first Anzac Day Bledisloe Cup Test next April, which sets up a three-match series between the bitter rivals for the first time since 2021.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

Whether a three-game series would persist beyond next year has been a hot question exercising pundits.

But Monday's announcement of an additional Test in Melbourne in 2029 will very much boost optimism that a permanent three-game Bledisloe Cup series could return.

That is because Brisbane has also secured the rights for the 2029 Anzac Day Test along with the 2031 instalment.

RA officials were coy on whether the announcement was a signal for a return to full-time three-Test series, and were unsure if 2028 would be similar to 2027 considering no Anzac Day Test has been announced.

An extra Bledisloe Cup Test would favour the Wallabies, who haven't held the trophy since 2002 and have been unable to win both Tests since it became a two-game duel in 2022.

In 2026, they were utterly humiliated by the All Blacks, conceding a mammoth 93 points across the two games, which dealt coach Les Kiss a harsh reality check ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup.

Wallabies admit they 'faced the music' It was brutal and confronting, but the Wallabies knew they had to face the reality of Saturday night's defeat to the All Blacks sooner rather than later.

Regardless of the three-Test speculation, having a Bledisloe Cup Test at the MCG next July is set to be a stellar moment for the sport in Australia as it ramps up preparations for the World Cup.

The Wallabies last played the All Blacks at the MCG in 2023, where a crowd of 83,944 filled the historic ground, which was the largest rugby attendance in more than 20 years at the time.

Last year, 90,307 watched the Australians' second Test against the British & Irish Lions, breaking the Lions' all-time crowd record.

"The Melbourne Cricket Ground is one of the world's great stadiums — and a jewel in Australia's sporting crown — and the Wallabies are proud to be hosting the All Blacks at the iconic venue in 2027," RA chief executive Phil Waugh said.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have played only four previous Test matches at the MCG, and this Bledisloe Cup encounter will mark 30 years since both teams took to the hallowed turf for the first time.

"The Wallabies and All Blacks have won two Tests apiece at the 'G and another enthralling contest awaits next year."

Australia will also meet the All Blacks at least one more time in 2027 when they face off in their second Pool A match of the Rugby World Cup at Sydney's Olympic stadium.

World.title: RLWC quick hits: Big crowds and bigger scorelines in week two
World.content:
The second week of the Rugby League World Cup was short on genuine contests as the tournament's haves and have-nots collided.

Aside from Australia's win over Fiji, where the gallant Bati gave the Kangaroos a hell of a scare, it was big scorelines across the board.

But with fans across three Australian states and two other counties voting with their feet, there are still plenty of quick hits from the second round of matches.

1. Tongan wall holds yet again

Tonga took care of business in their win over Lebanon. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

For the second week in a row, Tonga's opponent enjoyed plenty of field position and for the second week in a row Tonga's scrambling defence proved more than up to the challenge.

After holding England to 12 points last week, despite the English enjoying 34 tackles inside the red zone to Tonga's 18, they repeated the dose against Lebanon on Friday night.

Tonga down Lebanon in World Cup Tonga's win over Lebanon kicked off what's expected to be a lopsided weekend in the Rugby League World Cup but there's still something to be gained amid the blow-outs.

The Cedars came in with an offload-heavy game plan and had some success moving the ball up the field. By the end, they had 29 tackles inside the attacking 20 to Tonga's 30, but that was where they stalled.

Some of it was due to a lack of creativity but there were plenty of last-gasp Tongan efforts to deny Lebanese players who looked tryline bound, and it means Tonga carry a strong form line into Sunday's blockbuster against Samoa.

2. Samoa running riot over PNG is a sign of the times

Rarely will you see two halves of a single game more different than what Samoa and Papua New Guinea dished up in Port Moresby.

The Kumuls held the gloves up well through the opening 40, trailing just 14-6 at the break and could have been even closer had Robert Derby successfully grounded the ball for their second try.

But what followed was a procession: Samoa scored 50 unanswered points in the second half, as their size and athleticism totally overwhelmed PNG, who had just four sets in the entire stanza.

Of all the blowout results this weekend, this more than any other was a sign of the times. Rugby league's embrace of the set restart rule and the increased speed of the game makes it almost impossible for an underdog team to stay in the fight beyond a certain point and when things break they can break badly.

Samoa only had to make 36 tackles through the entire second and the Kumuls only got over halfway for two tackles.

They finished the game conceding six tries in 15 minutes against a side they had held their own against for the whole first half.

There were plenty of less-extreme examples of the same through this year's NRL season, most notably when a top eight side conceded the third-most points in a game ever, but it's been turned up to greater levels through this World Cup given the talent and fitness disparity and it stacks the deck even further against the underdogs.

3. France's woes continue in England smash-up

England ran out easy winners against a hapless France outfit. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

England beat the clock against their old rivals in Perth, running out 82-0 winners in a result that means France have conceded 160 points in as many minutes through their two matches.

It's hard to find any silver lining for Les Chanticleers and ahead of their tournament finale against Lebanon, the French game finds itself in a strange position.

The potential for growth or a return to the glory days when France were one of Test football's true powers is always the dream, and with two Super League clubs in Catalans Dragons and Toulouse — giving France more professional teams than New Zealand — they seemingly have the ingredients and infrastructure for improvement.

France just cannot seem to close the gap on their more illustrious rivals. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

All but two of this year's squad were home-grown players and since 2020 they have won nine of the 16 Tests they have played, with all seven losses coming against England or Samoa.

Problem is, across those seven games they have been outscored by a cumulative total of 394-44, with this England loss the worst of them.

There's greater pathways to the top for French talent than ever before but they can't seem to close the gap between them and the big dogs.

If anything, the gap has become wider. Nine years ago, in the 2017 World Cup, they played England at the same ground and lost 36-6 a week after losing to Australia 52-6.

Those scorelines aren't exactly a good time, but they're not a point-a-minute for two straight weeks either.

The Southern Hemisphere racing ahead of the north is a wider issue for the sport, but France are the collateral damage and they don't have a contingent of heritage NRL players to paper over the cracks.

4. Christchurch puts its best foot forward

Despite the result, it was a healthy crowd in Christchurch. (Getty Images: Kai Schwoerer)

Despite Esom Ioka's first-half hat-trick that briefly gave the Cook Islands the lead, few would have ever expected the Aitu to trouble New Zealand for long in their match at Te Kaha in Christchurch.

That didn't stop a sell-out crowd of 26,800 coming through the gates, marking the fifth biggest Test attendance of the past century in New Zealand and the highest ever for a game outside of Auckland.

It was a strong week of crowds throughout the tournament — Tonga and Lebanon pulled in more than 25,000 and Australia topped 40,000 for the second week in a row despite taking on Fiji.

But with the NRL expansion race heating up as the league prepares to hand out a licence for a 20th team, Christchurch showing up in droves did their chances of winning the bid no harm at all.

5. Fiji take Australia to the brink

Australia are through to the semi-finals of the World Cup after their win over Fiji. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris )

Speaking of that Australian-Fiji crowd, the 41,108 punters who packed into Lang Park didn't just push the attendance past that of the 2017 World Cup final at the same venue, they were treated to easily the best clash of the weekend.

On the back of an inspired display by five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe and a hat-trick to Castleford winger Semi Valemei, Fiji pushed Australia all the way before a late Jacob Preston try wrapped up a 36-22 win for the green and golds.

Consider the previous margins between the two (42-8, 54-6 and 64-0 in their last three meetings) and it's a measure of how far the Bati have come and how this World Cup is more up for grabs than one might think.

A couple of contentious calls and some killer instinct in key moments got the Kangaroos home.

But on what they've shown through two weeks, Samoa, Tonga and New Zealand will all fancy their chances of springing an upset should they meet Australia, who have wrapped up a semi-final berth in surprisingly shaky fashion.

World.title: Antonelli is two points away from the F1 title, and can win it next week
World.content:
With his ninth grand prix win of the season on Monday morning (AEDT), Italian Kimi Antonelli put himself on the cusp of winning his maiden Formula 1 drivers' championship.

The 20-year-old Mercedes pilot has been a class above the rest in 2026, and could have sealed the championship with his victory in Texas on Monday, but other results meant he had to wait at least one more week before popping the champagne.

Next weekend's Mexican Grand Prix shapes up to be the coronation of Antonelli as an F1 champion. Here is how he can seal the world title.

Antonelli needs just two more points

Heading into Monday's United States Grand Prix, there were still five drivers who could mathematically catch Kimi Antonelli in the race for the title.
